review_text:
The ugliest game ever made.

I think an incredibly important thing of note with this game is each individual element is relatively weak but as a whole it can be an enjoyable experience. Let me break this game down to three elements.
 
- World building and art style: The art style is of course the thing that is driving this game. I think it's relatively strong and the game loves to show it off at every chance it gets. It's kind of one-note but the game is only 5 or so hours so I don't think it overstays its welcome but it may for some. The world however I feel like is extremely lacking. I was drawn in and wanted to explore the world to figure out how it ticks but I couldn't figure out the logic behind this world as I'm not sure there is one. 
- Puzzles: They're nothing that'll really tax your brain. Some of the puzzles aren't really puzzles and more of just an excuse for the character to walk from this area to another. An aspect of a good puzzle is maximizing the time for a player thinking and testing things out in the puzzle and minimizing time walking around and waiting for animations to play. In that aspect, the game fails at it loves to revel in its art style and animation. 
- Combat/survival horror: I understand the idea of adding this in to the game. It promotes more exploration for ammo/health and breaks things up. I think a big problem with it is your melee weapon is absolutely horrendous. You can only use it to hit an enemy twice before you run away and wait for it to recharge. It's more aggravating than engaging when you have to repeat the hit an enemy twice and run away a number of times for an encounter. You also can't sprint to cancel a reload or weapon swap animation to dodge an enemy which will leave to some frustrating deaths. I know your character isn't some 1337 mega soldier and that's fine but I would expect him to prioritize his health and safety and sprint to dodge. Mostly the combat is serviceable but does get annoying at times. 

I would say the puzzle, combat, and world building are poor but they are fine enough tacked onto the art and atmosphere aspect of it. Just need to set your expectations correctly, I'd say it's worth it if you will be fascinated by the weird and disgusting things the artists came up with.

review_text:
This game is off to a GREAT start, but suffers from a few rage inducing quirks that need to be adjusted. (Reviewed after 9 hours of addicted gameplay)

The turning radius at low velocity is so large that when you miss, you end up driving AROUND the ball instead of adjacent to it, generally wasting 3-6 seconds trying to get back into position to even strike the ball. This causes unnecessary frustration, if i miss and go rocketing past my ball i shouldn't be fighting with a monstrous turning radius at low velocity just to get back to it. Also, several locations on tracks have details sticking out just outside of the map bounds, which look like you should be able to bounce your ball off of it, but alas, you are punished for your ingenuity with an out of bounds collider just before the ball reaches it. Several track edges on overlapping tracks tend to bounce your ball back instead of acting like a ramp, which would make sense considering its an inside corner, but no, it just bounces it back to you instead of continuing on and heading down the fairway. This is particularly frustrating if you find yourself putting, as if putting wasn't difficult enough! Could we maybe get directional dodging please? Sideways is a good direction to dodge sometimes...

The Curve prediction does not seem to take into consideration how much spin you're about to put onto the ball, is therefore inaccurate, and makes learning to curve properly an additional chore as you have to learn how much drift the curve will be from the center line as a result of side spin. 

I'm not sure whats up with the timing of the start boost detection either, but sometimes it doesn't detect ANY presses.

The tutorials are fine, but need to be more thorough. You learn nearly EVERYTHING From the loading screen tips!

There are a few XP lurkers out there that just sit in games until the time runs out, farming XP/Coin, forcing everyone to wait out the entire game duration. Please deal with them. If they haven't moved or touched their ball for the entire match and everyone else is already finished, kick them.

4v4 Team Racing when?

WOW, just WOW! this game is going down as one of my favourites of all time.

It hits me in two ways, in its perversion combined with its horror.

I love that nothing is told and everything is shown, exactly what you should always do when telling a good story. Show don't tell. There is a story in this game, but you need to pay attention to start to see it. Will you ever get the full explanation ? no, and that's the entire point. From HP Lovecraft's explanation of Gothic horror, the "unknown" is the most terrifying thing.

This also allows the player to create their own story to it. What do you think it's about ? You might be totally correct, and most likely, that's how it's supposed to be taken, YOU decide what it's all about.

The combat isn't great, and the game could have worked without it, but I also kind of see why they added it. The puzzles throughout the game are easy. The main focus of the game is mainly the looks, the feeling, the ambience. A solid part of it is that everything is alien, even the UI. It really puts you into the world more.

I would say the game is a bit short, but at the same time I'm not sure it would have been any better if it was longer. This is a one off experience of a game. It's the kind of game that you will keep thinking about for the rest of the week.

I hope we see a sequel that explores the world a bit more, and maybe explains just a little bit more, particularly about the ending. The ending somewhat comes out of nowhere and it does deserve just a scratch more of info.

What I think the story is about: (PLAY THE GAME FIRST)

[spoiler]
To me, the story seems to revolve mainly about a vastly superior and advanced alien race that has given in to sexual perversions but not for the sake of it but actually to reach an enlightened state and be able to pass into "heaven". They seem to use a specific type of creature to breed with and create new types of humanoids, perhaps as their new advanced selves, a new evolution stage if you will. Perhaps as helpers to get them into heaven. It's not fully clear to me either, but what is clear that there is a fetish for sex all over the place, especially at the end, that there is both a combination of pleasure and pain, and there is the idea of transcendence. However, all of this has led to their entire collapse. Things have gone very, very wrong.
[/spoiler]

review_text:
I have been playing STO for several years now.  For a number of months I was slowly grinding my way up the power tree with my first character, banging my head against some of the campaign challenges and just not making much headway.  Fortunately I was friended by a nice fellow in Germany.  (There is a notable German playerbase.)  He helped me defeat a particularly annoying enemy and got me a fleet invitation.  From there I asked a steady stream of questions and got very useful advice on in-game economy, earning upgrade kits, and similar topics.  
My advice to new players is to ask many questions and not be afraid to ask for help.  There are a number of details that are not even mentioned in the tutorials, but despite the never-ending stream of political bad takes in the big chat hubs there are even more decent folk who will take advise a newcomer.

The real goal of STO is, of course, "Space Barbie."  Dressing your crew toons in stylish uniforms or casual wear is amusing, but the bigger draw is the starship selection.  The game IS free-to-play, and the normal level grind will give you several opportunities to earn your choice of basic ships appropriate to the Federation, Romulan, or Klingon career paths.  Additionally, there are summer and winter events in which one can earn a free ship as well as useful personal gear.
Unfortunately for people without trust funds, the most coveted ships and gear are not free.  The in-game store has a decent sale from time to time but it is clear that your money is supposed to be theirs.  I kept to the ftp ethos for years but finally decided that a purchase now and then was not fatal.  To be clear, it is a luxury, not a necessity.  If something I really wanted came along, I would buy it only if I could do without a corresponding purchase elsewhere.  Most often that meant not buying beer for a little while, so we're not talking really large sums.  

Sadly, I can no longer make purchases because Arc decided I have to go through them.  I hope they enjoy not having that little bit of revenue stream any longer.

- high end content drops loot for areas 30 levels lower.
- Almost everything is neatly tucked behind a very nice RNG system that is designed to force players to grind the same thing for countless hours

Not sure why they call it New Genesis, game feels more like the end of a great franchise.

review_text:
GTTOD is extremely fun, don't get me wrong. But i would never recommend this game as it is now.

Let me say that the game is filled to brim with potential. It has many redeeming qualities but is in no way polished or refined in the state its in. Far too many insecurities and things i dislike. It has the best movement i've ever seen in a game before. I get this rush of dopamine every damn time I land onto a wall and go straight for the WALLRUN. oh GOD THE WALLRUN. The force of gravity feels natural and flowy, and the speed acceleration is so extremely satisfying. The shooting is also alot of fun, its alot of fun to land those hits and land melee attacks like kicks and punches. You can even stomp the enemies!

Here's where things kinda suck.

THE GAMEPLAY: I love the platforming, the wallrunning, and many parts of the levels that are based on movement. But GOD its so extremely repetitive. Each level is an abnoxious arena survival where the enemies run at mach zero and will *never* catch up.. Like.. EVER. The level design is abhorrent and basically insults the speed and mobility that you are given. All these small platforms and skinny bridges give you the middle finger due to how much they dont work with your speed and the pacing of the game. Alongside the enemies which are absolute PUSHOVERS. Literally just feels like a point-and-click game. I've never seem myself on the edge of my seat while fighting. Reaching the extremely late waves which claim to be difficult, finding it to be nothing more but a race to see whether you can shoot before they start firing at you. PLEASE, IM BEGGING YOU TO INCREASE THE SPEED OF THE ENEMIES! Primarily what this game needs is a better environment, the enemies are slow and sluggish and it always feels like your speed is useless. You have NO reason to go full-speed and run across the map like you're able to because an opponent will NEVER bring you to do that. Enemies are too slow to chase you down and overwhelm you. Their bullets are too slow to feel like an actual threat, just something to encourage you to step to the left just a LITTLE. The stages are very claustrophobic and have a seemingly pointless high-ground where enemies barely move and take up space. You can avoid danger by just walking away, it'll take forever for them to do anything about it. We need a FASTER environment that can KEEP UP WITH US. This will make tensions higher and encourage us to use our insane mobility throughout the levels. I cannot stress how annoying it is to be able to run at mach 80 while these guys literally cannot move at ALL. Game would benefit from homing projectiles, chasing enemies, and literally anything that gets us to move. We should be outsmarting the enemies with our movement, not running away from them! Another thing is the guns, they all feel like they serve the same purpose. Automatic gun that shreds down hordes. Crowd control. Splash damage explosive weapon which is best for: crowd control. semi automatic weapons better at dealing individual damage but are mostly just: crowd control. The best we get are the single-fire weapons, these actually encourage us to aim and fire carefully and pick targets.

- THE GRAPHICS: dont get me wrong i love the neon aesthetic. Many of the sights and locations can be absolutely stunning but i hate the over-usage of neon outlines. All that depth that existed in the graphics are immediately destroyed due to the atrocious colors and the outlines which make everything blend together and look flat as all hell. More often than not it feels like style over substance. The use of bloom hurts my eyes, the pickups, props, and ESPECIALLY the enemies feel impossible to read because of all the effects and colors. The silhouettes of the enemies are even abstracted by the abnoxious glow effect. The only way to see which enemy is which is by their name, which you can see by hovering over them with your crosshair. This doesnt help because that'll become impossible to read through all the bullets and effects covering that, too. And besides, it only flashes for a second.

-EVERYTHING ELSE: Overall the game doesn't have much going for it aside from *some* fun gamemodes. But thats it. These gamemodes include new abilites, new guns, difficulty changes and an endless gamemode. These are fun but barely do anything to make up for what i had mentioned. Alot of my gripes in this game are based on fundamental features like the combat and gunplay. I do enjoy many of the tracks, but they're quite forgettable. The aesthetic and atmosphere of the game can extremely serene and relaxing here and there. But that's it.

Overall I dont think the game is worth it in the state its in. Thankfully its early access so its nowhere near its final state. But i definitely do wish it gets some sort of overhaul gameplay-wise. GTTOD feels like a casual experience just shooting enemies in the background until the next wave starts. The gameplay needs far more depth than what it is right now and feels very lacking. With a currency and shop systems that feel useless and unneeded. This game's design priorities feel like they're in the wrong place. They're far too focused on extra gamemodes, maps, new guns, instead of the base game itself. The pieces just wont come together. We need more attention on the level designs, the guns, and the combat especially.

review_text: The amount of broken mechanics make almost nothing other than wingsuit traversal fun. Planes and jets operate in this strange high-fantasy sense, as in you need to use a nitrous oxide boost to fly at any significant pace, then let it recharge to have power again while losing speed and altitude, like some kind of powered glider.. I'm not sure who made this choice but it's so groundbreakingly disappointing that they may have thought jet engines are too op or something so, "here's a boost and recharge thingy just go up and down and up and down, new and cool right??!!" If you like planes in video games at all, you will be greatly appalled. The forced FOV is horrendous. I feel like I am playing with binoculars and I can never seem to feel oriented in-game, as well as the ground-vehicle cameras swaying around when you drive and turn, blocking your view of... where you're heading... Offroad/hills, just don't, angular changes to the vehicle are followed by the camera aiming in-line with the length of the car, so you're forced to be looking up and 45 degrees off center at times, and it is visually exhausting to attempt off-roading. Combined with low FOV makes me question if they really play-tested much if at all. The only "vehicle" that feels good is the wingsuit, it is clear this is the core of what they tried to perfect. Cutscenes are also jittery and look pretty bad, on-par with ps3 graphics with slightly lower framerate. The overall world is cramped yet empty, all climates harshly bang up against each other in a giant Fortnite amalgamation. Even with all the mods I have installed, weapons I've edited, and vehicles altered to try and save some fun, but it still doesn't fit quite right. Overall, JC2 was far better, it had half the mechanics and all of them felt useful and done well, the map felt real, asymmetrical, and the sections were spread out and encouraged exploration. Bustling cities, high deserts, swamps and mountain ranges, we may never have that uniqueness again, at least not from Avalanche.

I actually only heard bad things about the game, like it was boring and had failed and someone who even wrote somewhere that it was so railroad straight, it never held any suprises.

There were so many optional ways and secrets. I sometimes wasn't even sure if I was going the way I should or an optional way.
Of course it's not an open world game, where you can go where ever you want at any time, but this is a story based survival horror game! Open world has no place here and I'm glad the game was the way it was.

review_text:
I hate to give this long awaited sequel a negative review, but it's what I think the game deserves. So what did this game do right and what did it do wrong?

Positives: 
- The setting is honestly amazing, the segregated train cars all have a lot of personality and are a great way to involve many different kinds of trolls and show the social imbalance between the castes.
- Music and art are both excellent, the game has a very charming aesthetic. The character animations are especially great... when they aren't extremely choppy.

Negatives:
- As mentioned above, some animations look strangely unfinished, which was a problem with the first game as well. Both characters idle sprites look like they are about 5 frames per second and I don't understand why such a used animation would be cut down to such a bare minimum. 
- A couple other small nitpicks bothered me throughout the playthrough, such as not being able to examine the items in your inventory. You start the game with items from the last act and the icons for them are too small to really tell what some of them are. I went through the whole game without knowing what the book in Xefros' inventory was. The hint system can also be pretty useless at many times as well. Rather than giving you a hint it usually just repeats what your current objective is, more like a quest log than any sort of hint.
- Much of the games 'puzzles' are unintuitive and unsatisfying to solve. In the second half of the game especially I found a guide necessary for me to advance without having to repeatedly interact with everything over and over again. This makes me question why Hiveswap even had to be a game in the first place when, in my opinion, nothing is being accomplished here that couldn't have been in the webcomic format we are more used to. Or even in the style of Friendsim/Pesterquest! Those games were mostly able to maintain the strengths of Hiveswap (the music, writing, and character art) while avoiding its weaknesses (having to waste time interacting with things repeatedly to see what you're supposed to do or just look up a guide). I for one wouldn't mind making the game more linear if it meant cutting out the annoying bits.
- It feels like almost nothing has happened in Hiveswap act 1 or 2! I could sum up all of the relevant events from both games in just a couple sentences. The 'plot' is progressing at such a slow pace that I wonder how act 3 could pick up the pace and resolve everything in a satisfying way.
- I also don't really know who this game is supposed to be for? Troll romance is explained to the player through Xefros for what would be the third time for someone who has read Homestuck and played Friendsim. You would think that would mean its intended for people who haven't read the comic, but I can't imagine recommending this game to someone that hasn't already read Homestuck, or at the very least Friendsim. The best part of the game was honestly just being able to see my favorite characters from Friendsim, and the only other thing that I'm holding out for in this series is how it will relate back to Homestuck. Like, remember those black and green monsters from Hiveswap act 1? Yeah whats up with those, we still have no clue at all what their deal is. So yeah, I'm not sure who the target audience really is here, it seems more like they're trying to appeal to both but not doing a great job at it.

In conclusion:
I dunno, I feel like most people already knew if they were going to get this game before it came out. I'm personally not going to recommend this game to my friends, neither those who have read Homestuck nor those who have not read it. The game often had unsatisfying solutions, some general lack of UI and polish, and didn't really answer any new questions or contribute to the Homestuck lore.

review_text:
Pros:
- Great Artstyle.

Cons:
- No narrative context whatsoever. I had no idea who I was or why I was doing anything, and while the world looks cool, it has no real meaning or reason behind it.
- Poorly done puzzles. The puzzles often have little indication or context as to why you are doing them or what they accomplish. Combine this with an artstyle that can make it easy to miss levers or doors, and you will often be running around in circles trying to figure out what you are supposed to do. Combined with the lack of narrative context, you often have no idea at all why you are doing something, which makes the puzzles feel unsatisfying.
- Awful combat. The combat is awkard, clunky, and unenjoyable, and for an adventure game, there is quite a lot more combat than there really should be. You could probably remove the combat and enemies altogether and the game would be no worse for it.
- $40 for a roughly 5 hour game with no replay value whatsoever? Given that even the first playthrough is not particularly enjoyable, this pricing is ridiculous. I only payed about 7 bucks for it and I'm still not really sure that was worth it...

All-in-all, this is a very disappointing game, especially given how much effort was put into the artstyle. If you like the artstyle and it's real cheap, maybe it might be worth it, but even then I don't think there is anything in it you wouldn't get out of watching a playthrough of it on Youtube.

It's probably an honor thing, but I totally don't get why she would even stay one year with those morons.

Most women are dumbed down and into that kind of thing. So I guess it will work for many.

review_text:
You probably already know if you want EHM or not. If you aren't a hockey fan, and if you don't like pretty deep simulation-based games, there's nothing for you here.
However, if you like those two things, EHM isn't perfect, but it is the best option in the genre. Sports Interactive know what they're doing, and EHM is no different, although it is a little barebones. It's a shame that, for what is ostensibly a new game, there's no modern features such as achievements. Thankfully it does have Workshop support, and it's here we see EHM's trump card.
EHM's modding community is what, for me, pushes the game from standard sports-sim to something engrossing. Real-world rosters and clubs, as well as facepacks, allow for something more realistic - and thus, fun. For me, trying to turn my beloved Calgary Flames from perennial bottom-feeders into an actual force is far more enjoyable than doing it with a fantasy club, with fake players. Without these mods, EHM is pretty sparse.
On its own, EHM is a tough sell. Even with it's fantastic mod support, it caters to a pretty small niche. If that niche includes you, though, you'll be treated to a game that demands time and patience, but yields great reward.

review_text:
this game exists on the cusp of both being good and being mediocre

Problems, in no short order:
[i]Most, if not all, servers are based within Japan.[/i] Previously, there were three distinct regions: NA, EU, and JP. All the servers were consolidated together due to low player population on any server that wasn't JP during most hours. Unless you're playing single-player, you'll probably have 200+ ping if you're non-JP.
[i]Slow update cycles, for those who are inclined.[/i] The development team [b]seems[/b] to be relatively small. While they're dedicated towards this game, the amount of content they can churn out may be a bit of a turn-off for those who are expecting substantial updates per season.
[i]Always-on(ish) game.[/i] The game can be played in single-player and offline in limited function but key things will be missing. Any DLC characters will be disabled until you reconnect. Any shop-bought cosmetics, for those who prefer fashion before form, will also be disabled.
The core gameplay is tied to the online matches, so you'll be unable to enjoy the full experience offline. [b]They are testing a single-player/offline mode that allows for full access to the game. Props to them.[/b]


Aside from those problems, the core gameplay of a dungeon-raiding/boss fight experience is highly tuned though. 
Balancing in-game ensures no character is particularly weak, nor is a specific character a must-have for a team setup. Most characters have a clear identity within their class, and there's few instances of "oh this character is just x but better".
[u]Ignoring the latency problems[/u], all the bosses have clear reads via the damage indicators that appear.
The various equipment items you can equip have a degree of customizability, and can be tailored for a specific experience or boss. [i]The entire end-game turns into a loadout-setup simulator essentially. If you enjoy it, bonus content for you![/i]

The game's alright, despite the steep asking price. So long as DIMPS continues to churn out content for the game rather than letting it fall by the wayside, the game is shaping up quite nicely since its rocky launch.

It feels like a product that exists because it has to, not because anyone actually wanted to make a quality product.

Game controls are too imprecise which will result in you being discovered, and frequently that results in almost instant death.

Combine that 'no fault of the player' death with a game save system that can lose you 40 minutes to an hour of progress and the game feels unbalanced and anti-player. I don't mind failing in a game but don't make me repeat an hour of gameplay when the failure isn't even my fault.

Other irritating game design decisions include the first contract being in a featureless white expanse that bores the hell out of you, inexplicably low sight lines and visibility across almost the entire map which means you're in pistol range 90% of the time and the first contract including a facility that will keep blasting out its emergency siren sound for an hour unless you mute the entire game.

In other words, the developers hate gamers. As a result I hate their game.

review_text:
tl;dr Game's good, but too broken to play.
There's a lot to chastise this game for. The ever encroaching oversimplification of once robust systems. The community in a constant uproar and argument over fair and unfair tactics and powers. The select few sludge pits that still only communicate through slurs. The devs that have no idea what does well and what does bad in their game, because they simply do not play it. The grinding. The microtransactions. The lacks of polish.

But I can excuse it all. I can move past all that. If it weren't for the crashes and disconnects. I have not had a play session in MONTHS that didn't end with the game still running. Unreal will break. Servers will break. UAC will break. And kick you out of whatever you're doing and you have nothing to show for it.

I absolutely love this game. I've always been a fan of hide and seek games like Prop Hunt, and this scratches that itch. I've always loved horror as a genre and have been a big fan of the walking nightmares that can't be stopped, and this game lets you feel it. I love big crossovers: even when they get kinda outta control like Fortnite or Magic: The Gathering. I love the gameplay loop, I love experimenting with powers and perks, I love being a goofball with the survivors, I love playing a little guitar for the killers. It's so much fun.

When I actually get to play it.

Tried the free weekend and...The game is 50/50 to me but leaning towards negative because of its technical problems. 
The game can be pretty badass at times but THE SERVERS AND PERFORMANCE ARE MADE FROM EXTRA OLD DOO DOO which is what has me on the fence about purchasing and leaves much to be desired.

-Multiple crashes to desktop whenever I played

-The tutorial does a bad job of explaining what to do in your first few matches which can make you feel so lost at times. 

-Youll have major desync and rubberbanding the entire match if you get a bad server (which is VERY common)

-The bugs are lower resolution at a distance plus their low FPS animations make it look like a stop motion skit. The bugs will rubberband like crazy all around the map and glitch through walls/structures. It really killed my immersion and momentum to want to play. It makes the game look so cheap and mediocre. The game looked so much more appealing and interesting the first year it was out.

-Lots of times your shots will just not register, especially if theyre faraway shots. Most of the time its due to desync so you end up having to lead your targets while shooting and hope it hits. I used nearly 200 turret rounds on a bombardier cuz I could see my bullets hitting him (wasnt blocked by armor) but I was getting no hit marker so it took no damage with those 200 rounds. I shoot an enemy right next to it and those hits register so idk whats going on man. 

-Youll die out of nowhere during battle and your body will go flying hundreds of feet away and hardly anyone comes to revive you so you better hope you have a veteran medic who knows how it goes. This is usually caused by the meteor showers, explosives or enemy ranged explosive attacks. Your teammates will smoke you on accident a lot too.

The biggest thing im scared of is the games population dying down again. I was going to buy this game months ago but decided against it cause a few people told me no one plays it anymore and it can take a while to find a match if you even do find one. 

P.S If those technical problems are fixed in the future ill change my review to positive but I know how it goes with Indie studios so I highly doubt we'll see any fixes for a while if any at all. I have faith in the Offworld devs though, I really hope theyre able to fix it.

Stuck this on my wishlist after seeing a promising trailer and bought it during a sale. In my minds eye the game was going to be something like an isometric, slower and more strategic version of 'mark of the ninja'.

After pushing through an hour of gameplay and still not able to feel any comfort with the control system I wouldn't recommend it. Controlling the camera is a pain and you'll be constantly dicking about with it while trying to make heads or tails of how you can navigate the terrain. And that's not a 'there so many meaningful options that its difficult to pick a path' kind of terrain, but 'I can't tell if the basketball hoops they have stuck to buildings without which your adept ninja couldn't scale them is two floors up or one floor up because theres nothing really to indicate depth and rotating the camera just so I can determine what should be fairly forthright information makes my eyes glaze over' kind of terrain.

Oh, and if you want to know how little this game feels like a stealth game, with a second character they introduce (seen as early as the first level) you can kill any number of guards at once within a fairly generous area.

So yeah. If you want to play a fun stealth game you're looking in the wrong place. Go play 'mark of the ninja' if you haven't already because that game does ninjas right.

Then, when it does come in, it comes in way too late in the story to make much of a difference, and for the most part is really mostly used as a gimmick for about the last 4 or 5 levels. Like a lot of the other tools the game gives you, to really use it to its full potential you'll have to make your own fun with it, so for those of you going into this expecting a more 'guided' or linear experience, where things are crafted for you to enjoy the mechanics, you might be a bit let down. IMHO, Boneworks is a game that was made not just with the purpose of being modded, but with the expectation of being modded.

I'm just kind of disappointed. Maybe it's just that I entered the PCVR scene too late to appreciate what it is that this game does or maybe it's just not geared towards my kinda thing but regardless, I can't play this game for much longer than 30 or 40 minutes without getting really sad and booting up H3VR

The Good:

- Guns rock. This is coming from a guy who almost exclusively plays VR shooters and shoots on the weekends as a hobby. Everything about it feels visceral and punchy in a way that makes the occasional animation related jank easy to overlook, with the exception of a couple guns which stand out as being particularly annoying to use the to the weight simulation.

- When the immersion hits, it HITS. Sure, the settings can be kinda bland at times, but even in those circumstances there are moments that stand out as being really awe inspiring despite how simple they are.

- The soundtrack, for the most part, is top notch. Even though blasting through generic NPCs with a Glock to the sound of synthwave should be played out by now, it most definitely is not. Not in VR, anyways

- The Tac Trials and the Rooftop Parkour minigames are so god damned cool, even if they kind of suck to play

- Driving is generally pretty fun, at least in my opinion. I've got good vr legs and love whipping around in the go-karts :)

The Bad:

Campaign too short, IK sucks. I don't care how cool or immersive it is watching a playermodel's arms move in place of mine while I smash open a crate, or rack the slide on a pistol, or shove a giant ball of trash around if the other half of the time its only purpose seems to be 'get in the way of everything the player wants to do'. 

It's one thing for a game mechanic to be super realistic and well built, and yes, the physics are generally very cool and fun to toy around with, but any sense of immersion or enjoyment of them is often broken by the unfortunate reality of physics engines, in that they all suck in their own special ways, and will break eventually.

That said, you shouldn't have to fight against a game's physics engine, especially in VR, unless it's designed for you to do so in a consistent manner, and consistent physics don't easily mesh with full player bodies unless you have full-body trackers or a lot of patience. It would be one thing if the game was more tuned to allow people to get used to and work around the jank and the artificial weightiness, but unfortunately, a lot of the movement in this game is just way too sluggish for such an important mechanic.

For instance, the game really tries to be a platformer sometimes, there's a whole section dedicated to it in the form of that godawful pillar level everyone hates. The problem is that you can't climb for shit and jumping is quite possibly the most unintuitive part of the game, with it being tied to a button that at first appears to make you crouch and slow down a bit and then has this weird sort of delay before your character's legs even lift off. 

80% of the time, you'll try to climb up, onto, or over something and your characters legs will get stuck, and you'll wind up sliding back down it like a shitty mall cop. I made sure that my height and arm length were set correctly and everything, and I still wound up doing all of, but not limited to the following things;

- getting my own melee weapons tangled in my characters arms somehow

- missing jumps that a toddler could clear with relative ease

- looping my arms through the rungs of ladders

- flinging myself off of obstacles that I was half wrapped around

Not to mention the fact that the right thumbstick, for some reason, controls your in-game stance, which as far as I can tell can't be disabled. As an accessibility feature, it could be nice, and I'll give kudos for that, but it's usefulness is kind of debatable and I'd much rather the controller bind be spent on something more useful

Also, the puzzles are generally difficult to figure out at first, because the game isn't great at explaining, and you can't at all tell when you're getting shot before you start to black out.

review_text:
GTTOD is a game with a lot of potential. While it might be trying to ride the wave created by games like ghostrunner and neon white, among others, it has some unique features and it feels like it has the potential to be its own thing.

The problems start at the point where if you're the kind of player who seeks any actual polish, the current state of the game has little to none of it.

The movement is clunky, the momentum and inertia feel wrong, you get big burst of speeds you don't feel like you should get sometimes, the dash and wall run don't always work how you want (you have a setting for it, btw) and the maneuverability mid air is close to non existent especially at high speeds. You know, that "can't change my jump direction" feels. The level design is on the bland side, and there isn't much interesting tricks to pull off besides wall jumps left and right, and inconsistent dash resets.

The combat is complete chaos, but not really the good kind. You have a ton of enemies shooting in every direction, with very little visibility and clarity in general (be it the enemies or the actual environement), it's hard to figure out what's going, why you're taking damage from every directions, why you are still alive in spite of that. The weapons are so generous that it makes them matter very little, i can have a pistol, a shotgun or a bazooka, all i need to do is look in the general direction of enemies and they'll die. The bosses are no different, just run around hoping not to get hit and keep shooting toward the boss.

The levels quickly all become samey, even though there will be some randomizations and you can get random power ups throughout the runs which makes the gameplay have a bit of a roguelike flavor, but that's not enough to make it interesting imo.

So sure, if you're the kind of person who just wants to start up the game, go woosh HAYAHH woosh all over the place, and bang bang BOOOM explosions everywhere while killing everything, you might have fun, but personally i found it becoming stale really fast. If you're looking for more than just random chaos and you expect some depth, this ain't it yet. Thanksfully Early Access means there's a chance it'll get better.

review_text:
I must admit, this is a pretty difficult review to write. The game comes as close to "mixed" as I can get it, but it does end up on the positive side. So, without further ado, the details. 

The story is really innovative and interesting. The whole idea of "game within a game" hasn't really been exploited that much and the various twists are quite interesting and keep you immersed until the very end. I'd say the story, and especially the setting, is the strongest point of the game. 

The characters are a mixed bag. Some of them are very roughly drawn anime cliches, while others are actually memorable and non-trivial. The fact that you never learn the true faces and identities of the characters and only know their avatars only adds to the depth. 

The gameplay... at the start, I really enjoyed the combat system. It has the proper mix of engaging timings and fun abilities to make it interesting. However, the longer you play, the less enjoyable it gets. A lot of the later enemies are just reskins, and you basically only have a couple of basic enemy types. At some point, the game also becomes too grindy and too easy - I guess that on higher difficulties it would be more demanding, but then again I cannot imagine myself grinding so many battles on hard difficulty.

The grind. Oh my, the grind. The game's setting is a virtual MMORPG environment and I at some point I got the feel that it was really realistic and that I was grinding yet another of my WoW characters to level 120. And that is not a compliment. At least in WoW, the different areas have variety. Here, especially if you play all the parts in succession, it simply becomes tedious and repetitive. Why the authors decided that virtually all of the story dungeons have to take part in the same, "go through three levels" cave is beyond me. There is no autocombat feature like in Tales games, no autokill feature like in Persona, you just have to grind the battles. With the same reskinned enemies. With the same enemies on the entire level - sometimes there's nothing else than packs of the exact enemy in groups of 3, copied and pasted all across the level. 

Also, nothing ever happens in the levels. Nothing. No fun and enjoyable encounters, no extra sidequests, most of the storyline quests are "do the same tedious dungeon to the end of its 3-level glory and then watch a cutscene". The levels that are actually a bit different are also annoyingly spoiled - why would anyone think that figuring out a teleporter spiral is too hard for an average JRPG player and you have to drop obvious spoilers on their head?

The amount of copy-paste happening between the three episodes is sickening. How much can you play the [spoiler]basic story hook - go through the Arena championship - do random quests and dungeons with friends for character development - fight the supernatural foe[/spoiler] routine? You guessed it - three times. The exact same routine. Even the "quests" deal with exactly the same NPCs and open you up to exactly the same tedious grindy gathering routines.

Chim-chims - these deserve a separate point. Who in the world would thought that it would be fun to include an almost completely non-interactive, completely devoid of any skill factor resource system in the game that amounts basically just to going to clicky spots and clicking to get resources? At least add a minigame for it (no, chasing chim-chims or even running from the assassins does not count).

And finally, Episode 4. A giant troll. Basically a shortened, feature-reduced linear epilogue that toys with you by giving you some of the most fun combat mechanics (the final rank job extension) and then literally giving you one dungeon to run them in. It really seems like some of the feature distribution was completely wasted. Also, the [spoiler]Lost Weapons[/spoiler]. When you get them in [spoiler]Part 3 from the start, they are already upgraded to Level 3 - you get introduced to a new option to upgrade them only to learn that the upgrade requires fighting a... level 135 monster. Great. You'll get there after you beat the final boss. Then in Episode 4 they're upgraded to max again.[/spoiler]

In other words - this game has some really nice features. The "Crimson VS" minigame is actually quite enjoyable. However, it also has an absurd amount of tedious grind and an absurd lack of meaningful story content besides the main story. If you play it, I recommend treating it as 3 separate games. Don't do it like me and try to play it in one run - you'll probably get increasingly frustrated like I did. Otherwise, I'd say go for it (but I'd still check out some other titles first).

review_text:
After the previous game, I can see how the RGG team decided to expand on the concept first experimented with in Y4. Yakuza 5 is a complete evolution of the gameplay and game structure first explored in the last entry. They went from four protagonists playing their stories in the same city, to having five different protagonists with an entire city for each of them (almost) to explore. This game is MASSIVE in all aspects that you can consider, which really surprised me when I first started playing it. 

Like the previous game, the story is split up into parts where each character takes front stage, with each restart putting you into a new city to explore, often filled with new activities to perform on as part of the many side contents you'll find around. On top of the main story which is connected to a bigger plot in between each of the character's segments, each protagonist also gets a side activity that gets briefly introduced as part of the main progression, that you can follow to take a break from the main gameplay loop and arguably play a completely different game on each. I do personally enjoyed these side modes a lot as I enjoy the great variety that this series offers on their side content.

As part of the main combat, it's pretty similar to the previous game's styles, besides the one character who is swapped for a new protagonist. One addition is a character specific way of spending their heat, which can be fun or annoying, depending on who you're using, Saejima's isn't that great and is more annoying than not when it triggers.

Completion wise, as expected from having five different cities, there is A LOT to do, as evident by my high play time logged, it is certainly a challenge for Completionists. Most of the actual objectives aren't all that difficult, there simply is an insane amount of things to do. One tip however: Play on Normal difficulty, Akiyama's Coliseum matches are NOT balanced for him and it is a pain to do them in Hard or higher. 
There's also the fact that for some god forsaken reason, they do not allow you to create Clear Save Files from Premium Adventure, and they explicitly tell you this. This means that if you plan to do future replays, you are only able to carry whatever progress you had at the Finale. I have no Idea why they chose to do this and I understand it's the only time they did, so... there's that.

Performance and engine wise, there is a massive improvement from Y4 Remastered, having played Y0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2, this game feels like a middle point between 0/K1 and K2, it is still the older engine but I really felt a big improvement that it almost feels like it's the Dragon Engine at times, transitions into battles are smooth and instant almost always, the other times they play a small cutscene to begin the fight, but that's mainly an aesthetic choice, though it can get annoying after repeated occurrences.

As a final comment, I often see people disliking this game a lot, and I feel like it mainly comes from it's massive length, I get it for a bit, but the game being built in five different stories and cities are what enable it to be this way. Another point may be that Haruka's sections are so different and pretty much it becomes a rhythm game altogether, as a fan of that genre myself I adored this part, but I could understand someone who may not be as ecstatic to be more annoyed by it than not, I do enjoy the big variety offered so I enjoyed this alternate play style when it came, it isn't as hard as I wish it could be at times, but mastering the harder opponents was a fun challenge.

review_text:
World of Goo is a fun architectural puzzle game. The basic idea is that you have a limited number of various types of gooball and you need to use them to build a structure that reaches the exit pipe on each level with enough left over to meet the level's requirements. A lot of the levels mix up that formula to varying degrees, but that's the basic starting point. It's a good game, but if that doesn't sound like your kind of fun you probably won't like it.
As to what makes it a good game, the level design and the variety of gooballs keep things interesting while being presented well enough to not feel overwhelming, the difficulty is mostly in the sweet spot between boring and frustrating (and you're allowed to skip a few levels if you're really stuck and aren't feeling stubborn), the humor is goofy but entertaining, and the music and graphics are well-suited to the game.
The only downside is that it's short with only moderate replayability. My playthrough was probably a bit quicker because I'd played it most of the way through before and remembered a few solutions, but it only took me five hours. It'll probably take someone playing for the first time a little longer, and a good bit longer still if they want to get the achievements and complete the optional objectives and build a really huge tower in the World of Goo Corporation minigame.

Villagers run away at the first sign of enemies, no matter how heavily armed and armored they are, which isn't the most helpful thing ever when they get outnumbered by slimes on day 2.

The AI, such as it is, seems to have two different settings: pretend to work, and gleefully do jack.

"Prepare to lose often!" works with games like Dwarf Fortress, because in DF the game is legitimately difficult. In Rise to Ruin, losing happens because nobody does any freaking work, and slapping a "game hurd tho!" label on it doesn't excuse crap programming.

Give it a chance if you like, but be ready to spend a lot of time waiting for your dozen builders to decide they feel like repairing the damage done to that house a week ago, or boggle as to why your maintenance and repair guy is delivering iron ingots to the toolmaker instead of fixing the sixteen forty damaged buildings you built the damn Maintenance post specifically to get someone to fix the freaking things.

You need three or four buildings just to make one operational (magic turret? need an energy collector, which needs to be powered from another building, which needs...), and the workers in those buildings do whatever they feel like, which is usually 'nothing whatsoever'. Got three people working in the lumber mill making wooden boards? Well, that one guy there is bringing logs from the lumber shack to the village center while you've got four buildings waiting for boards. So fun! Not like you need those boards to repel the endless army of weak monsters that will utterly destroy everything in sight while everybody runs away, so you can avoid losing on day 2! The coding is like the workers themselves: it does whatever it feels like doing, which is usually nothing. review_text:
This game felt too thin, with too little substance stretched over a very short playtime that does not justify its asking price. It harbours and hogs gameplay mechanics to prolong an experience as intriguing and captivating as observing concept art. Far too little and too late is an accurate description of Scorn, as it extends what little gameplay there is in a game that can be finished in four hours to obscure how barren it is. Speaking of barren, Scorn's Story.

Scorn dumps you in its world clueless with no hints, no markers, no objectives, designed for blind playthroughs, if you will. I initially liked that until I learned this method extends to the game's story. Far from what I would describe as environmental storytelling, Scorn instead walks the path of no showing and no telling. With not a single piece of dialogue, the game does not establish characters, plot or narrative, not even through other means. When I discovered a moral choice in the game, I was amused at how poorly implemented it was. This moral choice only serves to make the game feel unfinished. It's a single moral choice. One of its kind, of little impact and importance. It further establishes the feeling of what could've been, of lost potential, of snuffed excitement.

Visually, Scorn is striking and sombre, yet appealing and unique. It is, undoubtedly, the game's most substantial positive element. The puzzles often blur the lines between puzzles and basic problem-solving. The combat is tedious and monotonous. Once a second enemy enters, the player will take damage no matter what because wielding a thruster tool against projectile-launching enemies in confined spaces is stupid. I felt like the player and enemy characters were designed for different games. It was definitely bothersome fighting far-ranged enemies with a limited close-ranged weapon capable of two strikes at a time, and it added to the dull nature of the combat. I discovered that enemies mostly chase the player for a very short distance before stopping and even exiting the area; from then on, I simply went along with my business and did not engage in combat unless absolutely necessary. The other much more powerful weapon is only used for one section before being rendered useless; hell, the combat, in its entirety, is in two sections, and I'm using both "combat" and "section" very lightly.

The Cream does not recommend Scorn at its full price; get it on Game Pass instead if you want to play a concept art exhibition with a few "puzzles", frustrating combat, and soft locking. Oh God, the soft locking!

review_text:
This game is getting a lot of consistent work and polish, and I appreciate it, but it still falls into a major category of frustrating that I can't seem to get over, and that is that villagers, that backbone of your economy are complete idiots.

Builder is the default worker position, where the job assignment for the villager is "go get whatever is needed to build the building that is on the top of the builder priority list." It's not extremely efficient role but it's very versatile and useful, especially at the beginning of the game. However, if you have built too many buildings, they just... stop functioning; they get stupid and stand around like brain-damaged penguins. in the meantime, your town gets overrun.

If I decide to add 30 building plans to my town, let me do that. Don't have the game punish me for ambitiously planning ahead of what my town is going to look like. The builders don't need to drop everything, they can just finish what they were doing and move onto the next thing when they are done.

"That's not how the game is played!"

That's how I'm playing the game. If it doesn't let me play that way, I'm gonna stop playing, and this review will stay red.

Edit: Years in, achievements have been added, and villagers are still brain-damaged penguins. I spend more time dragging single resources to buildings and dropping monsters into sacrifice pits than I do playing an actual game. It's not compelling gameplay. This is a simulator desperately in search of a game. It's sad too, because if the villagers weren't phenomenally stupid, this wouldn't feel like such a slog.

Edit 2: Alright, I finally gave in and bought Rimworld. HOLY hell. Talk about exactly what I was looking for.

I know that the purpose of this game is to be god and let your humans do the work, the problem is that your direct action in the game consists of dragging items to objects, one at a time. It's TEDIOUS AF. The gameplay on this BEGS for increased direct engagement. Rimworld admittedly, isn't perfect in this capacity, but the ability to draft your pawns and make them do ALMOST exactly what you want at any give time sets itself apart from this game. I'm sorry, but this discrepancy has been the difference between fun and not fun. Rimworld is tedious, but it's fun, RoR is tedious, and it's not fun.

What will fundamentally change this game for the better is a spell that automatically supply a building with materials. You click on the unfinished building's resource with the spell, and the tool simply grabs the closest resources required to finish the project and drags it to the building, spending mana based on distance of said resources. At the very least, allowing the grab spell to pick up stacks of material would probably suffice. In the long run, a holy golem might be more efficient, but when give the choices between efficiency and engagement, watch players choose the engagement every time. Right now, the spells are badly implemented, an entire array of options that have next to little practical utility, all drawing from a single resource that you use to tediously drag and drop materials.

No, I don't think I'll ever upvote this game, not unless spells are seriously re-imagined and empowered in a way that reflect gameplay agency for the player.

review_text:
The reason I wouldn't recommend this game can be condensed into the following sentence: Rise to Ruins is not a game you win.

That's not to say it's especially difficult, or it has an unreasonable learning curve, or anything like that; it's that the game is literally not designed for you to "win" it; the devs have admitted as much in a post on the Steam forums.

The game's "enemy" (for lack of a better term) is "The Blight", which is this area of dark, diseased ground on each village map that spawns monsters. As time goes by in the village, the Blight spreads and spawns more monsters. You can hold the Blight at bay or even push it back by building structures next to it, but that doesn't weaken it; it actually makes it "angry" and causes it to spawn more monsters. The more time goes by, the stronger the Blight becomes. There is no way to weaken it, so, eventually, no matter how well you defend yourself, you will be overcome.

You may ask "So what's the point of the game, then?". Well, the point is to establish a village, set up defenses, grow the population, create harvesting, refining, and production chains, and then take all your excess people and resources and move them to a new village sector before you're overcome by the Blight. Once in the new village, rinse and repeat.

There is no stage at which you grow so powerful and well established that you dominate the land and destroy the Blight. Eventually, given enough time, the Blight will consume you, and you will lose.

There isn't even a "passive" win state like in a Tycoon sim wherein you've built up your city/business/factory/amusement park/whatever to its ultimate potential and can then kick back and admire it. The Blight and monsters are still there, and they will still reduce all you've built to rubble.

In essence, Rise of Ruins isn't about "winning", it's about "accomplishing as much as possible before losing".

I'm not averse to grinding at a challenging game until I've finally won it, and I have over 500 hours in XCOM: Long War to prove it, but if I literally can't win because the game wasn't designed to let you win, I don't see the point.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 Remastered Review

I've just finished what might be my favorite Yakuza game! Here are my thoughts:


What I Loved:

Visuals/World: The expansive world design is a significant highlight. The fresh new accessible areas are not only visually impressive but also offer a diverse range of environments to explore.

Soundtrack: This Yakuza game once again delivers excellent music and track choices. It felt more like an award-winning movie than ever before.

Characters: Introducing a new playable character with a compelling story, alongside continuing the narratives of characters from Yakuza 4, was a great way to tie up loose ends and revisit familiar faces.

Combat: After the issues I had with Yakuza 3 and 4, I'm happy to say that the combat is enjoyable again in this game. The previous problems have been refined and are now much more appealing to play with.


What I Didn't Love:

Length: While I enjoyed much of the game and did a fair bit of exploration, the story felt drawn out at times. Specifically, the middle of Chapter 2, to just after the middle of Chapter 3 felt slow-paced. It's great if you want more Yakuza, but I personally skipped some side content to speed up my playthrough, even taking breaks to avoid burnout before reaching the better parts.


Recommendation: As with my other reviews, this is the second-to-last mainline Yakuza game featuring Kiryu, so I highly recommend playing it if you've completed the previous games. It could also serve as a good entry point as a trial run, but playing it as your first Yakuza game would mean missing a lot of context and potentially being confused.

Final Thoughts: Despite a slow section, I still consider this one of my favorite Yakuza games, ranking up there with Yakuza 0. There's so much to do and see, even surpassing Yakuza 0 in terms of the number of areas and characters. I found it incredibly engaging, and the story is once again fantastic. You'd be missing out if you skipped this for any reason! Be warned!

Blood Dragon is an absolute blast.

It takes everything that made Far Cry 3 great and cranks it up to 11 with a neon-drenched, 80s-inspired aesthetic that feels like a fever dream of everything awesome about that era. From the very first moment you step into the world, you're hit with a sense of pure, unapologetic fun, and it's clear that the developers embraced the over-the-top, action-packed, and absurd nature of the '80s.

The game's storyline is both ridiculous and brilliant. You play as cybernetic commando Rex 'Power' Colt, voiced by the great Michael Biehn. The dialogue is filled with cheesy one-liners and a sense of humour that never takes itself too seriously.

The world itself is an open playground of destruction, with enemies ranging from mutant animals to futuristic soldiers, all brought to life by the game's vibrant, pixelated graphics.

The sound design is top-notch, with a soundtrack that perfectly complements the over-the-top atmosphere.

Overall, Blood Dragon Retro-Fuelled masterpiece. A love letter to ‘80s action films and video games, offering a nostalgic, action-packed experience that’s equally thrilling and hilarious. Whether you're a fan of the Far Cry series or someone who loves a good, campy action romp, this game is a must-play.

review_text:
So after 19 hours I'm ready to draw a conclusion - also because the game really annoys me with some game mechanics. In this review there might be some Spoilers so beware. Conclusion at the bottom.

[b] Graphics: [/b]
First of all - the game is all in all nice to look at, because it is based on the CryEngine. You have several graphics options etc. There is also a FoV slider - which is not always guaranteed nowadays.

[b] Story: [/b]
It's about a fictitious republic in Russia, more precisely the Republic of Siberia. After an uprising and a fight for independence, this republic is now autonomous, albeit by force of arms.
One is assigned as a sniper to kill important members of the said republic and to reveal their researches / secrets.

[b] Gameplay: [/b]
Let's get to the point that will last the longest.
This is a sniper game - you kill 90% of all targets or enemies with your sniper rifle, you have to take into account the distance and the wind speed (the game gives you help even on the highest difficulty level). This help is provided by a mask that you receive from your client at the beginning of the game. This mask has some useful functions, like detecting enemies, mines, weak points of vehicles and as already mentioned it helps with sniping. Also as mentioned before there are different levels of difficulty - in this case three of them. You are able to purchase different Snipers, Pistols and Assault Rifles. All of your guns can be customized aswell with Silencers, muzzle brakes, differenz Scopes, Ammuniton and of course Camouflages.

Let's get to the points that are annoying. It can happen that at some points in the game you fall through the map and have to reload it. There are times where your character or NPCs are having trouble walking some paths and sliding down some slobs is not really fun. At some terrain points it seems to me as if our "professional sniper" is the greatest amateur there is, he can't even climb a bigger rock without problems and move around there, no you have to keep on jumping like a fool to get one little jump further up. Most of the time when it comes to this point you will be seen or almost seen by opponents which is of course annoying.
The AI in this game is a bit split in two, in some moments the AI is not able to think at all - the next moment the AI is as smart as a supercomputer. You can snipe away enemies one by one without anyone noticing, but if you miss twice, EVERY enemy in the area knows where you are AUTOMATICALLY via TELEPATHY. If you can still kill the enemy fast enough, nothing happens, but if you wait about 2 seconds too long, you have to reload the checkpoint. Of course the enemies can also spot you trough objects and terrian, also the kilometer wide shooting with assault rifles (and hitting) is included. In some moments it is really easier to just kill all the enemies in the area (no matter if someone has been alerted), because as soon as you go to another area nobody knows what happened in the other area. Even if you work with mines, hand grenades and C4 or shoot your way out with an assault rifle, in my eyes a bit strange.
In every mission there are main tasks that have to be done and also "Challanges" these are completely optional. Unfortunately some of them do not fit into a sniper game at all. For example - kill enemies with hand grenades or mines, blind enemies with flash bangs etc. I find it a little bit incomprehensible what such tasks are doing there, I am there as a sniper to (actually) only kill my target and not to start the third world war.
The missions usually last between 25 minutes (if you already know where to go) and about 1 hour+ if you want to be extremely stealthy or your just not getting lucky. For the missions – you have 5 Missions and a Trainings Mission.

[b] Conclusion: [/b]
I think the game is not bad, but unfortunately there are so many little things that are simply not solved well (e.g. telepathic communication between the enemies).
I can recommend this game if you just want to have some action and don't mind taking out all the enemies instead of sneaking through.  On the other hand, if you want to play the missions the way they are supposed to be played, it becomes very difficult to recommend it..

review_text:
Do not write many reviews but after reading devs most recent patch note response decided I would give it a go. 

Positives: Beautiful environments, variety of weapons, gun play is fun
Negatives: I am going to be speaking specifically about the devs statement about not adding any difficulty settings/sliders. Not going to knock the lack of any coherent plot or story as they did say they were working on that (it is needed,  though lets face it, the action is the king with these kinds of game). Leveling system is simply overly complex as well. 

As a veteran of Dark Souls series, Bloodbourne, Black Myth WuKong and a variety of other challenging games (as all of which I have completed on console) I have found this game quite frustrating and I suspect many others do as well given the comment about refunds the devs made. In each of these above games, progression felt good, your ability to continue to improve to meet and defeat the various challenges thrown your way was frankly way more attainable. Enemy design was fair.I do not need to feel overpowered in a game (though that is kinda fun), just want to be able to find a relatively clear path to get stronger and progress in some reasonable amount of play time (the latter is key). 

The gaming population is trending older (avg age has gone 26 to 36 over the last 20 years) and frankly us old timers (I am 61) have jobs, family, a million other things to do that fill our day. We do not have as much free time and when we do and want to play a game we want one that’s fun, allows for an reasonable challenge, allows for reasonable progression, and has mechanics that are not confusing or take a bunch of reading or YouTubing to figure out. 

This game is simply cumbersome and frankly a bit of a slog.  Leveling takes forever as you get into higher levels, some enemy units are just way overtuned in areas making that progression overly difficult, and you cannot clear an area and then try to get back to an extraction point if you want to escape without going further with your hard earned witch fire without more enemies showing up again (this is in stark contrast to all the games I mentioned above BTW)

The guts for a fun game I think are mostly here, needs more work. A difficulty setting would go a long way to smooth some of these things out and make the game progression much more enjoyable and much more accessible to a bigger consumer base. 

Which brings me to my final point:
I have never understood this mindset of developers who say they will not add difficulty settings/adjust game difficulty. In an industry that seems to be constantly under financial strains, I would think the idea here is to create a good product that is desirable to as many potential customers as possible. It is a business axiom. I get the vision thing and that what you create will not appeal to all gamers (does not need to) but there are rather simple ways to increase your customer base without sacrificing your product and all the hard work and love you have obviously poured into it.

review_text:
Another Metroidvania game, although this one is more of a Meroidvania-lite game. Unlike others it is shorter with smaller maps with less power-ups needed to collect everything, at most you'd just need to buy a spell or two in order to unlock certain things without much backtracking needed.

[b]Pros[/b]:

The pixel art and animation is beautiful. Everything just flows to well and doesn't really hide itself in the background. The most important animations look quite gorgeous with all that extra care given to them.

With it being metroidvania-lite the backtracking really is cut down, at most you barely have to go back to get other items be it for yourself or quest items for others. A lot of the times you just need to take the long way around or just need one certain spell.

A lot of different weapons and accessories to make your own build as the game goes on, able to change it up as you grab new stuff to see what you find the most fitting.

Beating the game once unlocks other game modes to spice up new playthroughs, all three of them varied in a way with one of them having a huge variance compared to the other two as it even has a bunch of new dialogue.

[b]Neutrals[/b]:

This depends more on how much you want to play this game, because it is short. One playthrough on average would take about two hours. Even 100%ing would not take that long if you don't idle, or do stupid things like me.

Quests are kinda forced upon you, along with returning the reward. Should you bump into the character that gave you the quest, you'll be forced to give up the item even if you wanted it. There's also one questline that's the same thing three times and it just begs the question of why. He isn't even that important of a character, he is just kinda there.

Combat first time around feels stiff, it takes time to adjust to it because your character swings it like they know how to fight, but don't have the stats to wield that weapon, and there is no leveling to fix this.

Story is.. there. It exists, it isn't terrible, but I could of had the same experience with the game if it didn't exist. I'd say just experience the dialogue once if you want since it isn't very long, otherwise just skip through.

[b]Cons[/b]:

Dodge rolling is pretty weak in this game, aside from a select few moments, it often just puts you in a tough spot. The enemy is either ready to attack again when you just get back up or you rolled too much and were too far away for a counterattack. A lot of the time it is better to just jump around the enemy to hit them.

Fighting enemies is pointless. This game has no leveling system and since only a few enemies have a guaranteed droprate of one item. The money they drop is pitiful and a lot of the loot they can drop is also pitiful. They can just drop nothing most of the time. So it is just better to not fight anything that isn't in the way or a boss.


Overall it was a pretty nice experience. Really enjoyed the different game modes, especially the big one. Though I hope the next game these guys work on improves the system when it comes to combat, at least giving some reason to fight the random enemies, Also this game has the best Mimic design I've seen in a good while.

review_text:
[h3]Overall score: 9/10[/h3]

RHL is a top-down 3D looter-shooter. And it excels at it. The loots is diverse and meaningful, and combos well with a variety of playable characters, each with their own set of active skills and skill trees.

The world is genuinely 3D, despite the top-down style. It's really unique, I haven't seen another game do anything like it. You can hop over and onto cover, use high ground, fall into and jump over pits, there's a charter who can straight up fly. And it's all a view from above.

The loot is unique. You get a primary and secondary gun in a variety of classes (machine guns, pistols, snipers, shotguns, and more), a set of passive gear, which also has classes that certain characters can take advantage of, a potion for healing, and a relic. Relics are super cool - you need to go on a treasure hunt, solving puzzles and riddles to find the pieces to assemble them, then they level up alongside you to offer very powerful and possibly build defining effects. Loot also comes in a set of different rarities, which aren't just flat upgrades. Legendaries carry a unique effect, Sets reward you for equipping multiple items together, Exotics carry even more random stats than other items, Augmented offer a powerful bonus, but need to to unlock that bonus by completing a challenge, Uniques have fixed stats, but often have an effect even more powerful than a Legendary. There is no "best tier" - they all have a use.

Characters are all fun to play. They each have three skill trees, as well as a melee, utility, charge, and ultimate skill. It's nothing to write home about, but it just all works well. Also, the thematic design of them is all great, they each fit different playstyles, and there's a cosmetic system to alter how they look to a degree.

Art is great. It's colourful, but manages to stay clear. No issues with seeing anything because of all the skill effects, like with some other games.

Music is good. Not very memorable, but it works well.

Story is... probably not to everyone's taste. It involves time travel. I enjoyed it, but I can see not everyone doing so. It carries a humorous tone throughout most of it, but gets shocking serious at points. It involves lines like "A child crying, running away as the parents are being erased by time." There's a bit of tonal whiplash at points. It also ends kind of suddenly. It's clear the devs wanted to do more, but ran out of resources and had to wrap it up quickly. Overall, I'd say it's still good, but not without issues.

Overall, RHL is a great game. If you like the looting aspect of Borderlands, and don't mind that RHL isn't a FPS, you'll probably love this game. It's clearly made with love, and deserves far more attention than it's getting. Worth full price.

Also, as of writing this review, the score on Steam is "Mixed". The game had a fair number of bugs and other issues, but post-launch, it's all fixed up. So don't let the overall score dissuade you.

LEGO Jurassic World is exactly what you'd hope for: dinosaurs, chaos, and that signature LEGO charm all rolled into one dino-sized adventure. Whether you’re a lifelong Jurassic Park fan or just love running around as a tiny blocky T. rex, this game delivers.

The best part? It covers all four films from the original Jurassic Park trilogy and Jurassic World. That means you get to relive the most iconic scenes—from the T. Rex breakout and raptor kitchen scene to Owen Grady wrangling raptors like a boss. And all of it is done with LEGO's trademark humour, clever slapstick, and surprisingly great attention to detail.

The environments are beautifully crafted in that colourful, LEGO-fied way. From Isla Nublar’s lush jungle to the high-tech facilities of Jurassic World, each area feels alive and full of secrets to uncover. And yes—you can play as dinosaurs. That’s not a drill. You can stomp around as a triceratops, roar as a T. Rex, and even build your own custom dinos. It’s silly, it’s fun, and it never gets old.

There’s a huge roster of characters from across all the movies, each with different abilities, and tons of collectables, gold bricks, puzzles, and side activities to keep you busy. The game also has great couch co-op, making it perfect for playing with friends or family. It’s accessible enough for kids but nostalgic and fun enough for older fans.

I have 19 Pros and 6 Cons, But basically A lot of my cons are more personal flavor and can be condensed to "I like where the games Basics are I just wish it had MORE to it." 

Played it in my child hood. Continued to replay for like 10 years after every summer on my HD tv (Yes even with bad pixelation from wrong formatting). So glad it was remastered. So glad they added a 4th game. I'm so excited to play the 4th.  Truly, one of the most perfect dungeon crawlers I've ever played. I have not found another game that satisfies me like G.U does... when I get to the bottom floor of a dungeon to get that Gott statue, gosh darn it, I love collecting things. I really wish it was indeed an Online MMO (I mean with Weekly events and a lot more rare items and stuff). I am probably a Male version of Mistral mixed with Elks personality...For any .hack fans....now you know what I am like. I do so love collecting rare items.

Nostalgia and Love for the Series put aside,

My Major Pros(may not be a pro to you)
-Dungeon Crawler
-Friendship meter with Characters
-Some choice interactions(Basiclly good or bad choices)
-Multiple things to collect/break inside the dungeons)
-Can be grindy but if you know what you're doing its not.
-All your work can be transfered to the next Game
-very cool story, like-able characters(and some we don't like....Lookin' at you Piros...)

Cool Pro features: 
-Main character can swap between weapons(twin blade, broad sword, scythe etc)
-Equipment can be customized with items which add perks (Like +10% EXP or Elemental attacks etc)
-Lucky Animals, in dungeons if you can catch it grant you Items, buffs or other cool things.
-There's small events that randomly happen, Like finding a PVP battle where you save a npc from being PKed
-You get to upgrade your guild, and Sort of Run your shop. 
-You get a motor bike to upgrade and use in dungeons and out. 
-You can trade items with NPC characters directly
-Really cool battle system, custamizable abilities and Equally cool Data drain Battles
-You get to interact with a computer desktop to read mail and customize it.
-Theres a card game to play on your desktop.
-theres forums and youtube like videos to browse through for Lore and information.
-Save data going to the next game with your Money, items, etc

Cons:
-Honestly, The traps that are in the dungeons are few and far between, and they are really not hard to evade. Kinda wish there were some more adventure like obsticles. Like climbing ladders or ropes. Or simply finding a stone lost somewhere that you use to open doors. Or even swinging blades in halls you need to dodge. Need some More of that, more frequently.

- Surprises. In the dungeons I wish there were surprises like Finding a room with 3 chests and a npc thats like Choose 1 and it could be good or they could knock you out and steal an item from you. Or a Room that  had a few npcs with an issue. Like Loosing their weapons so you need to go find them. Kinda like mini quests that just randomly appear in a dungeon.   (There's a few surprise events like the PVP battle or finding some healers that heal you. But I think It needs more then that. I think the PVP battles is on the right track. Now they just Need More event types stuff.
