I tried, and I mean REALLY tried to like Arkham City. 

I bought this game in 2017 shortly after finishing Arkham Asylum, thinking as I'd enjoyed it enough, City would surely be even better as most seem to hold it up as the best in the series.

Since then it has taken me 3 attempts to finally actually finish the game, after starting from 0% in 2017, 2018, and finally now in 2022. I find it difficult to put exactly into words what it is that makes City so uninteresting to me compared to Asylum, but for whatever reason I always felt horribly bored playing. Admittedly, this resulted in my mostly playing through the game whilst in voice calls - which I'm sure contributed at least a little to furthering my lack of attention. review_text:
I thought I'd give it a try since everyone raves about it. And while it seems like it might be enjoyable, I'm hugely turned off by the horror genre lighting. I'm stumbling around in the dark getting killed by stuff I can't see, shooting anytime my target reticle turns red, caught in some kind of underwater maze? So confusing, thankfully the ammo and health items glow.

I like so many things in this game, and I tried the remastered version first and have the same primary graphics complaint in both versions. I cant see well in this game. to play i turn the brightness up (if it lets me, remastered does not) and everything turns grey instead of black. 

so i get the story that this underwater civilization goes mad for the same stuff you start collecting to give super powers, that part is cool. what i dont get is why this underwater civilization doesnt have more advanced lighting. what i mean specifically here, if these people, before they went crazy, built such a great city, why dont they have light bulbs over 25 watts? thats where this game loses me. immersion is cool, eye strain is not.

other notes: the lower framerate animations are funny in this game, like so much worse than halo combat evolved, but funny. all quality settings at max and the textures, especially character model textures, look kinda like quake era. why dont these people have faces? other parts of this game look great, sprites and shaders in particular, and the design choices on the object models (just not the textures). its just really hard to take this game seriously, they try to force a horror genra game on you with the lighting style (despite the fact that i get less eyestrain from actual horror games), then they muck it up with blocky textures, yet still try to win you over with shader effects.

I found a sweetfx or reshade for either the original version or the remastered, i dont recall and have neither installed currently. With proper reshade/sweetfx the lighting issues are mostly resolved. there is an unusual forced darkness or negative light effect that makes it hard to dial in the settings. 

its iconic, and that's the only reason i might recommend this game.

review_text:
This is a fun game. It has an, IMO, excellent story that's deeper than you would imagine given the art style. Combat feels fast and the gun play feels very satisfying. This is a loot and character progression driven title, Think a diablo like ARPG. There are some pretty cool weapons that really change up the way you play your character however, the rest of the gear seems a bit lack luster by comparison, with most often just providing stats. 
  
  Relic Hunters Legend packs a ton of secrets and puzzles for you to find and overcome. The game will see you hunting down different pieces to build relics and some of these relics provide very interesting game play advantages. The game really doesn't hold your hand with these hunts, either, there is a vague clue given for each relic part and it's up to you to figure out where you need to go, that is VERY refreshing in the current state of video games.

  The combat feels very smooth, the controls can feel a bit slippery at first and there is no dedicated jump key, but once you get used to that you'll be flying around the screen zapping baddies with you arsenal of weapons and character skills. Each of the playable characters feels unique and fill their own niche with the best and most powerful hunter being being Seven (fight me? lol).

  The sound is good, it gets a little repetitive at times with the same background music playing during a lot of the stages, but it's not that bad. Enemy design is pretty good and there is a fairly large host of different enemies that all do different things. 

  Balance in the game seems a bit off, I mean difficulty balance. It seems as though the game is very focused on grouping up because when you go from story to hard, the enemies hit WAY harder and have a lot of health. You really have to have your gear upgraded, which is a MASSIVE grind guys. If you are looking for a mostly single-player game with a smooth difficulty curve and lower gear grind, keep these points in mind.

  Overall, this game is great. I would have loved to have an AI bot companion of some kind for the solo gamers like myself and a little less of a material and currency grind for the lower levels in the game, but can still easily recommend this one to twin-stick looter shooter fans.

review_text:
I'll keep this as short as possible;

One of my favourite anime show is Rurouni Kenshin (or Samurai X as I've learned what it's called in the west). For some reason I kept thinking about the show frequently while I was playing the game. The era which the game takes place, music, story,...basically everything was perfect in my opinion. I guess it gave me similar vibes?

The game is amazingly as historically accurate as it can be. Well, obviously it is not but you learn a lot about the last years of Edo/Tokugawa period and how Meiji Period came to the scene. Information regarding to the historical figures (all of the LI's basically) are also accurate -of course not regarding the ones related to the story. 

You have 12 LI's to choose from. While the prologue of the story is the same for every route, every LI's story is remarkably different from the other. There is a main story going on and it too is mainly the same but it goes a bit differently in each route. It's like LI's are the different players in this story and you see the big picture from their and MC's perspective. The main event is there and you play a different role and although some things change, main thing doesn't. (Yeah, it may not make much sense but I don't know how to explain it better) 

Don't expect heavy & steamy love scenes. The romance is quite light all over. It is not a bad thing though, in fact, it was quite refreshing to play a game where everyone doesn't try to get into each others pants.

Each route has a good, bad and unrequited love ending. Also each chapter before the last one has an ending which is "game over" You have to see ALL to unlock all achievements so check how to "skip read" lol. 

The MC is the one of best among the otome games I've played. She is not a total pushover or naive girl you usually see in these type of games. She is not very strong (the reason is explained a bit in Edo Blossoms) or particularly clever but she is not annoyingly dumb which is a huge plus for me. She doesn't fall for the LI's because "they made her heart flutter with the smoulder" You can relate to her a bit at least. 

CG's, character designs and soundtrack are very good. 

Additional info: There are several Hakuoki anime shows & movies. I haven't watched them so I cannot sat which order you should watch or which one to watch. But one thing I know is that Hijikata Toshiro is the canon LI in those. It kind of makes sense even in the games when you think about it.

To sum up; probably the best otome I've ever played to this date (if I said "the best" for another, well it has been replaced with Hakuoki series) If you like otome games, this one and Edo Blossoms is definitely a "must play" for you.

review_text:
I got this game for free from a cereal box many years ago, and it was one of the first PC games I ever played, so it was cool to revisit the game again after all these years. There are lots of aspects of this game that do feel quite old, but it's still quite fun.

You're given a set of different scenarios and maps, and asked to build a profitable theme park by placing paths, stalls, decorations, and rides. it's quite entertaining to go from a large empty plot of land to a bustling theme park filled with hundreds of guests. It's a good thing it's so entertaining to watch though, as there tends to be a lot of waiting in this game, as you often run out of money and must wait for the park to make enough money back to build the next large ride. Additionally, although there's a good variety of different maps and scenarios which present different challenges, building a park tends to be pretty similar each time, so the game starts to feel quite repetitive after a while.

The game uses an isometric view, which gives it that iconic look you're probably familiar with, and it works fine most of the time, but it can be annoying to try and see things sometimes, as foliage or rides often get in the way. Things tend to be fairly small as well, which also makes things a bit hard to see. The UI also uses windows for everything, which makes it feel quite old, and can make keeping things organized a bit of a nightmare sometimes. Once you adjust the settings and controls to your liking and get used to everything, it's not too bad though.

If you do end up getting this game, I'd highly recommend checking out [url=openrct2.org/]OpenRCT2[/url], an open-source re-implementation of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 that adds new features and fixes bugs, and helps the game feel not quite as old.  I didn't run into any bugs while playing game and it ran fairly well, which was likely due to the fixes made by OpenRCT2. review_text:
I got this game for 99 cents, which is good, because if I paid full price for it, I'd be angry. And the worst part about it is that the game had so much potential! I'm not against these kinds of stories. The Omen, The Exorcist, Rosemary's Baby, I own all three of them. Playing as Damien (I mean Lucius) should have been great!

And for a while it was. The first few kills really did work, and I thought I got this game at a bargain. Loved the gore, too.

Then it started sucking. Not the story. That part is good all around. I really enjoyed that aspect of it. And for a game like this, the visuals aren't terrible either. No, I'm talking about the quests themselves. 

Now, I'm not against difficult games. Far from it. But they sprinted across the line between difficult and next to impossible unless you know what to do next. For the majority of them, really. I appreciated the Ouiji board (first and last time I'll ever say that) for giving me the much needed clues to get a rough idea, but once I found my next victim, the game would basically go "okay, kid, here's a giant mansion and a crappy map to get you through it. Go find this obscure item that you would have no reason to go looking for. Combine it with this other obscure item, then follow these contrived steps to get the kill. 

Now, this might have worked a little better if there were multiple ways to get a kill. And if the house were a little smaller. Not a lot, but just a touch. Then when you have no idea what to do, you don't have to spend half an hour looking through every room and drawer and hope you stumble across the next item. But nope, it's "do this, then this, then this, then this."

Again, I'm not saying that I want the game to be easy. But I also don't want it so difficult that it's contrived. 

But I was willing to overlook all of that for the story. It really was interesting. Until...

A game-breaking glitch. 

*sigh*

So in one chapter, you have to kill a guy by using your fire powers to burn him to death. Like most video game bosses, he takes three hits. I fought him about five times, and this is how it went: 1. It worked fine, I just didn't have my strategy down. Fair enough. 2. I hit him, then he... disappears. You're in a small dungeon, so there's no place to hide. He just vanished, forcing me to re-start. 3. He's immune to your fire. 4. He's immune to fire. 5. He's immune to fire. 

At first I thought "hey, I'm just missing. I mean, not sure how I can miss with a fireball bigger than I am, but whatever." But repeatedly hitting him (in an area where the crosses were upside-down, mind you) with massive fireballs at point-blank range and not giving him a scratch lets me know, hey, this game is broken. 

I kinda want my 99 cents back. Difficulty bordering on being too contrived I can handle. It's irritating, but I can handle it. And they don't do it all the time. Sometimes you can figure it out with what they give you. But oftentimes I'd look up the solution, expecting to see something that made me go "oh, I just missed that. Silly me" and instead getting "why on Earth would that be the next thing I do?"

As a final note, something that amuses me about this game: the upside-down cross. I know it's a popular devil image and whatnot, but ironically so. It's supposed to be a symbol of defiance, but, if you read the history of it, it's actually a symbol of deep reverence and respect towards Jesus. The apostle Peter demanded to be crucified that way, as he didn't feel worthy of dying the same way his lord did. Just a funny note. I know symbols change and all that, but yeah.

So overall, I'd give this game a 5/10. 5 for a great idea, decent visuals, good gore, some creativity, an a nice story, and -5 for... pretty much everything else.

Honestly, not that great of an experience despite desperately wanting to like it after having seen it a bunch on YT and the like.

The "roguelite" elements of it are very evidently a complete afterthought and were probably only tossed in in the last quarter of pre-release development. Your campaign protagonist and team start out generally useless, but even upgrading your protag's stats between runs and buying new abilities and this and that just do not feel that impactful. "Upgrades" very seldom feel like they actually do anything of value a lot of the time, especially when the AI doesn't tend to make many mistakes on account of being AI. They will see what you're trying to do and they will make the objectively correct play to counter it without fail, and a lot of the time that boils down to either being designed to have absurd stats in some category to brute force you or an ability that says "You are no longer allowed to play the game", or some mix of those.

The "Princess" team, despite overall being the second easiest team to beat after the Referee team from the end of the first act, is in my experience the absolute worst of the first two acts hands down. You will spend 95% of the game trying to make a play and having some ugly pink fatass FART on you and you just go flying to the other side of the ice, usually into one of their players who will check you. It's really just a reaction speed test to see if you can pass after seeing that FART CLOUD. Are we 10 years old again? Are fart jokes still funny?

Juvenile jokes aside, farting at the very least isn't one of the many AI abilities they aggressively use off cooldown to tell you "I hate you, fuck off and give me that puck. You aren't supposed to be playing", which is in my eyes one of the worst possible design choices they could have made. A million and one ways to say "Stop playing for a sec real quick, K?" with your biggest counter just being to aggressively pass between players and pray that there's no interception and that the guy you're passing to doesn't promptly eat shit too. Sure would be nice if you could buff defense too, instead of the asinine accuracy stat. But oh, I guess you can if you want to move at a snail's pace, which is genuinely just the worst choice you can make because you simply won't be able to apply enough pressure anymore to make up for the fact that:

Your goalie is a vegetable. A genuine vegetable. He will stand 8 feet out from his crease and just stare as the opposing team speeds towards him with the puck, making token gestures of resistance as they go around either of his sides and earn seemingly scripted goals. You let the other team take the puck to your goal, thus you are now on a timer to outdo them or restart. Sure would be nice if their goaltender seemingly never made the same mistakes yours did, more actively sticking opposing players and HUGGING that net like it was his momma. Ironically the most reliable way I've found to score isn't to shoot at all, but to stick my entire body into their goalie's arms and just -pass- the puck into their net right before he topples me like a jenga tower. I have no idea why that works, but the goalies seemingly have no idea how to deal with that and as such I try to make it a habit not to use it. 
Despite the game frequently telling me to stop playing.
But hey, I think I'm going to listen to the game. After nearly 2 hours of being told to stop playing? I think I'll do just that. Pass me that $20 back, devs. :)

review_text:
Honestly, i wouldn't recommend. It's supposed to be a hitman-esque game, with a touch of "devil child" horror. But the truth is that the hitman component is just too basic. You kill 20 people throughout the game. Pretty much each person gets its own chapter. You have to go by the script. You cannot just kill anybody you want and there are no alternative solutions. You have to kill exactly how the game wants it and when the game wants you to kill. The hitman gameplay is basically boils down to just finding out that exact set of actions you need to take in order to kill the target. But thing about hitman games is that they always offered multiple solutions to you, each with varying level of difficulty and reward. Lucius on other hand is painfully linear. In fact, you get a total of 4 abilities at the end of the game, but you pretty much only allowed to use them when the game wants you to.

The second problem is in the narrative. Since this is an indie company, the game just fails at presenting the game's story to its full extent. I am talking about animations, facial expression, graphics, and so on. Also, to be honest, even with all those issues polished out, the game also has another issue with the dialog. The characters just don't have enough to say. They run out of unique lines very quickly. Pretty much everytime you pass them by, they will be repeating the same lines all over again. It becomes annoying at some point.

Also, the controls could have used a bit of work. You get telekinesis at some point, and in order to move object away or towards you, you need to hold down both left and right mouse buttons. Then by moving the mouse, you move it towards or away from you, but the sensetivity is just off the charts.

Also, Lucius body prevents you from viewing everything in front of you. Typically, in 3rd person games, the character is a bit to the left or right, and sometimes the game even allows you to switch the view from one "shoulder" to another. That's the way its supposed to be. In Lucius, he is standing right in the center, and personally, i had to zoom out a lot to feel comfortable playing. 

The game has a very cool concept, but it just wasn't brought to its full potential really.

A very Gooey-Bridge building puzzle game

The game involves you connecting goo-balls together to help them escape the stage. The concept has been done before but instead of making bridges with materials, you're making bridges with different types of goo-ball to traverse the various environments. Each chapter has a different setting each with a reason the goo-balls needs to saved. Almost each type of goo-ball has a different ability to help build your goo-made bridge. The soundtrack includes calm and soothing tracks while also having dark and creepy tracks for the more industrial stages. It is a shame it isn't purchasable on steam.

Overall, World of Goo is a creative change from the normal bridge building games. The Plot, Soundtrack and the Setting give the game a dark feel but with moments of success with saving the goo-balls from being turned into products.

review_text:
I had 250 hours in this game on the US release, playing via the Windows Store here in the UK long before it officially came to the EU. At the start, it felt like a true sequel to Phantasy Star Online and Phantasy Star Universe. The gameplay was fun, the setting familiar, and for a brief moment, it looked like SEGA understood what made the older games special.

I was a huge fan of PSO1 and PSU—despite having nearly zero interest in anime or traditional JRPGs (I like a few select animes and jRPG games) What drew me in wasn’t flashy visuals or cliché character tropes, but the grounded, lonely sci-fi atmosphere. Those games had a sense of mystery, isolation, and quiet discovery. Storytelling came through ruins, data logs, and strange anomalies that made the world feel lived-in and eerie. They respected the player's intelligence and let the environment tell the tale. It was subtle, immersive, and truly unique for its time.

Then came PSO2, and it all went downhill.

Somewhere along the line, SEGA decided to cater almost entirely to the weeb crowd. I don't mean your average anime enjoyer, i mean the other kind. The game quickly devolved into a fanservice circus—anime girls in absurdly skimpy outfits, physics-defying "milkers," and an endless flood of immersion-breaking cosmetics that have no place in a sci-fi setting. Every corner of the game became infected with over-the-top cringe, and the atmosphere that once set this series apart was drowned out by loud, flashy nonsense and tone-deaf character spam.

The community? Just take one look at the Steam hub or any social space in-game—it's wall-to-wall gooner bait and terminally online degeneracy. It's not just disappointing; it's embarrassing. Again, its not standard anime tropes they have focused on as i can kinda get into that. They've gone so far into the gooner side of weeb culture its beyond saving. That's whats ruining the game. 

SEGA took a franchise that once stood proudly apart from typical JRPG fluff and sacrificed it for shallow appeal and monetised cosplay. They killed what was once my first MMO experience on the Dreamcast, and what could have been a masterpiece successor became a gaudy mess. PSO2 might still have decent combat and core mechanics buried somewhere underneath, but it's completely unrecognisable as a Phantasy Star game in spirit.

review_text:
There's a lot of good with GTTOD but also a lot more of bad.

To start off with, the pros:

- The game is beautiful. It looks straight out of TRON or whatever other synthwave/outlast wet dream you can think of.
- The sound design is stellar. All of the guns that I've played around with so far are beautifully designed from shooting to reloading.
- The animations are amazing and easily some of the best in the industry. I'm especially fond of the pistol, especially the draw animation.
- The time slowdown feels orgasmic. It's so fun to use.

Onto the cons:

- Some parts of the game are so, so, so slow. For instance, there's one objective where you have to kill a certain number of enemies while inside an arena to build the door. The problem is that the enemies barely come and you can't exit the arena to search for them. 
- It's pretty demanding. I was able to run it fine but lower-end systems are gonna feel the burn.
- There's not a lot of enemies. There's drones, suicide bombers, enemies with shields, enemies with swords, projectile throwers, fodder, and... that's it, really. Compared to other shoot-em-ups like ULTRAKILL or -- dare I say it -- DOOM Eternal there's a lot to be desired.
- There's barely any tutorials. You get taught how to wallrun and climb on monkey bars and that's really it. I didn't know about the time stop or grenade buttons until I accidentally pressed them in my first or second run.
- You're forced to start at a bad level with a stupid end goal every time you play.
- Enemies feel unfair and hit you instantly even in time slowdown.
- Movement can feel weird and janky and it can be hard to get onto walls or platforms.

review_text:
Game is fine. But it is a letdown in many ways.

Difficulty: Easy. very easy. Controls are lenient. You can easily miss jumps and go wrong ways and still hold combos. Died a couple times to weird game situations (not bugs).
The music is good. Not great like the Jet Set Radio games. But they would get stuck in my head and they were nice. The Hideki Naganuma are actually the only ones I don't care for. The music is more tame in multiple ways, less punk, more mainstream. Less exciting, more chill.
Game has many mechanics added to it that would be great to see in the previous games. No complaints there really. Maybe just that they make one so powerful that there is not much risk/excitement when playing.
Basically all the characters are super lame. The one I can think of is cool in a sensei kind of way, not a punk kind of way.
The levels are entirely forgettable. Every stage is walk around, spray some graffiti, then do some menial tutorials disguised as competing with other crews. The level design in terms of riding around and doing cool lines, felt lame to me. It feels like there are big obvious lines that you take, nothing really on the side.
The story is down to earth in this game relative to the zaniness of the Jet Set Radio games. But the zaniness meshed well with the punk nature of the Jet Set Radio Games. With this game, the combination of down to earth + lame characters + being not punk, doesn't work, and the story feels both flat and faux.
The "genre" now has skateboards and BMX which is cool, but it exposes one of the most egregious sins of this game: there are not many tricks. Even worse, characters do not have unique tricks! This may sound unimportant, but in Jet Set Radio Future, spamming the trick buttons looked nice and felt nice. In this game, the tricks are kind of cool, but there are only the few tricks that you are stuck with, and get old quickly. One used to be able to play a different character to change things up. Not so here.
The only thing that differentiates characters is which annoying voice you choose to hear. No stats, and as told above, the tricks don't change.

If this game added more tricks, tricks per character, and added a fun post-game, this game would be good enough for me to recommend. But it feels like a lame story that gave me no emotion and left me with no post game to play with.
If one didn't play the Jet Set Radio games, this game will be amusing, but nothing special nor impactful. But it is a moist version of the Jet Set Radio games, and feels incomplete/rushed out. You should play Jet Set Radio Future instead. Jet Set Radio is cool, but it is pretty old and janky.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 is a truly incredible and unique experience. It's not for everyone, in fact I would go so far as to say it's not for most people. But if you're intrigued enough to read reviews, it may just be for you. Everything I'm about to say applies to the game's intended and hardest difficulty, which I recommend you play on.
 Here's why this game is genius: the goal of most games is to be fun and satisfying for the player. All their systems are tailored to achieve that. The goal of this game is to produce a state of stress, anxiety, and desperation in the player -*but also a sense of hope, a sense that you can win.* All its systems are finely tuned to enable you to stay on top of the various things dragging you down (hunger, lack of time, exhaustion) - but only by the skin of your teeth. As you come to understand it more, you realize that the game, despite going to great lengths to seem unfair, is in fact very fair - it always gives you access to the things you need to survive and win, as long as you pay attention and plan carefully. But your life in the game is never easy, you always have tough choices to make, and relief is only ever temporary. This combination is what makes it so engaging - not to speak about the story, world and characters, which are all wonderfully weird and vivid. 
Only about 7% of players have the achievement for beating the game on its intended difficulty. Clearly, these design principles don't click for everybody. But if or when they do, this game becomes the most mesmerizing and compelling game out there.

review_text:
Scorn is a pretty unique experience. The bleak and hostile world that you explore is art direction at its finest. It showcases a very depressing and gruesome imagery of a world that is clearly on the brink of collapse just by observing its surroundings. One of the standout features to me at least is the fact that the entire game is seamless. Once you start first chapter and later the final chapter, you won't encounter a single loading screen at all. The only drawback to this is that you'll encounter some stuttering since the game is rendering new environments as you progress. As for the soundtrack, it helps amplify the experience with its ambiance and eeriness. It further highlights Scorn's tone and visuals to a T. So that alone, Scorn wins in the audio and visual department.

The story for Scorn if you can call it that, doesn't really lead you in on any details. This is mainly due to the fact that you get no exposition, no narrations, or any context for what is going on. All you know is that you wake up and you're on way to your objective. The rest is all left to the world building, the journey, and what you take from it. This leaves Scorn's story up for interpretation and open discussion which in my opinion works well.

In fact, the gameplay itself is minimal too with the information such as your health and ammo only being shown when you have your weapon drawn or how many healing items you have by looking down at your view model. While it adds to the immersion, it goes overkill with the fact that there are some puzzles in the game that are annoyingly difficult to figure out. Then there's the combat which is just ok. Now granted, most encounters can be avoided so you wouldn't even have to engage, but sometimes you are forced into combat since some of the battles with the creatures are in corridors where avoidance really isn't an option. Plus fighting the same enemy type over and over again gets real tedious.

Thankfully once you get through the worst, Scorn gets kicking into high gear towards the end which you need to see for yourself if you haven't already. Now the campaign is very short and there's no bonus content whatsoever. My hours and 100% achievements are proof of that. And while normally there would be cause for complaints for this, I think it works in the game's favor since:

A: Combat is annoyingly tedious and repetitive, 
B: You've just finished a bunch of frustratingly long puzzles do you really want to spend another 30 minutes on another one?

So really, the game ends right before Scorn's shtick gets stale and that's honestly the best way to finish it. 
Would I recommend Scorn? Absolutely.  It's a game you should play at least once... But it is not for everyone. Just be prepared for some of the hard knocks you'll face in its runtime. Also $40 is pretty high considering the campaign's length so grab it while it's on sale. 

TL;DR
Scorn is a masterclass in art direction, world building, and it's soundtrack. The combat is meh and puzzles can be cryptic. It's not that long, but overall a solid experience.

review_text:
Quite fun, very similar to Dwarf Fortress and Rimworld, some similarities with Creeper World 2/3. Some aspects of the game are much more intuitive and less frustrating compared to those two though (like "maintain" amount orders being built in), well done with that. The graphics are a considerable amount better, definitely more consistent (or existent, lol).

On the negative sides:

* The building (upgrade) queue seems like too much micromanagement. If I don't bump every upgrade to the top at least once, then they never seem to get done in a reasonable amount of time. 

* Villagers seem to not like multitasking, so proper assignment is always tedious. If you ain't got nothing to bottle, why not give a helping hand to water masters? Seems like an artificial difficulty that just distracts from main gameplay.

* Builders are in general super inefficient and slow, the spells given are a relatively mandatory addition. Finished buildings in the same queue as upgrades/new ones does get very very cluttered at some point. A separate queue for repairing/restocking would be nice.

* There's also no way to lock gates, it's very annoying. 

The final and dealbreaker issue for me is that you can't win the game in any remotely hostile gamemode, the monsters at some point are only challenged by your finger. God walls? As strong as American homes. Because of this I probably won't bother playing the game for too long, knowing I'll lose (or lack anything to fight) makes it lose the charm.

UPDATE:
When you do manage to push corruption back until the point that you've basically defeated them, then before the last night their last tiles disappear you're in for an unfair surprise. The game ramps up the difficulty tenfold (not exaggerating) meaning basically no villager defenses are going to be sufficient. They're one-shotting the walls, your golems and do so en masse. 

I managed to cause a bottleneck with god walls (those also get destroyed in one hit if they block) and I could hold down lightning and the amount of dead enemies just refueled the bar for an entire night. Still more than enough enemies survived to destroy ten maxed-out crystal (and a few stone golem) spawners, three artillery towers and all the villagers.

All that while the previous night the enemies didn't leave their corner. I'd understand if it were a gradual ramp up, but that was cheating. Like Mario Kart's blue missile or Civilization's AIs being set to higher levels, but absolutely no practical tools against.

So not only are your villagers very unintelligent, the enemy gets to cheat.

review_text:
So much yes. Ive written a review for this game prior but after playing off and on for the last few years of owning this game I saw that review button and wanted to re-contribute. 

Playing this game is a great experience overall and I would recommend this game a million times to anyone.
Rating: 10/10

The Art (OMG the art is so great):
This game has the most beautiful pixel art that makes the world seem really alive. almost everywhere you see is satisfying eye candy. Almost everything in the game that isn't an inanimate object has animations. People, animals, and monsters all have unique animations for most actions, rain collectors have animated rain pooling into the funnels, rain washes off the building roofs. There are so many beautifully animated particle affects that most items or objects emit including the UI itself! Weather/environmental effects really pull you into the world what with clouds casting shadows and rain making you feel chilly in the winter/fall. Literally at any time, just zoom into your village and look at everything and you can see how much work the creator put into the art. 

The Gameplay:
When playing the game it takes your usual top-down town simulator approach and has you making resource harvesting/refining buildings and houses to feed your people and keep them out of the rain. You are essentially a god that can cast spells to do all kinds of useful actions. These spells can range from calling down lightning strikes to summoning work golems or even blessing your pregnant villagers to create demigod children with improved stats (some spells you cant do unless you have enough villagers since they increase your mana)! You start off by choosing any area on the overworld map that you want to start your empire from and then over time you can migrate villagers from that map tile to the next, slowly making a chain of kingdoms each having their own history and layout. Watch out though, you have to do all of this while trying to defend against the ever growing threat of the corruption on each map and the monster waves that spawn from there every night.

Game Mechanics:
I cant begin to tell you how many hidden and unique game mechanics this game has. The villagers all live their own lives and do their own tasks while every villager, animal and monster has their own XP bar, stats and inventory. Monsters build evil buildings in the corruption that can increase the number of spawned monsters and when you fight back the corruption (it can be done but its so hard) every tile that gets removed can spawn more monsters even during the day! For a 2d top down game you will be pleasantly surprised that the environment can be manipulated in many ways as long as you have the spellpower or the villagers with the proper jobs to do it. When playing you will find that you can build a trade center to buy and sell resources/equipment but something it doesn't outright tell you is that when you sell stuff in one village the store in another village will let you buy the stuff you just sold (quick way to move stuff from one side of the map to another). Things like this are constantly surprising me and with the new updates being added I am sure there will be more cool ideas to try to improve your gameplay.

Community content:
Unfortunately there is a severe lack of Fan content for this game so it suffers greatly when it comes to looking up specific game play mechanic tutorials or finding neat challenges to try. If the community had more content creators making gameplay mechanic tutorials or fun game play challenges I think it would be way better received by newcomers. There is some great content though so one or 2 videos will basically show you how to effectively play the game so don't despair!

Closing thoughts:
At first I suggest new players look at a couple gameplay videos to get an idea of the way of things but as you play you will definitely notice when things are and aren't working in your village as the game has many useful an intuitive stat/event tools built in game to help manage everything efficiently. I have spent countless hours managing my towns, choosing what jobs villagers should be hired to, upgrading the different resource collection systems you can make, designing/upgrading defenses and managing the waves of monsters that attack most nights. Many, many nights I've realized it was way late and had to go to bed or I wouldn't get enough sleep because I am always needing to prepare for the next nights defence or fix an issue that popped up due to overpopulation or some random event. I will continue to play this game for a very long time and I suggest anyone who is curious and likes pixel art or town simulator games to give it a try!

review_text:
As entertaining as this game is, it's also terrible. This game deserves a good watch where someone else plays it, but you gain literally nothing as a player of it. 

Visually this game's serviceable and generally it's nice to look at. The mansion's a bit of an unintuitive maze, but over time you'll get to know it and used to it. 

The story's also very amusing and cheesy. That's the main reason to even consume this game. Being the child of the Devil and causing mayhem's always fun. 

But as to the gameplay... it's terrible. Honestly. This is a linear puzzle game with bad puzzles and a bad sense of linearity. Nonsensical puzzle solutions like not being able to fill cups with water or bowls with water, but instead only being able to use a specific sink and a specific bottle in the right order. Or instead of knowing who to kill, you have to walk around the house, trying to trigger a script to understand who the game decided to graciously let you kill.

I usually write more about the game I review, but it really deserves nothing more. Moon-logic puzzles, generally bad gameplay and sometimes broken solutions. 

Go to Youtube and watch someone's full playthrough of the game and you'll not only enjoy it more, you'll also waste less time and money. Usually a game has some value in being an actual game, but this one just doesn't.

If you came here looking for something to scratch the Dead Space itch (like I did), you'll be sorely disappointed. It's an entirely different game with an entirely different vibe.

Right from the start of the game unless you're being swarmed by multiple enemies at once, you rarely feel like you're in any real danger, which certainly takes away from the "survival horror" tag this game has. That being said, if you're a sci-fi or walking sim fan and just want to jump into a cool sci-fi environment and experience the story, I'd recommend it on a deep sale. Some games definitely are worth every penny at this price tag, but The Callisto Protocol is not one of them. I spent $16 CAD and I kind of feel like that might have even been a little steep.

review_text:
Be careful with this game. It is, fundamentally, a good game. The stories are incredible and voluminous after 15 years of development and writing. It's well structured to suck you into an online world of Star Trek that is deep and engaging. The new owners, DECA, are responsive to the players and seem to be competent in addressing issues. There are moments in this game, even now, after all this time, that take my breath away.

Here comes the but...

It is rapaciously, avariciously monetized on a scale that would make a Ferengi blush with embarrassment. The lockbox and acquisition mechanics are designed to be addictive and predatory. The value of what you'd need to break into ingame (elite) content *starts* at around $300 USD. DPS chasers spend thousands. The most efficient grind rate I've been able to achieve to harvest these resources (dilithium and energy credits) works out to be about $.75 an hour, and that's after weeks of grinding to even get to where you can do that (admiralty system access, enough ships in your fleet, etc.). Moreover, to do this at scale (as in more than $.26 per day), you'll need multiple characters combining resources.

Do you *need* to run elite content to enjoy this game? Certainly not. Can you enjoy this game fully in F2P mode? Absolutely. But I don't know anyone who has. You need to understand that you'll be jumping into task force operations where whales are absolutely obliterating the enemy in seconds. You won't even know why. There are lockboxes, annual bundle sales that run north of $100 USD, and the infamous Mudd's market. If (when) you must buy something, wait for a zen charge bonus to buy the zen, and only buy the item on sale.

If you're prepared to deal with this level of monetization, then you'll find STO to be a very full, engaging, and enjoyable experience.

review_text:
The core idea of Yakuza 5, four parts in four different cities, along with a whole slew of new minigames easily made it the most ambitious game in the series up to that point. In addition to all that, the game received a large overhaul in the areas of lighting and gameplay. It still feels pretty similar to Yakuza 4, but you also start to see the beginnings of 0 - it is more or less a halfway point. The lighting alone really gives the game a face-lift that makes it resemble what would later be 0 more than any of the previous titles. It also includes some new gameplay mechanics in combat: the additions of enemy reinforcements, enemies that run away and crowds that back up as you approach, opening the combat area up a little more. It also introduced Climax Heat Actions and AppStims that newcomers to the franchise may recognize from the Kiwami games (though there the former works more like red heat from Y3-4). A more unfortunate change to the gameplay is that weapons now have requirements to equip them; you increase your weapon ability by using weapons you pick up. Possibly the worst change of all, though, is how they handle Premium Adventure and NG+ in this entry. Unlike every mainline entry before and after, you cannot create clear data in Premium Adventure. This means that if you do NG+, nothing you do in Premium Adventure will matter for it. This idiotic system premiered in Kurohyou: Ryu Ga Gotoku Shinsen for the PSP and went on to be in the original Ishin release (but fixed for the remake). 

The music in Yakuza 5 is some of the best in the series up to this point with some truly great tracks that hype you up for the action and make the emotional moments even more memorable. The substories as well overall are particularly strong, though, unfortunately, these don't escape the iffy issues that the series sometimes falls into and in my opinion, they are particularly bad here as well being more prolonged than usual such as an entire substory about a mixer where the entire joke is “haha they're ugly aren't they” and another substory where the joke is essentially that they're fat. There's also a substory that's rather copaganda with an ending that's somewhat jarring. 

Another thing that really stood out to me is the sheer variety - and not only in terms of the four cities. It seemed to me the NPCs had more variety to them, between the random civilians to enemies. There's also quite a few unique locations in the main story and even substories. 

One negative thing about the game's story is that it has some fairly bad pacing problems. For the most part each individual part is fine but the end of each one is something of a cliffhanger and the plot is really put on hold to introduce each character’s storyline. However, the way the plot is laid out I'm not sure how they could have rectified this other than alternating characters every chapter or two and that could get messy fast with the amount of protagonists in this one. 

Part 1 starts off with… Kiryu? But why is he a taxi driver in Fukuoka? Why isn't he with Haruka? This game really likes its mysteries and you're hit with multiple right off the bat. Kiryu’s taxi minigames are very fun, especially when you start street racing to some really hype eurobeat. 

Part 2 is with Saejima and his part is… Decidedly rougher. His part doesn't really open up much at all until chapter 3 with his side story minigame and even then, he doesn't get his substories until chapter 4. The way his story is handled is baffling and really kills all momentum the plot had, unfortunately. The first two chapters are mainly cutscenes and dialogue but if you stick with it there is atleast good payoff on those chapters. Once things open up it becomes very enjoyable. 

Part 3 is very unique for the franchise - it features Haruka, now turned idol and has two different rhythm games and a multitude of other minigames as part of her career. It portrays some unfortunate truths about the idol industry that can be quite uncomfortable, particularly early on but I do think it’s important that they didn’t try to brush it under the rug. Partway through her part, Akiyama becomes playable, his story intertwining with that of Haruka’s and creating a really lovely dynamic for them. If Kiryu is her father, then Akiyama is like her uncle. New to this game for Akiyama’s moveset as well are some ridiculous juggling mechanics that allows him to do some Devil May Cry-esque float-y attacks. This part has the strongest set of characters in the game, in my opinion.

Part 4 features a new protagonist by the name of Tatsuo Shinada who is a broke ex-pro Baseball player turned nightlife journalist. He is a very charming and likable, down to earth guy even to the local bartenders of Kineicho, Nagoya. His moveset is very weapon oriented, with an unbreakable pipe that only does a little bit of damage. He later gets access to a master who will help increase weapon durability, as well. 

On the whole I enjoyed the story but unfortunately the story crumbles a bit at the end for me. The reveal of the final boss in particular feels like a massive asspull that actively made it worse for me.

and not only in terms of the four cities. it seemed to me the npcs had more variety to them, between the random civilians to enemies. there's also quite a few unique locations in the main story and even substories. one negative thing about the game's story is that it has some fairly bad pacing problems. for the most part each individual part is fine but the end of each one is something of a cliffhanger and the plot is really put on hold to introduce each character s storyline. however, the way the plot is laid out i'm not sure how they could have rectified this other than alternating characters every chapter or two and that could get messy fast with the amount of protagonists in this one. part 1 starts off with kiryu? but why is he a taxi driver in fukuoka? why isn't he with haruka? this game really likes its mysteries and you're hit with multiple right off the bat. kiryu s taxi minigames are very fun, especially when you start street racing to some really hype eurobeat. part 2 is with saejima and his part is decidedly rougher. his part doesn't really open up much at all until chapter 3 with his side story minigame and even then, he doesn't get his substories until chapter 4. the way his story is handled is baffling and really kills all momentum the plot had, unfortunately. the first two chapters are mainly cutscenes and dialogue but if you stick with it there is atleast good payoff on those chapters. once things open up it becomes very enjoyable. part 3 is very unique for the franchise - it features haruka, now turned idol and has two different rhythm games and a multitude of other minigames as part of her career. it portrays some unfortunate truths about the idol industry that can be quite uncomfortable, particularly early on but i do think it s important that they didn t try to brush it under the rug. partway through her part, akiyama becomes playable, his story intertwining with that of haruka s and creating a really lovely dynamic for them. if kiryu is her father, then akiyama is like her uncle. new to this game for akiyama s moveset as well are some ridiculous juggling mechanics that allows him to do some devil may cry-esque float-y attacks. this part has the strongest set of characters in the game, in my opinion. part 4 features a new protagonist by the name of tatsuo shinada who is a broke ex-pro baseball player turned nightlife journalist. he is a very charming and likable, down to earth guy even to the local bartenders of kineicho, nagoya. his moveset is very weapon oriented, with an unbreakable pipe that only does a little bit of damage. he later gets access to a master who will help increase weapon durability, as well. on the whole i enjoyed the story but unfortunately the story crumbles a bit at the end for me. the reveal of the final boss in particular feels like a massive asspull that actively made it worse for me.

review_text:
I received the game as part of a new GPU purchase (RX 6700XT).

As mentioned by everyone else, the graphics and audio are sensational. It's just a shame that the rest of the game isn't up to the same standard. 

The game is basically a single corridor, narrative driven walking movie. It simply does not require much effort or thought to play. The combat is sorely lacking, it really is just dodge left, right, attack and repeat. The boss battles are the exact same as any other combat situation making them pointless. There really isn't any point to changing the difficulty due to nature of the game mechanics. The stealth sections are tedious and do not require any tactics. 

The game ran 'mostly' fine for me (R7 5700X + RX 6700XT) using FSR2 at 3K resolution, netted approx 45+ fps at ultra with Ray Tracing on medium. The game does still hitch from time to time for loading, noticeable on a few select doors. The audio did cut out from time to time and I had one complete crash to desktop. 

Saying that, I enjoyed the atmosphere, the story was okay and kept me playing, the few enemy types to face are interesting (but are not new to the genre). It is something I'm happy to have played, it's something I won't be playing again however. 

Saying that this game was a Dead Space successor really hurt it. It would have been better off being an 'Until Dawn' style interactive movie and then it would have been so much better and negated the poorly implemented game mechanics it has. This would have been more interesting with a branching storyline and multiple endings.

review_text:
Bear in mind, these are my first impressions based on just over an hour of play after beating about four to five missions.

The game appears to be linear with only one method to execute kills.  This can get very repetitive, very quickly.  Sometimes this method can be very difficult to figure out and although the game will drop hints here and there but sometimes they can be as ridiculously vague as simply "I should find a way to mess with him".

The house is designed in such a way that I can take easily five minutes to run from one side to the other, but if you ran in a straight line it would take less than twenty seconds -- I guess what I'm saying here is that there is a lot of running in circles involved.  The cryptic scribblings on the map don't help very much in guiding you around the house, unfortunately.

The chores can be quite tedius and at times, similarly to the main objectives, it can be impossibly difficult to figure out what to do.  I was given a chore as simple as "take out the trash" but no further hints were given.  Cue what was about 10 minutes of dull wandering as I fruitlessly searched high and low for the trash (eventually caving and looking it up), and another 10 minutes when I searched for the garbage bins.

The game lacks mouse control in the inventory menu which makes navigation through the most utilized menu feel awkward and clunky, no idea how that happened when the game was only released on PC.

Overall, this game did not capture my attention like I thought it would -- initially giving me hitman vibes, I came in very hopeful for an open, "do the objective however you'd like", kind of game.  As a result, I can only recommend this game on sale if you're feeling particularly curious.

review_text:
Game is officially out, and here is my final review.

Single player: The solo time trials are super fun and a great time kill that might make it worth buying the game. The controls are smooth, the maps are cleanly laid out, and there is enough variation to keep you busy for a while. It's not too hard to 3-star every map if you practice it a few times, but some are going to be easier than others. The game-play is designed around "cores" that give you different abilities that can influence your play-style on each map. Find which cores work best for you, and tackle the time trial.

Multiplayer-Golf Mode: The golf multiplayer is a pretty cool and is what you would think of when first coming into this game. Some of the maps can take forever to complete, but it's a pretty solid concept. This isn't the main play-style of the game, but it was still a cool addition.

Multiplayer-Golf Racing: This is the part of the game that warranted me not recommending it. I have complained, as have many others, that the match-making for the game is absolute garbage. You will continually get matched with players that are really outside your skill-level, and there isn't anything you can do about it. New players try out the game, get their ass kicked by people who have played this game non-stop for a year, then they give up after realizing how out-matched they are against most of the player base. A large portion of the ranked community isn't comprised of new players, they are legacy players that have been grinding the game for over a year. This is frustrating, because in my opinion this is going to be the death of the game and has been my biggest complaint. I really though after seeing what the ranked playlist devolved into pre-1.0 a change would be made, but I was wrong.

Community: The community for the game is a cringy cult, and I would avoid the discord server. Not only is it a very "clicky" community, they are very toxic and aggressive to people who don't play how they want. If I am in a game I know I am not going to win, you know what I do? I leave. The point of a game is to have fun, right? You know what isn't fun? Being forced to play out a 5-hole series against somebody that is going to inevitably beat you. Just leave, accept the penalty, and hope to god you get matched with more even competition. Most of these toxic people rage if you leave(and I even received a few...colorful DM's), because you refused to stay in a game. I don't get the anger, because they still get the win and the points.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 my beloved.

You get to play as Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and Shinada.
All five were absolutely fun to play as.  Each having their own side stories.

On my first playthrough alone, I clocked in 88 hours, which was far longer than the 67 hours I did on my first playthrough on Yakuza 0.  And honestly, the sidestories were probably the reason I stayed so long, just as it was for 0.

Kiryu's at a debatable strongest here, as your bounding throws are completely free, Tiger Drop actually negates all damage through the ENTIRE animation, both attack and rewind.  And, you can negate all damage yourself by just entering dragons rage.

Saejima's still fun to play as and is great for crowd work. However, Tsukimino has a slightly minor problem where the map is so constricted that you'll likely fight a guy right as you get out of one fight.  I didn't have a problem with that though.  And, you can take a picture of Miku in there.

Haruka gets to be playable in game, basing it off as rhythm as she's now an Idol.  Doing various dance battles and the like.  And her music soundtrack is great.  It's got the songs that I'm willing to listen to outside of the game, among other ones.

Akiyama, he's still fun to play as.  He's got his kicks, and you can even do air combos with him.
Some people might say that having an air combo which apparently misses half the time was a waste on Akiyama, but I never had that problem.  He's either good, or he gets his ass kicked in by the Komaki duo.  

Shinada my beloved.  You get to have a baseball sidestory that is my personal favorite in here, rivaling that of Kiryu's Taxi Racing.  His combat is my favorite in the game, going above Kiryu simply because of "My Meteor Tackle" and his own version of a bounding throw.  He can get into grabs in multiple ways, and he's really good with weapons.
Continuing on that, some people say his weapons aren't very good, that being the sturdy metal pole, long pole, knife, and katana.        And to that, I say that you really shouldn't soley rely on his weapons.
Shinada already is great at fighting if you know how to use his overflowing amount of I-Frames.    I personally only pulled out weapons if I wanted to utilize the increased XP on enemy finish, or if I needed it as a solution to an enemy.  Just, don't be stupid with them and you'll get your use from them.


The story's fun, it has a lot of twists and turns, and the final boss has a lot of health, which I find to be refreshing.

But most importantly, Baka Mitai was introduced as a karaoke track for the first time in 5.   There's also Machine Gun Kiss, which is also amazing.

Anyways, Yakuza 5's a great game.  I'll be moving on to playing Isshin before I play 6.

The game itself is okay, however I recommend that you stay out and away from any Event TFO's unless you enjoy getting AFK penalties regularly for 'lack of contribution' and 'not doing enough damage'. 

I've been Observing these Events for a few years now, and here's what I keep seeing:
This arises from the Uber-God players with ship weapons that can and do reach all the way across the map--in violation of a supposed hard-limit of 10 Km for ship weapons and with damage yields that one-shot anything, including NPC enemies with 225,000+ Health and tear through their shields like they aren't a factor. I've been watching Iconian and Undine dreadnoughts and Battleships as well as terran Battleships and such get popped with a single shot from the Ubers.
You end up getting no shots in, or so few that the system assigns you an AFK penalty no matter how hard you try or what ship your flying.
I have no idea where the Ubers get these weapons and Impulse engines that let them zip a Vengeance class Dreadnought around like a Viper from Battlestar Galactica, but it's something that makes it impossible to compete against in the Event TFO's.
They cross the map insanely fast...not that most need to with their infinite-range weapons, and kill everything, leaving Normal-scale players like us with no shots or so little our efforts make no difference.

Play the game, but avoid the Event TFO's, that's my advice...you'll save yourself a lot of aggravation and frustration.

review_text:
In its current state I can't recommend this game and I really want to...

The graphics, music/sound and lore are excellent, the levelling system (aside from gear score) is great; However the game-play gets stale exceptionally fast because there just isn't enough variation in enemies or stages forcing it to become a rinse/repeat kind of process with the occasional forcing of doing levels again just to get your gear score up.

Giving the players the ability to forcibly end the level for everyone is plain silly especially if you haven't finished looting, it should only end for you when you step on the teleporter.

The ability to Combo with the use of various character abilities to Prime and then Detonate was not well thought out, especially if you're playing with the general public. More often than not they either don't use the skills required to set up the combo or the ability used to Prime outright kills the target making it impossible for you to use your skill to Detonate.

Edit 1:

They've fixed a bunch of the bugs and just generally annoying stuff like combos/ending missions but i'm getting more and more random crashes from unity which is a bit of a pain but meh it happens and i'm not too phased.

As I've progressed further into the game the balance between the characters is honestly a joke, Raff is hands down the GOAT and whenever one rocks up into your game that is a high level you'll basically sit on your ass and do nothing whilst they proceed to one shot the entire level without breaking a sweat. No amount of min/maxing will get any of the other characters even close because you can half ass a Raff build with little to no effort as long as you get the right items and lets be fair you really only need the Salty Galaxy Shake potion to start with and you're already destroying everything in sight :P

Edit 2:

There have been so many updates since my last edit but honestly in terms of game play not much has changed, its still the same game hence recommendation remaining a No.

The builds got a shakeup and are more viable on each character which removed Raff as the be all end all of characters, the Panzer character came out, we got more relics, treasure maps were added, they now let us play offline, we got more storage, combos got a sorely needed rework, the end game ADN content changed to a 3 day cycle vs a week, they added challenge mode which is just the same maps on a harder difficulty and we got the ability to upgrade weapons/gear and add stats to them. I'm sure there is probably a bunch of smaller things I can't actually remember or bother looking up and yet despite all of these changes I still personally feel that the review is correct.

I understand that people want me to change my review, mostly because of the time I've spent playing the game or because it's "the top review" but unless something big happens to make me want to change it i'm sorry to say its not going to happen.

I do constantly come back to the game and play it here and there in the hopes that something will make me change my mind but Rogue Snail just havent quite hit the nail on the head yet.

After an hour played for my coverage of the Humble Choice January 2021:
This claims it’s an open-world horror RPG and sure I can see where it’s coming from, but I find it more like an open-world survival game.  Of course, I’m only an hour in and it’s probably not that indicative of the full game which is close to a forty-hour experience.

The first half-hour is a set of cutscenes that feel very out of place and probably could have been done better.  Random s]tuff happens, people refer to stuff that the character clearly should know about and the narration doesn’t match the subtitles.  This feels broken at times and just not very polished at other times. 

Then the player gets to the main game and is presented with rather severe survival mechanics, and a town that seems to despise him or is out to get him.  There’s not really horror outside of one scene so far, and this is supposed to be a rather long game, so maybe this game changes over time, but all I found was a rather dreary open-world survival game, one I was not interested in continuing to play.  It reminded me of Disco Elysium which I loved exploring, but here I found the nature of this world uninteresting.

Maybe I’m missing something.

The simple crux of playing Left 4 Dead is that Left 4 Dead 2 exists. The sequel has more of just about everything, with nearly all of this game's content included. This game has fewer campaigns, fewer extra modes, and fewer weapons (including a complete lack of melee weapons). I've seen some favor this game for its atmosphere. Indeed, Left 4 Dead takes itself more seriously, skewer closer to its horror inspiration. But I suppose that's not why I play either Left 4 Dead game, especially given that both are multiplayer-oriented experiences. When playing with friends, much of the tonal nuance is inevitably lost.
I will concede that, from my estimation, this game's default lighting solution is far more playable than the sequel's. You'll still find plenty of pitch-black rooms, but it's not as prohibitive.
If I can praise anything unequivocally, it's this game's opening cinematic, which expertly introduces you to so many key gameplay elements, such as the various special infected to expect and the car alarms.
As I see it, there's no reason to play this game when you can get basically all of its content in the sequel, on top of everything it adds. This game has few advantages over its successor to justify choosing it over the sequel.

This game is like [b]Rocket League meets golfing.[/b] The concept is much more fun in comparison to its competitor, IMO. However, the game isn't without its flaws. I put 8 hours into this game so here are some of my thoughts.

[b]Pros:[/b]

➤ As I already mentioned, the concept is pretty unique, fun and addictive
➤ The mechanics are easy to learn but hard to master, also they are somewhat more complex than in Rocket League, making the game all that much more interesting
➤ Varied vehicle customazation
➤ A lot of active and passive skills you can equip
➤ Great amount of maps
➤ Active updates
➤ Free battle pass
➤ Decent achievements worth grinding for
➤ In-game mission which keep you coming back

[b]Neither:[/b]

➤ The playerbase is small, you tend to play with the same people over and over again, most of the matches therefore are filled with half bots but the queue times are short, meaning you don't need to wait usually more than a minute
➤ In the first hour you kinda get to know everything about this game but you can always improve when it comes down to your skills (for some it gets repetitive real quick)

[b]Cons:[/b]

➤ There are a very few game modes you can choose from (solo = time trial, more players/bots = casual + ranked)
➤ Uncertain future, due to the small playerbase, I can see the game dying in the near future. Most likely, I see the game going free-to-play (the fact, the game was already bundled just makes my theory all that more plausible)
➤ No voice chat (it doesn't matter since there are no teammodes, still it would be a nice thing to have and let those, who don't want it, simply mute it in the settings)

[b]To sum it up,[/b] it's worth giving this game a try. After all, the game is still in early access. I had the chance of trying a demo during Steam's next fest and it was, hands down, one of the best games I tried. Maybe wait for a bit. 

I have my [b]doubts[/b] about the future of this game as I said above and even though the game seems to be getting updated regularly, it's mostly new maps and cosmetics, there doesn't seem to have been any new gamemodes or any groundbreaking updates since the game was released to the public.

review_text:
Played it about two years ago but forgot to leave a review back then.

Let’s start with the positives.
The atmosphere in The Callisto Protocol is absolutely fantastic — the first half of the game is just amazing. The opening sequence is what really hooked me in and kept me playing it till the end. The game does a great job at building tension, mystery, and intrigue at the start. And I won't say anything about the graphics, it is just incredible.

But then things begin to fall apart.
The biggest issue I encountered was optimization. I played the game after the major patches had already been released, but I still ran into noticeable stuttering in several scenes during the second half of the game. This seems to be a persistent issue, and even players with high-end PCs may not be able to avoid it. So be ready for that.

Another major flaw is the story.
The first part had a ton of potential: beautiful environments, intriguing characters, and hints of deep lore. It really felt like the developers wanted to build a rich, immersive world. Unfortunately, the second half comes off as rushed. There are still some good moments and characters that expand the world, but they’re far fewer than what we get at the beginning.

A strong indicator that the game wasn’t ready at launch is the post-release DLC "Final Transmission." It is the actual ending of the game, and that says a lot about how incomplete the original release was.

I honestly wish Striking Distance Studios had one or two more years to finish and polish the game.

The game needed a more complete ending, stronger antagonists, and a few more interesting side characters. The villains especially felt underdeveloped. After brief interactions at the beginning, they largely disappear from the story until the very end, leaving a massive gap in the middle with little narrative tension. I don't want to spoiler a lot, but I think that we needed a more interesting secondary antagonist that would be like Hans Tiedemann from the Dead Space 2 who was EarthGov's Director of Operations on Titan Station and was trying to somehow save that place with the personal in it. 

As you can see I am also a Dead Space fan (especially Dead Space 2, which I consider the best in the series), and that is why I also want to clarify something important: don’t expect similar gameplay like in the Dead Space. That game is not a Dead Space, they are really different, stop expecting the same experience like from the Dead Space, you will just ruin your experience due to that.

The combat in The Callisto Protocol is heavily melee-focused, with ranged weapons serving more as backup tools. It’s a completely different experience. I liked the concept of prioritizing close combat, but the execution felt lacking. The melee system needed more variety, like combo mechanics, to keep it engaging over time.

So, will the story pull you in?
Probably yes, thanks to the cinematic presentation and strong opening. But I highly recommend playing it on a really good PC and giving yourself time to get used to the combat system — especially if you are a Dead Space fan.

Overall, The Callisto Protocol is a good game and has some standout moments, but the execution and technical issues hold it back. With better pacing, antagonist development, and polish, this could have been something even more unique.

Final score: 7/10.
A solid experience if you manage your expectations.

review_text:
"Lucius" is a 2012 third-person adventure game, combining puzzle, stealth, and horror elements. Developed by Shiver Games on the Esenthel engine, it follows Lucius, the son of the devil, on a murderous journey dictated by symbolism and an episodic structure. While the plot relies on overt symbolism, it offers a unique experience as players navigate a series of murders, each with its own set of challenges.

Graphically, the Esenthel engine provides a generic yet visually appealing environment, with detailed characters and objects. However, animations and hitboxes suffer from occasional glitches, impacting the overall polish. The mansion layout stands out positively, offering a grounded and intuitive design.

In the sound department, voice acting is commendable, effectively conveying emotions in cutscenes and in-game dialogues. However, lip syncing issues detract from the overall experience. The music, while thematically appropriate, is bland and repetitive, failing to enhance the game's atmosphere.

In terms of gameplay, "Lucius" falls short due to its flawed controls, lack of controller support, and a confusing control scheme. The linear and on-rails nature of the game limits player agency, presenting specific solutions for each level and hindering exploration. The powers, such as Telekinesis and Mind Control, are underutilized due to restrictive scenarios.

The game's repetitive nature, coupled with a lack of variety in gameplay, makes it more suitable for viewing on platforms like YouTube than for active gameplay. Stealth segments, characterized by irregular NPC patrols and limited tools, add frustration to the overall experience. The 40-hour achievement suggests a grindy aspect to the game, further diminishing its replay value.

In conclusion, "Lucius" offers a visually appealing and thematically intriguing experience, but its flawed controls, linear gameplay, and repetitive nature make it more suitable for watching than playing. Despite its neat surprises, the overall chore-like experience outweighs the positive aspects.
