review_text:
Game is a simple god-sim citybuilder mixed with tower defence.

TL;DR: It does some things right and can possibly entertain you for a while, if you like the premise. At the moment I cannot recommend it, because of some issues.


Interface:
First and foremost, the interface is rather clunky to use and doesn't do a particularly great job utilising the screen space and presenting the information to you.

The icons for many of the ressources are almost or entirely identical to each other (with only a colour difference) it does a poor job of presenting the information you need to you.

Many of the building categories only contain a few buildings and some are overfilled or have sub-categories, making finding the building you want to place take that extra bit of time, that slowly gets a bit annoying.

The job assignment list is unsorted, which makes it surprisingly unhandy when you need to move people around. Each entry also takes up far too much space on the screen because of the way it is presented -- Every single job could easily be on screen at all time if this were redesigned.

It may just be me, but integrating a "please give me a good steam review" notice into the main menu seems a bit shady.

It also doesn't help that some of the less user-friendly (and sometimes frustrating) gui choices have been confirmed by the dev to be intended so as to force the player into playing the way the dev feels it should be played.


No pausing:
An important deal-breaker for me is that when you press pause, the game locks you out of it. Only thing you can do while paused is look at some statistics. The reason for this is, according to the dev, that you should feel like you are a part of the world, so if time isn't running, you should not be allowed to see the world.

To me it is simply an unnecessary restriction that makes the game less fun when you are not allowed to watch your city and the map around it while paused -- no need to be able to interact with anything, simply letting the player watch his creation while paused should always be a thing in citybuilding games.

This is a game where you build a town made up of a lot of buildings of varying sizes often in areas where space is at a premium -- buildings you aren't allowed to rotate to make them fit better. So taking your time to count tiles and figure out where things can fit can take a fair bit of time. Maybe your current city is doomed, so you need to figure out how to improve your city layout before starting a new game. Whatever the reason, a pause that simply lets you see the map and nothing else would change it from frustrating to fun.


Game world:
Right now there is a single world map for you to play on. The world map is made up of a lot of playable chunks that offer the actual game areas. This works as intended to give the player a good selection of maps with varying difficulty.

Sadly, the game does not let you reset a single world map piece, but rather forces you to either delete the entire world or keep playing with already played maps locked off. Locked off, because if you won, there is no need to return and if you lost, the map is impossible to reconquer since it has been overrun by enemies.

It would be a big improvement to be able to selectively cleanse specific of the playable maps. 


Gameplay - city management:
The gameplay is rather straightforward citybuilding and ressource management (food/water/population/housing) mixed with god mechanics where you can cast spells every now and again. It works pretty well, even if the economy could need a fair bit of balancing.

Spells don't always work as intended (and I am not talking about the intended mishaps), which can be frustrating. For example when you cast a spell that is supposed to regrow forests, food, and crystals in the immediate area, sometimes a lot of things regrow and sometimes next to nothing does. It makes the spells feel less like reliable god powers and more like a lottery, which makes you feel less like a god and more like a sky charlatan at times. Maybe this is intended.


Gameplay - city economy:
A lot of micromanagement is needed to make sure your economy is balanced correctly (like having enough ammo/food/water stockpiled. This is made into a bit of a problem by the game not telling you which items despawn and which don't. So if you overproduce items resulting in things being left on the ground, many of them will simply dissolve -- and some will not (or do so very slowly). No way to know which items can safely be left outside or for how long.

This could be alleviated by the default "how many to keep producing" setting for buildings being set to "how many can fit into the storage space of the building itself". That some items take up 1 storage amount per item and other items taking up 1 storage amount per 10 or 20 items makes it a bit of a chore to fiddle with at times.


Gameplay - combat:
Combat is a bit of a mess, which I think is intended. It would however be nice if you have slighlty better control.

Your non-combat villagers either run away or fight. It is a bit of a crapshoot whether or not they do one or the other and sometimes they alternate back and forth every second or run directly into groups of enemies when running from whatever they feel they need to run from. Would be nice if you could tell them to either attack or run away always, since the mix just about ensure that they die if they ever go near an enemy.

Your combat troops will walk around as they please, and you can not tell them to guard specific areas even if every single enemy follows the same path (with only ghosts being able to fly through walls). So often your guards will be miles away for no reason.

Your towers seem to fire on whatever they please (usually first thing to get within range) with no regard as to whether or not the thing it fires can do any damage (ghosts are nearly impervious to non-magic attacks, so if a ghost slowly drifts into range of your wall of non-magic towers before a group of zombies arrive then the zombies will get to chew on whatever they like. Magic towers use a somewhat limited ressource to attack, so at times you only want to use them when it is needed.

There may be a hidden priority to the targeting, and if so it isn't clear how or if it works.

Having the option to tell towers to prioritise certain targets over other or even to ignore some types would improve the tower defense portion of the game a lot. 


Gameplay - winning:
There is no way to win yet.

You can lose a map by getting overrun, which then makes it impossible for you to do anything on it, and you can "win" a map by cornering the enemy and getting the upper hand. But there is no way to get to a "you win" screen.

Whether or not this is a good thing is up to the player.


Graphics:
A lot of attention has gone into making the world seem alive and it shows. The art style is by no means beautiful but it works well enough and all the little animations and things like build stages for every building helps and makes you appreciate it after a few hours. The art for the buildings could be improved a lot if the differences were more distinct -- they all basically use the same building blocks. 

While all buildings have its own art, the difference between (for example) your mining facility and your lumber shack or a house is not immediately obvious, so if you want to click a specific building, you will often click around for a while until you find it. It should not be necessary to memorise the building layouts in order to recognise them. Some buildings are drawn much better and include a lot of things unique to that building, making them instantly recognisable.

All in all, the graphics could be improved but grow on you the longer you play.


Conclusion:
The game has a promise, but as it stands now it feels too rough around the edges for me to recommend.

To achieve this, you can grab any goo and attach it to others, leading to them being connected through trusses. Goo balls can slither along these trusses, allowing them to move across goo structures and towards the exit pipe.

The goo trusses are rather flexible, meaning you'll have to keep an eye on the integrity of the structures you create, lest they collapse. This is further complicated by the fact that each level requires a minimum amount of goo balls to reach the exit in order to be completed, so you'll have to strike a balance that allows for as many goo balls as possible to stay free. To push this concept even further, every level contains a bonus challenge, tasking you with completing it in a set amount of time or with an even greater number of goo balls escaping. These can be rather tricky to complete and provide some nice replay value.

As you progress, World of Goo gradually introduces different kinds of goo balls, such as floating or flammable ones as well as various stage hazards. Through this, the game's basic premise manages to stay interesting throughout its runtime while maintaining a fair difficulty curve. Every level also contains some observational monologues provided by an unseen character. This provides some background information on the world and events of the game, though stays rather vague throughout, leading to me personally not really caring too much about it.

For highscore hunters, the game also features leaderboards for each level, allowing you to push your solutions even further. Similarly, all goo balls you collect throughout the games' levels are placed in a separate area, where you can use them to assemble a tower, competing with other for the highest one.

Presentation-wise, World of goo goes for a charming cartoonish look that complements its overall tone. There's some decent music playing throughout the game, though it is mostly atmospheric and thus rarely memorable. Overall, I found the game's atmosphere to be a bit too bleak overall, which certainly matches the lore it contains, but can feel rather dreary.

[hr][/hr]
All in all, I enjoyed my time with world of goo, in large part thanks to its interesting premise.

review_text:
My prior review was back before the 2.0 update with the inclusion of base building. I wasn't feeling things. PSO2 NGS highly requires you have people to play with to really enjoy the content. As someone with nobody and not looking to join groups, this game was leaving me feeling empty. I took a hiatus that was planned to be quitting this game if I found nothing of interest nor change to dynamics that would bring me back.

Update 2.0 adds base building. I'm happy with the addition, but as per usual the UI and menu flows in the game are just horribly clunky. There are things I wish I could change colors on, if not select from some textures, but can't -the typical issues I have with character items as well where for certain items what can be changed isn't enough to make thinks look matching with other items.


I can't even sell anything I have extra for in-game currency because the market to sell anything to other players is locked behind a paywall, so I either scrap it like getting 5 cents back on an aluminum can or it stays in storage.

Gameplay takes a while to get better where AI start to be a challenge to a rifle user (the recommended choice for solo play), and yet really the only way to put me in peril that the AI has is numbers and filling gaps in the attack of one type with the attack of another unit type.

A lot of the cut scenes are clunky and not smooth -plenty of big gaps between character dialog. I'm sorry to say the VA and model movements often aren't in proper sync. A lot of the enemies can't hit me to save themselves and the team behind this game seem to want to push constant rewards where you get shields and weapons that break the initial progression grind of the game (already boosted and with augments and hidden ability level). It seems they really want you to speed through the content to end game so you are left with the customization aspect and maybe dump money on buying AC to do premium pack purchases or roll the gatcha wheel (which is disguised as scratch tickets).

I believe I had about 40 hours on PS4 that aren't logged over here.

I still refuse to recommend this game -if you don't have people to play with and are not into seeking people out.

That said, even though I don't recommend it, there are those who may like it. It has been stable the entire time thus far and I've played far worse games. The issue is all in how it makes me feel playing it, clunky gameplay experiences, and that it can't seem to respect itself as being a game and yet fails to want to go all in on being some weird social app with deeply customize-able characters (which is also clunky) and yet also the main source of revenue for the game. I kinda wish they'd figure themselves out already and iron out the clunkiness.

review_text:
SEGA will never listen to reviews like this because they're a multi-billion dollar corporation that couldn't care less about what a bunch of sweaty steam users have to say, but i'm still going to throw this out there in hopes that new players see and don't waste their time and/or money on NGS.

i played on the original JP servers of PSO2 before the game got localized, and even then i kept playing on the NA servers before NGS. i have a very deep love for PSO2 and have spent multiple years of my life playing this game because of it. i always felt an incredible sense of community with the player base, and this game has some of the most fun raids/boss battles i've ever played in an MMO. 

that being said, i wanted to like NGS. in fact, i did at first. i figured the game would get better as time went on because it's probably pretty difficult to catch up to the 10 years worth of additional content in the original PSO2. after 2 years though, i haven't seen any substantial improvement over launch. NGS' world, despite being open and vast, is dead. even in the most full servers, all other players do is idle in spawn. occasionally there's people who chat, but in comparison to the original PSO2, even in the NA servers, the game is dead. it isn't hard to see why, either. even the hub world is bland and colorless. 

NGS lacks the creativity, spirit, and user-friendliness of the original PSO2. it's been 2 years and i still haven't been able to participate in any urgent quests because of the absurd grind. granted, i don't have the luxury of being able to sit and play every single day, but urgent quests were such an exciting part of the original PSO2 that it leaves a massive void for those who just can't carve out the time to participate like the could before. even the story is bland in comparison to the original. i really don't like a single one of the main cast you're stuck with, whereas even the class tutorial people in the original PSO2 had very unique personalities. NGS can't even make their gacha fun like original PSO2 could.

i wanna have faith that NGS will one day capture the same essence as original PSO2, but it's very frustrating waiting for it to happen. i just have to wonder what led to so many poor decisions with this game. ultimately, i wish NGS was its own separate installation rather than an addition to the original PSO2. throwing it on top only bloats file sizes, and not everybody has that kind of space for a game that isn't even worth it. for SEGA to localize a widely loved game only to toss it out the window a year later with a sequel that can't even live up to a fraction of the original's legacy baffles me. 5/10, if you wanna play, just play original PSO2 on the JP servers. the player count here can't even justify playing it localized.

review_text:
Overall, I enjoyed playing through Hiveswap Act 2: the art style was pleasing, the soundtrack was great and had several gems, the writing was on point and the story, while admittedly a bit on the boring side, was still something I enjoyed following. There are a LOT of different item and character interactions, a good amount of which brought a smile to my face as I was exploring the hellhole full of violence, death and segregation that is Alternia.

But the game has its flaws. It is too buggy for a game we've waited three years for, and I already had the same qualm for the previous game in the series. For example, I've had a handful of objects making me walk around the area for a good five seconds for no apparent reason upon inspecting them (the only one I can remember right now is the barnacle in the cave). In addition, it felt like the overall quality of the game's animated sequences had decreased quite a bit compared to Act 1's, which was especially noticeable during certain cutscenes.

What I found most annoying about this game though is how much backtracking the game makes you do towards the latter half of the story: while the things you did in-between the endless area switching you had to do were fine (pretty entertaining at times, too), the endless walking, door-opening, walking, door-opening, walking, escalator-using cycle made the story feel like it dragged on and on. That is a real shame, because I think I would have enjoyed this part of the story a lot more if it were not for the absurd amount of backtracking.

However, Act 2's saving grace is definitely the characters and their interactions with Joey and Xefros. Characters like Marvus, Tyzias and Elwurd made me feel like this whole ordeal was worth it - I have no doubt I wouldn't have bothered to finish the game if it didn't have such fun and interesting characters. I'd say this all culminated during the [strike]Phoenix Wright[/strike] legislaceration segment, which I thought was great fun and helped the characters shine. There are a few bad eggs here and there (Zebruh), but all in all, I really enjoyed getting to spend more time with the characters I got to meet in the Friendsim series.

Was this game worth the three years of waiting? No! The game felt way too short and buggy for it to be the case; if it had come out in Spring 2018, its initial release date, I wouldn't feel nearly as conflicted about it as I do now. Do I think this is still a good game? Well it sure has its flaws, but its upsides outweigh them just enough for me to be able to say Act 2 is at least a nice experience, at least in my opinion. I will absolutely lose my shit if Act 3 takes another 5 years to get released, though.

The worst change is that a few maps allow for gear 5 levels beyond the current cap, yet don't drop gear of that level. review_text:
🎭 “Free-to-play? Technically. Fashion-to-win? Absolutely.”

Let’s be honest — in this game, money mostly goes into fashion.
Even as a free-to-play player, you can grind for in-game currency and buy outfits from others (though they don’t come cheap).
The amount of character customization is huge — and looking good feels like a big part of the endgame.

The graphics are beautiful in their own unique way.
The world is open, vibrant, and has that dreamy sci-fi atmosphere that’s perfect for just walking around and zoning out.
Lighting, skies, and costume details are surprisingly good — especially for a free-to-play MMO.

Combat and gameplay?
Fast-paced, flashy, and satisfying.
Each class feels different, and switching between them keeps things fresh.
But like many MMOs, the grind is real — whether you're upgrading gear, unlocking skills, or chasing better stats.
Still, the movement and action feel smooth enough to keep things enjoyable.

The good news is, even if you take a break, it’s easy to jump back in and catch up.
Want to get stronger? You'll either need luck, or enough grinding to fund your upgrades.
Most of the time though… you’ll probably just blow your earnings on new outfits anyway.

Personally, I love just walking around, listening to the music, and soaking in the vibes.
Playing with friends is always a good time — but even solo, it still holds up just fine.
Sometimes that’s all I need.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol is to Dead Space as Lord's of the Fallen is to Dark Souls.

My wife’s boyfriend on the other hand says the Callisto Protocol is to Dead Space what Back 4 Blood was to Left 4 Dead.

It feels kind of The-Order-1886-ly in that it truly looks amazing but the game itself is lacking. That said, while the combat does get kind of janky at times, the atmosphere does feel tense and scary. To me it's a great example of like, sure, graphics in a game aren't everything... but they sure as sh*t can be something. What's funny is that this feels exactly like when Evil Within came out. A great survival horror developer branches out and makes their own IP complete with janky combat and difficulty spikes. And like with Evil Within, I'm actually enjoying Callisto. It won't be winning any game of the year awards, but it's still neat. I have a feeling this game will be appreciated more as time goes on, just like the evil within 1, people had expectations that didn't live up, but maybe later people will appreciate it for what it is, because this feels unique and fresh in gameplay and art direction and tone... if you like condemned, escape from butcher bay, dead space, the evil within then this is a must.

This game released at the best time for me. l needed a break from 40+ hr RPGS and open world games for a while. I found the game really enjoyable and damn the graphics look amazing to compliment the bone crushing melee combat. It’s not for everyone though, survival horror never is. It is extremely engrossing, the atmosphere and tone is amazing, the world is insanely detailed and the sound design is - excuse my French - fu*king spectacular. I had been waiting a long time for this game to drop and I was extremely satisfied. A linear, single player, story driven experience arriving just in time during a season bogged down by online competitive shooters. It's a breath of fresh air. What surprised me the most is it's an actual FINISHED game.

I think graphically and visually it’s a total knockout. Literally one of the best looking games I have ever seen ever in my entire life. Now, I'm someone who hates cinematic games and walking simulators and the game does have a bunch of that, but in the end I still enjoyed it. I think the most divisive thing is how clunky it feels. The combat as janky as it was, still felt satisfying and fun most of the time and the big complaint "melee focused combat" is totally false and overblown by the way. You'll be throwing enemies at spikes, launching items at them, secondary fire explosisions, power shot gun. Its a big mix. If you only melee it's honestly on you. They post added more melee finishers too, and they are intensely awesome ways to finish fights.

The Callisto Protocol is a solid 8/10 game in my opinion. Brilliant setting, graphically beautiful, sounds great I finished it and overall enjoyed the world and story. If you enjoy Dead Space I would say to at least play it through once if you get the opportunity. Don’t listen to people who are so fanatical about horror games that they don’t want you to have a good time. They want you to be in constant fear and stressed out. That’s not fun. It’s a game for people to enjoy, as video games are supposed to be not to cause stress or the feeling of having heart attack every time you play, f*ck that. It feels almost like an old school survival horror which I like, but with some modern jank too (walking sim parts).

Big picture? Game is flawed but way better than people give it credit for. Is it on the level of DS remake or RE4? No. Is it still a solid visually stunning action horror game with replay value? Absolutely. If you go in to the game to play a Dead Space game the way every other idiot does then no it’s not worth it. If you go in to play the Callisto Protocol it’s a hell of a ride. People just can’t get over that the game is not called Dead Space and it doesn’t play like Dead Space. The game is great for what it is. This isn't some epic narrative driven movie RPG. It's a blood and guts killfest. And I loved it for that, end of story. If you want a short and mostly fun (but janky) scifi horror game to get some of the DS vibes back I'd recommend it. 

Would play it again to get some more eye candy. And by eye candy, I mean the Asian chick from The Boys, of course.

8/10

The gameplay may seem measured or monotonous to some, but behind this rhythm lies an exquisite beauty. Combat animations are a kind of choreography, every attack, every movement of the hero is an art with a sense of weight and realism. The transitions between actions are impeccably smooth, which only enhances the immersion effect.  

The Callisto Protocol is an ode to visual mastery and creative daring.

review_text:
As a solid fan of survival horrors, I'd say this game was onto something, but ultimately did not deliver. I was hoping to get all the achievements for this game but I can't play this anymore.

I do hope for the devs to make a big comeback after this.

PROS:
- One of the best graphics for modern games. Not only does this apply to the characters, but also the environment if you pay close attention
- Cutscenes felt like a movie and I am a sucker for those
- Environment kills
- There was an instance in the game where a QTE will provide players another chance when missing the prompt. It was a perfect execution for that specific scene

CONS:
- Major performance issues. Too many instances of stuttering. Turning off ray tracing does not improve performance at all.
- No toggle option for sprint and the devs are aware of it since the button config displays as "Sprint (Hold)". I am not sure why they made such a decision but my pinky finger hurts everytime I play this game
- Weird combat loop. The focus is on close range combat and it felt interesting at first until you progress through the game then you'll realize that it's repetitive and boring
- Manual save does not work as expected. It's the same as the last autosave

review_text:
I’m not sure I’ve ever been so split about a game. I really want to love ATF but it’s got just enough issues to make me hesitant about recommending it to others. 

First of all though, the Pros:
- If you’re a fan of intense co-op shooters with a pretty steep difficulty curve this could be one for you. To master the higher difficulties and unlock the best weapons and mods you need to learn how different weapons excel in different situations, how to utilise throwables and wrist devices to their full potential and how to move quickly but safely through the missions. If you have a group of friends who enjoy a challenge then I think you will enjoy the moment to moment gameplay of ATF.

- There are regular updates to the game, both to fix bugs and exploits and to add new content and QoL improvements. 

- Cross-platform support is very clean and easy. Steam users can team up with Quest users and Oculus users with a simple party invite.

- You can choose between quick reloading (slapping the gun against your chest) or active (realistic) reloading. You get a significant damage bonus doing active reloading which I like a lot. Unfortunately quick reloading is undoubtedly the superior choice until you can get extended magazines from higher difficulties. 

Now the unfortunate Cons:
- There are some game-breaking bugs here. They are infrequent but if you’re unlucky, as I was, you can end up in situations where someone will get stuck in a wall or the floor which can mean the end of a run. Switching from smooth movement to teleport sometimes fixes this but other times the person stuck couldn’t access their menu to change this option. This is infuriating when it happens towards the end of a hard mission. If you fail missions in ATF you lose any unlockables you may have picked up, which is understandable, but it means that bugs like these need to be removed otherwise you’ve just wasted your time. 
Other bugs include enemies getting stuck in walls. Enemies that need to be cleared in order to be able to progress to the next area, so you end up running around spraying up the walls hoping to clip them so you can continue. 

- After passing a certain point the progression system is heavily weighted in favour of having a full team of 4 players to clear the higher difficulties. If you want to try it with fewer actual players (I have no interest in playing with randoms) you kind of need the weapon modifications that you can only get from those difficulties, so you end up in this awkward situation where the difficulty becomes a brick wall almost. I will admit the challenge of this can be exciting but then someone gets stuck in a wall and you wonder why you bother with this game at all. 

- If you’re here for story or immersion I would advise that you give this one a miss. The story is wafer thin and the world feels somewhat empty and uninteresting most of the time. I get why that is, the game can create hordes of enemies to send at you which looks amazing and the engine can only do so much, but I never felt immersed or impressed by the world. 

- You get bombarded with party invites from randoms in the hub. 

ATF doesn’t have tons of replayability for me. It’s a game I come back to occasionally to see what’s new and I usually have a good time whenever I do. However, due to some of the bugs that are still present I can’t recommend it unfortunately.

It's a massive improvement from SGW3 and honestly i want to give positive review, but still left numerous annoyance from previous game. This game is try to be both HITMAN and it's 3rd person arch nemesis, Sniper Elite but ended up failed try to be both.

The graphics is absolutely beautiful and everything feels more finished than previous game.

The reticle system is the best of other sniper game, it have bullet drop & distance guide but you still need to aim exactly where to shoot, the game never tell you where the bullet gonna land. Its a perfect balance no too easy and not too hard, i wish Sniper Elite implemented this in some way

Unlike Sniper Elite, this game is more on realism side than fun with a HUGE ASTERISK, it's annoying and inconsistent as hell.

First of all AI, while it's improved from previous game, it still annoyingly inconsistent. Sometimes the enemies have no idea what happened around him, but sometimes a single shot to a lonely enemies, and suddenly other enemy from far away noticed it. I like the idea that enemies will bring binocular and can spot you from a far, but it's weird when everyone can do it (not just officer, heck idk what officer exactly do)

2nd this game seems run great & very optimized, until you ran out of vram and first thing they do is reduce draw distance on enemies which is stupid on sniper game, the enemies you try to snipe just gone just because you step back a few meters (this is also the reason why maximum shot distance you did in game never exceed 400m)

While i love the reticle system, the distance measurement system is not, i prefer the distance measured by the scope, not the tags. Also tagging HUD is not contrast enough with environment, it's hard to to check where is the enemiy tags

The gadget and skills is either should be give to player in the first place or just useless. Also i wish the drone didn't exist for both sides, player drones is useless 75% of the time, and enemy drone is just annoying.

The player manuverablility it's realistic except when sometimes you can't scale tiny obstacle and those tiny incline, stone, marble can totally block you up and you need to jump or stand up which is again annoying

The level design is good, with many variation, but it could be better or make it little bit more fun/engaging, and fast travel should not exist in game, instead player could choose infil point at beginning of the contract

In the end i want this game to succeed, but it need to fix a lot of issue, especially the draw distance optimization, manuverability over tiny obstacle & overall game design and balance

review_text:
I recently finished this game but being honest I found it frustrating in several ways. 

As a plus, the graphics in the game look great - very detailed, scroll smoothly and obviously a lot of work has gone into the environments you move around in. 

However, I found quite a few disappointing things about this game:

- A manual save option is badly needed as having to backtrack to a known save point (sometimes a very long distance) is frustrating and time wasting. I also found that when you log in to play again after saving, quite often you are not in the same location you were in when you saved the game, not always but quite often 

- The reactions of the opponents is very poor. I found several times that you can walk up right beside an enemy before they become aware of you and sometimes not even then. I also found at times that they show no response to a soldier killed right beside them 

- I see some people saying they hated the aiming and firing process used in the game. It does take a bit of getting used to but once mastered, it is easy to use 

- When checking an area to tag enemies, I sometimes found that they just vanish as you are watching them and also sometimes they (for some reason) drop down to the bottom of the screen and vanish from play 

- There was a glitch with the health setting. I had been hit badly by enemy fire and had virtually no life left. As I fled, I stumbled over a high ledge and was sure I would be dead. However, when I hit the ground my health restored to 100% and stayed that way for the rest of the level no matter how much damage I took 

- There was also a glitch with climbing. I jumped into the air from a height to reach a ledge but missed the ledge. However, instead of falling, I was standing in the air and the game allowed me to climb the ledge I had been aiming for even though I was not close to it 

- When approaching the dam on the final level, I approached from the valley with the train wreck in it. It was completely empty right to the end and I was able to watch and tag enemies. However, when I went to return there were about a dozen enemies that I encountered and killed. They were meant to be there the entire time but when I first walked down the valley it was absolutely empty when they were actually meant to be there


Overall, this is a lovely looking game but it is badly let down by the issues I raised above and so I feel I couldn't recommend it. There is much more satisfaction, interaction and challenge to be had in the Sniper Elite games

review_text:
This is one of my "Greatest games ever, do not ever play it" recommendations. Ask me about it and I'll rant and rave about it for hours.

Some posts that hit harder after playing:

"If the characters suffer, you've got ok drama. If the reader suffers, you've got better drama. If the artist suffers, you've got art. If all 3 suffer, you've got typical Russian literature."
"In Russia, Game Plays You."

I went in entirely blind to this game - no videos or review guides. I thought I was getting some Bioshock style weird action game, with some stealth mechanics of a looter shooter. What I got was something that inspired genuine horror and fear without the traditional jumpscare. If possible and if you want the challenge, go into this game blind - without spoilers, know that you may need to restart once or twice once you get the hang of things.

This game was a dream, a collection of hardcore mechanics so artfully disjointed and then sewn together. It's a genuinely unique horror game: It does not have jumpscares or traditional stealth or an Andrew Ryan / Fontaine, because there's no time for it. Things are happening, Green Doctor Needs Food Badly, and resources are delectably rare. Despite all the brutally hardcore typical survival bars you gotta keep up, time is the most valuable resource, and on my first playthrough, dread started eating at me like a plague until it (ALMOST) consumed me entirely. Like XCOM or the early days of an SMT hardcore game, the odds are stacked against you, and it will be entirely unfair - especially if you're going in blind discovering the various ways the game will play you. Like those games, it's a challenge that seems insurmountable - unless you know the Lines.

This game is art. Nowhere else do you feel the intense pain and suffering of being thrust upon the role of Artemy Burakh. You wander the town, both in fear of being instant-killed in the night losing hours of progress, and in constant fear of the ever-ticking clock. You'll scavenge and barter desperately, attempting to make split minute decisions that will alter the course and lives of many - where murder and survival are both excusable and morally accepted, even from someone who vowed to never cause harm. Play it on the intended difficulty, and go in blind for some pristine hardcore suffering (at least on your first try before looking up tips). Like a Souls game, the uncompomising gameplay difficulty is a story in its own right, which weaves together a connection between the inputs you make, the brutal inventory choices you are forced to make, and Artemy's excellently aggressive dialogue choices. Like a good piece of media, I'm left with so many questions, so much regret, so much inspiration. Truly, one of my favorite games of this year, and I played and loved Sekiro and AW2.

Side rant, I love being insulted by a character and then shouting that they don't know the Lines like I do (things I definitely shouted while streaming before seeing that was a dialogue option), or being told shitty orders by a pawn and the chat line is just a hearty "Piss Off." A reflection of my own soul.

Dread will consume you entirely. Only those who know the Lines can mend it.
Thanks, Pathologic.
I mean, you know... Fuck you, but... Thanks.

review_text:
I bought this game on sale, and just recently got to it after watching one of the creators dev vlogs. To be honest, there just doesn't seem to be a point in playing beyond the first 40 or so minutes at the moment.

GTTOD plays like a mashup of Risk of Rain/Muck, Doom/BPM, and somewhat, Ghost Runner.

The game has you rush to find the orange door at the end of each level. Once you find the door you must kill enemies to open said door to proceed to the next level. At the start of each level you can start a shrine that will spawn enemies that get progressively harder as you fight, but these enemy kills don't contribute to opening the door until you reach the door and activate it... they are only spawned to offer you a challenge and some money to buy guns or equipment. As a bonus, once you complete the level with the shrine activated you get some sort of randomized "Buff".

It sounds like a fun loop and the whole story idea of "Climbing to the top of a mountain" sounds awesome. But after playing 13 or so levels... that sense of "climbing to the top" just isn't clear. I fought a level 4 sentinel, and several levels later I fought a level 2 sentinel... why is the later enemy weaker? Am I making progress or am I not? The repeating level layouts didn't really help the case, so by that point I figured the game simply never ends because it is in Early access.

While guns, Gun slots, and equipment can be gotten fast enough (and are all mostly satisfying to use)...
Buff accrual is too slow in this game. Games like BPM, Muck, and Risk of Rain all had a pretty decent rate of Buff Accrual since you could pick up buffs from shrines or chests.

As the Early Access would let on, the game isn't ready for release. It needs work and the developer knows and is hilariously vocal about it in his lovely Dev VLogs on steam. I'm keeping this game to support the developer and because I look forward to seeing what this game can become, but my review will not be kept as "recommended" out of hope or pity. It will change to that when the game becomes more fleshed out and progression becomes more apparent.


Minor Notes to DEV:
* Tutorial was appreciated
* Level design is mostly nice... some parts need more clarification on intended direction, some parts feel like there is only one real path to the end. The first level with the wire fence I walked around in circles about 3-4 times before I found the door.
* Add some way to scroll up and down display Settings in case you don't have or use mouse wheel
* Add a window to look at all of your current buffs in detail
* Add a QuickSave option if this is intended to be an endless game without any goal aside from padding stats against the ever strengthening enemy

This review contains spoilers of the story sections seen in the game.

While it's a bumpy ride to say the least, Hiveswap Act 2 is where I feel that the Hiveswap series finally finds its footing. Act 1 was a nice novelty and Friendsim was a mixed bag with highs and lows, so it was nice to feel an actually solid entry that feels worth getting to for Homestuck fans.

The first few sections play similar to Act 1 where you progress through the game in typical point & click fashion and just comes across as alright. However it's around halfway through the train that you reach one of the major sections, featuring the teal and jade caste who also so happen to have the most interesting characters from Friendsim. The bulk of Act 2 is spent in a trial where the player has to try to put together evidence, and this is certainly the most mixed bag section... the trial itself wasn't the best put together as it's hard to reach logical conclusions on our own like an actual puzzle, however engaging with each character and exploring different dialogue trees did have me invested to the end.

The train car after the trial is the lowpoint of the game for me, it just drags on. While there's a few interesting moments, it  loses the momentum for me that the trial was building and I sort of wish it was just.. skipped. Luckily the game comes back around in the end to really raise the stakes in an interesting way, making me looking forward to Act 3.

But please... do better by your developers and fans alike. There are a lot of decisions still being made that clearly does not have the game's best interests in mind.

review_text:
I might recommend this game if it were solely a historical visual novel (but that wouldn't remove the problem of historical revisionism and romanticization) but since Hakuoki is marketed as otome game, I cannot recommend it as such. It can be easy to fall for one or more of the love interests (I surely did) but the meaninglessness of the female MC that the narrative creates by always prioritizing the love interests and the lack of care given to her by both game and love interests, Hakuoki Kyoto Winds (and Edo Blossoms) fail(s) at romance.
[hr]Kyoto Winds is the first part of this edition of the Hakuoki franchise. The split into two is justified by the change in tone and game mechanics but even being half the full game's length, KW is still too long - mostly due to the abundance of love interests. Originally, the franchise had 6 love interests and while I do like two thirds of the new 6, I would have preferred it if some characters' routes were cut or the overall game were made less repetitive. This game is unplayable without a guide and if you look at one, it would seem there were many choices to make here. But when you look at their nature, you'll find that they only serve 3 functions: 1) getting MC to be in or avoid situations where she can interact with certain love interests, 2) making you choose between love interests and 3) gaining or not gaining the affection of a certain love interest. {In Edo Blossoms, the choices are only type 3) and an additional choice type which is completely redundant.} [b]If you like VNs where your choices matter (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Hakuoki KW and EB are not for you.[/b] Another thing are the endings which, apart from the good endings, are mostly redundant and insignificant. The bad endings all end in either the MC or the love interest (LI) or both dying, whereas the unrequited love endings are either "LI leaves MC behind" or "LI sacrifices himself". [b]If you like VNs where each ending, good or otherwise, adds something to the game (experience) (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Kyoto Winds isn't for you. [/b] {A similar thing can be said about Edo Blossoms where they added Game Over endings but those are just premature bad endings.} [/hr]
[hr]Aesthetically at least, this game does not disappoint. The art and CGs are great, the music is solid but can get on your nerves if you play through the whole game.[/hr]
[hr]Overall, if you're interested in this game, just watch playthroughs of it online. Neither KW nor EB are games that need to be played since they are linearly structured and probably the most literal definition of "visual novel" - a novel with visuals. And Hakuoki doesn't need your money, it's getting enough at home because everything Shinsengumi-related is highly popular in Japan (thanks to the romanticization of the past and yearning for a time where samurai still existed and were fighting against change).[/hr]

review_text:
[h1]On the path of esoteric gunfights[/h1]

As a fusion of first-person shooter and dark fantasy, Witchfire blends roguelike and soulslike elements into an unforgiving battle for the life of your gothic sinner turned witch hunter. The moment you step into its cruel world, corrupted and twisted by witches and their hellish minions, your life turns hostage to the last couple of bullets in your revolver and the crumbs of stamina only enough for one last dash.

Where Witchfire truly excels is in its uncompromisingly challenging shooter mechanics, delivering combat where every shot is weighty and explosively satisfying. Even the starting revolver provides incredible pleasure from the recoil, the feeling of steel weight in the hand and the dull crack of an enemy’s skull being split. Of course, this isn’t enough to defeat the hordes of undead and other witches’ degenerates. They will swarm you and weaken you with madness. They’ll shoot bows and pelt you with spears, call in heavy halberdiers or musketeer squads whose marksmanship is no less than yours. Or even summon an entire ghostly galleon, hovering in the sky and shaking the entire level with the roar of its cannonade.

In order to progress, you’ll have to undertake raid after raid. Gather enough experience to level up, unlock new weapons and magic, and eventually gain access to new locations. The layered upgrade system, filled with meaningful choices, encourages exploration and experimentation.

Leveling passive skills is not the only way to get stronger. Seek quests — kill foes in different ways or under special conditions — and collect rare resources to unlock new weapon perks. Layer spells atop your arsenal, and witness unique combos emerge, where magic and gunplay entwine in unexpected symbiosis. Relics and artifacts, hidden across locations or forged in your sanctuary, add yet another depth to gameplay and open up various battle tactics.

Finally, you can raise your Gnosis level. It provides a deeper dive into an esoteric insight of witchcraft and hidden truths — stronger enemies emerge, new mini-quests whisper secrets to you, and challenges intensify. Simply speaking, Gnosis functions as a difficulty system tied to rewards and exploration. With every ascent, the prizes grow richer, and you unlock more areas, regions, gear, and gameplay mechanics.

Visually, Witchfire is a triumph, complemented by sound design, that heighten tension and immersion of this grim dying occult world. There’s no point in talking about it for long; you can only experience the beauty of this world by going on a witch hunt yourself, armed with a trusty shotgun and spells that burn everything in its path.

review_text:
I'm one of those people who got hooked by fans euphorically praising Pathologic 2 as a work of art, letting you experience feelings unknown in most video games. I was told to "skip doing research and just play it blindly".

Well, I dont think it worked out for me. Pathologic wants to be an interesting experiment on creating a specific dreadful experience. But it's also very much a video game. It has so many meters to keep track. And when it wants to raise tension, it just invents more meters. 

At some point, you're just not seeing the game world anymore, You're organizing your character like an excel sheet. There is so much distance between you and the game world. 

I feel like this would work better with it ditching a lot of systems, just experiencing the game world under the pressure of time and working out moral dilemmas. Focus more on that thick writing. As it is now I dont think Pathologic 2 was worth my time and I would only reccommend it to survival game fans.

review_text:
Homemade Vanilla Bean Custard Ice Cream

INGREDIENTS:

1 1/4 cups Heavy Cream
2 1/4 cups Whole Milk
2 Vanilla Beans or 2 teaspoons Pure Vanilla Paste or Extract
3/4 cup Sugar
3 Egg Yolks

INSTRUCTIONS:

To make Custard Base Vanilla Ice Cream (with egg yolks):

Combine the cream, whole milk, and vanilla beans into the medium pot.
Start to heat mixture over low heat.
Whisk the sugar and egg yolks together in a small bowl until fully combined.
When the cream mixture reaches 95 degrees or feels warm to the touch, remove from the heat.
Carefully, add 1/4 of the cream mixture into the yolks, whisking constantly until blended.
Do not add all of the cream mixture at once to the eggs.
You want to slowly add heated cream a little at a time to temper the yolks.
Whisk the tempered yolks into remaining warmed cream mixture.
Return pot to medium-low heat.
Cook the ice cream base over medium low heat until it reaches 185 degrees or is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Remove from heat.
Remove vanilla bean pods and scrape vanilla beans into ice cream or add pure vanilla extract.
Pour ice cream mixture into a bowl to cool.
Fill a large bowl with ice. Place the container of ice cream in the ice bath.
Stir often and let cool.
When the ice cream base has cooled, pour into ice cream machine and churn according to manufacture's instructions.
When finished churning, transfer to airtight container.
Allow ice cream to harden in the freezer for 30 minutes to 1 hour.

review_text:
I really wanted to like this game, having played and loved the demo.

But while I appreciate what they were trying to do, it's more frustrating than fun. I was expecting XCOM meets Tenchu, but got a more one-dimensional game.

Level designs in spite of their size seem full of bottlenecks that limit your approach, sometimes to a specific character. You also can't choose specific characters to take on a level, and you get a sense levels are intentionally designed around specifc tactics and approaches. I was hoping for customizing what you bring to the mission, but you use the same lures/distractions tools you get early on, save for the occasional mission-specific item. 

Controls also are frustrating. Attacking enemies for example sometimes requires pinpoint accuracy of clicking the enemy, otherwise your character just stands there. Also don't like how your character speed slows to a crawl when detected. It's also counterintuitive how stealthy or unstealthy attacks are. The ninja guy takes a whole day to finish his "stealthy" kill animation, giant, armored samurai guy can sneak up to people and hide undetected in a bush. Civilians are inexplicably spooked by your presence even if you're just walking around, in spite of all the armed samurai walking about.

For a plus, the Japanese dialog is great--clearly they had somebody native scripting and acting out the dialog. Visually is another story--it looks like some generic asian-fusion design, where clothing, hairstyles, architecture look like a Westerner's view of what feudal Japan was.

This game is 15 years old, and they are still adding new content. Where they used to have to chart their own narrative course due to a dearth of Star Trek; the newer content does a decent job of incorporating storylines from the new shows into the existing STO cannon.  

Why do I keep coming back, I have fun. When I don't on the shelf it goes, ready to reimerge in few years again

review_text:
This game is not without its flaws and will likely be love or hate for a lot of people.  

The overarching story concept is great, though the writing leaves a lot to be desired (and some of the voice acting is obnoxiously bad).  Combat mechanisms are unique and interesting.  There is a large cast of characters that can join you as party members, but there is really no compelling reason to party up with most of them.  

The biggest cons to this game are the repetitive level design and the fact that it is extremely easy to become overpowered if you veer away from advancing the story at all.  

I would still recommend the game, particularly if you're a long-time .hack fan as I am.  I'd only played volume 1 on PS2, so this collection was a great find for me.

Especially the fact that this game handles all that action with a good performance is another plus point.

Yeah, besides that, there isn't anything in particular I disliked about this game. Sure, the story is garbage, but I didn't come here for the story anyway.

And I know that the Just Cause community dislike this game but to be honest I don't care. Maybe it's true that Just Cause 3 did it better but it didn't stop me to have a lot of fun in Just Cause 4.

So, as someone who always wanted a game that gives you the freedom to do things straight out of an over-the-top action movie, Just Cause 4 was like a love letter to that.

Awesome game!

review_text:
this game is an extremely mixed bag. i have a lot of thoughts on it and they're hard to structure so here's some important ones in list form:

- the rooms in this game feel far emptier than act 1. there is not a lot to interact with (besides people) in the environment and a lot of the item combination dialogue give very generic "no" responses, which directly contradicts act 1's philosophy of providing witty, helpful, and unique dialogue for every item combination. it makes you not want to try using them, and most of the items in your inventory sit around and fulfill no purpose, except for when they suddenly do.

- this is sort of a continuation of the first, but i feel as if a lot of the charm from act 1 is missing. the lack of item interactions is a huge part. act 2 seems to focus a lot more on interacting with the characters surrounding you, but a lot of them are rather one-note. i personally found act 2 less funny than act 1, but there were some good interactions and it ultimately comes down to personal preference. i think act 1 has the superior writing out of the two, though.

- the interactions between the two main protagonists was by far my favorite part of the game: their dynamic is enjoyable to read and i love reading the conversations they have. it's very wholesome, and it's one of the places where the game really shines. the art is beautiful as well, and i got really excited at seeing all of the cute reactions and expressions everyone has. i know this is only one bullet point, but i have a glowing adoration for both of these elements of the game, and i had a lot of fun moving through the world because of them.

- following that, i also really enjoyed the story, though i admit that is entirely personal preference and i have seen opinions that differed. during the last part of the game especially, without spoilers, i was tense and excited and really interested to see how things would play out.

- the gameplay is rather weak at times: there's a lot of backtracking in the latter half of the game and a lot of players have expressed frustration with the puzzles. the game does not often provide any meaningful guidance that would allow you to think through things yourselves. it usually comes down to a lot of tedious trial-and-error, and i personally never felt very rewarded when i did get a puzzle right.

- there is a part of the game that is an extended ace attorney parody, and it is by far the worst part of the game, story and gameplay wise. the logic and answers are extremely convoluted, and the segment overstays its welcome tenfold. it actively drains the rest of the game's experience and is an enormous black mark on a game that could otherwise be viewed favorably.

- i enjoyed the myriad ways the game can branch off, and i think it's interesting to think about how those may affect future acts. i really love achievement hunting and replaying games, which was a significant draw towards act 2, but the AA part of the game makes that concept far more frustrating, which goes to show how the worst parts of this game brings down the product as a whole.

i would recommend this game if you like homestuck and enjoy the troll call cast, though i would hesitate to extend that same welcome to any wider audience. a lot of people have had very different experiences playing this game! i had fun and i think it's possible for a lot of people to have fun too. it's a decision you need to make for yourself.

lastly, and i think this is probably the [b]most important[/b] part, and would be a mistake if it were left out of any review:

fans have had to wait for this game for three years, and to be frank, it is rather buggy at times and feels as if it's been cobbled together and rushed at many points. it has had a complicated development lifecycle involving a lot of bad luck, bad decisions, endless delays, and a lack of transparency, which makes it really hard to trust the developers. furthermore, and this might honestly be one of the worst parts of the game: there is no credits page. none. none of the people who worked on this game are given any sort of acknowledgement for their hard work, which is not only horrible to the contributors, but extremely suspicious. i couldn't truly say why nobody is credited (their response as to why is rather unsatisfying), or why the game has taken so long for a product that is rather disappointing, but something messed up is going on in this game and behind the scenes, and i think that should be considered before you give them your money.

[b]edit:[/b] credits have since been added, but their reasoning for not doing so upon launch is extremely flimsy and it's almost certain they lied in their response addressing the situation. i cannot verify if the credits include all of those who have previously made assets for the game but are no longer on the team, but at least some of them are, and further speculation should not really be on a steam review. consider that issue remedied, at least in part

EDIT: I scrapped my old review as the problem was fixed with the new update, but there's still a serious problem with this game.

It's a good game. All you need is the NHL rosters from the Steam Workshop and you'll have a game that is well-worth its full price. That said, the main problem with the new patch and/or rosters mod is that star players ask for way too much money, and they don't come down on their price until just before the start of the season, and by that time, no one is trying to sign them so there's no competition. review_text:
Another one of those games that would benefit from a "meh" or "so-so" rating.

With the lack of Star Trek games available (even the old ones are difficult to get and run) it is rewarding to have a game where you can step inside the universe once more. The character customisation is great as is the wide selection of uniforms. I started the TOS storyline and the look and feel of it is real nice with several references and nods to the series. The graphics are as good as we've had in a Star Trek game and the TOS story is decent if incredibly short, though I could have done without the one character and plot from Enterprise that everyone hated.

But whilst you will enjoy the setting and feel of the universe the gameplay will have you incredibly frustrated. If you ever played Star Trek Away Team then that is essentially the away team gameplay here except you only control your one character and have a 3rd person perspective. You will walk down straight, linear corridors with enemies stood waiting for your approach and you just click on them to start attacking till they are dead. Trying to evade fire is usually more frustrating than its worth as your camera loses focus (largely due to the horrible control system). So you end up just you and the enemy standing opposite each other shooting and relying on power ups to win. There is a "shooter mode" that attempts to bring a fortnite style control system to the game but it is even worse. 

I read a lot of reviews that said ship battles were the saving grace of this game and I have to say I am unsure on what they were talking about. Ship battles are incredibly frustrating, again it is about spamming power ups rather than tactics. You can't target subsystems, can't direct allies who to attack and there is no way to command from the bridge. The brilliant Star Trek Bridge Commander this is not. 

Then there are the dozens of bugs. When a Klingon throws a grenade at my character she will react to the explosion throwing herself backwards from the blast onto the ground a good two seconds before detonation. If you tell your ship to fire beams only the sprite for torpedo fire will still show when your ship fires. Things like this destroy immersion and leave you this little annoyance. 

A lot of the missions are repetative once you have done the initial 12 mission starter set. I accidently started the ST Disco Stammets storyline and it was pretty attrocious as well as breaking the rules of the Star Trek Universe. How can you recreate a hologram that is a mental replica of a person also with all their memories and experiences? Don't make me geek angry game!

The game could be great. Get rid of the stupid point and click web based game controls and implement something similar to those employed by every other survival/3rd person game on Steam. Go play Star Trek Bridge Commander and implement the same control and combat system. That would at least give the game the platform to be great.

So it is with regret I have decided to uninstall this game, me wanting a good Star Trek game badly won't make this game any better and I am tired of being annoyed by it. I have only had 15hours in the game so haven't got to the grindy pay-to-win elements that drive most people away, what is the point of getting through the horrible controls, gameplay and bugs just to hit that brick wall?

review_text:
[b]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds[/b] is a remaster of the game "Hakuouki", originally released on PS2 in 2008. I'm not a fan of dating simulators, but that game caught me because of  history of Japan in Edo Period. I was pleasantly surprised that there are no kisses, words of love or erotic content, only hints. This is a naive, in some places stupid story about friendship, self-sacrifice in the name of duty and love. I as a person with a heart of stone, can say for sure - nothing caused my tears no matter how awful the ending was. I guess, the game is mainly oriented towards romantic and dreamy female players, and it would be foolish to demand something brutal, terrible and cruel to a nervous tic. 
[i]There are 12 routes (three endings for each character). In total: [b]36 endings.[/b]

Recommendable  routes(IMHO): Hijikata, Harada, Toudou, Nagakura, Iba, Yamazaki, Sakamoto and Kazama's.

[u] Pros: [/u]
+ 12 romanceable guys,  so you'll definitely have your favorite at the end of the story.
+ Fully-voiced dialogues (except main hero) in Japanese language, not just a few phrases. This part is more important for me than anything else. 
+ Nagakura's  seiyū. Gosh, this guy did a wonderful job voicing him. Every time he put a goddamn smile on my grumpy face. 
+ "The Comedy Trio": Harada, Toudou and Nagakura. Without a doubt - best part of the game.
+ Fascinating  CG's. I bet artist sold his soul to the Devil for such talent. I wish I could draw like that one day.
+ Opening  theme "Ruri no Sora e". Already added in my playlist, but other musical composition  aren't especially memorable.
+ Lenght. My first walkthrough of Hijikata's route took about  10 hours. 
+ Mini- encyclopedia. If something causes questions, the game will explain.

[u]Cons: [/u]
- To play other route you must skip tons of text you read before. 
- Cannot skip credits after route was finished. I don't mind to read  it at first, but I decided  to beat up all achievements, so pretty annoying . It was fixed at "Edo Blossoms".
- Sanan's route. I have no clue why his route was added  in the game. He enjoys the fact that he is no longer a human and I fully agree with him: he is inhumanly boring. I'd like to romance Takeda instead.
- I used custom character's name "Chizuru" but nobody called her by the name. Fixed in "Edo Blossoms".
- Some glitches(black streaks) in Sakamoto's route after using "force skip".
- Chizuru. She's a typical Mary Sue with ultimate abilities, such as fast healing of wounds and making tea.More than 50% of the game she complains that she is not a human and completely useless  to the Shinsengumi. Yukimura doesn't have any interesting character traits, what would make the player worry about her.  But this is a common problem of the "Otome" game genre.

8 "Go back to your room, kid" of 10

review_text:
What started out as a love letter to JSR quickly turned into a disappointment. Trust me, I wanted to love this game, as a fan of the original Jet Set Radio, but the game has so many issues that I can’t in good faith recommend this at all.

Firstly, the stages are too spacious, nothing is happening within them. There aren't many cool landmarks and most of the stages begin to blend together at a certain point. The level design is something the original game did well, but here, it’s just not fun to grind through through them. A certain point you kind of lose interest in exploring at all.

Secondly, there is no energy to this game. Remember how the original Jet Set Radio opens up? With Professor K’s iconic JET SET RADDIOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO blaring into your eardrums. That game commanded your attention from the start and you, the player, knew you were in for a ride. Here, there’s no voice acting. Sure, we get some grunts and a few short words here and there from the many characters, but you can’t help but notice that something is missing from the cutscenes. Everything feels so quiet… so lifeless… despite the game wanting you to be invested its story.

And that finally brings us to the story. I will say right of the bat I didn’t like it. The story started off well but halfway through, I was bored. Could it have helped if the game had a better presentation with voiceovers as well? Maybe. But the writing just isn’t that interesting. I thought it took itself a bit too seriously.

The music is great, possibly the best thing about the game and I’ll leave it at that.

review_text:
I tried hard to love this game...and I did! But I can't recommend it, not without some major caveats.

First things first: the look and feel of the game, its environment, lighting, and sound design, are 11/10. Ebb absolutely killed it and I'm happy they took as long as they did to do so. Fans of Giger, Beksinski, and Cronenberg will be drawn to this game for obvious reasons. In Scorn, your feeble, tormented character wanders around a cold, disgusting, biomechanical superstructure, a monumental and unwelcoming presence which wholly envelops you, making you feel like a speck of dust: small, forgotten, hopeless, and insignificant. Sickening machines of unknown purpose stand ominously next to piles of gore. The croaks and gurgles of ungodly creatures echo through the skeletal halls. Everything you see and interact with is hideous and captivating, in the best way. I'm not only impressed, but inspired by the wickedly immersive and thoughtful aesthetic experience of this game. It's something to aim for. Other studios and projects will struggle to carry tone and artistic vision the way Ebb did with Scorn.

The level design is also phenomenal. Orderly, geometric floor plans are broken by tasteful asymmetry, dilapidation, and corrupted organic growth. Each chapter has its own architectural styles and motifs that gave them a unique flavor as you progress, a reward in itself. Verticality is a huge aspect of the layouts, twisting and folding back on themselves, which succeeded multiple times in making me feel like I had wandered far away only for me to notice that I was above or next to an area I recognized. This is also a huge part of the aesthetic experience, as you'll be shouldering around the tight throat of a hallway one moment, then come out to a stunning, decaying vista the next. There were probably a dozen moments in this game where the view in front of me was so stunning, my jaw fell open and I had to just stop in place and take it in. Even backtracking was rewarding in that the paths in reverse had details of their own.

But wait, how much backtracking? A good amount, and that leads into the first downside...

Initially, the gameplay is not unlike a point-and-click adventure, in that you walk around, find items, and use those items somewhere else. Immediately in the first act, though, after wandering around and inspecting all the interactable things on the level, I was confused. Eventually I worked out that I needed to [spoiler] solve the (now infamous) sliding pod puzzle [/spoiler]. Not only was it too subtle that this was even a puzzle at all, I found the "cues" for what you had to do to solve it kind of unintuitive, already a concerning sign for a puzzle game, made even more concerning by Scorn's minimalist approach. I play a lot of logic and puzzle games, so I enjoy a tricky or "hardcore" challenge like this, but it gives me pause in broadly recommending Scorn. It demands patience in a way that will turn many people off in its first hour (and I've seen many reviews to this effect). To be fair, the puzzles from that point on felt more intuitive. But considering it's the first major roadblock you face, I think the devs could have better eased the player into it, guiding them a bit better. Be prepared to backtrack and search around while you determine if you missed something earlier. And, unfortunately, be prepared to encounter things while you backtrack and search.

So yes, let's talk about the gunplay, this game's weakest point by far. Scorn is not a shooter. I remember early on when it was announced, there was more of a focus on the gunplay, but Ebb seems to have de-prioritized that element, and I'm glad they did. But I wish they went even further. The combat in Scorn is unnecessary and feels stapled on - for example, most enemies you can and should avoid altogether, or fire one shot at then run past them rather than try to kill them. It's like Ebb either didn't want to let people down by removing it, or throw away the weapon art assets and design decisions they'd already worked on, or both. I feel like the combat could be removed from the game and it wouldn't have had less of an impact on me; in fact, its inclusion is distracting and too tastes too "game-y" compared with all the wonder of its environment. I've seen other reviewers hope for something like the "safe mode" in SOMA, which optionally turns off enemy encounters altogether, and I agree. The best compromise I can imagine is for enemies to still be around, maybe [spoiler] still block your path sometimes in the case of the big "charger" guys in the later acts [/spoiler], just not aggro or attack you. Then they're more like an interactable part of the environment and you can consider the impulse to kill them or not.

Other people seem to have crashes and graphical issues and stuff, but I haven't experienced much of that. Assuming they'll patch that out, I haven't factored that into my recommendation.

[b]Overall I would recommend buying Scorn on sale if you are interested in a challenging aesthetic experience over compelling gameplay, willing to play it with patience, and willing to forgive its shortcomings.[/b] The current price point of $40 given its length (appx. 5 to 8 hours) is a bit steep. However I will say that if you're speedrunning this game, you're totally missing the point. Play it slowly. And it /does/ have replay value, but not if you're only motivated by Steam achievements, lol. I will definitely be playing this game again.

Some grab-bag improvements that could be made:
- As many reviews mention, checkpoints should be more frequent, especially right after completing a puzzle. There is no reason to make players repeat these sections if they die.
- Only show controls which display on the pause menu that are currently available and relevant. I was stuck on a part where I thought I couldn't switch weapons, because there's a control simply labeled "Switch", and it didn't do anything. Turns out this "Switch" control is only available during the last 5 minutes of the game - so why is it shown on this screen the entire time? I think it would make more sense to only show that control during the small section where it matters. Similar idea with the weapon and item controls as they're unlocked.
- Would be nice to holster my weapon when I'm just walking around. Better for screenshots and immersion :)

Criticism aside, kudos to Ebb for an incredible art game and I can't wait to see what they do next!

review_text:
This game's core design revolves around timers. Timers, if used sparingly, can add to tension. When abused to this degree, though, it destroys the gameplay. There are 5 timers going at any given time (Hunger, Thirst/Stamina, Infection/Immunity, Exhaustion, and Health), and at the base setting, the aggression of the timers is infuriating. If you want to experience this world at a semi-enjoyable pace, do yourself a favor and set all the bars to their most forgiving setting. It is set up to be a multi-playthrough game, but with probably more than 20 hours of dialogue menus and 10 hours of sprinting around for fetch quests and trying to barter for resources, why would anyone want to go through this a second time?

I picked this up on sale, and I have to say, I still don't feel it was worth it. Unforgiving game design can add tension under the right circumstances, but overdone it can ruin a game. Multiple timers, constant backtracking, constant fetch quests, and hours of text dialogue are not good game design - they are a lazy attempt to add length and tension rather than coming up with more interesting design and allowing visual world-building to show how dire the situation is. The world is beautiful and the atmosphere is great, but you will have no time to stop and take it in. You will eat multiple times per day while still starving to death. You will run all the way across the map to receive a quest all the way at the other end of the map, then you'll die of hunger or exhaustion because you didn't spend half the day trying to barter with the locals. The game is nearly unplayable even lowering all the difficulty sliders to their easiest position, and every time you die you not only lose maximum health (across every save you would attempt to load) but also your survival meters remain where they were when you died - so if you died of hunger, guess what? You're still hungry but now have lower health. I could forgive almost all of this if you didn't spend so much time in dialogue menus, because then when you load your save you have to go back to sprinting across the map to click through the same laborious dialogue menus. An excellent world, a brilliant idea, and a beautiful premise executed in the most egregious and unplayable way possible. Spend your hard-earned money on something else. I'd get a refund, but I spent so much time in dialogue menus I missed the refund window.

review_text:
I can really only recommend this game if you get real cheap (right now it's 90% off and thus $2 making it worth it), but since the normal price is $20 I can't recommend this game. The reason I was interested in this game is because of the obvious: you're the son of the devil and you kill people. However the story doesn't really go beyond this (just the brief musings of the detective at the end of a chapter). You barely, if at all, get to know any of the people before you kill them. When there's no personality or character development with the characters then there's nothing felt when you kill them. I could forgive this if the ways that you setup the deaths of people weren't the very definition of linear. This too could be forgiven except the steps you take to setup the deaths are also very unintuitive. They aren't even puzzles; it's just a process of figuring out what weird way the developers want you to setup the next person's death. There's almost no thought or intelligence involved on your part.

Another thing I was interested in, like most people I'm sure, are the deaths themselves. Considering this game was supposed to have earned an AO for Adults Only rating from the ESRB (refused to avoid complications with release) I was a little disappointed. A couple of them are gruesome sure, but they've got nothing on some of the fatalities in the Mortal Kombat games (which are rated M for Mature). There is a kill that Lucius himself gets to personally make, but I was highly disappointed when we don't actually get to see Lucius do it. One minute he's standing there, and we know what he's about to do, but the next he's done it and we saw nothing. Boo!

You are slowly given 5 different powers to make these deaths happen. They can also level up in power when you make a new kill. Only problem is the concept of leveling them up is absolutely pointless because there's only 1 way to setup the death of a person and you are always at the right power level to do it. You don't get to use certain powers when you think you could either, because again there's only 1 way to make the deaths happen.

Pros:
+Voice acting was decent or better, especially Lucifer's.
+The basic concept.

Neutral:
+-A couple of the deaths are cool. Most are forgettable.
+-It's pretty easy to get lost; a minimap would've been nice. At least there is a map and a marker telling you where your kill target is located.

Cons:
-The story lacks any depth beyond the obvious, and the characters themselves are given no time to develop or have much of a personality so that when they do die we the players don't care one way or the other.
-Figuring out what to do next is part luck and part tedious searching of rooms and objects to find the right thing to interact with.
-Completely linear death setups that don't allow creativity of your mind powers or anything else.
-Mind powers have no depth despite being able to level up.
-The graphics are pretty poor. Could be forgiven but the animations are also lacking which doesn't help the already lifeless characters.

Despite all this I am interested in the sequel and the promise that it corrects some of the issues here like linear deaths.
