review_text:
After The Fall delivers a distinct take on the cooperative VR shooter formula by plunging players into a frozen, alternate-1980s Los Angeles overrun by mutated creatures known as Snowbreed. Rather than leaning on the usual sun-bleached apocalypse aesthetic, the game wraps its ruined world in ice, snow, and biting winds, creating a uniquely harsh atmosphere that immediately sets it apart. The backdrop of abandoned malls, skeletal high-rises, and buried streets adds a chilling sense of isolation even when playing with a full squad. From the first mission onward, the hostile setting works in tandem with the action to create a constant feeling of tension: every echo, every distant roar, and every frozen alleyway reminds you that survival here is earned through grit and coordination.

The gunplay and physical interaction are at the heart of what makes After The Fall compelling. Weapons feel substantial and responsive, rewarding players who enjoy the tactile rhythm of VR shooters—slamming a magazine into place, racking a slide, or dual-wielding against an onrushing horde feels satisfyingly grounded. Each firearm has its own personality, and upgrading them over time adds a sense of progression that keeps missions engaging. The game strikes a good balance between arcade-style accessibility and immersive realism; it never becomes overly complex, but it still demands enough physical involvement to make firefights feel thrilling and high-stakes. Facing a charging Snowbreed brute or a swarm erupting from the ice becomes a chaotic, sweaty moment where instinct mixes with muscle memory.

The cooperative design elevates the experience further. Missions are built around four-player squads, and the game’s difficulty scales in a way that makes teamwork essential. Reviving fallen allies, managing ammo under pressure, and coordinating defensive positions all prove crucial, especially on harder difficulty levels where enemy numbers swell dramatically. The social element gives After The Fall much of its longevity—playing with friends or an active online group transforms otherwise straightforward missions into dynamic, unpredictable encounters. Communication, even minimal, adds a sense of camaraderie that fits naturally with the desperate fight for survival. The hub area, where players meet between runs, reinforces the feeling of a small but determined survivor community carving out life in frozen ruins.

Progression is anchored by collectible floppy disks that unlock new weapon modifications, items, and upgrades. This system encourages repeated play, nudging you to refine your loadout and experiment with different weapon builds. While simple, it provides a steady reward loop that complements the game’s run-centric structure. Each completed mission brings new resources, pushing you to take on tougher routes, face more aggressive Snowbreed variants, and continuously improve your arsenal. Over time, the challenge ramps up in a satisfying way, making early missions feel dramatically different once you’re better equipped and more experienced.

The game does, however, show the limitations of its scope. Content variety is one of the main criticisms—mission layouts follow a similar pattern, enemy types are somewhat limited, and the absence of a strong narrative means the world’s backstory remains mostly implied rather than explored. While the moment-to-moment combat is engaging, players looking for a story-driven VR campaign or a vast sandbox may find the structure too repetitive. Technical issues, such as occasional matchmaking hiccups or minor graphical glitches, can also interrupt an otherwise fluid experience. Yet even with these limitations, the core loop remains enjoyable because it leans so heavily on atmosphere, gunplay, and the energy of cooperative action.

In the end, After The Fall succeeds by focusing on what VR does best: immersion, physical engagement, and shared adrenaline. It offers a polished cooperative shooter experience wrapped in a striking frozen-apocalypse aesthetic, delivering a steady stream of intense firefights and memorable co-op moments. While it may not offer deep narrative layers or expansive mission variety, it compensates with tight combat mechanics, strong social features, and the satisfying grind of upgrading weapons and tackling harder routes. For VR players seeking a reliable, action-packed co-op game with a distinctive atmosphere, it stands as one of the more memorable entries in the genre.

review_text:
I wasn't expecting much given the other reviews.  But honestly, it's not bad at all!  I had quite a bit of fun.

The premise is that you're a very good sniper hired by some mysterious guy to take out some bad guys in Siberia.  The game takes place in 5 regions.  Each region has around 5 (give or take) "contracts".  About half of the contracts are to kill someone, and the other half are other objectives such as "destroy the research" or "find the evidence".  Each region also has two "bounties" (optional targets) and "challenges" (such as "do this and that without killing anyone").  In brief, I would describe the game as a "sniping-focused murder sandbox".

I think the gameplay details are pretty well handled.  The length, story, and difficulty were satisfactory.  The upgrade tree is a nice addition.  The challenges are quite interesting, some of them very much baffle me.  

My main praises go to the variety of approaches you can take towards completing the contracts and the design of the bounties.  Although this is explicitly a sniping game, it's clear that the developers intended to allow you to pursue other styles of murdering.  There's a good amount of freedom within the sniping itself as well.  Various targets can be eliminated from multiple vantage points.  As for the bounties, I really enjoyed spotting the rival snipers that overlook the bounty targets.  Sniper vs. sniper action is fun!

My main qualm with the game is that the gameplay loop can get a bit repetitive.  While there are one or two interesting twists in the contracts as the game progresses, I don't find it enough to keep the gameplay fresh over 5 whole regions.  There are also a few minor silly hiccups, from getting stuck on geometry a few times (easily resolved by reloading to the last checkpoint), to a typo here or there, to scout drones magically producing bloodstains when shot.  But I don't find that any of this severely impacts the fun.  I don't think I've ever found myself frustrated at the game, which is a good sign!

The various reviews complain about an omnipotent AI, but I can't relate.  Here is a brief description of how the AI functions, as far as I can tell:  Information between the enemy soldiers travels quite quickly.  When you're in a sniping spot, and an enemy sees another enemy get sniped by you, then word of this spreads rapidly, and pretty soon the entire base is taking cover.  Some enemies will also take out binoculars to look in your direction.  That does not mean, however, that they know exactly where you are.  Only once you are directly spotted (or in other niche scenarios) will the enemies go into combat mode and actually come for you and/or shoot at you.  None of this will happen if your kills are unnoticed, so as long as your kills are done in a well-planned order (which is not easy!), it's possible to clear some bases without the enemies having any idea what hit them.  Of course, what I've just described represents a far more intelligent group of soldiers than what would exist in real life, but I did not at all find these AI mechanics frustrating or more illogical than the usual video-game fare.  I would not say it's perfect, but from a gameplay perspective it seemed acceptable to me.

In sum, I'd give this a 7 or 8 out of 10.  If you're seeing this on sale for 5 bucks, it's definitely worth it.

review_text:
To the Moon is a story-driven point-and-click game that's about two scientists who travel into a dying man's thoughts in order to create a new set of memories for him. It has one of the best stories I've ever encountered in gaming. The portrayal of the characters - the man, who carries a lot of regrets, his wife, who suffers from an unidentified (in-game, at least) condition, and the doctors themselves - is all spot-on and reminds me a bit of the characters in a Miyazaki movie. They're all a little flawed and clearly world-worn without being characatures. This world isn't black and white.

I can tell that the story is a very personal one for the creator, and I can strongly identify with it - I share the main character's love for Animorphs, for example. The details of the story are all very realistic and resonate with me greatly.

But the gameplay brings this way down for me. You just walk around clicking on objects and occasionally playing a flip-the-tiles game. There's no challenge or thought whatsoever and the gameplay sections are unbearably dull. The only fun moment for me was the one puzzle that actually requires a little work to solve, and ironically involves obscure Animorphs trivia, which I thought was hilarious.

The story is great, yes, but it's not a story that's suited very well to an interactive medium like gaming. This should have been a short story or a short film, not a game. Let's compare it to Brothers. Now, I know it's not very fair to compare To the Moon to one of the best games of all time, but bear with me. The story in Brothers is less interesting than the story in To the Moon, but what makes it compelling is that Brothers' story is powerful specifically because it is told through an interactive medium - a game. The game's message relies on you learning to control the characters. In To the Moon, on the other hand, the attempt to shoehorn "gamey" elements into it significantly mutes the impact of the story because it interrupts it every few minutes with annoying, fiddly searching about.

So that's why this gets a thumbs down.

review_text:
Yeah, it's fun. And makes a great early impression.

But after a bunch of soft-locks, chasing the 1000th guy around a tiny rock because he wants to play hide and seek, watching swordsmen glitch in every possible way, etc, I find I'm not having any fun.

The guns are cool. The spells are cool. The builds are cool. But the moment to moment gameplay fizzles for me. In this game with no real melee options baddies are constantly spawning directly behind you. Playing with a controller is a hassle just because you need to turn 180 so often.

Also, this game is so mini-map dependent, it's crazy. It's one of those games where you end up looking at your mini map more than anything, and without the mini-map on you'll constantly be stabbed in the back and miss every chest. I literally just watch the mini-map during boss fights, or any major incursion. There's so many graphical effects going you can't make heads or tails of the action anyway. So I just look at my mini-map, have the red dots and spray and pray.

I die a lot too, and it never feels good. Falling instantly kills you, even if you're supposed to have one free death. You get knocked off a cliff by enemies. One of your own weapons will often kill by knocking you backward, making it just unusable.

Spells are another frustration, if my spell cooldown doesn't come back I'm just dead. The timer is a lie and it only lowers the cooldown on enemy kills. I'll be stuck in a tense fight hoping the 1/100th of a cooldown passes and I can cast an important spell. It never does. It never will.

If I have to reload in a bad spot, I'm dead. Getting trapped in melee happens a lot. Leading to you often having to just sprint for open air before risking a fight, even with basic enemies. Shotguns are terrible in this game.

If a bunch of invincible swordsmen jump on me from a cursed chest, I'm dead. The curse chest that makes only one enemy vulnerable at one time is one the most tilting things ever. Because of the enemy's love of hiding behind small rocks.

Losing everything on death sucks. Yeah, I'm not super familiar with this genre but, regardless, it sucks. It makes me just want to put the game down when I die, not do another run. And you don't even get the loot you had back when you recover your body. Wow. Great idea.

Just as an aside, people don't really get Dark Souls do they? The secret of the games is that they aren't actually hard and that you never ever actually lose progress, just a handful of souls on death, which are always easily replaced, or you get the back from your blood pool.

Games like Witchfire, where you lose all progress on death, are not soulslikes. They're stupid. And frustrating. And when From Software made all the great strides forward in game designs these guys didn't pick up a clue.  Why you don't get the stuff you dropped on death is beyond me.

Also, if you get softlocked in the game you can't kill yourself, so you have to quit and literally lose all progress, (weapon kills, everything) Dark Souls also thought of the solution to this a long time ago.

 I keep finding more and more stuff that's just a struggle. And then I'm struggling to just have fun playing the game, which is what video games are for? Right?

This game is too much work. Maybe they'll fix it.

Also, I posted all this stuff in the forum but I don't think the devs read it. So maybe this'll help.

Yadda yadda yadda, I think this game will be a definite thumbs up when it reaches 1.0. Right now it's still baking.

- Unique art-style actually looks great 
- Gameplay is fantastic and highly replayable
- Character abilities are hilarious and add a lot off interesting gameplay deviations

- This may have been addressed since, but when playing co-op against AI, the AI seemed suuuuper smart and made it difficult to progress

review_text:
Like many other reviews already said, great visually but whack gameplay.

The games setting can be described as disgusting and ruined alien facilities. Which is the perfect setting for a “biomechanical horror” type of game. The environments look really nice, as well as all the tools and contraptions you use, which have well-made animations. So it is no wonder that the atmosphere is also quite good, it really makes you feel like you are trapped in a place you want to get the hell out off. There is no clear narrative, and it's more of a game where you have to piece together your own meaning of what actually happened in the end.

Regarding the gameplay itself, the puzzles are more like small labyrinths where you need to find the right contraption to interact with, which allows you to interact with yet another contraption somewhere else. So, really a lot of walking around slowly and not much actual thinking. Sadly, the combat can't make up for the bad puzzles. Enemies are just an annoyance that makes solving the puzzles even less fun. The game also doesn't have a single textbox or something explaining anything, which can add a bit to the atmosphere, but it's also kinda annoying if you don't realize for half of the game that there actually is a healing or weapon switch mechanic. Admittedly thats somewhat my fault.

If you want to play this game for its visuals, it can be worth it, but if you want any fun with the gameplay itself, I cant recommend this.

review_text:
This game has a lot of small issues that together make it very painful to play. The gameplay itself is a lot of fun, but that just makes the issues more frustrating.

1. Performance is very spotty. I have a 2700 Super and a i5 10400, and even playing on "low" I frequently have  moments when the game completely stops rendering for a second or so when there is a lot going on. Any time there are a lot of zombies, interacting with your gun becomes unreliable, and sometimes my gun floats away for a couple of feet before snapping back. It's not a tracking issue or general issue with my machine, because I've never had any of these problems in Onward, Contractors, Pavlov, etc.

2. Speaking of weapon handling, it's extremely frustrating that there's no option (that I can find) to use your trigger to pull back the charging handle. The detection of where you want to grab is very wonky, and you'll often end up just grabbing your gun when you want to chamber a round. It gets worse when performance drops, which is of course the worst possible time.

3. The AI is basically worthless. Playing with 3 bots is almost as much use as playing with one human who has never played a VR game before. They mostly just get in your  way by blocking doorways, and then complain about you shooting them. The only useful thing they do is revive you, but you've only got about a 20% chance that they'll choose to do that instead of running around failing to kill zombies.

4. Speaking of the terrible writing, every time you do a mission, you get all of the "story" voice acting all over again. If there's any difference in the script each time, it's very minor. The worst is at the end of the "Relay" mission, when you have to sit there listening to them wrap up the story long after you've finished killing the zombies. Also, the AI's only have a handful of voice lines, and repeat them endlessly. My favorite one is the guy who says "You're afraid of the dark, Mal?" despite the fact that there's no character named Mal and no one else has said anything to prompt it.

5. When you start the game or end a mission, you're dropped into a closet that you have to leave to enter the lobby. You can't tweak your weapons (or even see what you have equipped) in the lobby, so you have to run across the lobby to a separate room. If they are going to insist on making you enter a special loadout room, it would be nice if it wasn't literally the farthest point away from where you spawn.

6. Moving things around in the loadout room is very unintuitive. Instead of grabbing things with your hand or laying them down, everything is based on what direction your hand is "pointed". That means you'll often pick up the wrong thing, or drop something in the wrong spot. It's also a headache grabbing your holstered weapons if there's a grenade or gun laying on the ground at your feet, as it will usually try to pick that up instead.

7. Grenades / health / pickups are stored in your wrist like in HL: Alyx. The problem is that the items stored on your wrists are only illuminated by the environment. So if you're in a dark room (which is 80% of the rooms), you won't be able to see if you have a grenade stored in your wrist or not.

I'm sure I could keep going until I hit the character limit, but no one is going to read this far anyway. The game is fun but it needs a couple dozen tweaks to make it not infuriating. I usually start out excited to play, and end up annoyed.

review_text:
Pro
The over-the-top 80s retro-futuristic theme is incredibly fun and stylish.

The game doesn’t take itself seriously and is packed with cheesy humor, references, and one-liners that perfectly capture the vibe of old action movies.

The neon-soaked environments and synth-heavy soundtrack create a unique atmosphere that stands out compared to other shooters.

Gameplay is classic Far Cry with stealth, shooting, and open-world exploration, but streamlined into a shorter, more focused experience.

The Blood Dragons themselves are a creative addition, adding unpredictability and chaos to fights.

---

Con
The world is smaller and the missions more limited compared to a mainline Far Cry game, which can make it feel short-lived.

Some mechanics and objectives repeat too often, making the gameplay loop a little shallow.

Rating: 9/10

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a wild, neon-drenched homage to 80s action movies, packed with humor, style, and explosive fun. While it’s not the deepest or longest experience, it makes up for it with personality and charm.

review_text:
Although this game aged extremely poorly in many aspects, it still is a unique experience which deserves to be played at least once. 

We will play as Lucius, a kid who is the son of the devil. Chapter by chapter we will be tasked by our father with killing people inside the house we live in. 

First it will be staff members, a maid, the butcher, up until more “high profile” targets. The killings must be disguised as accidents, in order to avoid and deflect suspicions about us. 

Every kill will increase our power and eventually we will unlock new abilities, like telekinesis, mind control and fireballs.

The game is really explicit and graphic in depicting the murders, showing exactly how every victim dies with plenty of details. The story is pretty well written too, conveying a nice black humor sort of noir mood.

This is greatly enhanced by the soundtrack, which gives great moody vibes and perfectly fits with every scenario.
I must say the atmosphere is overall on point and works very well.

The mix of action and kind of “point and click” gameplay is smart but doesn't always work, and I found it pretty difficult at times. Some actions required to progress are really unintuitive or need a lot of exploration and trial and error to figure out. The fact that some important objects arent highlighted at all and often blend with the background doesn't help one bit, thus at times I had to help myself with a guide.

Another low point of the game is the presentation, which I guess is the aspect that aged the most poorly. Still, the overall style is consistent, albeit not looking great even compared to other indie games from the same time period. Also sometimes the game is a bit janky, with some hotbox issues which require some extreme precision to work.

Overall though, it was a fun experience and I really enjoyed being the villain and decimating the unsuspecting victims. If you can get past some ugly-ish graphics I'm pretty confident in recommending this game!

review_text:
This games wishes for you to suffer. I am not talking about a difficult game where you can master, mess up, and even get a bad ending; this is a game that was made for you to loathe it while playing it.

Now, on the surface, this sounds fun. After all, having the odds stacked against you and legitimately having a chance to lose is awesome. I love difficult games. However, this game is not difficult; it's a knowledge check.

If you do not wish to be spoiled, do not hover over these. However, I consider these the bare minimum you'll need to play the game and not want to shoot yourself. 

[spoiler] Hoard food, the game time speeds up. Literally, it speeds up. If you do not hoard food, you are going to starve and it's not even funny. The game moves twice as fast towards the ending. Even traveling takes multiple hours of in game time. You will not have time to get a lot of food unless you do it early. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Do the antibiotic questline for the panacea or Rubin will die no matter what. This is stupid, and simply a knowledge check from you. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard fingernails, do not use them early in the game. The cost will rise from one fingernail per fast travel to two. You will need a bunch of them in the late game to have a chance at good time management. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] As stated earlier, time does move faster, and it's a lot faster. Account for that in any way. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] You can get herbs by going to the south east of the map past the steppe to the steppe village. Do this in the early days or you will have a bad time. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard shmowders early, do not waste them, the little girl with a bob hair cut can trade shmowders on top of the dead item shop. Trade with these people as often as you can. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Honestly, even hoarding shmowders is only if you care enough to save the people in this game. Unlike Pathologic Classic, there is no real penalty for letting people die; you do not need to save anyone. I think that was a horrible decision since you're literally a plague doctor and it added natural difficulty in the first game, but fuck me amirite? [/spoiler]

These mechanics should not be a thing in the game. The increased time mechanic is not present in the original game and makes this game go from an extremely difficult plague sim to a gamey video game that the creators made just to mess with the players. A good example of increasing difficulty that made sense and was executed well before this is [spoiler] that individuals have lower plague resistance as the plague goes on [/spoiler] and [spoiler] In order to save a character, you must intentionally infect yourself. [/spoiler] Both of these difficulty increases appeal to the narrative and allow some type of management from the player. 

TLDR: You do not fight a plague in this game, you fight the devs. It is a big disappointment if you enjoy the early and mid game. Just play the first game.

Over the years Star Trek Online has settled into the role of being the ultimate Star Trek fan simulator, in my opinion. There is an original story and world that exists here. For you, there is the option to basically play any ship (especially if it was one of the main 3: Federation, Klingon, Romulan) that appeared in cannon or original star trek online ship of your dreams. Same goes for weapons and crew looks.

You basically fly around with the ship and crew of your dreams within this star trek universe. New stuff is added regularly from various pieces of star trek. That is why the community is still here or comes back from time to time. I use the Alita class with basic star trek online style uniforms, weapons, and gear, so it was easy to straiten out my head cannon dreams.

That being said, there is a lot of things locked behind pay walls for various reasons. Some are much much frendlier (regular 1 time cash shop stuff with benefits) than others (loot boxes). Some things are borderline impossible to get without spending a ton of money or effort. With over 12 years on this game I can also tell you it was easier to grind for what you wanted in the past than now, but there is enough free stuff and other goodies to ensure that you aren't gear locked out of the standard story and side missions. The important thing, ships, fairly easy and/or strait forward; but not always cheap.

Overall if you ever wanted to do star trek stuff using your own dream ship and crew in the equipment you want, this is THE place to do it.

review_text:
The art is great, but that's about it.

The game is artificially extended with slow walking, slow animations, backtracking, and other tediums. But overall is actually quite short. 'Combat' is tedious and frustrating, if you miss a shot or two, you're dead. And if you don't die there, you die later because you don't have enough ammo or health to proceed to the next 'checkpoint', and you can more or less softlock yourself forcing you to revert to an older save.

The most egregious issue is the bugs. I had to look up walkthroughs to figure out if I just wasn't doing something properly only to see others do exactly what I had done without issues, loaded an earlier save, played through more tedium to reach the spot where the bug prevented progress, and voila, i was able to continue. I got it on sale for 13 bucks, and I'm glad I did. If not for the bugs, the game has a playtime from start to end of ~3-4 hours, and fails to introduce or use new gameplay mechanics effectively. The puzzles are either simple, or tedious. There was a crunch for time before release, and it shows with the lack of care put into polishing the actual gameplay/story beyond making it a visual piece. If you like giger-esque art and you're getting it for that, expect a gruelling experience. If you like action horror games? Theres not much action. If you like walking simulator style atmospheric horror games? You probably wont get very far either. It's more or less a visual piece with a few gameplay mechanics haphazardly tacked to it to make it sell better. But if you got the game and enjoyed it? I'd recommend trying 'Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay' as a comparable (and more polished) experience.

review_text:
This game has a lot of potential and I've been playing it on and off since it's EA release. This game currently is not worth your money and at this pace, may never be. The devs have been consistently updating the game, but a lot of the updates are straight up bad. 

Despite people complaining about the immense disparity in the enemy AI vs your teams AI and ESPECIALLY in regards to the goalie since launch, this problem has only gotten way worse. Expert mode is an absolute joke now because even the freebie level on the first slot of your run is at risk of getting the puck once and firing it in because your goalie will absolutely never block. Your AI never positions to defend properly or set you up for good one timers or to protect a shooter.

The enemy AI on the other hand is perfectly positioned at all times. You already have to contend with enemy teams having better stats and talents/abilities, having to also deal with the game actually griefing you is too much. You can be up 5 goals and the enemy will get 5 breakaways and tip it in perfectly every time. Every shot is a rebound they will magnetically get and they will fire it in anyway. It never feels fair or fun, it just feels like bullshit. You're not losing because of any skill issue, you're losing because the game cheats.

To be clear, these are also not the ONLY issues, these are just the ones that upset me enough to finally review it and thumbs down. Stuff like buying superstars and abilities clogging up the pool and making the RNG worse than ever have been called out for ages and never fixed. There's a create a player / team mode and it's completely useless since it can't be used in the roguelike.

The game is not good enough to carry these issues. It used to be understandable since it was early access early launch, but they've had plenty of time to listen to the community and fix it and it's worse than ever. Until the devs shape up, don't bother.

review_text:
Hakuooki has about 60+ hours of play time

You need Hakuoki: Edo Blossom for the romance half of this game. I am playing through both games back to back which is emotionally draining (in a good way, the games are really getting me in the feels). If you want to crush the games I recommend not following in my footsteps. 

Kyoto Winds is more slice of life than a dating sim, with a darker setting. If you are a fan of post-apocalyptic this is a great title for you. You have cast of 12 male characters with most of the stories having overlap since it mostly takes place at the Kyoto Head quarters of the Shinsengumi. You visit locations and more "hangout" with the Routes interest. Each is managing to stand out so far. Currently Hijikata (Edo only) -> Okita -> Harada -> Yamazaki -> Saito -> Ida -> Toudou. Harada is probably the least complicated (in a good way) making him in my opinion the Best Husbando material and Yamazaki was a dark horse.  After playing Toudou I ship him and the MC as the cannon romance since they instantly hit it off. 

All 12 LI have left an impression on me. I am least looking forward to Sanan and Nagagura. Where the cast succeeds is the fact they are all grown men and it is alluded to most of them engage in philandering. Primarily the cast is singly focused on the conflict around them and their duty. However you do get to see many sides as you witness their friendships as well their more serious sides. There is a lot of bickering between the cast which is great. The interaction with the MC serves more as emotional intimacy but refrain from taking the final steps because they want the MC to live a normal life in this chapter. 

The MC: Her world is crumbling and expanding at the same time, which can make her seem passive since she is a side character in a bigger story. She is also caught in a military campaign which limits how much she is able to accomplish since she is surrounded by skilled fighters. Each Love interests forces her to grow in a different way which makes the intimacy memorable. Each man also is conflicted with duty and honor vs self preservation which they confide in her as she is a third party... your basically the resident counselor. Minor spoilers, some of the cast have survived suicide attempts. 

Knowing the pay off this game is well worth it if you plan to pick up both titles. There is lots of memorable play time.

review_text:
Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts or SGWC (for short) is the perfect game for Sniper enthusiastics.
If you have played a Sniper Elite game this game will feel very similar, however in this one you are forced to stay in a FPS POV. From the start the game will show you different weapons, bullet types and utilities. I do recommend starting a mission and testing it there, instead of the shooting range since a mission has a lot more diversity and will show you how the game works. After completing your first Mission you will get rewarded with credits which you can use to buy new weapons, unlock your skills and utilities. The game has 3 difficulties for each mission. The game rewards you with a slow motion bullet tracker for a precise long shot kill. The only downsides of this game are the following: Sometimes the enemies/cameras/turrets can spot you even though you are clearly hidden. Also sometimes the enemies can immediately notice if there is someone dead even if they are not next to the corpse, which can annoy the player who is clearly going for a stealth walkthrough. There is a "Load from last Checkpoint" option that you can abuse, which makes this game a walk in the park in higher difficulties which kinda annoyed me, but i think this compensates for the bullshit I mentioned before :) . Overall, if you enjoy a sniper based game, you enjoy a stealth/ninja play style and you enjoy using different utilities to approach a mission, this game will suit you well. I finished the game 100% with all achievements in 24 hours but I enjoyed every minute I spent on this game.

After beating the game, the ultimate OCD challenges are also worth a try (especially if you don't even know what it is like me after the first run). 

What impressed me most was its epic soundtrack by [i] Kyle Gabler [/i] (which is free to download on his website) and unique art style. From the uplifting [i] Ode to the Bridge Builder [/i] to the epic and emotional [i] Best of Times[/i], the haunting melody showed me that music from a game can leave such an impression. Later on I learned that a deeper and darker meaning lies behind the fantasy story, which I wasn't actually a fan of but is magnificent anyways.

review_text:
Quite nicely designed tower defence, but it is so slow it gets boring.
Nothing is happening on the first 15 hours on a new map, you just autistically build your village and defences on 3x speed, then you get maybe an hour of decent gameplay before your village is overrun.
The game lacks progression, you have a shit ton of maps but you don't have a goal except for a lazy "survive for one year on each map". One year is roughly 10 hours of gameplay, to "beat" the game you need to spend about 300 hours, the game gets boring long before you match the win condition. Instead of the steady progression we've got XP, perks, lootboxes and stuff - the best practices from the mobile gamedev to elevate repetitive gameplay and keep the player in the game longer, except it doesn't make sense here.

This is still an early access game that could have been much more, but instead decided to bail out somewhere in the middle of development.

review_text:
BOMB RUSH IS ALL CITY!!!

This game is dope! You can tell it's been made with passion and a team that has much love for Jet Set Radio   and urban culture in general. The aesthetic from character and environment design through crisp animations, stylized shading and bright colors is very inviting and immersive. The story, which I didn't expect all, does have some twists and turns that go a bit deeper which is a nice extra despite the game being a lighthearted experience. The characters are loveable from the start. The soundtrack is original and cool, exploring the levels is great fun and I while the mechanics are simple they are really satisfying once you master them and are able to zoom throughout the levels and achieve practically infinite lasting combo streaks. Some stuff I could do without is the entire wanted star system, it's just annoying. I get that it fits with the whole illegal graffiti thing but I just wanna skate man! A toggle for it would be great, maybe unlockable after finish the story so that I can 100% complete the rest in peace without annoying cops following me. I know we can use the restrooms to change outfits but it's just cumbersome and breaks the flow of the game. Stuff I'd like to see more of: more characters and worldbuilding! It was fun finding random characters while skating and interacting with them and getting quests, more of that would be great. Having the hideout of the oldheads as an exploreable place would be sweet, stuff like that. Other stuff is just straight up confusing. Like the phone game. You can earn points/currency which I expected I'd be able to exchange for something but I guess it's just a gag that is useless? Played it once during the first hour and haven't touched it since. But all that are just gripes to avoid glazing the devs too much. Overall this is a super fun and stylish game that is like a breath of fresh air, so grab it! If you're a completionist you can squeeze out a lot out of BRC.

review_text:
At first, Bioshock amazed me. The opening is very well done, the music just clicks with the amazement of any player looking at the wonder that is Rapture as first seen. The setting is fantastic at first: A utopia, as considered by the city's founder, would only be viable underwater in the middle of the pacific. And the buildings and neon lights, like a 60s city, but with whales and fish swimming around, reinforced glass tubes connecting the buildings... It's fantastic. And then, you start entering a building, and hear cries of distress: the inhabitants monitoring new arrivals didn't expect you, or anyone to arrive. And as you stop, someone tries to get to you and help you, they're killed by a mutated woman, with hooks instead of hands. 

She disappears, and slowly through the first level of the game, so did my amazement and wonder. One of the tubes connecting buildings has its glass broken and starts leaking while you're on it, but it doesn't convey a sense of distress. You kind of have the feeling that the water is barely rising so that any idiot can escape the tube. (Also, the pressure on the seabed would probably do a lot more damage.) The first plasmid (a genetic modification that reflects in magic, in this case Force Lightning) just feels like a basic attempt at emergent gameplay, and it's the best plasmid: You can stun splicers (mutated humans) and insta-kill them with a wrench, at least on the first levels, or temporarily disable turrets and other robotics to hack them and turn them against their allies. It's nice, but could have been used better, and the other plasmids are either mostly useless or the emergent gameplay created from them is more basic than this one: oil + fire, and ice + shatter foes with crossbow, basically.

Gunplay is pretty weak: the projectile speed for the machine gun doesn't feel right, the pistol is pretty much a Half-Life 2-like pistol that has a ridiculous recoil yet doesn't feel good, the shotgun is kinda meh, etc. The enemy variety is very low: There's turrets, whether stationary or flying on helicopters, 5 kinds of splicers that, even though they behave differently, they look pretty much the same and scream the same deranged stuff. Finally, there are the Big Daddies. They come in two flavors: Bouncer, who rushes at you like a bull, and Rosie, who will kick your ass with a proximity mine launcher. They feel good at the first times, but then you realize their HP is severely bloated and that's mostly why they're hard. But you keep on doing that because, whle you have a choice, it's much more beneficial to just kill them instead of ignoring them (they will ignore you unless you get too close to them or the Little Sisters.) There are no new enemies after the first third of the game or so, only elite versions with even more HP bloat.

The level design would be good if the objectives weren't so annoyingly placed. At least 7 of the 12 levels (not counting the first one or the final boss) consist of you being led to a nearby objective to keep going to the next level, find out the objective is blocked and you have to unlock it by exploring the entire level. It just feels wrong. The levels are "kinda open-ended" but with linear objectives, and in some cases ist's annoying as hell to get to an objective, backtrack to an area you were previously in and then, only then, to have to go through where you have just gone to, but farther into the level. With respawning enemies this just turns into a massive pain in the ass, and it's just you traversing through the same stuff 4 times.

The presentation is very good, the 50s art-deco style is very well presented. As for the story: It has some nice biopunk stuff, but it's pretty much about the plot twist, part of which they decide to shove in your face and make it obvious a few hours before and the other part a pleasant surprise: [spoiler] You're not playing Bioshock, Bioshock is making you play it.[/spoiler] After the plot twist halfway through, well, the game should have ended right there. The quality takes a nosedive into a pretty underwhelming final boss (though, underwhelming final bosses exist in most FPSs I've played so far) and an ending that depends on a certain choice: This choice makes you Jebus Lord and Saviour or LITERALLY WORSE THAN HITLER. It's even worse that Dishonored at that.

Buy it on sale, I guess?

review_text:
All in all a pretty solid game (after its rough release).

Positives:
- The exploration and the lore behind it is quite solid, exploration is rewarded with background knowledge to 
  Black Iron Prison and  expensive goods that you can sell for upgrades that really make a difference
- Combat is hard, dodging is harder because its hard to tell where the enemy swings from, but with damage 
   upgrades to the baton and shooting weakspots, you can get out of trouble fairly quickly

Neutral:
- Lots of backtracking, which is often rewarded, takes a lot of time though
- At certain places you are hit with a choice where to go and you never know which is the right path and 
   where you can get more stuff
- Plays a lot like Dead Space, for me personally not an issue since I enjoyed Dead Space quite a lot and a 
  different setting with similar gameplay is always welcome 
- There is an enemy with two heads, if you shoot one enough the enemy will split off the dead half.
   Though no matter how much you shoot both heads, the moment one half is split off, the other 
   regenerates almost completely and that is not quite clear, given the fact that the alive half can be covered 
   in blood and completely destroyed, but still having tons of health.

Negatives:
- Manual saves do nothing, if you drop a save and load into it you will just be dropped at the last autosave.
   This is the most bothersome when you stop playing or the game crashes.
- Loads of instances where you are getting overrun with ammo when you dont need it, but when you would 
   need it you dont have any at all (see boss) 
- Theres two boss fights:
   - If you dont know whats coming for you, you are screwed. In my first run I shot all my ammo at the first 
     boss, unaware that this boss doesnt take damage from ranged weapons. 
     This decision basically trashed the rest of the game and I had to fight the final boss with almost no ammo 
     whatsoever.
  - If the first boss didnt makle it clear enough that it cant be hurt by bullets and it still isnt clear while 
     fighting the second boss you will most likely dump all your ammo on the first phase and have none left 
     for the second phase, where you actually need the ammo, and no, you dont get any ammo when entering 
     the second phase and I dont believe that the ammo you get before the fight is enough to finish the 
     second phase.

TL-DR: I would recommend giving it a spin yourself once its on sale again. And if you do, dont do the same 
            mistakes I did and maybe start out on easy since medium already is quite a ride.

review_text:
This isn't just a review of G.U. but also the entire .hack franchise.

I would absolutely not recommend .hack at all, but I will admit the idea of it is very interesting. I don't think a whole lot can really be done with the whole "game within a game" setup, but the real plot of the franchise is actually pretty cool. That being magic died a long time ago, but its slowly coming back through technology, specifically its starting to manifest using MMOs as its pathway, in particular the MMORPG known as "The World".

The issue is that this plot is done in probably the most uninteresting way possible. The OG series takes so long to get through only for a whole lot of nothing to happen. The anime bored me out of my mind and I can't remember anything of plot relevance happening aside from the ending. The "games" (really just one game with four seperate discs lets be honest here) were awful too, I couldn't even make it past the first one because I think it might be one of the crappiest RPGs I've ever played. Watched a playthrough of the rest and it takes forever for interesting plot moments to happen, and even then they are so short lived. Its a whole lot of nothing really.

G.U. is an improvement over the OG series, credit where credit is due but it still falls short of what I would recommend. I will admit I did not fully beat G.U. but I did make it past volume 2. I kept trying to convince myself to finish up the post-game content for v2 or to move on to v3 but whenever I considered it I just had this voice in the back of my head keep saying "There are loads of other great RPGs that you could play instead when this game is only a 5/10 even in its best moments." The two biggest praises I can give G.U. are 1: that the story has much better pacing and it feels like things are actually happening at a slow, but fast enough pace to keep my interest. Once again the anime was a whole lot of nothing though. 2: The combat is infinitely better than the combat in the OG series, alas it is not good enough to convince me to beat this series but there is real potential and room to expand it into an actually great combat system should Bamco ever decide to revive this franchise.

I think there is real potential in the series, and I would be interested in a reboot or something but the series that we currently have lacks a story solid enough to be memorable and lacks any truly fun gameplay.

I like this game but I wish I could leave a mixed review. While doing your tricks you press the same buttons and that's fine. It's not just about the tricks the key  to enjoying this game is rhythm. But this game has other poor design choices. Such as heat which builds during the gameplay loop forcing you to break from the fun part of the game to reset it. And combat which is quite literally button mashing enemies until they die. 

Gliding across the arenas and maintaining the combo is perfect and well tuned using grinds and special meter, but the comboing itself is so lackluster. This key aspects REALLY sticks outs when you are gliding across the very thoughtful and ingenious map design. The ONLY comboing you can do (comboing being moves that earn you points) without just jumping on the environment is pressing ur three buttons which typically only press when you are grinding on rails. Where as skate 3 for example had a billion different set of moves you only HAVE NINE TOTAL OVER THE WHOLE GAME (3 different moves for the 3 mounts). 

The devs didn't even have the foresight to implement the existing mechanics into comboing. I hate to be an armchair dev but there was missed potential. LIKE JUST DISMOUNTING YOUR RIDE AND HITTING VERY COOL SLIDE ON THE GROUND AND THEN CORKSCREWING INTO AIR WHERE YOU HIT A COOL AS FUCK FLIP ANIMATION. But wait ITS ACTUALLY IN THE GAME YOU JUST DON'T GET ANY FUCKING POINTS (WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE GAME).

BUT the environment is cool my god the art style is wonderful and the story is actually interesting and completely unexpected. It's basically umarangi generation if it cosplayed JSR or Tony hawk. Cosplaying only because it emulates those games. Yes I'm complaining, only because I love this game and just wanted more from it. 

Should you buy it? Yeah, on sale. Because while the art direction is amazing the gameplay will leave you with some questions and even some disappointment. This easily could've been better if the devs cared enough to update the game.

review_text:
PSO2 and PSO2:NGS, I can say after first starting in the Japanese Server during the launch of Episode 4. I started out alone and with no prior knowledge going into the game. The game itself does what it offers, a vast customization system, flashy but a bit janky combat, expansive skill trees (that you now have to pay AC and SG to fix in the classic version, but completely free in NGS), and a wide array of players from across the global.

The classic version first is very unforgiving if you're a new player as many events and handouts are no longer existing. With most players being veterans who've already completed the game and the final quest HTPD (The Primordial Darkness Hard Mode), Masquerade depth 999, and the time attacks of Rondo to flex with each other on. However on the NGS side you can jump right in and pick up and put down at your leisure. The story will carry you throughout the early progression as you get handouts and things to help you along the way.

Towards the Starless first part quest is when everything in NGS has to offer for you is fully unlocked, so you can skip the remainder of the lackluster story if you want to jump right in to the "endgame". For F2Ps there are things like dailies, weeklies, dext farming, and alnothe farming to be your main source of N-Meseta. However dext farming requires a more specific set up to min/max in which in a good group or a private farm you make 1.5m-2m meseta per hour spent (with either meseta boosters or 100% Rare Drop Boosters + 1 Hour Auto Sell Passes as the drops there adds up to your meseta count when auto-sold.)

I will be real with you though, with the game pushed from the ESRB to T to M, there has always been a slew of extremely lewd and cursed players who are unhinged and ERP in the local town hubs. Central City being the main criminal for that. People can be either toxic or cringe depending on how you approach them, but there are always a good bunch around. Making friends and connections will do you wonders in the game, both Classic and NGS.

Though the game loop is lackluster at best, having friends and making small and big goals helps you continue to want to play this game. I myself have spent 12k hours into this game, yet still find enjoyment despite I am beyond burnt out, fed up with the toxicity and lewdity, and have completed most major content in the game including HTPD in Classic. Would I recommend this game I would say both "yes" and "no". Yes, if you are the fashionista who loves cosplay, looking cute or cool or both, taking screenies with friends, alliances, or yourself, or don't have much time to grind so to do dailies and weeklies then scoot off. No because the game though not completely finished in NGS is brutal when it comes to gearing. As most things boils down to overly expensive augments, preset abilities, and expensive upgrading. Being a loner type will only get you so far as you'll be limited to solo only content or try-harding to the point you drop grands on the game.

My TL;DR if you do decide to play, find your niche, make friends, make a cool unique avatar, and just be yourself. It's both the game I love and hate, and could have been potentially one of the best Anime MMORPGs of its time. But because of sega's greed, monetization, and poor management, the game falls short of what made Phantasy Star, Phantasy Star.

review_text:
This is a bad game unfortunate to wear the Star Trek name.

Sure it starts off quite fun with a lot of veneer on the surface as you start to recognise the voiced actors from the various shows. But after getting blown up for the umpteenth time in ship-to-ship combat, I wish I could get my money back!

What's that? It's a free-to-play game, you say?

I know, but I still feel like I've been cheated.

The game is woeful in its tutorial only teaching you the basics whilst expecting you to trawl through menu upon menu to find extra keybinds you didn't know your character could benefit from that WOULD HAVE BEEN NICE TO KNOW AT THE TUTORIAL LEVEL!

I can't stand games like this; they look like they're promising you so much, until you sink some time into them and you quickly realise that an awful lot of boot polish has been applied onto a wooden statue only to be clobbered over the head by said statue.

The space combat is so lacklustre that you find yourself dying over and over again without ever really knowing what you're doing wrong. You just get spanked (and not in a good way!). Hints would be welcome if you keep dying to the same foes (who magically regenerate all their health when you go right back in by the way!) to at least offer you some guidance what you need to upgrade.

I haven't got time to source external sites for data to study which weapon combinations are better than others for my ships when I game TO RELAX not for endless frustration at doing different things over and over again but getting the same RNG results. It's utter cr@p!

I wanted to like this, I really did, but I just can't recommend it for what I've got out of it... hair-tearing frustration at seeing your ship get destroyed because the RNG loot drops you get after a fight just WON'T give you the weapons that give you a fighting change against enemies you should be obliterating.

This is looter-shooter at it's most banal and I haven't got anymore time to waste without having something more substantial to show for it.

If you ignore this review, then that's your call, just know I don't want you to have anywhere near the frustration I've had when other games are actually ENJOYABLE to play!

This isn't. Not when the risk-reward just is not up to snuff.

This review is a heavily truncated version based on the upper character limit for Steam reviews. For the full version, watch the video.

It seems like the developers have learned from their previous mistake, at least somewhat. While the game still features an open world design with five maps to explore, it now no longer invokes Far Cry as much anymore by having you endlessly drive around the place and fill the map with tons of pointless markers. The sniping gameplay, the core around which everything else is built is better than ever. As before, you need to take wind, bullet drop off and even the travel time of your bullets into consideration. This can obviously be a bit of a challenge if you don’t have an intuitive way of knowing where a bullet is going to land once you fire it. 

Contracts actually has a neat little twist in the way it provides aim assist to you, in that it doesn’t give you the exact point the bullet will hit, instead just showing a general drop off curve along which the bullet will travel. I like that this increases the skill floor from the previous game somewhat but keeps it accessible to newcomers. However, the previous games allowed you to turn this aim assist feature off entirely and the hardest difficulty didn’t even allow using it, which you can no longer do. And even while I wouldn’t have turned it off myself, reducing options for players is always worthy of criticism. 

So if the sniping gameplay is better than ever and some of the faults of the previous ones haven’t made a return, this game must be quite good, right? Well, unfortunately not. 

For one, even though the maps are no longer typical sandboxes, they’re still incredibly annoying to navigate. Usually, you have three or four places on each map that house objectives, but enemies are present even outside of them, so walking around from place to place makes no sense for the most part if you can just bypass everyone with the fast travel system. But even fast travel is implemented in a fairly shoddy manner. I’ve had it happen multiple times that enemies spawned within meters of my own location upon loading the section of map and even when starting a level, which is incredibly annoying. 

Thankfully, most of the time, the enemies were entirely unaware of my presence. That isn’t to say that enemies don’t still exhibit the infuriating ability of spotting you halfway across the map whenever so much as one of your bum cheeks sticks out of cover. It’s just that enemies behave entirely unpredictably here. It’s almost as if the game decides at random whenever it gives the enemies super vision, so progression through these levels can really end up testing your patience. And it’s not like you don’t already need to bring buckets worth of patience to begin with, since whenever enemies are alerted to your presence, they immediately hunker down and refuse to move even an inch and the game takes an eternity to reset them to an unalerted status, even if you leave the area entirely. 

I’m overall not a big fan of how the actual mission sites are designed either. Contracts usually give you two targets to kill per map, while the other objectives revolve around retrieving something from somewhere or planting explosives. Can you tell where those two ideas conflict with each other already? That’s right, we’re playing a sniping game, so the thing players want from that is shooting enemies from as far away as humanly possible. As in, not even setting foot into an enemy compound if at all possible. Not that that’s even doable, since most of the time, the compounds are located between mountainous terrain or other hindrances that the game for some reason refuses to let you climb over. You only get to climb up ropes, ladders and ledges that are clearly defined by the game, there’s absolutely no freeform way of approaching these levels. You’ll have to do it exactly as the developers intended. 

Having to retrieve something from somewhere or planting explosives means you actually have to infiltrate every single compound on the map, meaning that Contracts wants to be a stealth game as well. But again, enemy visibility is so arbitrary that this is already a losing proposition. And given that I personally was there for the sniping gameplay, I mostly accomplished all the goals by methodically taking out enemies and the actual targets from afar, strolling into the compound without any resistance and gathering whatever needed picking up with no enemies in sight. Why would I pick up a game called Sniper Ghost Warrior and do something other than sniping? That’s what I’m here for, but the game tries as hard as possible to make it about anything but sniping. 

Take for example the challenges you can do in each level, like it’s a fu[i][/i]cking Hitman game or something. Each map gives you a bunch of additional challenges to complete, from killing the targets in a predetermined time limit to doing the entire mission with just your knife. That last one is actually given in the same map that also has another entirely different challenge of killing an enemy from over 300m distance, as if the game wants to brag about all the replay value it has. 

If you’ve paid attention, I mentioned that not all of Far Cry’s habits have returned here. And I also mentioned enemy tagging a few paragraphs ago. So yes, just like in the Far Cry games, most of the time you’ll start every infiltration by keeping a lookout for all the enemies and tagging them on your HUD. And I have to ask, why can we only tag enemies with the binoculars and not directly with the sniper scope? It’s just pointless busywork to switch between the two every single time you notice an enemy you haven’t tagged yet while scoping. But that’s not enough in the way of finally getting to the shooting. As mentioned before, the game also features certain compounds with jamming equipment that disable tagging entirely and prohibit the use of the drone. I don’t care that it’s realistic for someone to set up an anti-drone perimeter, it’s just not fun. 

Speaking of realism, the game also wants you to exfiltrate every single site after completing the objective. It doesn’t matter that in my case, most of the time I had disposed of every single enemy in the compound before I got to the point where I needed to pick up something. I still had to walk out of the place in order to get to the designated exfiltration spot. And why did I have to go to those spots to just upload some data? Seriously, why do I even have to do that? I have a constant connection with my handler, why can’t I just upload the data from wherever I am and just move on to the next part? This entire rigmarole is only there because this Contracts wants to be a stealth game. But it just isn’t a good stealth game, it’s moveset and gameplay are too static and contextual to provide the necessary freedom for emergent gameplay and its levels are designed in ways that don’t incentivize stealth. Especially given the fact that you have a god[i][/i]damn sniper rifle at your disposal, so dealing with enemies from a distance is not only what most players who pick up a game called Sniper Fu[i][/i]cking Ghost Warrior show up for, it’s a preferable alternative to trying to infiltrate these compounds unseen.

It’s a shame that CI Games simply can’t manage to knock out a good game in this series. They’ve tried so hard and it’s sad to see that the competent sniping gameplay is once again wasted beneath layers of forced stealth gameplay, schizophrenic enemy AI, highly funneled level design that disincentivizes clever traversal and non-existent writing. Heck, even the one thing the previous game excelled at isn’t around anymore and that’s the music. So in essence, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is another sub-par entry in this series and as such, I can’t really recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore fans of sniping gameplay.

seriously, why do i even have to do that? i have a constant connection with my handler, why can t i just upload the data from wherever i am and just move on to the next part? this entire rigmarole is only there because this contracts wants to be a stealth game. but it just isn t a good stealth game, it s moveset and gameplay are too static and contextual to provide the necessary freedom for emergent gameplay and its levels are designed in ways that don t incentivize stealth. especially given the fact that you have a god i i damn sniper rifle at your disposal, so dealing with enemies from a distance is not only what most players who pick up a game called sniper fu i i cking ghost warrior show up for, it s a preferable alternative to trying to infiltrate these compounds unseen. it s a shame that ci games simply can t manage to knock out a good game in this series. they ve tried so hard and it s sad to see that the competent sniping gameplay is once again wasted beneath layers of forced stealth gameplay, schizophrenic enemy ai, highly funneled level design that disincentivizes clever traversal and non-existent writing. heck, even the one thing the previous game excelled at isn t around anymore and that s the music. so in essence, sniper ghost warrior contracts is another sub-par entry in this series and as such, i can t really recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore fans of sniping gameplay.

review_text:
This is an unfinished (Oct. 2018) but ok little city-builder game with a promising "world" level added to the mix. On the basic city scale, the game doesn't do too much new in terms of mechanics, but has great style without doing anything too wrong either. In that sense it's a perfectly fun game, but if you're looking for a city-manager there are simply deeper and more polished options out there, with Banished and Rimworld both being vastly superior. That said, the hierarchical "world" level is where Rise to Ruins has a real chance to set itself apart from the pack. In its current state, your territories can send resources and people to neighboring regions in order to speed colonization- neat but nothing crazy innovative. If the developers push the game in a direction making world level interactions more compelling and interactive, they could really establish a niche for Rise to Ruins. I'm thinking world level events like big corruption battles that are easier or only possible if multiple territories team up to send golems/resources, but the possibilities are vast with the god mechanic as well.

In its current state, the game is not bad. I spent 20+ hours playing it until I got bored, which is pretty damn good for an early access game. That said, I'm giving this the thumbs down for two reasons: 1. negative comments are read more often and 2. there's no reason to play this right now, no matter if you're a fan of the genre or completely new to it. There are just much better options out there for similar price tags. Wait for full release, Rise to Ruins is promising but simply too derivative right now to warrant purchasing.

review_text:
bought the game hoping for decent action game, didn't get that.

stayed for 300hrs to figure out whats good, what works, how it works etc.

in the end, the experience is layer 1 shallow, there is virtually no skill expression, and the gearing/content loop is absurd, although they're *attempting* to address some of it in *season 2* they are still not fixing the fundamental errors that make this game absurdly unfun.

>progression is complete dogshit

you will spend the first 70-80hrs of your game experience just trying to reach rank 100, post season 2, the grind to 50 will be reduced, but the worst part of it (85-100) will be untouched. there is also no-one playing the content of the lower ranks/world-tiers. CPU/bot lobbies are dreadfully slow and teach you nothing of the game, even worse, is that the content you're doing is Co-Op quests, which by r100 you will find out all the knowledge you have accrued is absolutely worthless as r100+ content is exclusively boss raids

>the enemies don't fight you

you either roll the enemies to death in half a second, or you find arbitrary ways to avoid or mitigate them entirely. this includes bosses, but with how bad the ping is, you essentially just smack a big wall until it kills you (you're only dying in EX) for an action game with perfect guards/dodges, you almost never use them (also a DPS loss.)

>the gearing is abysmal

in endgame, you will need to setup your build with a specific set of equipment with desirable traits. getting a legendary item, is pretty fucking rare (1 in 10 on average iirc) then getting the item for your class-type (1 in 6) AND then getting the correct legendary trait (1 in about 5 or so depending on the item) AND then you need to farm several legendary and epic items to take stat lines for to create a desirable item. for every character. for every build.

weapons are almost entirely worse as for most characters, 75% of legendary effect options are ass, and one is locked to a specific element. even then, you require a weapon of every element that character has access to, with desirable traits, desirable legendary effect, then its RNG whether or not its EX (objective 10% dps increase) and if its lv.98-100 (average loss of 1.2% per level iirc)

in my 300hrs, with what i consider to be extremely lucky (and i was always 4-stacking in one of, if not, THE fastest party on the entire game) i was only able to fully gear up 2 characters. (silica/eiji) most players will never get fully optimised gear unless they're 500hrs deep.

i won't even go into how some of the BiS traits like crit have like a sub 2% chance of even appearing on gear, or the fact blue rarity and below cannot be used to take traits from, as i'd be writing a 50k word international crisis report.

>combat is very bland and expressionless

all characters share the same attack sequence profile, there are no jumpcancels to take advantage of, guard/dodge cancels are often suboptimal and have an arbitrary cooldown between uses and are very clunky. every character essentially boils down to "find optimal normal attack chain, find optimal skill, use off cooldown and repeat" with absolutely no exceptions. a lot of the top-tier characters have basic skills that can be indefinitely looped for easy, free damage.

as expected, there are no hard execution characters, one resource heavy character who is bugged as fuck, a couple of gimmicks that are mostly shared amongst several cast members at the same time etc. combined with a lack of response from the enemies, there is just nothing satisfying or fun. again, basic overview, but i only really have negative things to add.

>balancing (not just character balancing)

the roster is horrendously balanced, from characters having easy damage that infinitely tracks and has no weaknesses to characters who carry every utility, to characters who literally do the exact same thing BETTER than another character because "lol", and some characters who are incapable of doing virtually anything. the balancing is an absolute mess.

element damage fundamentally in my opinion upsets the game balance entirely, and makes balancing the game impossible from a developer standpoint. element adds a flat 20% additional damage boost to any damage done on an enemy, provided you hit them with the element they are weak to. (relink anyone?)

where the issues comes in, is that all (besides 3) characters are missing at least one element from their weapon roster. and mobs, where present in boss raids, might have a different elemental weakness than the boss, and finally, the BIGGEST problem, is that all characters have at least one elementally-locked skill.

the issue here, is that certain characters now have certain parts of their moveset completely made redundant or useful based on ONE select piece of content. sometimes an ENITRE CHARACTER becomes completely unplayable if their missing element is the weakness of the boss in current rotation. even worse yet, characters can have legendary effects on their weapons to change their elementally locked skill into a new element, which is also fixed to one type only, and grants a FURTHER 20% damage boost vs. that element. making gearing and character power even more matchup dependant.

as explained earlier, its also completely unviable to use multiple characters for specific bosses/quests, as you would quite simply never gear them in time.

element simply makes or breaks your damage performance, especially considering elemental damage stat lines are commonly one of the best overall damage increasing options, alongside the elemental damage boost mod that can drop in missions. (elemental damage is also capped out to 100%... because fuck you in even more hyper-specific scenarios)

there's also stuff like skill cooldown on crit that breaks the game, but it is what it is.

so in the end, you will be playing a game that requires 70-80hrs before you can even properly start playing it, with extremely shallow combat, no progression, an endless grind that you cannot win, with poorly balanced characters and mechanics, whilst having a concurrent playerbase of under 300 people. yeah i'd probably buy it in a sale for a laugh in 5 years time.

review_text:
[h1]After waiting over 3 years for Act 2 to be released, I can sadly say that it was not worth the wait.[/h1] The effects of development hell are pretty apparent as there is obvious cut content in the early sections of the game. Promised characters like Charun and Zebede are completely absent despite being shown in the now deleted announcement trailer back from 2019. Hell, in Zebede's case, an entire mini-game was just cut because players found it too hard and is now only accessible to Day 1 players. Also, Act 1 featured fully animated cutscenes, while Act 2 only has animatics. For those not familiar with the term, not of the cutscenes are actually animated, they simply cut from frame to frame and this is usually used as a storyboarding technique. The use of a shortcut technique to avoid time on animation and the cut content really tells that the painfully delayed product was actually rushed despite the 3 year time period they had.

That's not even factoring that the finished product is very underwhelming on its own. The vastly detailed and cruelly engaging world of Alternia is limited to just a train for three-quarters of the game. When I think of an alien world to explore, I'd want to city the towns, cities, caves, forests, deserts, or one of a kind biomes that I would never see on Earth. The train route also makes the gameplay and area progression a literal straight line. The problems with the game's map layout becomes even more apparent when the final section of the game has you do backtracking. Like, a lot of backtracking. I know it's a point and click game and that already limits what you can do with the gameplay, but please do something over than fetchquests. Oh, and if I wanted to play a Phoenix Wright game, I'd play a Phoenix Wright game. After playing through both all the Danganronpa games and the Phoenix Wright trilogy, I can safely say that the Hiveswap court case is a gigantic waste of time that you can just have the answers hand-fed to you in. It's boring and really overstays its welcome. Onto a topic I actually enjoyed, the multiple options you could take to solve some of the game's puzzles was actually really well done! It's not something along the lines of multiple endings, but I enjoy the ability of having multiple solutions to a single problem. On a final note on this incredibly short game, I hope you like the song called Ticket to Ride. Because that song and the several remixes of it will be all you hear once you step on that stupid train.

I don't think I would be nearly as bothered as I am with Act 2 if it wasn't for the terrible management choices Hussie (and to a lesser extent the WP team) made. Andrew Hussie has shown a complete lack of care for Hiveswap, yet refuses to allow other people to continue the story he has no care for. In between the release of the two acts, Hussie started 4 other projects that ate up time and resources that could've been devoted to Act 2. Even after Act 2's release, Hussie has started yet another project and left the Hiveswap team despite the original kickstarter promising 4 acts AND Hauntswitch. This combined with The Odd Gentleman leaks really gives me the impression that we'll either never get future acts or that the quality is going to take a drastic dip. For those who aren't aware of TOG leaks or how they're involved:  TOG was a studio that Hussie initially hired to work on Hiveswap but cut ties with them after they supposedly "stole funds". What seems to have actually happened was that Hussie was an abusive boss that set unrealistic goals for the dev team that could've changed on a complete whim. Projects, models, concepts, drafts, etc. would be nearly completed and Hussie would decide he's not happy with it at the very last minute. There's more to it, but I'd rather you find the initial reports on it, as I'd risk inaccuracy even further. I have chosen to believe the claims against Hussie as they would very easily explain the lack of a court case for TOG allegedly stealing crowdfunded money. 

[b]Overall, I am not happy with Act 2 because of the final product we got and because of the complete disinterest shown by the project's "head".[/b]

The veteran player base is toxic, and treat newbies struggling with contempt.

The only reason to play this game is if you want something star trek since the star trek IP has left us with practically nothing else to play.
I'd LOVE to see star trek get an actual decent game, instead of an at best 5.5/10 MMO

review_text:
It is absolutely not a perfect game, there are small but infrequent bugs and the social/family aspects of the game are pretty bare bones, but it is a good game that I enjoy nonetheless, and keep in mind that this was made by only two developers. 

The artstyle is adorable and pleasing to look at. The music can be repetitive but it's relaxing to zone out to.

 The gameplay is good, there is a story but it's definitely not the most in depth and there is little to no reward for following/completing it. Where it really shines is the various randomized quests you can take on from the villagers. They always give you something to do, and you never know what kind of cool things you could get as a reward. Just be careful during selection because some quests are impossible to complete if they ask for something out of season, and you can't discard quests until they naturally expire on their own.

The aging system is fun, seeing the original NPCs experience different lives each playthrough is a cool touch, and it's fun to see how different your town looks year by year. Getting to play as your kids is pretty awesome too, but I do wish you could have the option to play as a child if your heir is still young when your main character dies. It feels weird to just suddenly age up to an adult when the kids born before you are still kids! Perhaps it could be an optional choice, for those who just want to move on and get their character married, but I would love to experience my character's childhood to feel immersed. Gameplay wouldn't have to change at all either, because you simply inherited the farm as your new job!

The difficulty is very customizable, you can remove aging, illness, minigames, and item decay to make your experience as stressful or peaceful as you want. All I really do is remove the fishing minigame because it's a lot of work for not a lot of reward. I also only take on one quest at a time because I get overwhelmed easily, but I've seen plenty of people with huge lists of quests to occupy themselves with if that's more your style!

Overall, there is room to improve, but the devs slowly continue to add updates and content as well as bug fixes, and I'm excited to see where things go from here! I would definitely recommend this to anyone who likes farming/life sims, and the actual Sims franchise as well!

Take on the boss team at the end of the map, and if you win you advance to the next map.  Earn rubber to spend after your run on attributes, new players that can be on your team, and new skills, all to be used in future runs.

My one complaint would be that the game feels a bit short.  It is still in early access as of now, so I would hope at some point by official release there is an endless mode added, where the boss teams get progressively more difficult.
