After 4 months of not playing this game, I think I should revise my review. 

I was extremely hyped for this game. When it launched, the first 2 months were really something magical. 2 second queue times for 20 player lobbies, Getting familiar with all the characters, leveling up, killing bosses. 
As time went on, the magic started to wear off a little sooner than I'd hoped. New content was just too slow in coming out. The skill ceiling would alarm a claustrophobe. The optimal routes were quickly picked up on so variety went out the window. Enemy AI is just too passive. The game became a snoozefest. Extreme Boss raids added some excitement, but there just wasn't enough overall to keep me engaged. I've got a good 300+ hours out of it, but the way my engagement fizzled out... It was a hot and fiery relationship that just stopped meeting me halfway which soils the fond memories I've had. The DLC is too expensive and for what? 2 characters for $29.99 MY GOD. 

I'd go on and on, but I'd rather not let this review go on any longer. 
One final note, it's been an honor, all of you. Fellow Raid members.

At a certain point mid way through the game you won't get anything new.

Theres just nothing really here besides the story and small additions to generic FPS gameplay. Funny with how much positive press it got and for gameplay theres just not alot here to care about, even less about Infinite. Turn on Stereo Mix
Disable Steam UI

review_text:
This game has some good aspects. The story missions are generally good. The space combat is one of the best capital-ship-style that I've come across. The away team missions even have an optional third-person perspective in addition to the more common MMORPG interface. But it's not worth the time unless you are willing to sink several hundred dollars for a lifetime subscription or the cash shop, or are willing to put in a whole lot more time than I was. First, the gameplay had frequent lag and rubberbanding, which is apparently the result of my using a WiFi network instead of physical cables. Second, the events are pushed too heavily for me to engage in a few hours of casual Star Trek fantasy each day. Third, I ran into a bug where the game kept removing items from my ship and putting them in my inventory--every time I transitioned to a space section.

If you REALLY need a Star Trek fix in an interactive mode, this is the best I have found. But, that's just too low a bar to mean it's actually worth my time anymore.

This is tough call because the game can be fun but it is really no where near finished and the devs are already trying to push this out of early access alpha and dumping money into playing for actor cameos. Game modes are pretty lacking, there are only 2 maps each with their own faults and only 4 game modes which can make the gameplay very repeatable. As of right now the only thing that can keep it interesting are the mission mutators and those are in some serious need of gameplay balance. 
The player classes were just recently revamped in update .7.0 and while overall the classes are good there still needs to be some adjustments to abilities and gameplay for each. 
All in all this game needs a lot of work before it can be considered finished and it just does not seem like the devs are doing that. I am kinda flabbergasted that they would put money into paying for unnecessary voice acting at this stage vs working on the flaws of the game. Hopefully, things get better because I really do like the game and it is fun playing with a bunch of people.

Being hit also leads you into further chain hits because your stamina bottoms out of a hit. Meaning that the enemy that just hits you usually can do so again. Lack of healing, the guesswork of small in health mushrooms of is this poisonous, or not, is never explained, and changes constantly, so you get into a lose lose, or dont trust deal. The currency of this game is abysmally slow, even with a character that excels in getting it. 

Everything out-ranges you, is a bullet sponge for all but a few weapons. Elites are damage sponges, perfectly capable of chaining you 100-0 because of the stamina matters, or just ranged multi-shot that destroys your health, and bosses just are abysmal to face between two tapping you and just being faster than you. Many things get shielded teleports in which they can just no sell your shots, which is beyond frustrating. And these are basic enemies that can do this. Not elites, Not bosses, those get that standard as part of everything, and you can expect them to teleport the moment you fire on them. 

Your weapons, even the long range ones, have beyond pitiful range, and the aggressive falloff damage turns most weapons into chipping away at best. Your close range weapons might as well be ignored, your melee does better and more damage than they do. I kid you not.

Coupled with insanely aggressive cost multiplier of scaling of stat ups, Means you squeak by on multiple runs of a basic map to get enough for a single point that feels worthless.

Save your money, buy a bad or average souls game, fps, or other clone of your choice. There are infinitely better options for the cost of this game. I dont think i'll be able to get a refund, but i'll danged well try.

This game should have remained on epic where it could die in obscurity.

review_text:
Two good steps forward, one big step back for this franchise.

I'm enjoying the more challenging cornering and ground physics. It really shines on rougher tracks where finesse is key to maintaining good speed and fast lines. I also really appreciate a more open tuning system to get your bike setup the way you like it, and tune your bike for your lines at different tracks and surfaces. These feel like really awesome improvements to the gameplay.

I really love the choppy rutty tracks in this game with these 'pro' physics setup. It takes way more finesse and control, and feels awesome. I've noticed in longer races, the deformation eventually just flattens out the lines, rather than make them choppy or blown out. I get why this works this way, but it would be cool if lines got rougher and harder over time, rather than smoother. This is really apparently in long motos, where the A.I leaves a 5 foot wide perfectly flat race line through the whole track, which brings me to my next point.

The AI seems largely unchanged and is as slow and one lined as any of their other games. They simply follow the same path around the track lap after lap, never changing lines and providing only a challenge for the first few motos while you get comfortable with a setup. After I found a good base setting in my second ever moto, I've been easily 2-5+ seconds a lap faster than the A.I, which is hugely dissapointing. By my estimation, Milestone expected the increased riding difficulty meant the A.I is inherently more challenging. It works to a degree, and I think they're probably on to something with that formula. If the A.I took different and varying lines, which made the track rougher and more difficult over time, riding smoothly and fast would be more challening, making the whole game much harder and more fun/realistic.

The most maddening step backwards is the in air controls. The scrub and whip, apparently 'helped by' Tim Gajser is the absolute wost it's been yet. Gajser, while an amazing rider; is apparently a very poor gameplay designer. I am mostly shocked that they took such a huge step backwards on a feature seemed to be improving all too slowly. There is no longer any 'feel' in trying to lean off a jump, it doesn't matter how fast or slow you move the control sticks, the rider simple snaps the bike sideways in which you have to counter steer back to land safely. It's absolutely madenning how bad this is, at least in MXGP3/MES you can control the speed and amount of english you put on the bike. Why are you struggling so hard with this Milestone? I just don't understand after all these years of being dragged kicked and screaming to adding more control and feel, you've now completely gone backwards again. It just doesn't make any sense whatsoever.

Graphics are great, sound is great. They're continuing to up the fidelity and it all looks and sounds awesome. The career mode and sponsor stuff is all fine and pretty good so far. It also runs great on my iMac with bootcamp. I'm really bummed there is still no FOV adjustment for those of us who primarily ride in first person.

Overall it's a fun game, and a welcome installment. I just wish the A.I could go as fast paced as Milestone does at releasing these games.

review_text:
I just finished To the Moon, and wow… I don’t think I was ready for this. My eyes are still wet, and my heart feels both heavy and warm at the same time. It’s not the kind of game you “play” in the traditional sense—it’s the kind you live through, quietly, almost like reading a book or watching a memory unfold. And then suddenly, you’re crying because it hit you in a place you didn’t expect.
River… oh, River. What an unforgettable character. She’s not loud, she’s not dramatic—she’s gentle, quiet, and impossibly human. The way her love and struggles are revealed piece by piece is so beautifully done that by the end, I just sat there thinking about her long after the game was over. She doesn’t just feel like a character; she feels like someone you once knew, someone you wish you could hug.
The story itself is simple yet devastatingly powerful. It talks about love, memory, regret, and the things we hold on to even when words fail us. And every moment is carried by that incredible soundtrack—those piano notes will stay with me forever.
It’s rare for a game to make me cry like this, but even rarer for it to leave me feeling grateful afterward. To the Moon is not about action or puzzles—it’s about empathy. About understanding someone’s heart, even when it’s complicated, even when it hurts.
If you’ve ever wondered whether a video game can make you feel something truly profound… play To the Moon. Just make sure you’ve got tissues nearby, and maybe someone to talk to when it’s over.

[updated to positive in the meantime]

I'm giving this game a negative review despite loving it. The reason is that I want to draw attention to the negative sides that I don't feel get mentioned often enough.

First of all, there are still bugs in the game. After so many  itterations, one would have thought that things like trading and contracts would work flawlessly, but nope, you'll still run into situations where you need a save file editor or create another GM just to get the game to follow hockey rules.

My other and biggest issue is with the way this game compensates. Let me explain. I've been playing EHM since the very first version, probably spent thousands of hours on all versions together. One thing you have to realize is that this game is essentially a numbers generator, working with probability and such. Thing is, if you've been playing this game long enough, you'll find ways to build fantastic teams, with (probably)  the best coaching staff in NHL history and you can pretty much win the Stanley Cup with any team by your second, in a worst case scenario 3rd season. But! The game detects when your team or player start producing extraordinary numbers, and it will start compensating to keep things "realistic". Won too many Stanley cups in a row? Well, you'll lose in the playoffs, no matter what you do (tested by replaying the same saves when things got weird on countless occasions). You'll win with the same team next year, but the game won't let you win, say 4 times in a row, just because. Same if your team is scoring too much. Built a scoring machine with 1st line level players on your 3rd line? Well, bad luck, because you're gonna get punished by periods where your team will refuse to score, until your goals scored total returns to a "normal" value, then, without changing anything, you score again. Same goes with winning games. Winning 90% of your games mid season? Well, here's a drought, it'll end once you're around 75-80%, then you'll dominate again and the cycle repeats.

Bloody hell EHM, let me build super teams if I want to, don't punish me for finding ways to work the system. Sheesh! What's the point in learning to play a game if it will punish me for that and promote mediocrity?

Otherwise, I really enjoy this game and I value the work they put into it, it's a great game, but the compensation system can be incredibly irritating.

there are no subtitles, and sensitivity setting is not enough; it is always too low. performance is horrendous. it takes like a solid 5 seconds to enter a building. FPS is always low.

review_text:
PS2 was the golden era of JRPGs. It's got "hack" in the name. It's basically an isekai set in an MMO. I wanted to like it, but I didn't.

There are a lot of cutscenes with hammy EN voice acting and animation that hasn't aged well. The main char has a world-champion level awful personality in the early game. The combat is very basic, and the gameplay is basically running through identical small areas over and over. Between fights it's just clunky, opaque gear management and having to remember to re-equip party members.

I sat through an hour or so of introductory video catching me up on the prior games which I had not played, but the plot of Part 1 unfolded so slowly and the gameplay holding it together was so slow and stale that I couldn't force myself to keep going after the first 5 hours or so.

When I'd given up, I skipped to Part 4 to see if it got any better. The core loop seemed exactly the same - tons of wooden cutscenes, boring areas and samey fights. The combat had opened up a bit (after you gain 100 levels playing prior games) with weapon switching and a range of skills, but the return on investment doesn't seem to be there for a four game series. At least it only cost me $5.

review_text:
When I firsts started playing it I went "Man, this feels like playing a new Dreamcast in 2025", and it is!  But it's unfortunately for both good and bad reasons.  It has a fantastic visual style and sense of audio-visual aesthetics that makes me want to spend time in it, but totally fumbles the bag when it comes to level design and basic modern design conveniences, and will constantly get in it's own way of the fun.

The stunt and combo mechanics are fun and a meaningful improvement over it's predecessor (Jet Set Radio Future), and they make me want to just play around, but most of these future city environments feel simultaneously cavernous, empty and weirdly linear for a game about trying to combo tricks and they feel less fun to navigate.  And just when I'm getting info a flow with the game it has this bad old-school cutscene system where triggering events will yank the camera away from what you're doing just to highlight a basic level event like the cops appearing or where to go next, when they could have indicated that to me from my character's perspective like any other modern game in the last 10-15 years will do.

And then there's the janky stuff that just feels straight out of the old Jet Set Radio/Future games, like the boring police combat, bad forced camera angles during certain boss fights (big Sonic Adventure vibes here),  the awkwardly sequenced audio and the static cutscenes that don't do much to add life to the story that peaks 10 minutes in.

If you like what you see from the videos then you'll probably enjoy it and I did have fun here, I think i'm just disappointed that 22 years after Jet Set Radio Future this game doesn't feel like it makes the leap forward it should have.

If you want a lego game by Tt that isn't glitchy and is playtested well, go get something else.

Now, as a gamer for my entire life and an aspiring game dev, I can tell you this is the most glitchy game by a AAA company I have ever come across.

As the game goes along, more and more things were ignored within development. FPS drops become more frequent as the game progresses, and parts of the game refuse to register, leaving you stranded, annoyed, and having to restart a level. Then there are the random, even more fun glitches where it continuously changes your character on any button press, rather than just "Y". The raptor level, level 1 of Jurassic World, is especially glitchy and where I've become too frustrated to continue when hitting another level breaking glitch.

All in all, the people working on this game had something else going on that was more important. If you want a bug free game that is well polished and playtested, find something else. Show Tt they can't just let this crap slide.

I come here to tell what most have said before: this game should not have combat or it should be designed in a different way. 

The game has permanent health, limited recovery, far away checkpoints and a combat system based on the fluidity of movement of a walking sim. It's a shame that with such a strong atmosphere somebody managed to ruin the game just by saying "but it can't be oppresive if there's no real tension", without that decision this game would no doubt have extremely positive reviews. Also, the shift into combat-oriented gameplay happens like 30% into the game and it goes from 0 to 100 in the span of like 10 minutes, I don't know what the purpose of that was but it really makes you appreciate how good the game is without combat just to take it away from you.

As an extra sidenote, from my 3 hours of gameplay almost one was me fixing an audio issue that the devs have neglected for a least one year from what I've been able to find, it's kind of a rare bug but if you feel like the game is too silent, it's not a feature, it's a bug.

review_text:
[h1]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, all badges unlocked, every mission completed on Hardcore, every optional objective cleared[/i]

[b]Shadow Tactics is a ruthless, rewarding stealth tactics game that demands precision, creativity, and patience.[/b]
Completing everything is not just about learning levels. It is about mastering each character’s toolkit and finding the perfect moment to strike.

Set in Edo-period Japan, you command a team of five specialists: a samurai, a ninja, a thief, a trapper, and a sniper. Each mission is a sprawling sandbox of overlapping patrols, line-of-sight puzzles, and timing challenges. The level design is meticulous. Every shortcut, hiding spot, and climbable wall has purpose.

[b]At 100 percent, the game becomes a logic puzzle with blood.[/b]
Ghosting maps, speedrunning, or taking out every guard without raising the alarm offers wildly different experiences. The badge system pushes you to play levels in new ways, forcing creativity even after a full clear.

[b]Each character feels distinct and essential.[/b]
You are not just solving stealth problems. You are learning how best to combine skillsets. Distraction into trap. Grapple into shuriken. Katana into smoke bomb. The synergy is the solution.

The story is understated but effective, with grounded performances and solid character development. It builds tension and payoff through quiet moments, not spectacle.

Few games reward mastery like this. Fewer still make the process so satisfying.

I don't know how non-.hack players would feel about this game but it's pretty good. Compared to the original series, it's not the best but it's still fun getting to play in The World.

With the randomness of certain things, some of the extra content can take forever to complete if RNG isn't on your side which isn't great. I'd rather that time be filled with actual content, not just warping in and out of fields until I finally get the results I want. There's some bonus content I know I'm just not going to complete because the time spent isn't worth the reward.

For me the original series felt rich and immersive and I could spend hours on end in the games without getting bored but G.U. feels like a 20% story and 80% tiny little side chores that are barely engaging. I loved seeing the bonus dungeons after completing the games in the OG series but in G.U. the post-game content falls flat for me.

Still, if someone loves .hack, I'd still have to recommend playing G.U. because any .hack content is better than nothing.

review_text:
A great idea, executed in a not-so-great way. That is Lucius, a horror-focused action adventure.

So, the idea is great; a free roam game where you get to kill people like in those famous horror movies we've all seen. You'll be using items and powers to kill off these people. It's not all that straightforward though. You have to solve little puzzles to complete objectives. And every time you complete one of these objectives you're one step closer to killing a certain someone.

But it's all executed in a mediocre way; the inventory is cumbersome to use, but manageable. The 'stealth' missions are terrible; there's no way to see where a certain character is so you'll bump into someone frequently. And sometimes the hints you get just aren't clear enough, which results in you doing the wrong thing. And when it's Game Over you have to start the mission all over again (including sidequests).

It's an interesting idea though. And I would love to see a(n improved) sequel someday.

[Rating: 65/100]

review_text:
Set against the backdrop of 1860s Kyoto—a time of crumbling empires, brewing revolution, and supernatural secrets—Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is an otome visual novel that mixes historical fiction, political intrigue, and tragic romance with elegant storytelling. Originally released as part of the Hakuoki series and later reimagined for the PS Vita and PC, this version is both a solid entry point for newcomers and a rewarding expansion for returning fans.

You play as Chizuru Yukimura, a young woman searching for her missing father in a politically unstable Kyoto. Along the way, she crosses paths with the Shinsengumi, the infamous samurai police force loyal to the shogunate. But all is not as it seems—beneath the rigid honor and discipline lies a darker truth involving secret experiments, hidden pasts, and the supernatural.

Yes, this is a romance game—but it's also a war story. A slow-burn drama about loyalty, sacrifice, and personal identity in a world on the brink of collapse.

Kyoto Winds introduces a whopping 13 potential love interests, each with unique personalities, routes, and endings. Some are stoic and principled (like Hijikata), others are warm and protective (like Okita), and a few are wildcards, including newcomers not present in earlier Hakuoki entries.

Every route branches early and often, with meaningful choices that affect not only your romantic outcome but also who lives, who dies, and how much of the game’s deep lore you uncover. The emotional payoff is often gutting—don’t expect sunshine and rainbows. Expect to suffer beautifully.

What Hakuoki does so well is tone. The writing is mature, atmospheric, and drenched in a sense of historical melancholy. It’s not just about choosing a romantic partner—it’s about watching people you care about wrestle with duty, mortality, and fading ideals.

The romance feels earned, not rushed. Chizuru is more than a passive observer—she grows, learns, and stands up for herself, even if she’s not a sword-wielding heroine.

The game doesn’t shy away from tragedy either. Many routes reflect the grim fate of the Shinsengumi in history, lending weight to even the tenderest moments.

Visually, Kyoto Winds is stunning. Character art is elegant, with detailed kimono designs, expressive portraits, and beautiful backdrops of Edo-period Japan. Every moment—be it a quiet snowfall or a heated sword clash—feels drenched in mood.

The soundtrack matches perfectly: subtle, traditional, and often tinged with sadness. It doesn’t overwhelm but enhances, especially during emotional turning points.

As a visual novel, gameplay is limited to choices, but Kyoto Winds offers plenty of quality-of-life features: fast-forward, auto-text, a flowchart to track choices, and multiple save slots. That said, the pacing can be slow, especially in the common route (shared across multiple characters), and newcomers may feel overwhelmed by the historical detail or sheer number of branching paths.

Also important: this is only Part 1 of a larger story. It ends many routes on cliffhangers that resolve in Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms, so be ready for a two-part commitment.

Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is a haunting, emotionally rich visual novel that goes far beyond romance. With layered characters, beautiful writing, and a strong historical setting tinged with fantasy, it’s a standout in the otome genre. If you’re looking for swoon-worthy samurai with tragic pasts, quiet yearning, and poetic goodbyes, this game delivers in spades.

A slow-burning, beautifully drawn saga of love and loss—just make sure you’re ready for heartbreak.

Rating: 9/10

It is worth noting that all servers but one are inactive so if you hoped for an immersive experience with a variety of different servers with various play styles, this isnt the game.

The animations are janky and limbs seem to merge with one another, especially when you fall, the legs sprawl out.

The only active server follows a realism style of play which causes rule-breakers to join because it is the only server you can play on with others. If you have ever played 'The Cenozoic Era', this game is similar but with more animals and instead of the product being free, its overpriced.

In terms of quality, the early access price is not worth it. £5 would have been a fair price for the quality of this game in this stage. Roblox games are performing better than this.

review_text:
Good MMO in a sea of shite, it's a Whale's paradise but still very F2P friendly. 

Star Trek Online is made with love and passion from the developers, they've got the original actors from the TV shows to reprise their roles and voice act in well written story. There are plenty of story arc for the players to play through and explore more of the Star Trek universe. Most of them are written very well and kept interesting enough to hold the players' attention at all times. 

You gotta love this game's music, the main character selection screen has got the BEST background music ever. I have looped the game in the background over the years just for the music. 

The graphics has not aged well, you can see that most evidently on ground where the textures are disgustingly bad to the human eye. However, an advantage of low resolution texture is the extreme fast loading times between areas. It takes no more than 30 seconds for me to load from one area to the next.

Now, combat in this game is unlike anything you've played. Space combat where you pilot your starship is one of the best PvE combat system in anything similar. you can move in a 3D environment (3 axies XYZ) and position your ship for a broadside barrage of lasers. Your starship can be further customised with different weapons and loadouts to varied styles. It's glorious, Beam Boats to Cannon Volleys and Torpedoes build.

Now for what you have waited for. Is the game P2W?

Yes. Like all MMOs, STO has been alive for 14 years. You don't have a MMO running for 14 years without massive player's whaling. Most of the best DPS consoles and traits(captain and ship) in the game are obtained from Lockboxes(Lootbox) or from Zen Store ships.

Fortunately for you F2Ps, it is not all lost. You can reach very competitive DPS numbers by just spending time in the game and reaching Lvl 50 to unlock the Reputation system which has BiS gear for free. Some of the story mission also award you with very good end game scalable gear. Every story basically give enough for 1 level up each time, so you can reach max level (65) in a few days if you grind long.

This game is still good, you're be joining a friendly and knowledgeable community. Besides, this is the ONLY good Star Trek game out there.

Same as the previous one - don`t waste your precious time. This part of Arkhamverse is the worst Batman game ever created. 

Minor spoilers below:

- Lots of characters, far less reasons why they are actually here. Remove Robin(or better kill), Two-face, Cat, Grundy, Joker, Ra`s Al Gul, the entire Tyger faction and nothing major changes.

- Main story. Half of it - regarding the creation of this superprison - is actually awesome. The other - regarding the cure - well...it`s so stupid. I understand that developers tried to continue Asylum`s plot, which was basically a mess. And they failed.Also, Hyth Ledger`s Joker was great. Suicide Squad`s Joker was great. Origins` and Knight`s Jokers were great. But  this hysterical bitch IS NOT the Joker, just some random cosplayer. 

In the end they force Cat to choose whether to save the Bat or flee. But two games later we find out that mercs were already prepared to take down Joker and Arkham Knight himself was watching over Bats. So this choice didn`t make any sense.

Even if noone would have been there to stop the clown - there`s a Superman in Metropolis, so the imbecile was doomed anyway.

- Challenges. What`s the reason in their existence? Waste of SSD space - random copy-pasted moments from campaign, but without story. 

- Hugo Strange. I hate psychiatrists. Their looks, their smug behavior, their overconfidence, would have strangled and/or bleeded every last one of these sons of...what were we talking about? Ah, the game, right.
So...why they actually chose this old bald as$hole as Bat`s nemesis? He isn`t Lex Luthor - no money, no charisma, no good looks, nothing! It took him 1 sword stab and that`s it - the greatest villain. Don`t make me laugh.

- Alfred`s pajama still doesn`t protect Bruce from anything. Look at armor from Origins and Knight - these outfits are badass.

- Who are Tyger mercs? 

- DLC`s. Boring.

- Bane and Deadshot boss fights. Pathetic.

But:

+ Combat got better. More bone-breaking combinations, predator moves and my favourite "disarm and destroy".

Thankfully Origins rebooted Batman in a more dynamic way.

review_text:
Slow, boring and tedious.
All the talking bout it's being difficult is lies. Battles don't provide any challenge, most of the time I've played with my eyes half closed, the only thing truly kills in this game is it's extreme boredom. Enemies are slow and stupid, most of the time just fuss around to give a player even more time to breathe. Elite variants don't seem to be interesting either, like there is a guy, who spawns a shield and heals under it. Well, ok. Sometimes there are a bunch of melee enemies preventing you from entering the barrier and killing him, but mostly they are too scarce and helpless to make a difference. Even a thought of traversing an empty map from one enemy camp to another eventually becomes so haunting, i don't want to start another run.
Roguelike elements are lies. You get random bonuses for farming (i can't call it a fight) enemy camps, but they all are so minor, variety is so low, they don't make your runs different at all, don't affect a playstyle a tiny bit. From one point I've started picking em randomly, like they don't exist at all.
Weapon variety is laughable. Range is heavily nerfed for balancing purposes, headshots provide a comical ~25% damage bonus, which results in bolt action rifle taking same amount of headshots and bodyshots to kill a minor enemy. 
To make the game harder you need to lvl up "gnosis", so for a while you will be stuck in hilariously easy earlygame with the smallest amount of enemies per square km I've ever seen in shooter genre. I thought the game eventually become harder, but no, i guess i need more grind to progress further towards harder encounters, but i can't force myself into this boredom. This game feels like an one huge tutorial, which never ends. 
I think devs should make a difficulty sliders, like health, damage, enemy quantity multipliers, various handicaps for players to let em tune more "high risk, high reward" style of action. Otherwise there is nothing to do.

review_text:
Writing a review for a game I don't recommend yet experience love and hate for is a very difficult prospect.

At the current time of writing, I've spent too much money on this game than I even care or dare to admit to myself, and I've spent more time on it ( 1275 hours ) than it rightfully deserves and yet I've played the bare minimum of the story, prefering to avoid it entirely. So then, what is it that attracts me to this game? What is it that keeps me playing despite how much I dislike a lot of it's attitudes?


Let's start with what I hate.

I hate how they keep pushing lootboxes constantly. Every new ship is pretty much hidden away behind a lockbox. You don't have to get them is the argument and it is indeed a valid one, but it fails to understand and take into consideration that all those ships are the popular ones that people want to have. Of course I understand that if they had put all ships in the C-Store, the game would most likely not seen the light after 10+ years of being alive.

I hate how there's bugs around that are 8+ years old that still haven't gotten fixed.

I hate how the character creator has only seen removal of features as opposed to improvements.

I hate how limiting customization can be for characters and ships.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 is kinda hard to describe. It's a very bizarre open world survival horror game about a small town being ravaged by plague. You're a doctor and you have to figure out what's causing the plague and how to create a cure, all the while being stalked by people and unknown entities. Similar to Dead Rising's time cap, you have 12 days to complete the game, which is around 25-30 hours. 

The town and it's people feel like they belong in another reality, in an uncanny valley sort of way. The atmosphere is filled with dread and hopelessness. From the moment the game begins, the town seems like Purgatory. The whole town will slowly start to become insane and men won't be above murder for long. Sound design and music are top notch. Voice acting is limited, but it's understandable because there's tons and tons of dialogue. It has an insane amount of interesting lore in it. The writing is absolutely unforgettably phenomenal. You boot the game up and you're immediately immersed in this weird, dark, terrifying world. 

For a long time, you'll probably end up having absolutely no idea what the hell is going on, and most characters seem to be speaking in riddles! And if you ask them about what's going on, they seem to have no clue either. NPC's can lie here. Unlike in most RPG's, you can't trust people face-up. They have their own agendas and world views. If you believe everything that every NPC you meet says, you'll end up getting screwed over.

Gameplay itself is nothing special, but it's by no means bad in any way. Basic FPS controls with looting and sneaking. Melee combat and shooting is fine, although I have to say, any kind combat in this game is like a dizzying nightmare. You'll be horrified to know that a fight is about to start. Killing and dying is fast, the combat in general is vicious and uncertain. Dying is the last thing you ever want to happen. If you're anything like me, you'll probably do everything in your capabilities to avoid a fight of any kind.

The game as a whole is like one massive puzzle which you will most likely not figure out the first time playing, and you'll probably end up starting over, which I think is intended. You're supposed to learn from your past mistakes and try again. The game is absolutely brutal and making big mistakes can easily lead to having to start over. But things become manageable once you understand what is required of you. It doesn't require complex pattern recognition or lightning fast reflexes, quite the contrary, the game is slow in terms of combat and survival mechanics. It's all about carefully planning ahead and thinking for yourself.

I love the description on the store page, it sums up the difficulty pretty well: "An uphill battle. Your own body is only waiting for an opportunity to give up and betray you. Things are changing from bad to worse and the odds are stacked against you."

I highly recommend this masterpiece if you're willing to test your sanity and patience. There's nothing quite like it. Pathologic 2 blew my mind, it's easily one of the most engaging and unforgettable experiences in entertainment I've ever had. With that said, it's definitely not for everyone. It's not a fun game at all and it isn't trying to be, it's an experience. Many times I felt needlessly tormented and stressed out about things like whether or not I am going to make it somewhere in time, or if I am going to run out of supplies, and if I do, what depravities would I  have to do to get myself back on track. But the reward of seeing more incredible dialogue and lore and seeing where everything is going was always way more than enough to keep me going. In many ways it even gives everything it's distinct flavor; you're suffering just like the rest of the Town is. 

I guess Pathologic 2 even made me kind of obsessed about it for a few weeks. Not sure if there will ever be anything like it again, but it's definitely altered my view of art and entertainment in general. It's by no means the timeless Holy Grail, but if we ever get to see the perfect piece of entertainment, it's on these tracks.

"Convenience is poison. One must accustom themselves to pursue any intention as soon as it appears, regardless of difficulty. Otherwise one burns out, gives in to doubt, starts fearing oneself. The bolder the dream, the more surely it becomes dust when the moment is lost."

The story, at least from the very beginning, sucks.  It assumes I care about my character and that I care about whoever my character is working for, and this predicament they are in which has brought him to this point.  I actually started to write this review, realized I might have overlooked some background the game had given, and went back in to replay it.  Nope - there's nothing here to compel me to care about the characters - this is purely "kill the other people because it's your job" as the motivation.  At this point I can't say I'm sure I'll leave this installed on my system.

ADDENDUM:  Allegedly Peter Marinker is a featured voice actor in this game, so I'll give it another try just because I really like his voice.

review_text:
This is overall a recommend based on about 90 hours of gameplay combined between a Windows MiniPC (AMD Ryzen 7 5875U, 32GB RAM) and a SteamDeck OLED 1TB. For background, I only watched the .hack/sign anime series and played the first game in the PS2 series when I was a kid. I am doing this rating after completing all 4 games. 

Overall, I give this a RECOMMEND but barely. I’d overall say 7/10. 

THE GOOD:
- Nostalgia: I do appreciate some of the connections to my childhood (Mac Anu, Hidden Forbidden Holy Ground, layout features, etc.). 
- Leveling system: I personally think they do a good job of trying to find different types of maps as you level up and go from game to game, so it feels like the dungeons are different but the overall concept/mechanics are similar. 
- Story; Story is okay, though I think they could have put more into the last game. 
- Memoir system: You can never really not know what’s next between the map and memoir, though this further encourages mashing skip through the crazy number of cutscenes. 

THE MEH:
- Amount/Balance of Cutscenes: Way too much and what’s the point because you can skip through almost all of them very quickly. It almost became an instinct by the time I had played it for maybe 10-20 hours.
- Gift System; The stupidest way to equip your party members. Why??
- Party System: It doesn’t really give you much reason to consistently use all of the characters. Some come and go but there are a couple early on that can carry you through Game 4. 

THE BAD:
- No cloud saves: This alone is a big hit. I have yet to own another game that doesn’t have cloud saves. Just not forgivable and also keep in mind if you uninstall and haven’t backed up, your data is gone. 
- Optimization is terrible; The lag on my PC is the absolutely stupidest thing ever. Lumina Cloth was laggy as hell (and you spend a long time there, fun). All of the Skeith fights, including the final one, and many bosses were stupidly laggy. Imagine playing through 3/4 games on a laggy as hell PC only to  find out that the SteamDeck runs the game flawlessly, but have to cope and play the last game BECAUSE THERE ARE NO GD CLOUD SAVES!!!

So overall I think the game has a cool story (if you don’t fall into the temptation to skip the cutscenes). I would BUY IF ON SALE but NO WAY JOSÉ AT $50 PAL.

This game is the bane of my existence.  My League of Legends.  I just do not have the competitive drive that seemingly everyone else has in order to enjoy playing the game on either Survivor nor Killer side.  Yet I keep coming back like the abusive ex-wife that gave me a heroin addiction because there's just this SOMEthing about it that I somehow enjoy; not that I could put it to words.

Playing Survivor has become a gamble of who's going to get Tunneled first and for me personally dissuades playing in a squad as you'll always have a friend twiddling their thumbs with nothing to do for potentially 10-20 minutes while they wait for the match to be over.  Lesser capable Killers who don't use Meta perks such as myself risk every game being a punching bag to a Bully Squad or Gen-Rushed by a team of Survivors they could just never find.
I hear the development team knows how unfriendly DBD is to beginners, but it's not just the overwhelming amount of Killers with different abilities and Perks with different interactions, but the PLAYERS just as well.  I've seen many times where a Survivor is inadvertently tunneled out of a game because they're not as well knowledged as the rest, and witnessed Killers whom have only JUST downloaded the game absolutely demolished by well-versed Survivors.  As someone who markets themselves as a "Casual" gamer, these are serious turnoffs for myself and I can reason many others as well.

It's just a shame that there isn't anything that properly competes with DBD that'll last.

100% in ~130 hours

Great game, and might be my favorite of the series so far (0, K1, K2, 3, 4). Each of the 5 main characters has unique side content [spoiler](taxi, hunting, dance battles, baseball)[/spoiler] that, for the most part, is fun and interesting. The story overall was coherent and engaging with a few twists that, thankfully, didn’t involve any rubber bullet nonsense (Y4). It took awhile to complete this game because there is an insane amount of content available. 

To 100% you’ll need to complete every mini-game objective, which wasn’t too hard, but some mini-games were extremely boring; looking at you sea fishing, comedy team, VF 2, snowball fights, and air hockey! To meet the eating requirement, you'll need to consume over 560 food items from an innumerable number of restaurants across multiple cities. The terrible hostess mini-game returns where you spend hours talking to these 5 ladies instead of doing anything fun. The coliseum also returns, but this time comes with an excessive grind that must be repeated on 4 total characters. For each character, you’ll need to complete at least 40 knock-out matches without losing just to unlock all the levels for that single character. Losing a match will drop your rank almost as fast as you can gain it.

Lastly, the last few bosses had way too many QTE events. It felt like there was a QTE after every single tiger drop. An infrequent single button, or sequence QTE is fine, but these all smash a button rapidly for 10 seconds for.. action? 

I know I've been complaining a lot, but it really was a great experience that vastly outperformed some of the others in the series. I would gladly recommend this game to any Yakuza fan that doesn't plan on getting all the achievements. Getting 100% in this game was borderline masochistic at times.

review_text:
First, my preface; I have been playing Animalia since about a year after it released, albeit not over a large number of hours. I play every few updates to see what has changed over time. For animal survival games, my go-to is The Isle, but I was hoping Animalia would provide a slightly less intense experience. However, thus far the result has been disappointing.

1) The game isn't the best looking or moving. The static elements of the game look just fine, but it's the player models, the things which are most important and you spend the most time looking at, which need serious work. Every single model has something wrong with it either in the way it moves or the way it looks. The transitions between gates are either slowed down to allow for a transitional animation that isn't there or jolt you into the next gear like a stick shift that's transmission is about to go out. Jumping is an awful affair on animals that have it. Swimming is stupidly slow and difficult. And with the new O2 system, you're more likely to drown than make it across a river that wouldn't be that hard to cross otherwise. Also due to the O2 system, Crocs can barely stay underwater, meaning you can't get the jump on players coming to take a drink. Climbing with leopards is a tedious affair. Most trees aren't meshed for it and those that are have such spotty meshes that it's hard to tell whether your leopard is going to fall through the branch or glide a few feet in the air but still technically be on the tree. Forget about actually hunting from up there! You're completely visible to all players on the sparsely foliated trees, and if that wasn't enough; you can't control where you're going to land when you jump down in addition to leopards not having a vertical pounce attack in the first place.

2) The map is almost completely empty. If you're buying this game to explore a beautiful map and see all the unique locations the creators have built, please take your expectations down a notch. The map that is currently available is more akin to the Day of Dragons map than that of The Isle: EVRIMA. There are vast swaths of badlands where no players ever go, or are ever incentivized to go. There are only a few locations where everyone tends to congregate, meaning you have to hang around those locations as well if you either want A. to interact with another player on the map or B. ever want to find food as a predator. There is a large jungle canyon network on the map that can take an hour or two to get out of if you don't know the way. It would be fun if you had a chance at encountering something scary there, but most players steer clear of it after getting lost in there once or twice with no food or water.

3) The game doesn't feed carnivores. One crucial aspect of a survival game is feeding predators via NPCs when they are nearly starving due to either a lack of other, weaker players around, the player actively hiding from another, stronger player, or other such circumstances. Animalia just doesn't have this. Dotted around the map are carcasses which sort of serve this purpose, but are once again just opportunities for players to congregate and chit chat IMVU style. There's no experience of trudging through the badlands and spotting a lizard in the distance that might just carry you over till you get to the other side. There's no nearly starving as a juvenile but finally managing to catch that smaller mammal you've been working on for half an hour. There's no experience of sitting in a bush as a young bachelor lion at night in a foreign pride's territory and them locating you via the gazelle the game spawned to quiet your growling stomach. There's no learning to fish as a croc, even, because they added playable crocs before adding AI fish for them to eat. AI has been introduced by server modders, but the tiny affect their mods add to the game does not make up for the massive hole in the fabric these developers are trying to weave. The developers have mentioned AI several times, to my knowledge through rumor, yet have chosen to add multiple new species to the game instead on claims that the AI is taking longer to develop. Well, I think I speak for most of the player base in that we'd rather get bare bones AI into the game over another shoddy animal model which adds no value or playability to the game.

4) Combat is... strange. Fighting carnivore v carnivore (or non-tank herbie) in this game is just a game of who has the smaller ping at the end of the day. Whomever can keep on target, without hitting a lag spike, wins. The combat in this game is just so different to the nature it's trying to emulate. review_text:
Pathologic 2, at the time of this review, has one route out of three published. This means the Haruspex's route must stand alone, while simultaneously convincing players to be interested in the upcoming routes. Unfortunately, if you look past the survival mechanics that occupy most of the player's time, it comprehensively fails to deliver on its fancy narrative themes or give its characters depth.

The first thing the game tells you is that Pathologic 2 is literally a play in which the player is the main actor and the audience. A corollary is that the other NPCs are just there for your benefit, and aren't working towards their own goals. The two competing healers don't do anything to hinder you (besides give you quests), and many, many other characters' arcs have been rewritten to focus on the Haruspex, breaking the motivations that made them well-written in the original. This is perhaps most apparent in the fact that there are no factions: the player is tasked with caring for every person in the town, for no other reason than "his father told him to watch out for a list of kids", but the future of the Town has nothing to do with those people.

Everything revolves around the Haruspex, and yet nobody will tell you anything. There's a constant stream of "go away, we're having an important conversation that doesn't involve you", with occasional deep-sounding vagaries about fate and puppetry. This is intended to keep you interested in the upcoming routes, but frustrates the route's ability to stand on its own. Characters frequently say the Haruspex is too stupid to understand their activities, which falls short of being a running joke and becomes deeply uncomfortable given that he's the game's only Indigenous PC. At the same time, you can meet characters' "Reflections" that tell you the NPCs' innermost feelings, which a) stops the game from ever showing these feelings through actions, and b) limits their characterization for the upcoming routes.

Pathologic 2 has received wide acclaim in gaming journalism for its high-concept themes. (For the record, this constant praise let the lead writer fly under the radar as a child groomer for years). But the theme receiving the most attention- the Haruspex's mixed Indigenous identity- is explored through a shockingly racist set of quests (it's revealed that [spoiler]the Kin aren't harmed by the plague because they're a mindless, faceless mass who don't think for themselves[/spoiler]), and ends with a binary choice that completely fails to accomplish what both the antagonist and the director tell you was the point of the game: [spoiler]the Haruspex is meant to connect the Town and Kin, but the actual choice is which one of them you want to kill[/spoiler].

The other big theme is the meta of characters' fate being set within the video game, and leads to what I think is its best concept: an ending where [spoiler]you reject your part in the game and leave the Town to journey with your companion, a personification of Death, forever[/spoiler]. However, despite the game's insistence that "you have to break your fate to become truly human," this is framed as unequivocally the worst thing you could do! The game contradicts itself on both of its thematic selling points, and never offers the player an appropriate narrative conclusion.

Death itself is a core topic in Pathologic, which is why this game's failure to incorporate it is so jarring. While almost any of the NPCs can die, none of their deaths affect the game whatsoever. In contrast to the original, you can get any ending with all of your adherents dead, and if someone does die all you get is a few lines about how sad it makes the Haruspex feel. The way the game tracks player deaths is nicely done, but this combination just reinforces how the player is the only person who matters in the Town.

A few positives: the game has really high-quality textures and lighting, and the game balance gives you a solid survival challenge with varying accessibility options. The tincture-brewing mechanics are a huge improvement from the original. The herb collection is enjoyable, and there are a lot of great one-line NPCs (shady shop guy my beloved...). Best of all is the Fellow Traveler's character, who appears throughout the game to give exceptionally relevant conversations and advice.

However, the optimization is notoriously bad: every single outdoors asset is loaded all the time, including when you're in locations that aren't even related to them like dreams and windowless buildings! The omnipresent level fog doesn't do anything to fix this, and just cuts off your vision at an arbitrary point. Going through the entire multi-stage introduction when you start a new game is agonizing. There's also a baffling feature where wounded townsfolk will always run away from you faster than you can catch them. But the real issues are all in the narrative. Every time I think about this game, I realize it's more badly written than I thought.

The game's really only good for taking pictures in. Half of its problems are unfixable parts of the Haruspex's route, and the other half will require a huge amount of retconning to handle in the upcoming routes. It's not well written at all.

So I'll recommend the game for a certain audience, if you get your expectations straight. It's mainly an atmospheric puzzle game, any lore the game might convey will be through the scenery and it's up to you to interpret it. The fps shooting definitely isn't the core mechanic but the threat that enemies pose certainly conveys a sense of vulnerability.

They put most of their effort into the aesthetics and the labyrinth-like levels are nicely crafted. The animations of the surrounding fleshy bio-machines are meticulously mechanical, detailed and over-complicated, that helps to inspire wonder and horror. Is Flesh punk an aesthetic theme yet?

It took me 4 hours to beat, and there's no replay-ability that I know of, so for most people the full price might not be a good value proposition. It was a short experience that will leave a lasting impression.

I've only played a couple of hours but I already had some quite dissappointing moments in the game.
Basically the game feels that it only can be fun if you've already played it and know every corner and secret beforehand. Experiencing it first time is not pleasant.

Bad level design. You can't backtrack and collect loot you were unable to take because you have a limited inventory. You have to know beforehand that there will be a shop soon to sell loot.
You have to know beforehand where to go first because you will be locked out of loot and secrets if you accidentially chose the main story path through the level. It's not really evident which passages are optional.
Enemies appear out of nowhere on script. You can't really see how many enemies you're fighting. Their number can increase midfight just because.
GRP throw an enemy will collide and stop midflight even with smallest collision. Looks unnatural. You lose energy on bad throws and it doesn't feels right.
Some enemy attacks are unavoidable and will damage you no matter what.
If you know beforehand that there will be an enemy you can cheat around it.
Enemy health is a mystery. Some times it takes 5 hits to kill sometimes more. You can't really see why.
Most fights are scripted so you can easily win them only if you know how to approach them. But level design is so poor that most times it's very unevident what was the intent of the level designer. So lots of reloads and experimentation which are not fun. Because you reload even on a slightest feeling that fight is going not good. Hard fights are fun to go through only a few first times. Some time into the game you understand that every fight is only hard if you have approached it wrong.
The most unnatural thing is when you fight multiple enemies they all wait their turn. They can easily rip you apart but they line up and wait while you go through them on at a time.
Game lightning is a physical strain for eyes. Even if you increase gamma.

And now I think I've played enough to rewrite my previous wall-of-text review by condensing it into something much shorter.

Although you're expected to lose often (as intended), this game is very addictive; it is on the same level as Dwarf Fortress addictive. And just like Dwarf Fortress it ruins your life by stealing away the hours from you.

The game hooks me in for hours but there is no carrot, only an endless supply of stick.

I can't refund the game, nor would I want to. Fair is fair, I played the game a lot and the dev deserves the money. But I wish I could just give away my copy of the game so I could not be tempted to play it again.

In a nutshell, I don't recommend this game for these two reasons:
1. It will ruin your life
2. There is no cake

I won't lie. I did have some fun with this game. However there are some MASSIVE issues here that ruin the entire experience.

- Your goaltender is absolutely brain-dead. I cannot tell you how many times the enemy team will be kept out of the my zone for the majority of a period but will get one measly scoring opportunity and it will go in every single time. Its is ALWAYS, one shot and one goal. It would be different if you could buff the goalie to not be a moron but alas, that's not the case. You are stuck with that idiot. It really sucks all the fun out the game for when losing just boils down to, did my goaltender poop the bed or not?

- I know its supposed to be a kooky fun game with wacky mechanics but most of it just boils down to removing your ability to play. How many different forms of "you can't play the game" did you need to put in?
You have your players turning into ice, losing their stick, being checked down by the enemy, being checked down by the goalie, being checked down by the referee, being forced to dance disco, losing your stick being farted away from the play, etc. The creativity here was severely lacking. Games that base their difficulty on taking away your ability to play are so common these days and I'm really tired of it.

- It took me maybe an hour to an hour and half to beat the campaign but on top of that it honestly feels like after about 3 hours or so, you've seen all the game has to offer. The "rogue-like" aspect of it is paper thin and I do not think this game is worth 20 bucks. This should have been closer to 10 dollars.

review_text:
This game is the definition of mid. It's just pretty generic in so many ways, the combat, the story, the progress trees, all serviceable, but not memorable, engaging, or interesting. The whole game just kinda feels like a grind. It's only like 10-15 hours, depending how much of a completionist you are, but it feels like 50 because every area is a lumbering slog. Hope you like crawling and shimmying, because that's like 10 percent of the total movement in this game. Hope you like clunky, tank-like controls, because your guy moves like he's carrying a backpack full of watermelons.

There are single digit variation of dungeons in the game. So far I've only really seen 4-5. There may be more, but I doubt it. Based on the dungeon design, combat is unavoidable. That itself isnt' a problem but the game does a good job of making sure you're leveled up quickly. However, it means that a lot of the battles are going to be fluff since you get heavily reduce exp and you can only escape them with an item.

Picture the complexity of arma paired with the simplicity of roblox. On top of that, the game itself is horribly buggy and terribly designed right off the start. The plot is the exact same thing it always is, but with a new coat of paint. The graphics are marginally better than the second game. 

This 'game' is just an utter scam. It's the Madden of third person shooters. It makes even the newest Gears of War games look like bouts of divine creativity. The maps are always identical to one another and offer no variety. The worlds are always empty and devoid of life. The AI is always horrible and bland. The combat is always horribly uninspired and boring, offering nothing unique at all. Animations are practically recycled from the old games, just like everything else within this horrid experience. 

The first real mission is an escort mission, which have always been the worst thing to ever exist within these barely passable games. They always involve horrible pathing from the drivers, terrible map design that leads to glitches and the vehicle getting stuck, and laughable enemy spawns that you can literally see. The FIRST mission in this 7 0 D O L L A R G A M E is an escort mission where the car gets completely turned around 3 times in a row and then breaks, getting stuck for zero purpose. Full health and at every tutorial ridden junction it stops at, the AI fails to move on when you clear the path and just sits there. 

The tutorials are even terrible, forcing you into buggier sequences where you're forced to jump through their terribly conceived hoops just to progress. The tutorial introducing Grappling hook loadouts, which might have been fun were it not made by apes slapping a keyboard while starving, was so horribly broken that it locked me out of weapon switching. I closed out of the menu accidentally while trying to do it and the game decided that I was no longer worthy of playing. I couldn't grapple anymore, couldn't switch weapons, couldn't reload, and restarting my objective didn't fix that. 

Every popup in this game, of which there are many for some reason, makes this game lag. You're constantly getting popups about achievements, milestones, feats, or just your score compared to your steam friends who also play this game. Even if you have NONE, it still pops up non stop and the entire game freezes every single time this happens. I'm on a 2080 with an i9 and this game can't handle its own popups. The frame rate is stable, but the entire game freezes every time you kill anyone because you get a popup telling you about it. 

I have not seen such a blatant scam of a game in ages. This feels like it was made by a team only kept motivated by indentured servitude and the knowledge that their families will die without what little money they receive. I got this from Humble Bundle and I feel horrendously scammed. This game having even mixed ratings, let alone positive ones, is the prime example of how and why the gaming industry has become a joke so old that everyone's tired of even thinking about it. 

What a fucking joke.

It is tough to evaluate the Yakuza 3-5 set of games. They are plainly a step back, graphically, mechanically, from the prequel Y0 and remade Kiwami 1/2. This feeling continues into Yakuza 5, which like Yakuza 4 before it is a narrative split with more playable characters than just Kiryu. Unlike 4, where Kiryu was kept in reserve until later, we start with Kiryu here and end up with a plot that involves five different characters in four different cities - including Haruka, Kiryu's (formally adopted? I forget) daughter, who is chasing her dreams of being an idol by getting into street dance battles. Yeah, really.

There were big chunks of the game that actively repulsed me. Saejima's portion of the game, which is spent part in prison, part in a completely imagined version of a city, part in the snowy wilderness, and part in the actual version of that city, is particularly bad in this regard. I might have fought two tigers in Kiwami 2 but I'm not here to hunt bears in the snow, with traps and rifles and all that stuff. Haruka's part of the game, while narratively important, is also quite a jarring shift and while I didn't mind the departure, it's also a long interruption from the big yakuza plot that's been brewing now for two games. 4 was an interesting shakeup to the formula but this continuation of 4 was not a good follow-up to that shakeup. There were parts that I really enjoyed but overall... eh.

I really, desperately want to like this game but I just can't

I love Star Trek and this is a fun way to run around in that universe. I'm normally not a fan of MMO games but this one plays more like a single player game so that's a plus. The environments and gameplay loop is pretty simple but again, I don't mind at all

But the space combat... I cannot for the life of me figure out how to have fun in space. It doesn't matter my tactics, my ship, my loadouts, every combat is the same. Fly around trying to keep my shields up so I can land a few hits then run away as fast as I can and hope my shields come back so I can do it again. Then I still explode several times

I've watched a bunch of playthroughs and advice videos but it's the same thing every time. Ship combat is abysmal and unfortunately, that's a full half of the game

I played a few dozen hours of this game through the Arc launcher a few years ago before I put it away and then tried it out again through Steam to see if it was better and it is exactly the same

It's not fun in any way

review_text:
Alright, I’m probably going to make some enemies with this one, but whatever.

First, let’s talk about the main selling point of the game: its atmosphere. Heavy, morbid, gory. That’s what made me buy it in the first place.

Now, the story. Utterly meaningless. The first person who dares tell me it’s “poetic” or some other nonsense I’ve read online, I’ll make them eat their keyboard. The story goes in circles, leads absolutely nowhere, and tells us nothing.

The music? Practically nonexistent. You get a bit here and there, another piece after four and a half hours of gameplay when you enter the final area, and that’s about it. And the people who said the silence was meant to “enhance the oppressive atmosphere” shame on you. That’s complete nonsense. A good soundtrack would’ve amplified that atmosphere ten times better than silence and random ambient noises.

The gameplay mechanics are archaic, they made me want to quit more than once, and the combat is absolute garbage. Slow, punishing for no reason. I felt like the game was breaking some fundamental design rules, like enemies being able to charge attacks while I’m stuck in an unskippable cinematic finisher on another enemy I didn’t even choose to finish off.

And sorry, but €40 with no discount for six hours of gameplay? Yeah, look it up the game barely lasts that long. Even at €12 on sale, don’t buy it. Just watch someone get paid to play it instead. It’s more frustrating than enjoyable.

Yes, I’ve been harsh on Scorn, but I honestly never thought I’d play a game that would make me want to hate video games altogether.

review_text:
[h1] It definitely was an experience, though a lot less cathartic than the original. [/h1]

And I'm not talking about "I've already seen it" kinda feel. In fact, it is a very different game, enough to justify being a sequel, not a remake. It works a lot better as a game, the mechanics finally enhance the narrative and you have a much harder time to escape all the challenges it throws at you, which makes the struggle element so consistent throughout, but it lacks... a narrative punch. Yes, now people can actually die of the plague! But... it feels like they made them more bland because of that? EDIT: I checked. Yeah. It is true. Even if the kiddos from the Isidor's list die, it changes... nothing. So the game built around the idea of mortality rewards you with nothing if someone dies AND doesn't punish you if they die? That's bullshit. Honestly, I feel betrayed here.

With some characters, they did find an interesting way to re-introduce them. With others... They became less. I can't say I felt strongly about characters other than Burakh's friends and the kiddos, and even then, not to all of them. 

The music is so not present, that sometimes I forget that it's even there. There are hardly any tracks I remember right after completing it, while the original is a treasure trove of great music. A bigger focus on ambience felt fresh at first, but by the second half I was bummed out that I can't run around the town vibing to the otherworldly tunes of P1. 

The intended difficulty is a lil overtuned, I'd say. Yes, now it is the point that you can't be everywhere and help everyone. Still, I barely have any time to finish up with the important biz! And the time is starting to flow faster and faster with each passing day! The game really expects you to loot the infected/cured parts of the town to keep your balance and meds up, but howwww, whennnnn. And deaths causing permanent effects on you and the city is cool, but the way Mark talks to you after you die is so eugghhhh.

I like how they overhauled the haruspex part of the gameplay. It was soso not obvious where to look for the herbs, or how to mix them to get something decent, but here it's pretty easy to understand and it does a good job of tying the narrative of being a traditional medicine healer into the gameplay. Being chased by the entire town for cutting out organs right in front of their eyes was thrilling. And assigning separate trust levels to each region of the town is a great idea. 

And speaking about the narrative... the message it tries to convey is iffy, yeah. I may be misremembering P1, but I feel like the overarching idea of progress vs traditions was better presented there. Here, it feels wrong. The way they portray the kin is... oof. I don't wanna spoil stuff, I'll just say that I think they done them really dirty here. 

[h2] It is still a great game, and I like how they reimagined lots of things, but I can't shake off the feeling that something is very wrong at the core of it. [/h2]
 
TL;DR: Instead of "ooooh, cooooool" kinda mindfuck of P1 I got "huuuhhhhh, whyyyyy?" kinda mindfuck of P2
I think I prefer what the Marble Nest was going for than the main game.

review_text:
Scorn has an incredible art style, good animations, and well-crafted level design. Visually, it’s a masterpiece. But beyond that, it falls short.

The game is very short—I finished it in just 6 hours, even taking my time exploring and admiring the world. There’s also no reason to replay it, as there are no choices, secrets to find, or alternative game modes. There’s no story context either: you don’t know who you are, what you’re doing, or why. The lack of guidance, combined with unexplained controls, made finding my way especially frustrating. The environment is alien, filled with buttons and interactive objects, but the game never makes it clear where to go or what to do next, leaving you to wander aimlessly and hope you're in the right place.

Combat is clunky and unrewarding. Ammo and health are scarce, and there’s no stealth option, making fights more of a hassle than fun. I ended up avoiding enemies altogether, either by waiting for them to despawn or simply running past.

At 40 Euros, I can't recommend it. For under 15 Euros in a sale, maybe—if you love the art and atmosphere.

review_text:
This is by a landslide THE MOST CLUNKY platformer I've EVER played!

The combat system needs A LOT of work.
- Weapon swings are stupidly slow. I actually cringed when I first picked up the gladius and tried it out. If you give a real life mace to a 7 year old, he's gonna swing it faster than the MC of this game swings a freaking gladius (which is designed for quick stabs btw, note to the devs).
- For some bizarre reason, the devs decided that when somebody extends their arm forward whilst jumping forward, all of their momentum from the jump magically disappears and you drop down like a rock...

Other than that, the game throws A LOT of cheap shots at you. For example: you're being conditioned to believe that your shield can block anything, including axe swings from orcs 10 times your size, or even explosive projectiles. Then there's that one random boss that damages you if you try to block it (which is a one-shot on veteran)...

Then there's the bosses... The design is pretty cool and the fights are entertaining, but a lot of them are very cheap and unnecessarily long. The ice boss for example: you triggered it, see the blizzard, cool effects and everything, then you get ready to fight it, but oh wait, you get insta hit if you didn't instantly jump on a platform after you regained control.
There are a lot of examples of such cheap shots. They're cheap shots because you're usually only going to get screwed over by them once.

Then there's the hitboxes... oh boy... suffice to say, they need A LOT of work. Often times you will stab an enemy, with your weapon literally overlapping the enemy, but no wait, the game decided you didn't actually hit it and proceeds to hit you instead. Then there are hits that land half a meter away from you, that still bizarrely hit you.

There's also the fact that they decided that the autosave shrines can't be re-triggered, so if it's right before a boss, enjoy having to keep switching your equipment around after every death, because there's no way to save again at the autosave shrines...

EDIT:
Beat the game, oh boy, does the game go downhill for the last quarter of the game. It seems like enemies are just being thrown at you in the cheapest ways possible just to slow you down as much as possible. You will end up just ignoring them and run past them, which will make things 95% easier. This last bit of the game was BY FAR just tedium and not enjoyable at all.

The second to last boss is kind of broken (Kana), her attack hits you before the animation actually shows a slash, and her dash attack makes her invulnerable even a second after it's been finished.
Usually in a game like this, when the boss uses a strong attack, it leaves them open for punishment, and Kana certainly shows that, what with the boss standing with her back towards you for like a second after the dash. But nope, she's invulnerable during that time.

The boss before that (the spider archer), you just literally have to put a small rock on the button you assigned your shield to, and you will win the fight lol.

The last boss was the most disappointing one so far. Very anticlimactic final boss, it relies exclusively on cheap gimmicks (summoning other enemies that heal her).

review_text:
Gotta say, I wasn't expecting this much from this game:

It's an incredibly detailed Hockey simulator that says "Early Access" but besides some UI changes that could be made, looks like it could be a full-blown game right now. It's a game that is easy to lose yourself in and you know you want to come back to play it once you've shut it down. Even though right now the game doesn't have actual NHL rosters in, it is incredibly easily to download the real rosters and facepacks to go along with it. The Blueline website does a better job than EA has ever done on their NHL games at updating their rosters; you can expect an updated roster almost once a week during the regular season from the website. 

There are a couple of problems with the game right now, obviously. The trading in the game doesn't work very well. You never see a blockbuster trade in the game and teams are constantly sending good players that are underperforming through the waivers. On my simulation Dion Phaneuf had a 50 point season but when I put him on the block, the best trade offer I can expect is a couple of 3rd or 4th round draft picks. This could be because of his salary, but I still think the game's trading mechanics need to be a little reworked.

If you are looking for an extremely detailed GM simulator than Eastside Hockey Manager is the game to get. Don't let the "Early Access" deceive you, this is a game that is easy to waste hours on and is challenging and rewarding. Recommended to anyone that loves hockey and wants to know what goes on behind the scenes!

Great game! A hell of a lot of fun and a great deviation from the SocCar genre.

Something to note though:
While the gameplay and aesthetic is similar to Rocket League, you can't go in expecting the ball physics and car physics to be the same. The ball will slow to a halt and curling shots is much more exaggerated, which both make a lot of sense given the fact this is a golf game. Also to note is that dodging (double tapping the jump key) doesn't auto-align your car the same way either. Turbo Golf Racing is it's own game, and just because your a Rocket League god, you can't expect to jump straight into this and be at the same level. What's obvious quickly, and in my opinion excellent to see, is that this is very much a game with a low entry level, but a high ceiling when it comes to skill!

review_text:
The game is great! I'm a Trekkie at heart and now I'm living it (well, virtually anyways).
The only thing...
the 8000 refine limit on dilithium. I know the reasoning, preventing "inflation" in the dilithium-zen exchange and encouraging monetization, but no one ever actually trades zen for dilithium -- why would they? once they have zen, they have the currency for the absolute best stuff, there's no reason to downgrade to dilithium, and since ships beyond T5 can't be attained with dilithium, only zen or a long grind, maybe the occasional energy credit purchase from the exchange (which still takes either a long grind or a real purchase), there's still a huge monetization incentive.
Now, I get why you don't want players to have unrestricted refinement... being able to buy too many phoenix reward boxes could actually lead to less monetization incentive, but dilithium is also essential for equipment upgrades... which is a core part of the game. And... yes, I'm aware of the way you can "exploit" the exchange to transfer refined dilithium between characters... but that doesn't address the real issue... all that dilithium ore you've accumulated on one character that you can't do anything with... so perhaps instead of limiting all players to a flat 8000, you could use some sort of tiered limit... at level 1, 8000 is a lot, but at level 65, it's nothing, and you're definitely earning ore much faster than you can refine it... and to tackle the potential problems this could theoretically cause with increased dilithium transfers in the exchange... maybe you could impose a limit on the dilithium exchange... though, like I said, no one actually trades zen for dilithium, and we really just want to use that ore that's in our accounts staring us in the face that we can't do anything with... if we could just refine that... there'd be no need for the dilithium-zen exchange at all. I get why you don't want someone being able to purchase 200000 phoenix boxes at one time, but 8000 is just too limiting. It would make more sense if the limit leveled with us, starting off low, possibly even less than 8000 to begin with, and slowly increasing as we ranked up, to an amount, say, modestly more than 8000, say, between 10000 and 19000. really, having the amount be a 5 digit number, even if its only 10000, could go a very long way.
