Alright time for an updated review. 

Still no patches to fix the rampant exploits, You'll have people with uzis firing explosive ammo, people glitching through doors and breaking runs, and more. nor the broken Index controllers, nor the left handed mode.  I feel like it takes me 4 launches for every 1 good one I get.

You still lose your acquired Items and harvest, even after the patch claimed to have fixed it. So watch your progress and custom built guns continually disappear on you.

Then sit for 4 minutes waiting for a player who crashed at launch while you stare at a blank screen until it times out.  It's actually faster to just exit the game entirely and restart it, than waiting for the timer.

Oh, and I hope you enjoy making 3/4 of the way through a map and then all players get disconnected, and you lose your sound.

Under all of the problems, It's a fairly enjoyable game, but with all the issues, it's just disappointing.  It's a month after launch and there is nothing in sight as for fixes on the things I listed, plus all the other issues.

They released the game early to cash in for Christmas, and now all of us have to hope it isn't going to turn into abandonware. 

Add it to your watch list, and keep an eye on the patches to see if they legitimately fix things.

review_text:
Well, it is a good game for me. It is a not-that-short-but-not-hat-long game. The game takes around 15-20 hours to perfectly complete it. Just like the others have mentioned about the good sides, I am here just to confirm them. However, while there are many good things in this game, some bad parts are still clearly observable. 

Let's start with a good side. Honestly, I am so satisfied with my time spent in this game to play as an assassin, AKA Seeker. The presentation of this game is very simple. You are an assassin called Seeker. You start each mission by getting contracts from your employer to kills those influential people with their battalions. Yes, those people are bad guys, and your employer will clearly explain the reasons of killing them to you before starting each mission. Sorry, guys, but there is no any plot twist here, bad people are still bad, this is not Far Cry. Hence, you are a hero in this game, saving the world of being destroyed.

If you just want to be an assassin killing bad guys with guns (mostly a sniper rifle) and various technologies. Well, give this game a shot. You won't regret it. I bought this game just because I wanted to play as a sniper, that's all. 

However, there are some drawbacks that you may perhaps need to consider. First of all, an auto save in this game does not do its job well, resulting in reloading the game approximately 10-20 minutes before you get killed. You may be able to experience a situation where you manage to kill the whole army but stupidly get a damage from falling, making your 20 minutes of killing enemies in vain. Secondly, there are some bugs that may irritate you. According to my experiences, I used to kill one dude from behind, but that dude was close to the wall, causing my character stuck in the wall without being able to do anything but load my save game again. Enemies in this game possess an Aimbot, allowing them to accurately shoot regardless of your speed or distance, ensuring every shot hits its mark which is very hilarious and annoying.

Beside from these, I have no problem with it. As I said, the game is pretty fun and enjoyable for me.

review_text:
I can only reccomend this game to two kinds of people. If you're a fan of the original .hack series (Infection, Mutation, Outbreak, and Quarantine), you'll be able to enjoy this game as a continuation of the story, and for familiar gameplay with a few new twists. The only other group I can recommend Last Recode to is people who played the console release of the G.U. trilogy, and are looking to play the new fourth chapter. For anyone else, my criticisms follow.

First and foremost, I found this game to be buggy in a way not related to the story of rogue A.I. causing glitches in an online game. The game has, in my experience, a tendency to freeze. A lot. The game freezing has been such a constant problem across all volumes that I got in the habit of maintaining two save files just in case it decided to crash while saving and corrupt one of the files (though this has not occured at time of writing).

Secondly, the game is a bit easy. You might struggle a bit early on in Vol. 1, but it doesn't take long to get to the point where in any story areas, you're just cruising through without ever feeling threatened or challenged. It actually takes more effort to keep from getting to a point where you're high level and decked out in the best gear than it does to get there. Especially if you're carrying over data from one volume to the next - which you should be, it's the intended way to play and you miss out on some content by not doing so - you'll get to a point where with very minimal play outside of required sections, you'll never really need to worry about the story getting too tough to progress. Money ceases to be an issue vey quickly as well, as you can easily earn tons of it, and most of the time, using items isn't needed.

Third, there's some especially notable problems with Vol. 1 in particular, just in terms of story and pacing. After a short tutorial sequence, the game finishes off a brief period of story before you can get back to the action, ending in you getting sent on ANOTHER tutorial. One which largely covers the same things you just got done being taught. Further, there's an extended sequence in the story that involves entering a tournament. This is perhaps the most aggrivating element of the entire trillogy. Every single round of the tournament ends in getting kicked to a cutscene right before you could have finished the opponent off. This is not an exaggeration. It's literally every round. You NEVER get to actually win a round of the tournament. This is made worse since pretty much all of the scenes focus on your character being "outmatched" or "not ready" and getting pushed to his limits/forced to rely on his special "protagonist powers" to win in some way, shape, or form - made even worse by the fact that, as I noted earlier with the difficulty, it's not at all unreasonable that you'll have 10+ levels and better gear over your opponent and be able to end them in a single attack...if the game didn't force them to survive at 1 HP, that is. Fortunately, the games get better as they go on, but these early moments can make it hard to push through to the more engaging parts.

All the issues can be overlooked, but overall I just can't reccomend Last Recode to anyone who isn't already a fan, because without that level of investment, it's just not going to feel worth it.

The hours talk for themselves.

You can say this is one of the "must-plays" for the otome category. You can never go wrong with this game (or franchise, to be exact). Tons of routes, stories, MC that doesn't make you want to personally offer your own backbone so she stopped being a doormat. Though admittedly, there's one or two routes where she gets a bit annoying with "I want to be helpful" notions, even though she's already helpful enough in her own way, and perhaps she just have too much of a backbone to rush into a battle even though she knows very little sword skill. Yeah, MC actually fights sometimes, though most of times she still ended up being carried/saved by the LI(s).
The story does a great job to turn LIs with seemingly negative personality into something more redeemable and likeable, and gives shine to characters that don't seem to do much with the MC, but actually has a lot of dealings. There's not much romance going on, save for several routes. Kyoto Winds is like the introduction pamphlet to the actual otome, Edo Blossoms, which I haven't played yet, but looking forward to it. If you want an otome that goes straight to the romance points and not being talked hours and hours into historical facts (there's only one kiss CG in the game and it's on the forehead!), Kyoto Winds isn't for you, unless you can bear through it before you can finally play Edo Blossoms. Personally, I like this game very much and even I don't mind playing this without the romance options.
It's very much worth the price, and I'd totally recommend this game to any otome fanciers out there who haven't played this yet. Seriously, just play this already.

Really fun game so far, playing on Hardcore for shits and giggles and man is it a kick in the balls. I don't understand the gripes against the slow attack speed some other reviews talked about considering one of the very first equips you get from the shop increases weapon attack speed by one.

Final boss needs a buff though.

review_text:
I saw this game's trailer a super long time ago, and was in love with the HR Giger aesthetic it had going for it. Because of the super mixed reviews, I waited for a $10 sale to pick it up. Without spoiling much, I'll try and list some pro's and con's to see if this game is going to be for you.

PROS:
>Very immersive, minimal HUD elements to distract you and being able to check your health reserves and ammo by just looking down at your character model was a really great choice.
>The environment design...wow. Just wow. This place really looks and feels like hell (in a good way). Biomechanical, living structures and lovecraftian landscapes all over. Not something you see represented in games often and I think they knocked it out of the park aesthetically.
>Gunplay feels nice, even the reload animations are visceral. Combat not so much, but I'll talk about that in cons.
>Completely silent story? No dialogue at all? I'm here for that. All-environmental storytelling and leaving a ton of it up to interpretation is a pro for me. I like being able to think about a game after playing it, and when it's not all spoon fed to you it leaves a lot of theory-crafting to be done.
>Graphical fidelity is beautiful. AAA looking graphics are pretty impressive for what I'd assume is a small team of devs.
>Able to 100% in about 6 hours. This could be a pro or con for you, but for $10 I'd say I got my money's worth out of it.

CONS:
>Some of the puzzles really blow. With no dialogue or tutorials anywhere there will be a few puzzles that you will have no idea what the objective is, leading to a ton of time wasted just tinkering around.
>Having to wait an incredibly long time for environmental animations. A lot of the waiting kind of feels like padding the time out. Expect a lot of pulling lever animations and then watching the environment change for the next 20 seconds, it's going to happen a lot.
>The combat isn't great. You don't really have enough ammo to deal with everything which led to me trying to avoid fighting where I could, but this led to a lot of damage taken trying to run past enemies in 4 foot wide hallways.
>The gimmick of the last level [spoiler](not being able to use your hands)[/spoiler] was incredibly annoying and almost led to me getting softlocked. I left one of the final boss battles with 2 hits remaining, then the game forces you to take scripted damage twice after that, leading to me dying over and over. I had to backtrack to find a health station, and after seeing a bunch of other people complaining about it, I don't know how the devs didn't anticipate this happening.
>Ending felt kind of out of nowhere, definitely not a 'traditionally satisfying' ending but that's probably to be expected with the tone the game takes.

All in all, if you are a [i]patient[/i] type of gamer who likes brutally dark storytelling, doesn't mind solving some puzzles (or looking up a guide when stuck), AND you like biomechanical/HR Giger aesthetics, go for it. It's not the best game on earth but I love to see unconventional, weird, crazy games like this. I'm glad it got to see the light of day and didn't get canned by censorship for it's heavy themes. This feels more like an artpiece than a game, and I almost feel like it would be just as good if not better if the combat and puzzles were absent. I had a great time just soaking in the atmosphere and taking screenshots. I'd give it a 7 or 8 out of 10, purely because I want to see more stuff like this get made.

review_text:
You play Lucius, a formidable six year-old child. Born on the 6th of June, 1966 (you can do the conversion), Lucius has the honor of being the anti-Christ and all the light-hearted responsibilities that come with it. Visited by his dad on Birthday number six, Lucius is tasked with carrying out the whims of his father: murdering all the inhabitants of Dante Manor.
The game is comprised of nine separate chapters. Each begins with a voice-over and a notebook entry on who your next target is, and concludes with a grisly homicide and a follow-up visit from Satan to grant Lucius new powers and to bolster old ones, such as telekinesis, combustion, and mind-control. While many of the kills are creative, entertaining, and sometimes morbidly funny, what the game often requires of you to reach that moment of satisfaction often results in frustration.
As an anti-hero six-year-old Satan spawn, you’re quite the amalgam of bad-ass and unsuspected hitman – but without much motive or directive. Each kill requires you to piece together sporadic clues to determine what items or tools are necessary to manipulate your target or lure them into places they might not otherwise go (such as face-first into a stove top element to light a cigarette).

The entire game takes place at Dante Manor, an enormous, sprawling estate with dozens of rooms to explore, drawers to rifle through, and objects to steal for your nefarious ends. While the ultimate demise of each target is often original and unpredictable, reaching that moment typically mimics a “Take object A to manipulate object B to get target C to do task D”. As such, there is little freedom in getting to the end result. This is not a sandbox game and does not follow the open-ended format of, for example, the Hitman and Manhunt series – but that difference isn’t necessarily a flaw, as it serves a purpose by bolstering the narrative.
For those who enjoy all aspects of the discovery process, clicking around in different environments and ultimately finding what you’re looking for can be rewarding – although the emotion I frequently experienced was exasperation. With little feedback that you’re on the right course, the game can quickly stop being fun. Because of each mission’s strict requirements, the intended payoffs act more as a relief to pent-up frustration for finally getting it right. There was nothing more disappointing than going into the kitchen and being unable to pick up the butcher knife. The mission requirements are often unclear, as almost the entire mansion is free to roam from murder one. Further, there is no initial tutorial on the sequential nature of your murderous imperatives, so you’ll need to start clicking early, often, and indiscriminately.
Graphically, the game isn’t ugly, but a lot of the colors are washed out, the lighting is unrealistic and interferes with other sources (like the outside light interacting with ambient light), and the animations are jerky. The cutscenes are entertaining but suffer from poor camera placement and direction. Subtracting from the presentation are the unacceptably long load times. This compounds frustration when occasionally you’ll fail a mission because someone may have seen you wielding a screwdriver that you had no business wielding, or overtly using your telekinesis, drawing attention from those around. There are no waypoints, so if you fail, you’re back at the beginning, but first you’ll be staring at a load screen.
The in-game music features some fun, weird, bugle-filled atmospheric tracks, sometimes employing the cellos, violin crescendos, and orchestral choirs that are common of the horror genre. Sadly, the music is often on short loops, and can get annoying or simply feel out of place during parts of the chapters. Speaking about out of place, the game’s voice acting is B-rate at best, suffering at times from a poorly-translated script and inadequate direction. This was especially disappointing due to the game being heavily story-driven and reliant on verbal or conversational cues that felt detached.

Despite the game’s ambitious premise, its many shortfalls overshadow the things it actually does well. The murders are always a treat. Coupled with Lucius’ deadpan death-stare and the ludicrously lavish and ridiculous ways in which targets reach their bloody ends, there is often a sick, dark humor that pervades the game. This is also apparent among the surviving residents and workers as they’re picked off one by one, slowly slipping into depression or insanity, and little Lucius just stands there, taking in all the madness, while still conducting his everyday business of putting away his toys and brushing his teeth (these are sadly further nuisances – chores – that break up the narrative but add to the hilarity).

review_text:
EDIT: Quick addendum to the part where I talk about the issues with RTX, you can get past the infinite loading screen by just waiting for an absurdly long time... Another thing I forgot to mention is that RTX also breaks some of the game's scripting, so cutscenes either lose their audio entirely or it's completely disjointed, audio and music cues trigger too late and character dialogue can break as well.

Despite the fact that I kinda like the game from a technical and graphical standpoint, the animations and facial rigging are really good. I cannot recommend this game to anyone because outside of it's technical aspects, it's a very mediocre, poorly designed, badly optimised and barely functional mess.

Let's start with one issue that really grinds my gears: Ray-Tracing:

Simply put, the game completely breaks if you enable it. It may work once or twice, but after that you have to disable it if you want to keep playing otherwise it will just permanently hang on a loading screen and never actually finish loading. What is the point of adding a feature that you don't even optimise the game around? God forbid I want to experience the game with RT on, I want to see how it is utilised and how it affects the atmosphere. It worked for me initially and I got reasonably playable performance, the only downside was the increased loading times however it would actually finish loading, then it just stopped. Krafton is not interested in fixing this problem because they've written this game off as a failure and don't want to dedicate a day or two to troubleshooting the problem... or they can't get ChatGPT to fix it for them.

Gameplay wise, it's extremely repetitive, enemy variety is low and the strategy for every encounter is exactly the same, barring 2 notable examples but those are spoilers. It's a melee focused immersive horror game, the controls are extremely simple and enemy AI has been neutered to the point of being trivially easy and not even remotely threatening, even on the hardest difficulties. Hold left or hold right to dodge and alternate to dodge more than one incoming attack... that's it, there's no timing required, there's no learning patterns, just hold a strafe key, button mash and repeat.

Story is practically non-existent, it's every sci-fi/zombie story rolled into one, characters are one dimensional and have extremely basic one-note motivations. It's as stock as it gets, and the big twist is literally something you saw coming hours before.

Mercifully the game is not very long, so you can get through it in about 6 hours. Why you would subject yourself to a game that is barely functional and a worse version of a better game series that has been left long dormant without a proper ending, is entirely up to you. Me, I like this game as a benchmark for new hardware and to stress test my PC, it's graphically intensive enough to basically be this generation's version of Crysis. But outside of that, there really isn't a reason to play this over games like Dead Space, Alien: Isolation, etc. 

Additionally, Glen Schofield, creative director of the original Dead Space and The Callisto Protocol, left the company in 2023 so fat chance we're gonna see much else coming from this series.

review_text:
Graphics/sound quality 7/10: This game is not new by any means, and there is some parts of it that look janky/uncanny valley with the characters. I don't think it's a particularly bad thing given the context of the game, but I think they were more focused on quality of story than they were on quality of graphics. 

It would be a 4 or a 5 with just graphics alone, but the atmosphere of the game is portrayed extremely well and is closer to an 8. The sound quality brings it down a bit though, as there are some certain sound effects that can be rather jarring and repeat often enough to break immersion. 

Gameplay 6/10: The premise is good, the mechanics are lacking. There is a lot of weight to your decisions and actions in the game, but the pacing of movement as well as the clunky inputs can often be frustrating. This frustration can be compounding as you get further into the game and run into your own consequences. The only reason I give it a decent score is because that is partially intended. Otherwise, it would be a 3. The difficulty can be adjusted in many ways to accommodate though, and I would recommend this if you are having a really hard time.

I will put this up to dated engine restrictions, but this game is extremely punishing and plays more like a puzzle game than anything else. If you aren't someone who is patient (would recommend playing over time as compared to rushing it), this game will be very frustrating to you. Taking the story in parts, like 2-3 days per session is preferable to prevent burnout.

Story 9/10: One of the most intriguing stories delivered through mostly text dialogue I have ever played. Both "out there" and grounded in the plot at the same time. All the characters have their own personalities, and you may find yourself feeling one way or another towards them as the game progresses. The overarching themes and narrative are both perpetually confusing and clarifying as time moves forward. There are a few lose plots I feel like they didn't develop all the way, but maybe I missed something. There is a lot to unpack with this game, and I think you get your moneys worth just with the story alone (I have not played the DLC). 

The weight of your choices and the urgency of choosing options leaves many unanswered questions on first playthru... you will not have too many answers at the end of the first playthru. I would play the first time without any guides/story look up, and then youtube other story elements if you find yourself unable to continue with future playthrus.

As someone who played this game for hundreds of hours, I enjoyed watching it grow and become more complex. The reality of the situation for the game today, though, is that the complex systems and ramping-up of the game require you to do things in a very specific way. It becomes a game of "How long can you stick to this specific plan?" rather than a game with multiple ways to succeed and move forward. You need to build a maze-like area for the tower defense portion, but if you make it too long, the monsters will just break down your fences anyways. So it's about learning what you can get away with, and then doing exactly that over and over again.
As much as it pains me to write this review, I can't recommend this for anyone new unless you're looking to figure out a complex gameplay path, memorize it, and stick to it.

For myself and apparently many, many others, this game is unplayable.
Something to do with Realtek and Creative soundcards.
I have 39 minutes logged and that is just from the increments of testing the exe over hours worth of searching the net and attempting every kind of fix we could think of.
I thought it may be the Steam port but in our search for a solution even came across people who had this issue with their physical copy.
The best result we came up with was -nosound, which let the exe load properly but as you might guess, left us with a game that had NO SOUND.
That is not by any means an acceptable solution for a game regarded as "atmosphereic".

This is a pretty big title and the soundcards in question are quite common.
There is absolutely no reason this issue sould have made it through production, let alone not be patched for the decade since its release.

If you do not have the cards in question, I suppose you could buy the game without issue (?)
If you are running Realtek or Creative soundcards however, my recommendation is a resounding "NOPE!"

What I "can" recommend however, is that if you or someone you know has this game and cannot play it due to such issues and have yet to leave a review, please do so by leaving a negative recommendation citing your inability to play in the review.
Perhaps if they receive enough of them, they will actually get off their butts and do something about it.

review_text:
Sometimes all a narrative game needs is a good story and you can forgive the faults. However, To The Moon has everything going against it despite having a very unique and interesting story.

The dialogue is quite bad. At some times cringeworthy, and other times just missing the mark on a joke/reference. It feels as if the author knew the destination for their story, but didn't put enough effort into how the characters would get there.

The music does all the heavy lifting. Due to the terrible dialogue, the game relies on the amazing soundtrack to carry you through the story beats. This is the biggest strength of this game because the music completely nails every setpiece. I'm confident if they removed every line of dialogue from this game, used only emotes and sprite work, this would be a knockout.

The controls are frustrating. Since you are really just walking around in this game, easily moving your character around should be a top priority. However, your character advances too many steps in a button press, leaving you to run into many walls because you overshot.

A very unique story dragged down from the sum of its faults.

review_text:
This game is for anyone that enjoys playing sport sims and loves hockey. The control you get in this game is unreal - literally every aspect of managing a team is presented in this and you are free for the most part to do whatever you want as the GM and head coach of your team. You can be very involved and contribute to every detail that makes up your club or you can be more selective and only manage certain things. It's all up to you as the game can run many parts of the team on its own. 

The coverage this game has is pretty amazing as well. You have the NHL of course as well as the AHL and ECHL for the NA minors as well as many European leagues and other overseas leagues. Canadian juniors as well and even the SPHL, which is a minor league lower than the ECHL, so practically any league you might want to play is likely in this. Another thing very enjoyable in this that I mentioned earlier is the game has a lot of depth in regards to how much you can put into the game. Everything from a team's lines and PP/PK units to much more intensive things like every player's individual tactics such as their focus on being more defensive or offensive, how hard they hit, IF you even allow them to be physical, how ambitious they are with passes and shots as well as their tendency to dump. Pretty much it's a control freak's dream if they wanted to be a coach and it's all there in this. 

I don't have any serious complaints as this game is very well made and you can tell a lot of thought was put into it based on the options you have in it. It truly is a sim game where you can manipulate everything to your liking. I'll just say if you're new to hockey it is not the game you want to try your hand at until you learn more about the sport as the learning curve is more suited to fans of the sport and not a casual gamer who knows little or nothing about the nature of hockey and the business involved in the sport. If you're a fan of the game and want to try your hand coaching or even just running the show as purely a GM then this game is for you, no question.

Controls: Acceptable
Music: Good
Graphics: Decent retro
Story: Flimsy

- Hospice related workers that are unprofessional and disrespectful toward the client/patient are usually fired.
- People who make it a job to help others do not treat people they help as burdens. 
- Young children do not all talk like the kids in Talladega Nights.

- The random shouting of "HADOOKEN" during dramatic moments was not acceptable.
- The Final Fantasy style encounter with the squirrel was not acceptable.
- Do not use names from Sci-Fi characters to name people in a somewhat modern time.

FINAL THOUGHT:  So yeah, I guess the plot is sad, but only because he has been neglected by a selfish wife, and the people he hires to get some fulfillment in death, treat him like a burden.
 Stopped playing after 90 minutes.  Biggest disappointment for me since Fable 3.  Glad it was on sale.

The only redeeming quality about this software is the environment you're in and the music, otherwise its a boring, tedious walking sim. Sure, there is technically "combat" and puzzles, but each feels like an afterthought sloppily thrown in to justify it's existence. 

All in all, this is software that completely rides the coattails of the artists and art styles of Giger and Beksinski while otherwise bringing nothing interesting to the table. 

If you want to immerse yourself in the vibe of this software without having to trudge through it's mediocrity, here are my recommendations:

1: Go buy some art books that showcase the works of H.R Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński
2: Go buy some of Lustmord's music
3: Sit in a dimly lit room with just enough light that you can easily look at your new books, thrown on a Lustmord album (if you've got some nice headphones, that's a bonus) and spend an evening flipping through the pages.

review_text:
This review does not cover every weakness in this game. SEGA does not know how to utilize their resources to provide meaningful content for one of their most beloved franchises. If you put enough hours into this game, you will see many flaws with New Genesis and it boils down to the fact that the NGS developers do not play their own game. This review won't guide you through all the problems, but I will highlight one in particular.

NGS will always put in the barest minimum effort and expect to profit from it. You deserve better.

Over the course of 2 years and 4 exploration zones, the Halpha continent is basically complete. As of writing this review, NGS is celebrating their 2nd Anniversary with an event that rewards players with goods from a limited time trinket shop in exchange for seasonal points. I will use this example to fortify my next paragraph that summarizes the remainder of the game's "content". If you are new, seasonal point gathering might be a great time to group up with friends and grind out a combat zone or Limited-time quest, earn some points, spend it on the shop. If you have been playing for 2 years you've already seen this event structure 10 times by now. It is monotonous, unimaginative, and most egregiously, recycled. The NGS Team performs a copy-paste of their previous event and hopes you can't spot the difference. Each time this event returns, it is an insult to your time, your effort, and your intelligence. Daddy SEGA knows that customer engagement is important to profits, so giving you an mindless task  every "season" is a perfect example of scamming players of their time (possibly AC) for a product they've been recycling since its introduction. 

You say, "But that is just a transient event. What about the permanent content?" True, a lot can be said about the quantity of "permanent content" presented in the current version of this game. But I ask the question to the veterans: 

"How many VR/Purple cube/Blue cube tile-set instances filled with monsters/bosses would it take for you to realize that the content releases have zero deviation?"

You've fought these monsters/bosses before, now NGS has kindly repackaged them for you to fight them again. And possibly again! Congratulations on a higher score-- or a faster time. Give me a fucking break! How much of this game is speed-running through cube-rooms shaded over with a VR texture that burns your retinas? It takes less than an afternoon for a developer to create (or recycle) a purple/blue cube arena for you to play in. Are you enjoying something new or what SEGA wants you to perceive is new? Do not praise NGS for new or innovative content, because nothing you've experienced is new. You have been doing the same dodge/block/parry combat against recycled monsters/bosses, just in a different backdrop.

PSO2: NGS does not intend to create a fleshed-out game. There is no effort put into creating meaningful activities. Developers are just clocking into work to meet a deadline on their next poorly executed project -- that is probably a VR cube room that spawns a boss; it will ship with almost zero play-testing. Every week some whale pays for AC, so that the NGS developers can keep the lights on at the office and continue scamming you of your time. So if you are still asking "Should I play this game?" The answer is: You deserve better.

This is a weird game. It's got great visuals, a great concept and the shooting isn't bad...but every system in the game comes off like a prototype from inexperienced developers. 

- No way to upgrade your gun stats
- Player upgrades have INCREDIBLE diminishing returns
- Difficulty settings are missing: you can't pick what difficulty map you want to run
- Guns have no range, but enemies have near infinite range
- Game forces you into close combat but cripples you with cooldowns and stamina limitations
- Very few guns that actually matter, and a small pool overall
- No melee weapons

review_text:
I know this is going against the grain some. A lot of this game is very good. Visually very appealing. Very good controls (I played on the Steam Deck and had zero issues). Really distinct characters with unique mechanisms, nifty new twists in levels (I liked the disappearing snow footprints), and the combinations of the characters really changes how you play. I also liked the Shadow mode that lets you create a simultaneous string of actions to pull off big moves, though I am not sure I truly "got it" and ever truly took advantage of it.

But, the game starts to get really hard. I lost interest after I finished Mission 5 (assassinating Yobu at his castle). The level was so tightly patrolled that it felt like a very tedious, trial and error slog of slowly peeling back and onion to do anything. I spent 30 minutes after I finally assassinated the target just trying to sneak my characters out to the escape point as they added even more guards and patrols. When the game focused on cool powers and figuring out the fun way to do something? I enjoyed it. I liked the experiment. But, by level 5 it just went from "neat puzzle sandbox" to "tedious puzzle" and I put it down after completing the level.

I think the true way they want you to play this is going through the game to learn the levels and the mechanisms. Then, go BACK through to pull off more challenging requirements, or do it without killing or being seen. That all seems fun if you have infinite time and really want to invest. But, I wish the game's approach to difficulty went a different path and not just "infinite guards." It's very cheap, so I definitely got my money's worth the for the 7 hours I played. Still, if asked, I wouldn't recommend it. Not my favorite stealth game.

review_text:
Haunting and phantasmagoric, Scorn is a convulsing nightmare of an experience. The game showcases some of the most stunning visuals and sound design the medium has to offer. I frequently found myself stopping just to absorb the striking level of detail in the environments. There is a strange and alien story unraveling before you, solely communicated through Scorn's immaculate environments. Strange whispers echo the halls while gurgling, fleshy masses comingle with machinery. The atmosphere is laid on thick and refuses to let you go until the game's final striking and thought-provoking moments.

Scorn is less of a game and more of a visual and auditory experience. In fact, Scorn is at it's best when it's not trying to be a game. I found that the pacing was disrupted by the gameplay and puzzle elements and would have much preferred exploring the world uninterrupted. What sparse mechanics Scorn does present are never explained. For example, I found myself in a section where I only had one bar of health and copious amounts of enemies. I kept dying in one hit and couldn't understand how I was supposed to complete the area when I die so easily. I only discovered that I could heal myself by accident when I stumbled upon the key to do so in the menus. I don't need or want weapons and combat when the world and the story it tells is this engaging. Scorn really would have benefited from embracing more of a "walking simulator" design principal and forgone the tedious combat though I will say the deliberate obfuscation of all of it's mechanics does lend itself to a sense of this space being truly alien.

Scorn, while rough around it's edges mechanically, is a one-of-a-kind and unforgettable journey through a demented alien landscape that I will be thinking about long after I've uninstalled it from my machine. It's not for everyone but no great piece of art is. Giger and Beksiński would be proud.

review_text: Not as much time in this as I would like, but I can already kinda tell this isn't as good as some of it's contemporaries. It's not bad, but there's a handful of lacking QOL choices, such as no real way to track what individual villagers are doing, so I'm left wondering why my buildings aren't getting done when I have more than half of my people set to build. review_text:
If I'm being brutally, BRUTALLY honest, this isn't quite what I was hoping for in a successor to the Jet Set Radio games. Now I mean, don't get me wrong, after 20 something years, I'm glad we got SOMETHING but... see, it's like being forced to try vegan bacon when you've been raised on actual meaty bacon for so long. It's just not the same. No matter how hard you try to convince yourself of the minimal difference, it's still different enough that it simply can't quite hit that same level Jet Set Radio had.

For one, the game is kind of missing a lot of what gave Jet Set Radio it's personality. Like DJ Professor K, aka the guy who basically narrated a lot of the story in JSR while also hosting the pirate radio station that played the awesome soundtrack. Bomb Rush unfortunately lacks a character like that and while in JSR, all the music in the game was available from the beginning, you have to go out and actively FIND the music in collectibles in BRC. The method of story-telling is also done directly through the characters too, which while I don't mind, I feel like they could've done it a bit better than they did. In spite of the fact that characters interact with each other, I can't help but feel a disturbing lack of personality where there should be.

While Hideki Naganuma (the guy that made JSR's soundtrack) himself did contribute some songs to the game, the issue there is that there are also a bunch of indie music in the game that simply just don't sound like they belong in a JSR-like. That's one more thing about JSR, the whole soundtrack was composed by Naganuma, meaning he had full control over transitions and understood whether the songs meshed well in those transitions so that it didn't feel jarring when they change between each other. Here, you can tell whoever handled the audio in this game doesn't quite have that same understanding. They try... just not very well.

I feel like with all these foundational complaints however that I'm painting a bad picture. Is this game bad? No, in terms of gameplay, they did great capturing the feel JSR had. Sort of. They did have to take some liberties to make it work in some areas but overall they don't do a bad job of it. And while the story is kind of confusing and doesn't make a whole lot of sense in certain areas, JSR didn't exactly have an academy award winning story either so it's not like I can make that comparison fairly.

For those who just want a one-paragraph review: 7/10. A bit lacking but not necessarily bad. Definitely worth the full price for what it offers but reign those expectations if you're looking for something that encapsulates a modern-day Jet Set Radio game.

There were only a couple of things I liked about this game. The first was that I didn't have any technial issues with the game itself, no crashes and no dropped frames that I noticed, it ran smoothly, nothing to complain about there. The other was that most of the story was decent. 

As for the gameplay, overall, I did not find it enjoyable and close to zero replayability. Even though I purchased this during the summer sale, it was not worth the 5 and I am very unlikely to play anything else in this series. 

As in most action games, this game is centered around combat with some puzzles.  

The combat started to wear after only a few fights and this feeling only got reinforced the longer I played.  I believe the combat system is called "free flow", which appears to be a fancy way of saying  button masher with a timing element. To be fair, the variety of tools and moves available added some complexity.  While the combat may be superficially attractive it has very little real depth and is more cinematic than anything else.   Even perfect fights were oddly unsatisfying and often felt wrong on some level due to the somewhat clunky timing and occaisionally odd attack sequencing.  I can honestly say that I diskliked every character, sometimes for different reasons by the time I finished the game. 

The puzzles were ok at first, but after solving a few they did little other than stretch the game out and by the time I completed the main storyline finishing anything I missed was just a form of self flagellation.

review_text:
So, honestly, I feel torn on this game. It has some really fun bones, some really cool base systems, but nothing feels like it works together. Everything feels like it has a rough edge. Inventory management ends up being clunky, dropping down from ledges is positively disorienting, and sometimes grabbing something seems to grab something entirely unrelated simply because the game decided that was the more "relevant" option. It's also somewhat threadbare on content.

Performance is [i]rough[/i], even on my decently beefy machine (64 GB DDR4, AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, RTX 2080 Super). If there's more than a few recently-dead zombies, I get enough frames dropped to be motionsick.

I almost feel bad not recommending this, because it's fun. It's enjoyable. But I feel like $40 is too much of an ask for it in this state. I'm not upset I bought it, I am a little upset that I bought it for the full price. If you see it on sale, I'd say pick it up. Even still, if you think you'll enjoy it, you probably will, but just be aware of what you're getting into.

review_text:
Very nice game that I can highly recommend. I played it in 2024 and I am still finding it fresh and funny compared to 90% of all modern games. This is like a parody of all famous 80's action movies. Not a single one was spared with Blood Dragon. The story and scenario is so funny that you will smile for every line if you understand the point of it of course. Simply a must play just because of that. 

I am also finding a gameplay dynamic and the fact that you can't die on the island from falls in combo with fast pace running across game world, really pulls you into the small but interesting world. There is not too much to complete here and in 8-10 hours game time you will find just right amount of material for playing. There is also a leveling system (on a basic progress) and weapon upgrades which also is interesting addition. After all this game is more of a DLC but probably extended into a standalone game because Ubisoft saw a potential for separate game.

Graphics is simply... different. It has so much lightning that sometimes can be distracting but it is a selling point of game play and setting. I find it nice but I honestly couldn't play long sessions in this game. Soundtrack is awesome. From main menu theme to game play music. You have to listen and enjoy it.

I have nothing negative to say about the game. More than 10 years after release, I am even more happy to play it now in 2024 when I miss good old FPS even more. This is Ubisoft I like. 9/10

review_text:
This is going to cover a lot. I dont structure reviews very well so this will be a cluster fu... a mess. Enjoy.

I REALLY did NOT enjoy this game.... I really want to give it a thumbs up anyway because it is a high quality game (great graphics, no bugs etc) and its obvious the developers (small indie team) put their hearts and souls into this; I wish the big triple A studios put as much effort into their titles. It doesnt feel fair to give it a thumbs down just because I didnt have fun playing it, but their overall rating is so high I dont think my down vote is going to ruin their rating :) 


Lets begin...... The game takes place in an "alternate reality" town during a plague, you essentially investigate the cause, try and help people and ultimately try to stop the plague all while trying to keep yourself and a handful of main characters alive throughout. The game is really difficult and I usually enjoy that (especially in survival games) but something about this just annoys the heck out of me and leaves me irritated.  You have to watch your hunger, thirst and monitor your infection level - make sure you dont catch the plague.  Food, medicine and clean water is really hard to get and becomes exponentially more so as the game goes on.  You have to CONSTANTLY ( i am not exaggerating) loot trash cans for trinkets like buttons, yarn, marbles etc and trade with NPCs for scraps of food. There are men, women, and kiddos but there are only a few preset models for each-for example, if you see 5 men in a group, 3 of them will look identical, hopefully that makes sense, I really didnt like this, ANYWAY... On top of always worrying about getting a nut or crumbs of bread to not die of starvation you have to CONSTANTLY worry about gathering enough herbs to craft under powered medicines to keep the main characters alive. You also have to maintain your gear and equipment which degrades INSANELY fast...as the plague progresses certain areas of town will be infected and there will be thugs who will attack you on sight... there are a few different weapons you can get, lets say you have a gun, you shoot a thug 2 times and you not only lost 2 bullets which are EXTREMELY expensive and rare but your revolver now lost 1/4 of its durability.  To repair it? Oh, well on top of all the other items you need but cannot get, you need to try and round up the scrap items to repair your gun/knife etc. 
You can wear special clothing in infected areas to SLOW DOWN the rate you become infected...  you wanna cut through an infected area? throw on your plague boots and take a few dozen steps and see the durability has dropped significantly...wanna repair your clothing? You know the drill, go loot for junk, try and trade with all the npcs who look identical, nobody wants what you have, rinse repeat. All while having a VERY limited inventory.  It is just too much for me personally, I didnt find this fun.  Your character WILL die multiple times but the game goes on, its actually part of the game in a way.... IDK. 

This is a "parellel universe" type situation. Its a world that looks like ours, but there is a "supernatural" force at work and the people use A LOT of lingo and terminology you will not understand and its used so often it got annoying to never understand what exactly is being said to me. Your responses also contain this weird jargon and you will not know what youre saying back to these NPCs.   

The main mission/ point to the game is essentially racing back and forth across a map to a bunch of main characters at different times and talking to them.  Quests are timed so youll never complete them all...  You get a "quest" to go see character 'A', you make your way ( at great cost) to get to this person, they are - and always will be- a stationary NPC. People in the reviews say your choices matter and will have consequences but id like to say this isnt as dramatic as you think it would or should be - in my opinion of course. Your "quests" and "decisions" are STRICTLY dialogue choices. You have a conversation that you wont understand and get more of the strange story and thats about it.  You can try and save certain main characters if they get sick, or let them die, and if certain characters die then youll lose out on some dialogue with certain characters later on but thats my point is its only dialogue..... You go to a character, you talk to them, chose dialogue options, and the convo/quest ends. Based on your dialogue options this will set up certain interactions with other stationary NPCs later on.   You dont go on missions with these characters or anything like that... Its just you talking to stationary NPCs and picking dialogue and inbetween these "interactions" you are scavenging junk to trade for junk to survive. 

I think a large part of the game for people is getting attached to the world and characters? Thats what makes all the different dialogue trees interesting for them, thats why trying to save them is fun and thats why they get so invested? Not sure... but for me its just... shallow. I dont see the magic everyone else sees.  

A thing that appealed to me in reviews  was the decay of a city while the plague takes over, but it wasnt as I thought itd be. The city is made up of a dozen or so separate "sections" or "zones".   The length of the game is 13 in game days, and on a set schedule 2 zones/ sections of the city become "infected" with the plague.  During this time if you walk through either of these 2 zones you will slowly get sick so you avoid these areas and just walk around them. Then after a day or two those 2 areas go into a "after plague" phase where a bunch of thugs wonder the streets but there is no more sickness, then after a day or two the zones recover to normal as 2 different "zones" go into plague mode.  My point is: its not like you slowly notice the sickness spreading throughout the entire city as time goes on and things completely go to hell... its just certain zones at certain times... no matter what, 80% of the city will always be normal. The plague is only in 2 sections at a time basically and it spreads at a scheduled interval.  To me that really breaks immersion.

Id say before buying this game you NEED to watch a lets play on youtube, seriously.  Its hard to explain why I find it "shallow". People will read me saying "shallow" and argue that the lore and story is super deep and theyre right (but its not interesting), im talking about the actual game play. The weird language and lengthy conversations to read (it isnt voiced)  left me mostly wanting to rush through the convo instead of stop to carefully read all this confusing jargon that didnt make sense. 

Its very story driven. VERY.  Maybe too much for me.  The choices and consequences dont seem as dynamic as people made it out to be. the actual game play is just you looting, trading, and constantly starving, always having somewhere you need to be, never having what you need ALL just so you can read a conversation with a stationary NPC.  It just didnt spike my interest. 
Because I never formed bonds with these characters & because I wasnt able to fully dive into the lore or story it made the "struggle" of the game pointless for me.  
I didnt find the looting of items, trading for scraps fun.

I did find out how to cheat tho hehe.  I figureed out how to add items to my inventory, it took forever but it can be done.  Heres the problem, even with cheats the game was a drag.  I gave myself clothing you otherwise cannot get which is the "crow costume" the plague doctors wear (high plague resist), I gave myself what looks like a 98K rifle, a "wehrmacht" helmet and uniform, ammo, ENTIRE fish etc.... so I could travel anywhere and do as I pleased, shoot thugs, stay healthy... but IT WAS STILL a drag because using the rifle a few times left the damned thing broken, the clothing would degrade, id end up hungry five minutes later. Even cheating isnt fun.

review_text:
Scorn is a totally unique game that is not for everyone. The environmental storytelling is incredible, the art is jaw-dropping and intricate, the grotesque scenes are picturesque and uncomfortably beautiful. There are many things I would describe as gut-wrenching and disgusting, but as someone who has played countless horror games, I found that to pull me in to the experience even more. I enjoyed the puzzles and figuring out where to go quite a lot. The game does not give a shit about holding your hand as there is no dialog, no hints, you have to pay attention to detail and find your way through this dismal, broken world. I totally loved that about this game. Each level is DENSE and very complex to digest. There's so much to get a grip on in each area, and it feels as if every nook and cranny has been lovingly crafted by a team of fine artists. The gore is abhorrent, the body horror had me reeling and leaning away from the screen. The monstrosities that loom over you in this bleak world are ominous and vaguely sad. Everything drips in the classic art style I've come to understand from East European game developers- a collective consciousness utopia inevitably ending in disaster that is a staple in portraying communist authoritarianism. Games like Stalker, Darkwood and several others also feature this theme, and Scorn portrays it with aplomb. I highly, highly recommend this to fans of other East European sci-fi and horror, you'll likely fall in love with it immediately. 

That being said, the combat is definitely the biggest detractor to the fun I had in this game. The clunky movement and gunplay forced several restarts to some relatively easy to kill enemies, and before you get the shotgun(?), the pistol(?) is very underwhelming. As a horror game with puzzles, it's a fantastic experience and I had a lot of things to reflect on after finishing each chapter about what I had just seen. As a horror game with combat, it's more stiff than the original Silent Hill or Resident Evil in terms of movement. You fire slow, you run slow, you reload slow, and enemies have an unusually good chance of hitting you with attacks, in particular the enemies that look sort of like chickens. The final boss also had an annoying habit of firing 3 grenades but 4 explosions would happen, which killed me multiple times. I was not frustrated by the austerity of the world or puzzles, I was only frustrated by the handful of enemies and the fact that I couldn't quicksave to skip the cutscenes that have to play before each encounter.

This game is a tragedy compared to Boneworks. I don't remember things just breaking as often as it does with Labs. Examples. For some reason, you just get stuck in ladders while climbing them. Like meld with them. Tried for five minutes to get off a ladder and figured out I was somehow clipped into it and pinned. Minecart level? Had to reload over a dozen times because the minecart just stopped. Would not go forward. Couldn't get out of the minecart. Just stuck.

What made me quit was the Gokarts. I flipped over because I'm sure the Index controls are just garbage. I couldn't right myself either. Instead of changing the control scheme where you could use a trigger for acceleration, I had to hold the thumbstick forward. This made controlling the damn thing a nightmare. 

The physics are a nightmare as well. You seem to be heavier than you should be. In Boneworks, the physics were like this, but without the feeling of your character weighing an absolute ton. It translates into drunk movement. It's very sloppily done. Like no effort was put into it. Add to that guns (or digital gunstock) screwing up your aim. It bumps into you well before it comes close to your body, throwing off aim. That's if bumping into a wall while aiming doesn't twist your limbs or wrist in a weird way making aiming impossible. Had the shotgun, couldn't figure out why I could not aim forward after bumping a wall. I let go of the fore-end with my left hand and watched in amazement as my right wrist in game twirled the shotgun around like a majorette twirling a baton. From bumping into a wall.....

It's pretty clear that they just got lazy with this one. Boneworks sold, so we can just rest on our laurels with this one and people will buy it. Maybe they've turned into Bethesda and just let modders do all the work now. Who knows, but it seems like they didn't even get the fundamentals from the first game right before launching into the new additions. Just scream of laziness.

review_text:
It's a frustrating game. When I got it, I was hoping it would be one of those games you can easily sink 100 hours into without getting bored, but now I'm 8 hours in and I don't think it will be. The game doesn't even try to explain itself to you, so you're supposed to learn through trial and error, but the problem with this is that trial and error can only give you a vague sense of what's going on, I'm still left confused about the details of what these buildings actually do or how my villagers will actually do their work. 

Defending against monsters is much easier than just keeping your villagers alive. I always lose due to my villagers starving, never to the monsters. I've seen lots of other reviewers complaining about their villagers starving, so this seems to be a pretty common issue for new players. I think that's a failure of the game to explain the basics of food management to the player. I always build and fully upgrade a farm and a kitchen early on, but that doesn't seem to help since food primarily just spawns in the wild, the farms don't seem to do much, and I'm not really sure what staffing farmers do. Do farmers just collect wild food? If I staff the farm with multiple farmers, will the crops grow faster? How much water is needed in order for farm food to grow? These are the kind of questions that you'll never get answers too in the game, no matter how much trial and error you do. 

I'm still giving it a thumbs up, because I think it's a decent strategy game, it's cheap, and clearly some people out there really enjoy it. Personally I'd give it more of a 5/10 - not bad, not good. If I went through the trouble of looking up how you're supposed to play this game on you tube or something, I would probably enjoy it more, but at the same time I don't like copying strategies from other players, I prefer to find my own way in these types of games, but I can't really do that when there are so many unanswered questions about how the game works.

review_text:
God fucking dammit Steam needs a "mixed" review.

If there is anyone out there who still doesn't own it, I would actually recommend this game to people who like:
- Batman lore
- open-world games
- streamlined reaction time based combat mechanics

My problem is that I like neither.

There are some things that this game does *very* well. Moving around the city by gliding and jumping from roof to roof, listening to the bad guys chatter, swooping in and fighting crime, and the whole being Batman thing feels really good. Graphics-wise it is still pretty impressive. The story is interesting (it depends on how much you like the lore I guess). The production value (world design, voices and dialogue) is insane for a 6 year old game. 

I just don't think it's deserving of that 95% rating and those remarks of it being "one of the best games ever" that people keep throwing around. It's actually a simple and linear game, cleverly disguised as an open-world game and with a very well executed Batman skin on top. None of the game mechanics are intrinsically "fun" or valuable on their own. They only make sense once you put the Batman skin on top of them and most of them are fluff, to keep you busy or advance the story line. Combat is basically a very elaborate cut scene, whose outcome is decided through quick time events (see the on-screen prompt, react by pressing the proper button). The combat system is what dissapointed me the most I'd say. "Detective mode" is basically 3D pixel hunting. Stealth is mediocre, feels tacked on and scripted. The "open world" part is just there to keep you busy going from A to B while following the story.  The combat mechanics, gadgets, puzzles are all just thrown at you from the start and will create the illusion of a complex game, but a lot of it is just fluff. There really aren't a lot of mechanics to "master" in the game.

However, everything looks *cool as fuck* and I think that's where the game shines - if you aren't looking for particularly deep mechanics or a sense of challenge, the game is gorgeous and spectacular and is maybe enough to keep you glued. There's a lot of stuff "to do" and achievements to hunt so if that's your thing, you're going to love it. 

But if you're looking for something more interesting, deeper mechanics, more complexity layers, look elsewhere. This is definetly not a stealth game - it's no Thief, Hitman, Splinter Cell, Dishonored. It's a linear experience cleverly disguised as an open world game. And it's definetly not one of the best games ever. One of the best produced games ever, yes, but mechanics wise it's very shallow.

grenadier is peak enemy design rofl

gnosis as a progression system is so fucking braindead. you can tell there's absolutely 0 effort and/or thought put into it. and stop pretending 'but you can just grind to be strong too' is an excuse for this poorly designed enemy scaling. you are effectively discouraged from using a new, non-upgraded weapon because they just don't pack that punch at all. Imagine a fucking auto shotgun taking 5 shots (in a 10-bullet mag) at point blank range just to kill a random lowest-tier ranged mob. running out of imagination? fortunately you don't need to imagine anymore because that's already in the game and it's called gnosis fucking 2.


More detail at the bottom because these are not as important:

95% of in-run blessing (arcanums? i'm super good with these names) also adds close to nothing, rendering the remaining 5% must-picks. 

In the former category you get: less flinch when damaged, but costs stamina; +chance to drop healing potion (in reality this is 99.9% negligible); +damage when low hp, +1 healing potion carry capacity, +chance for missed shots to not consume ammo, +defense when casting/switching/reloading, and the majority of elemental blessings (unless you have a elemental-focused weapon like midas' burn)  They are either extremely situational or has negligible effect or has very low uptime, you pretty much don't feel their existence.

review_text: No game, upon its completion, has made me feel as disappointed and as enraged as To The Moon. What was supposed to be an emotional journey through an old man's memories to fulfill his final wish turned out to be a horribly offensive and inconsistent story that isn't subtle about its hatred. There isn't much gameplay, but I didn't mind that as the focus of the game is supposed to be on the story. The tone is all over the place. It aims to be a heartbreaking game, but the constant unfunny commentary from the two main characters (one of whom makes blatantly sexist remarks to his partner throughout the game) ruins any tension the game would otherwise build. This is one of very few games that features an autistic character (the game never directly tells you she's autistic, but it's heavily implied), but she is treated as a soulless husk whose abilities and limitations are wildly inconsistent. Every other character treats her as a problem to be solved, so it wasn't surprising to find out the developers have donated to Autism Speaks which is considered by autistic people to be a hate group. This game boasts its representation of neurodivergent minds but strips its character of her autonomy and turns her into an animal to be studied and ogled, and these are dangerous stereotypes that real autistic people already have to fight. I don't think any real autistic person was involved in the making of this game. I really wanted to like To The Moon, and the glowing recommendations and reviews I saw made me think that I would, but its disgusting sexism and autistic rep make me hate this one. I won't be recommending it to anyone, and I will be trying to remove it from my memory.

review_text:
Traveler's Tales' LEGO series, based on various licensed properties, has become somewhat of a staple in many video game collections since its inception with the the 'LEGO Star Wars' games, so after seeing 'Jurassic World' I was ready to go through the LEGO tie-in game, and after a couple of days, I've been left with a dissappointing experience.

There have been many other reviews already talking about the plethora of bugs within the game, and I ran into quite a few myself, two of which halted my progress and forced me to restart the levels I found them on, one of them prevented me from building something because I previously broke some nearby boxes, which is very counterintuitive for a bloody lego game.

However, they also included voice acting for this one, and whilst it's heartwarming to hear Jeff goldblums' laugh (and voice in general) come out of a LEGO figure, the age of the audio become apparent, since it's taken from the original 'Jurassic Park' so the difference in quality between audio from 2015 and 1993 is seen rather easily.

This leads to another problem with the game. It isn't funny. Aside from a chuckle or two I got from the raptors and their shenanigans, none of the humour appealed to me. This is partially to blame on the inclusion of voice acting, since the strength of previous LEGO titles was the physical comedy, it was probably one of the main reasons I loved the LEGO series, but it's been diminished significantly in favour of mediocre verbal comedy, which takes away quite a bit of enjoyment from the game.

The game is strangely anti-death aswell, but I won't dwell too much on that, just know that nodoby dies in LEGO jurassic world, including one character who survived being eaten by being thrown back up a short while later.

However, there is fun to be had in LEGO Jurassic World, the gameplay is as strong as ever, it's still the standard LEGO game affair, smash everything and anything breakable in sight, and attentively searching the levels for the minikits (Most of which are well placed) still manages to be both fun and challenging. A lot of detail has also been put into the open world aspect of it. There's also the option to play as dinosaurs, which is as epic as it sounds!

On the whole though, it's a bit of a mediocre experience for me, but would I recommend the game? Short answer: Probably not. If you love the other LEGO games, you'll probably like this one (If it works for you), however, if your new to the LEGO games, don't buy this one. Get 'LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga' Instead, It's not as buggy, cheaper, funnier and is based on a better film franchise.

TL;DR: Dissappointing. Weak humour, but still has good lego collectathon style gameplay. Not even Jeff Goldblum and playing as a T-Rex could save this one.

Final Score: 6/10

review_text: I'm not sure that I would call Scorn a good game, but I don't regret playing it. The art of Scorn is phenomenal ranging from grotesque to arguably beautiful, especially in the final part of the game. I think that Scorn is best as an interactive art portfolio rather than a video game. Unfortunately whenever the game tries to step outside of being interactive art issues arise. This is most apparent in the combat which feels incredibly scuffed. There are only really three enemy types in the game followed by a mind numbingly boring 'boss' in the final act. Combat is very stiff and just generally awkward. I understand why this game did not get a great reception, it was marketed as a horror fps. The issue is that all of the fps elements feel like an afterthought that the devs added so the game would have broader appeal. If Scorn was just a puzzle game and scrapped the combat I think it would be a better experience. Even now the steam page claims that this game is 'open ended'. It is not. It is a completely linear walking sim/puzzle game with clunky combat thrown in. Despite all this, I still think Scorn is worth playing once to experience some fantastic digital art. I just think devs should not be afraid to market a walking sim as a walking sim.

review_text:
An interesting Metroidvania with survival aspects and rather difficult on the higher difficulties. Item usage is a big part of this game and you don't get increased movement options and abilities like in other metroidvanias, but there are a wide variety of spells and items with different play styles that still makes the game entertaining.

As mentioned in other reviews, the combat is pretty slow and there are no iframes meaning that you get one shot by pretty much every multi-hit attack in the game which can be annoying, but it is fun to plan out which items can best counter different enemy types which is where a lot of the strategy comes in.

One complaint that I do have is that because combat is slow and getting hit once is really punishing, there is no reason to use any melee weapon other than a dagger since it's the only weapon fast enough to reliably get in melee hits and this makes all other melee weapons practically useless which is unfortunate since there are some interesting weapons available that you can't really use. 

Magic is versatile and fun and there are multiple items that allow you to use magic more later on in the game. 

Overall, this is a pretty fun game and I recommend it.

review_text:
This game has come along way and has alot to offer anyone who likes a good FPS.
There's a whole bunch of unloading on some bugs, and that just feels good.  On top of that, I like to throw out some quotes from the first movie in Local chat, "c'mon you apes, you wanna live forever?"

There's also some strategy.  
As you level up the different character classes, you have some options about which gun you use for that class.  It's not so widely varying that it's mind numbing right.  Like, there's not one single loadout that everyone uses because it's the best right.  That gets boring.  There are some classes, where you see some people favor one particular rifle, while others favor another particular rifle.  I like that.  Some games become bland because a certain class has a specific best "load-out" and everyone uses it and that's boring.

It's also important to know base-building.  Sometimes, it's best to build a tightly packed, multi-walled base to protect the arc, while in other cases, you'll want to extend walls up against static objects to create the barrier. 

Teamwork is definitely helpful, and as you play the game, you'll see where it's important to not only have a variety of classes, but also why it's important to even just load a dude's gun when wave comes.  

Again though, it's also simple enough that if all you wanna do is get in and kill bugs, you can, and that's satisfying.

I think the developer is doing a good job of trying to maintain a good balance to the game, with the changes they make.

review_text:
I've been playing this series since EHM 2005, although it was EHM 2007 that I put in hundreds of hours.  This version of the game is an iterative improvement over EHM 2007.  It appears to be a conservative migration to SI's latest app engine, but maintains a very similar flow to EHM 2007, not the latest Football Manager game.

With that said, this game is simply spectacular.  I've only played a few games into my season with this version (so I'm not an authority on the state of completeness) but what I've seen so far is fantastic.  I've had some gripes with FHM 2007, fortunately it appears that quite a few of them have been addressed.  The fact that SI is bringing this game back is astonishing considering how they unceremoniously dropped the game after pirating concerns shortly after it was released in 2006.  Those of us with the Mac version really got screwed since there were some terrible bugs that were never fixed.

Regardless, I'm really excited for the future... If this game gets half the attention FM gets, we're in for a treat.  I have a feeling what we are playing now is a wait-and-see product- see what the respose is to this conservative effort and decide if it's worth investing any additional effort.  Judging from the response so far it should be a resounding YES, this game deserves 1st class attention!

Anyway, newcomers from FM are going to need to be patient, the UI is no where near as mature as FM.  FM has had the benefit of many years of iterrative development... while EHM has been in stasis for 8 years.  Even if this release just brings EHM up to date and nothing more, we all win.  Hopefully next years release will start incorporating some of FM's ground breaking systems.  

This game is worth every penny whether you are new to the series or upgrading from EHM 2007.  My favorite sports sim ever, hands down.

The entire game is basically just boneworks post campaign content extended to a whole game (not a bad thing as the post campaign content was genuinely amazing) w a small campaign thats more of a glorified tutorial.

+ Gunplay & sandbox was improved (other than the fact that the guns are more inaccurate)

+ Runs & (usually) looks better than boneworks most of the time

+ Spectator camera was improved majorly

+ Ascent, Home, and the intro level are genuinely amazing and the campaign should of been like those levels.

+ (daddy) Ford is back

+ more guns

+ leaderboards (please fix them)


- Game requires an SSD, or face hour long loadtimes (this is genuinely a stupid thing to require for such a small game)

- Melee was downgraded for a glorified "hit until they die" instead of boneworks amazing limb system

- Climbing is jankier than boneworks

- Game is basically on life support until the developers communicate with us, only being held with mods

- Campaign barely shows off combat in any way, OST is less prevelant than boneworks.

- No zombie warehouse?? really??

I really wanna recommend this but I genuinely cant if youre going in with the expectations that itll be even slightly like boneworks, as its at the moment more of a downgrade. The only reason why I began playing this more and more & bothered reinstalling was due to the fact that Ive 100% and done everything you can in boneworks, I even completed the campaign when it was still 1.0, even with the bugs and jank I still enjoyed it. With this game, I genuinely cant recommend it in its current state.
Play it after 100%ing boneworks & feel like biting the bullet for a more mediocre product thats also more expensive.

review_text:
[h2] Introduction [/h2]
We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip is a cooperative escape room puzzle game developed by Total Mayhem Games. It's another entry in the We Were Here series. In this part, we focus on repairing the ship in order to escape from the abandoned amusement park. The developers offered the game for free for a limited time, so I was able to claim it at no cost.
[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
The core of the game lies in its cooperative gameplay. Players control separate characters, unable to see each other directly. Escape requires constant communication via walkie-talkie, describing their surroundings and collaborating on solutions. This mechanic is consistent with previous games in the WWH series.
[h2] Graphics [/h2]
While it may not be groundbreaking graphically, there's nothing to complain about. The graphics are pleasing to the eye, effectively capturing the atmosphere of the setting, and the level design is very well executed.
[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Since communication relies heavily on walkie-talkie use, clear and well-crafted audio is essential. The game delivers, with crisp voice transmission, good environmental sounds and pleasant music.
[h2] Story [/h2]
We have exposition and justification for our actions, but the story has never been the main focus of these games, and the same is true here. However, that's okay for the game.
[h2] Enjoyment and Replayability [/h2]
Solving puzzles with a friend brings a huge level of satisfaction and is extremely fun. While the core story can be completed in a single sitting, the game offers some replayability. We can replay challenges to achieve better results. While a bronze ticket is enough to pass, in good company, attempts to obtain a gold ticket are never dull.
