review_text:
There was a chilling feeling washing over me in the first hours of [i]Witchfire[/i], and it wasn't due to the ghosts breathing down my back. It was a sinking feeling that I had done all of this before... but where?

Open world zones with activities marked on the map?
Small dungeons I could descend into for a timed activity?
Stats I could improve using resources?

It wasn't until I picked up and fired my first revolver that it hit me. [i]Witchfire[/i] is a single player [i]Destiny 2[/i]... and I love it. It's everything great about MMO-style looter shooters without anything to get in the way. The game valiantly charges through the mires of hostile, addictive game design trying to mess with your gray matter, with no microtransactions or in-game purchases to speak of. Instead, [i]Witchfire[/i] hearkens back to classic ARPGs like [i]Diablo II[/i] and [i]Grim Dawn[/i], focusing entirely on your growth through various hard-earned means. Every delve into the witches' territory leads to some interesting decisionmaking, especially once the higher Gnosis (read: world difficulty) tiers are unlocked and the game starts getting really  mean. 

The game feels incredible to play, with immaculate sound design and spectacular particle effects. Weapons are the highlight, with excellent foleywork and great punch to each one of them. Machine guns spew bullets down range, while shotguns rip the air apart with their blasts. When I compare this game's revolvers to [i]Destiny 2[/i], know that I am doing so in the highest praise, as the latter game has some of the best gunplay this medium has to offer. Enemies die to bullets yes, but also glittering electricity dancing between them, or roaring flames colouring the surroundings in a faded orange light. With a dev team at the helm that utterly nailed it's dark gothic steampunk aesthetic, you're left with a compelling power-fantasy toolbox that feels great to traipse around in.

Probably the coolest part of [i]Witchfire[/i] is how cryptic the entire experience feels. You're almost completely isolated, a lone warrior against impossible odds, staging hectic raids into cursed territory just to put pressure on the enigmatic Witch. It's an extraction shooter, but also an RPG. It's a looter shooter, but it also has some survival horror and resource management mechanics. It's a game about shooting a lot of red-tinted ghost guys in the face until they go away, and about waxing and wayning power like a rollercoaster from hell. One minute you're obliterating whole swarms of enemies, and the next you're traipsing around a new zone in fear from the onslaught that's about to befall you. 

This is a really compelling little title that I could see easily being worth the asking price, with a healthy amount of content and some really fantastic weapons. If it looks up your alley (or the ghost of [i]Destiny 2[/i] is slowly dragging your mouse cursor over to the purchase button), you should really give it a try.

590.7 hours. That’s how long I spent inside “The World.” I laughed, I cried, I screamed at corrupted save files, and somehow... I still want to dive back in.

This game is special. It’s not just nostalgia — it’s an [b]experience[/b]. The story pulls you in, the music hits deep, and even though the gameplay can feel repetitive, I never got tired of it. I got so far into the game — nearly to the last chapter — only for my file to get corrupted. Yep. 590 hours gone. Just like that. I stared at my screen in silence, questioning my entire existence.

But here’s the crazy part — I still want to start over. That’s how much I love this world. The story, the characters, and that emotional connection you build with Haseo and the crew make it totally worth it. The music alone deserves its own award — it’s atmospheric, emotional, and perfectly fits every scene.

The combat system isn’t the smoothest, but it gets the job done. I was way more into the story and the vibe anyway. The visuals are polished, the art is clean, and it’s wild how good everything still looks for a remaster of a PS2-era game.

If you love anime-inspired RPGs with deep storylines, memorable characters, and that nostalgic MMO vibe, this game will grab your heart and never let go. Just… back up your saves, please. Learn from my pain.

review_text:
I love the overall vibe this game has. The artstyle is great, the music is fun and the animations are really well made. Optimization is nice as well. The gameplay, however, gets boring and repetitive real quick. There's basically zero depth and no challenge at all. All you have to do it spam graffitis to get into "crew battles" in which you only have to take corners while grinding rails to increase your multiplier and spam your three tricks to get more points in order to beat the other crews score by miles. The movement is fun, but it's really basic. There are no fancy combos you can do and the skateboard, BMX and rollerblades all do the same thing with different animations. The cops are useless and no threat at all. The biggest challenge was working with the horrendous camera during the final boss fight. The dream sequences were pretty cool and a little more challenging. I think their difficulty should've the one outside of these sequences while they should've been even harder.

Navigating the map was a little weird at times as there are sometimes only one or two ways where you can go to the next part of the map. If you reach the mall you'll know what I mean.

I finished the game within 6 hours. Considering the length, lack of depth and high asking price, I can't really recommend the game. I got it for cheap on Humble Bundle which made it okay. Don't get me wrong, it's still a high quality game, although heavily overrated. If you don't care much about gameplay and just want to vibe to the well made soundtrack and world, you won't regret getting the game on sale.

review_text:
Lucius is one of my favourite horror games, so much so that I play it every Halloween. 

This is the first game in a trilogy of Lucius and starts it off very well, firstly if you are looking for a game with heavy gameplay, this is not exactly what you are looking for, it's a third person game with fairly straight forward puzzle elements to it. Come into the game without expecting indepth gameplay you will be rewarded.

The story is the real meat of this game, you are following a detective named McGuffin (yes really) who is investigating mysterious deaths occurring around a wealthy family manor. However you are playing as the culprit Lucius who is the child of the family, which no one suspects is the cause of the deaths. Every day you will wake up and get a target that you have to figure out how to go about killing them. The methods you go about killing them in this game are very linear, there is only one solution on killing each target, which is perfectly fine. Some of the death scenes are very gruesome and will have you shocked on the first viewing. Some of the solutions can be difficult to figure out especially in the later half of the game, but nothing is far out that you will never figure out.

You can tell that this game was developed on a budget and thankfully the game does not take itself too seriously, however  you can also tell that the devs really tried, they have put a serious amount of effort into this game and it shows. I recommend this game to everyone especially with how cheap it goes. 

This will get you into the Lucius series, which the future games are just as good (Yes even Lucius II)

review_text:
Lucius is an interesting game, which sadly doesn't live up to its full potential. 

It's effectively a linear puzzle game set in an open area. While you can get all of the items you need in game at any point (and I would recommend you to get them early because the game starts putting trials around getting some of the items later which can be skipped if you get them early on), you can only use those items in order as the missions require them.

The game has a few issues: AI can lock you into parts of the map, the autosave doesn't seem to save at a lot of points making you redo a lot of what you have already done in the case of mission failure or getting bugged (and there's no manual save option), The voice acting is bland and often does not sync with the character animations, and the hints the game gives you to help you proceed often don't really help as they are far too obscure.

Some assassinations are difficult, some are very straightforward. There are two "boss fights" if you could call them that, one of which resorts to a linear finale...

There are stealth sections which when you first do them you will generally learn them through trial and error (due to a lot of insta fail sections), but after you get the "forget" power you basically run through them laughing like a wizard, because despite the power being limited use, there are more than enough uses to easily abuse it.

The game isn't entirely bad, but its not what I was hoping for and does not live up to it's full potential by restricting playstyle despite the large amount of powers and interactivity given to you. It's more like an interactive movie than a game. It was still enjoyable despite all its faults, especially with the gruesome cuscenes, but I can't really recommend it.

review_text:
OK, how do I even start? I was thinking about some good points to start with, but... there are none. I've only played to Vol 3, as it has a proper ending for whatever story they tried to make, and I have to assume that Vol 4 just adds more of that boring crap.

OK, three volumes. They are all (mostly) the same game, down to the same collection "quests" and how you progress the main story by doing arena fights. Oh, except for vol 3 which ends the initial story eventually... and then just pulls a new even bigger baddie out of the hat. Although this time around, they just beat it up somewhat quickly, because they don't have another three volumes.

And while the game claims to be set in a MMO, which it is, they completely failed to actually create that game. The dungeons are utterly boring and repetitive, and there's no story for the players to follow.  I can't see why anyone would ever want to play the MMO.

But, for some reason, whenever a character wants to tell me something about the "real" story, they make me go through these boring dungeons and only tell me at the end for some reason. Either that, or they send me an "EMail". Which, btw, is what drives most of the story -- NPCs telling me something they do or don't know or assume, or NPCs telling me something they found out. My job is to go through the never-changing dungeons and hear what NPCs tell me.

Oh, did I mention that the game is about certain players with ingame superpowers of some sort that nobody else is supposed to know about? Yet, the game doesn't mind if I put characters that aren't supposed to know anything into my party when going to those meetings or doing stuff they aren't supposed to know about. The game just feels randomly mixed together. In volume 2, you're even suddenly getting messages from another person you've never heard about that's supposed to be dead, leading you to special weapons... again, no explanations and no context.

The characters are often annoying, starting with the protagonist himself whining about a character that we've never met being unconscious in the real world due to the weird stuff going on in the game. Which is a bit of stretch, but whatever. Unfortunately, the story never actually develops in any way and just drags on and on and on, until vol 3 deus-ex-machinas it to an end.
Other characters are often annoying as well, especially Endrance, but we're in 2020 so I'm not allowed to go into specifics.

And then there are the Avatar battles. These have no levels, no gear, no skills, no items, nothing. They are a lot like QTEs, as attacks have one specific way to avoid them.

Feel free to play it if you really want to; I just don't see any reason to recommend this to anyone.

review_text:
Blunt review THIS GAME WAS MADE WITH CLEAR LOVE AND PASSION AND IM GRATEFUL TO THE TEAM WHO MADE IT AND REALLY LIKE THE IDEA BEHIND THE GAME HOWEVER I HAVE SOME ISSUES AND IT WOULD BE UNFAIR NOT TO AT LEAST GIVE MY OPINION

Im only giving it a negative so more people will see it . This game is good. HOWEVER. Many people are thinking of this as the next JSRF. It is a good spiritual successor but it definitely has a different vibe than the JSRF. The music and the story have a very different vibe to JSRF and while this isn't a bad thing i feel JSRF was a bit more lively and focused. The music in particular has a distractingly different tone and feel that I'm personally on the fence about. I'm not sure why they chose a song about @ss to be the most frequent song in the beginning but it feels odd. 

The movement is good and fluid with good intuitive responsive controls but the way combat is handled feels out of place and a bit forced as im not sure why  they added sweep kicks to a game like this. 

I really miss the levels of JSRF which felt more lively and expansive with more character where as these levels feel a bit flat.  The characters themselves are interesting if a bit too far on the wacky side for my liking where in JSRF the gangs felt like a groups who had a theme and had uniforms almost but were still all believable in the setting even poisen jam with their monster outfits seemed to fit here we have a ginger necromancer and his army of zombie frankenstien bikers.

The addition of foot traversal seems odd to me and I feel it makes the game less focuses and having to swap from board to walking just to slide under something breaks the flow especially when it takes so long to take out the board.

As interesting as the new graffiti system is the JSRF method while less interactive allowed for a feeling of flow instead of reaching a point activating your jetpack to hover in front of a wall in mid air for a few second while i fail at drawing a pentagram slows the pace and a setting to swap to one click or the 3-5 section murals of JSRF would make speed up the pace. 

The art style is lovely and Im a big fan. The cluttered compact buildings and alleys really brings across the same feeling as the areas in JSRF. While at certain points the areas seem (As stupid as it sounds) videogamey with an example being the billboards layed out clearly for the purpose of wallriding where as in JSRF they would have been around the level in locations where they could be used organically and comboed as you go from a to b where as here they feel like they are part of the path instead of feeling like an optional flourish to be used for style points. 

The graffiti art is beautiful and interesting and fits well each gang has their own style and all of them feel suitable and interesting. 

The story is alright. A lot more focus is put on the story with long cutscenes and a lot of dialogue. Not a bad thing but for those of us who prefer the to lean more into the gameplay the JSRF style of short cutscene for context and then you get to freeroam with the odd cutscene to add a bit more info from time to time would have been preferable and I feel like the story is missing a bit of energy like where is the half mad underground dj character? I really miss the sort of energy hearing him talk about how he got so nervous for a date he forgot his underwear. 

TLDR : Game is decent. If you expect JSRF 2 this is close while it is very much doing its own thing but it is fun game with charm and love and great attempt at meeting standards that are admittadly unrealisticly high as with all nostalgia blinkered opinions.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol Review: A Stunning Horror Experience with Some Rough Edges

First things first, the graphics in The Callisto Protocol are absolutely incredible. Even in performance mode, everything looks fantastic, from the environment to the detailed blood, guts, and gore. The death animations are particularly well-done and stand out as some of the best I've ever seen for each enemy type. While they can get repetitive if you die often, there’s an option to skip them, which is great for someone like me who takes a few more hits than I’d like to admit.

The combat is... okay. While it’s not without its flaws, it can be engaging once you get the hang of it. Dodging enemy attacks becomes routine after some practice since there’s no timing window for the dodge, making it fairly easy to avoid hits. However, the combat's biggest issue comes when you’re up against multiple enemies. The lack of a stagger feature, even after landing a power hit, can be frustrating. It’s annoying to get the first swing in only to be immediately slapped down by the enemy. And the weapon-switching animations? They're painfully slow and clunky, which can really interrupt the flow of combat.

After a while, I found the difficulty spikes to be too much. I decided to lower the difficulty to "combat" mode, which made things more manageable without completely taking away the challenge. That said, even on this setting, it’s still easy to get overrun in certain sections. I imagine New Game+ would be where the real fun lies, with a more forgiving pace and power-ups making the combat feel smoother—but I’m not sure if I want to replay the entire game to get there.

What really drew me in was the promise that The Callisto Protocol would be the horror gamethat I might love.. I love fighting back, tired of puzzle infested horror games with limited combat..  offering an atmosphere filled with tension and fear. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite live up to that hype. While the monsters are terrifying to look at and the gore is top-notch, it didn’t give me the intense, pulse-pounding experience I was expecting. It didn’t have the creeping dread of something like Dead Space, where every corner feels like it could be your last. There’s a lot of ammo lying around, and with waves of enemies constantly coming at you, the game doesn’t build that slow-burning fear that makes a horror game great.

Another downside is the enemy variety—or lack thereof. You encounter the same types of mutated humans over and over, and even the bosses feel repetitive, with a particular fight being recycled three or four times. It detracts from the sense of escalation that should come with each new challenge.

That said, The Callisto Protocol has its redeeming qualities. The visuals are amazing, and when the game works, it really works. The story is solid, and there are some genuinely thrilling moments. It’s just unfortunate that the difficulty spikes, repetitive enemies, and combat mechanics drag down what could’ve been a truly memorable experience.

At its current price point (around $7 on CDKeys), I’d still recommend giving it a try, especially if you’re a fan of horror games. For that price, it’s worth experiencing the great visuals and story, even if the combat and pacing leave something to be desired.

review_text:
This is a game that feels VERY fun to play once you get it down.  I can't wait for the full release, it's improving all the time.  It's an excellent extraction shooter that forces you to learn the enemies, weapons, spells, synergies, and obstacles instead of grinding stats (though it certainly helps to level your magic cooldown stat).  Also exploring.  It's very fun to explore new levels, it feels terrifying like getting to a new place in dark souls.  You know you're going to die a bunch of times then look back after a few hours and wonder how it went so poorly before.  The power of experience and hindsight.  The weapons are pretty fun and while I have my favorites I can't point to any BAD ones.  Just ones I prefer less at the moment.  I was able to make more or less "anything" work to varying degrees of efficiency, but once I felt free to actually equip something due to how it worked with the rest the game almost feels easy.  In a good way.  It took many hours and many runs to work out what I wanted to do and to aquire the stuff to do it...then to practice different situations. 

I remember staying on the scarlet coast for many a run just advancing timers, telling myself I'll upgrade my gnosis soon.  The decision felt very impactful, and like a roller coaster once it picked up speed it became inexorable until the process was finished.  I eat gnosis 6 for breakfast now.  I wish it got harder.

review_text:
Honestly, I like the concept of this game, as a colony game with spells, but there are too many negatives for me to recommend. 

This game is incredibly slow to play through.  Each day takes an hour, and your colonists take FOREVER to build and deliver resources.  If you queue up 5 buildings, it can take literal days for your colonists to deliver and construct them.  Priority setting on buildings seemed inconsistent at best regarding what order my colonists would construct things, causing them to finish things even slower it seemed.

Colonist AI is atrocious.  They will frequently wander close to the corruption and die because they wanted to pick up some items.  There's no way to set an area for them to not wander around in.  Other times they'll run up to an enemy that will kill them in a few hits (fire elementals).  You just have to know that this will happen in your playthrough, because the game doesn't let you control your colonists in any way to reliably save them from themselves.

Worker management is tedious and unhelpful.  When workers are idle, they don't do other tasks that need to be done.  If you assign workers to make ballista bolts until storage is full, once they finish they'll just sit there.  So now if you want to be efficient, you have to unassign them from the bowyer building and place them somewhere else, and then reassign them when you want more.  I can't believe more people don't complain about how confusing the slots system is for buildings.  For example, a single farmer will comfortably take care of 3-4 farms without idle time.  But if you build 3-4 farms, there's enough slots that you can assign like 12 farmers.  If you assign those 12 farmers, 10-11 of them will be completely idle as you really only should have assigned 1 or 2 farmers at most.  The game doesn't warn you that you have idle villagers either.  The ranger's outpost is another example of this problem.  If you want to have most of your workforce being idle, throw a bunch of people in there, because rangers are completely useless in this game.

Water carriers don't prioritize farms in this game.  I've had fountains full of water and my farms are dry.  You know why?  Because my guys assigned to water distribution are delivering water to houses that are already nearly full of water and in no danger of running low anytime soon.  

Most spells are garbage.  There's lightning, fire, magic missiles etc.  You can drop a useless meteor on some enemies and do a little damage.  But why should I use any of these when they're horribly inefficient and I can instead pick up and drop an enemy into a building that kills them in one hit.  Though that ends up being horribly tedious as well.  There's the grab spell, but you can't pick up more than 1 thing at a time.  You wanted to help build?  Then you have to tediously pick up and drop 1 resource at a time onto a building under construction, when they usually take 32 resources MINIMUM for the lowest tier.  And for some stupid reason, you're penalized if you're not quick about it.  If you hold onto a resource or an enemy for too long, your mana starts to drain, so you better be quick!  This game just loves to hurt your wrists.

On the other side, there are 3-4 incredibly OP spells.  Harvest is ridiculous, and will net you 100 wood/stone or more with every cast. Something that would take your colonists a literal day to chop/mine is now done in seconds.  You don't even need to build a mine or a tree harvester building with this spell.  Holy Potatoes and the regenerate land spell combined with harvest means you don't really need farms either, they're that OP.

Don't even bother trying to do animal husbandry.  The breed rate and butcher rate is so ridiculously slow that you might need 10 animal pens if you actually wanted to use them to feed your colony.  But again, you shouldn't even bother tbh.  Just use Holy Potatoes and get all the food you need.  Even if you don't use that spell, just eating raw vegetables from your farms works perfectly fine.

There's a general lack of information in the UI.  What's the difference between raw meat and cooked meat?  I couldn't tell you.  My colonists will eat both as far as I can tell.  Do the animals I keep in my animal pens and chicken farms eat my vegetables or are they grass eaters?  Beats me.  Are eggs and boiled eggs from my chicken farm any better for my colonists than raw vegetables?  I have no idea.  None of that is explained anywhere that I can tell.  

The lack of a tutorial when you start the game.  I think I understand the game clearly enough now, but honestly this game could have used a longer tutorial when first selecting an area and playing through it.  I see enough reviews that this is clearly an issue.

The tower/defensive balances in this game are not well balanced.  Golems are straight up better than defensive towers.  They're cheaper, mobile, don't require ammunition, don't require any sort of maze to build (which can be walked through by some enemies anyways), and can help you offensively if you build lights right up against the corruption.  Literally building mass golems is the best strategy I've come across.  There's also armor and weapons you can equip your colonists to fight with, and an outpost building you can use them to patrol with.  Why is this even in the game?  Colonists are so fragile in this game, you can't control them, and you generally need them doing other stuff that I can't fathom why the dev thought anybody would want to send them to the front-lines, especially when you can't readily replenish them.

There's also no way to technically be offensive against the corruption in this game.  You may happen to have some golems wander close enough to the corruption that they'll attack something and draw some aggro, but there's no way to specifically order your golems, or even colonists, to attack and clear out an area, which is quite sad.

Speaking of that, colonist spawn rates is another issue that slows this game down.  It's entirely random when you have nomads join you.  Apart from nomads, you can also gain population through childbirth and by buying workers to join your colony.  The problems?  Childbirth is as infrequent as nomads and quite often the children will not make it through childbirth.  Nothing you can do about that.  And you're lucky if you actually see more than 1 worker every 3-4 days (2-3 real life hours) for sale.  They're that infrequent.  Actually, because those workers show up at the merchant station, its actually beneficial to pick up your merchants and kill them so that more slots are available for workers to show up.  No penalty for doing that.  That's how ridiculous it is.  I can have an abundance of food, housing space, water, and defenses, and I'm still being bottlenecked in population by something completely out of my control.

The pause button doesn't let you scroll around the map, or view things.  It throws a screen in front of you so you can't see or interact with anything.  I just wanted to pause and take a look at a battle or plan out some building placement, but screw me I guess.

I really wanted to like this game, and the dev seems to care about his game and seems like a nice guy, but there are too many flaws and design and balance flaws that I have with this game to recommend it.

The concept of HITMAN 666 is really well used with a lot of good ideas but spoiled by the many bugs that persist and unclear objectives. You play the son of Lucifer and your goal is to kill everyone around you, but you'll often be left with a person to kill but no method of doing so. If the game had been better at explaining what you're supposed to do, it could have changed a lot of things, but the scenario is fine for the majority of the game, a little goofy around the edges but still good for a game from 2012 and above all visually beautiful for an independent horror game.

review_text: Purchased this expecting some good Left 4 Dead in VR gameplay, ended up uninstalling after 90 minutes. Went through the 15 minute intro but once the training wheels were off and it came down to playing some multiplayer with friends the matchmaking was downright broken. After the intro the game puts you in a hub world with other players populating a server. Me and a friend tried for over an hour to join eachother, but the closest we got to entering a match together was being in the same hub world. We would join eachother's party, but once the host started the session, only the host would load onto the level, everyone else would remain stuck in the hub. This happened repeatedly. Had we not been communicating on Discord we would have had no clue anything was even going on. We tried private lobbies, public, with AI, without AI, changing server regions, manually entering lobby ID's, none of which made any difference. After about an hour and a half we gave up and uninstalled. Not worth the hassle, considering the gameplay wasn't all that different from Arizona Sunshine anyway. Consider avoiding if you plan on playing with friends.

review_text:
Pretty interesting 2D side-scroller. I've only played through once and on normal difficulty for reference.

The story is basically what the description if the game says. Not much else except a few side stories. There are 3 multiple endings you can get but I've only gotten 1 so far, but it was decent. Nothing crazy or really engaging but okay enough to keep me playing.

The gameplay is relatively easy and simple. Enemies follow basic and repetitive attack patterns. Most bosses took me 2-4 tries. The final boss was really disappointing, super easy and only a few attacks. There's a large variety of different weapons and magic to fight with. I will say that I didn't delve too much into the magic aspect of combat as I mainly used a weapon and shield. The shield is incredibly OP in this game. It blocks like 80-90% of attacks in the game and you can just infinitely block.

The art is fantastic and the soundtrack was good. The art is probably a big reason this game gained some traction. All the girls are really cute.

It's a solid game but for me it just lacked excitement. Definitely worth giving a try but I would wait for a sale to pick it up.

That being said I think what it shows us is something that is a very interesting one and I'd love to hear more intepretations of it.

If you have the patience for a game like this, go ahead, if you don't, I wouldn't get it, maybe just watch a summary if that's what you're after.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol...what a "disappointing" game... !!! BUT !!! ...the slip-up is not on the part of the game (because the game itself delivers everything that you would be expecting from the survival space horror genre) the blame should fall on the publishers ! Yes...yes..."what the actuall f*ck?!" right ?! Let me break it down to you....

As I mentioned before...The Callisto Protocol (TCP) is a survival space horror game, as the genre states for itself...YOU r IN SPACE, fighting for your survival, surrounded by an eerie apocalyptic atmosphere. Year 2320, the story follows Jacob Lee, a starship captain who survives a crash landing on the Jovian moon Callisto, only to be captured and confined against his will in a high-security prison. -BLACK IRON PRISON-...and shortly after that...comes the virus outbreak...and your fight for survival...

I dont want to spoil the story...the game is SOLID...whether you are an "old Dead Space veteran player" who is looking for the same "Dead Space" feeling in a new skin...or a newbie regular gamer who is looking to try out this game genre...you are at the right place with TCP, because it delivers everything you would expect from this type of game. 

THE MELEE COMBAT - is raw, brutal and bloody. Just like in Dead Space, but...the close combat is way more advanced in TCP. The melee system they made is very enjoyable, you have to time right your attacks, blocks and deflections, otherwise you will get punished by the enemy. In other words...you can easily kill ALMOST all enemies if you time your attacks and blocks right....but if you mess it up you´ll die very quickly...not to mention if you are surrounded by multiple enemies.
 
THE RANGED COMBAT – is in my opinion always superior in this type of games because its always better to maintain distance between your enemies...this is true in TCP too. Again...its just like in Dead Space...you can dismember limbs (hands, arms, legs, heads) thus slowing down and killing your enemies. For that purpose you can choose from many weapon blueprint types...like shotguns, pistols or rifles. To wrap it up...the ranged combat is good...but nothing revolutionary...

GEAR
   
You can also upgrade your gear...wheter its your gun or melee weapon...the upgrades are bought with „Callisto Credits“ which is the in-game curency. Credits can be collected on the way, as you explore your surroundings. In this game...its worth to explore hidden places, instead of pushing forward the main story line. The upgrades are essential...if you want to make your life easier.  I have to mention...that it was a great disadvatage to have a limited inventory space...which forced you to leave essential or valuable items behind...you cannot upgrade your inventory...it upgrades when you are deep in like 70% of the storyline. I think thats a flaw... 
 
THE WORLD in TCP...NOT OPEN WORLD

...strictly only story based areas and hidden rooms. Although the space around you is limited...the quality is on the level...and I mean masterpiece level. It delivers the dark virus outbreak type of feeling. The developers did a really good job there with the prison, the harsh outside frozen world, the underground tunels/colony  or the hyper-modern laboratories where the experimentations took place. All this + with the added jumpscares...random monster noises, the crawlings, crying and suffering inmates and prison guards...makes you feel like you want to get out from that place. You are checking every corner because you never know where you´ll get jumped by the next enemy. The music or soundtracks also adds to TCP feeling. So the music is good and it forms a finished whole. Especially the ending song.  
FOR those who are looking for some interesting features...Dina Nakamura, Jacobs female inmate friend...is played by the actress Karen Fukuhara, she is famous for her role in “THE BOYS“ as Kimiko...(she was one of the reasons I wanted to try out this game)...and daaamn what a performance she delivered with her character in TCP... Also...for the Star Wars fans....the prison guard (he is making your life a living hell) who is played by Sam Witwer...also known as the actor who played Starkiller in “STAR WARS THE FORCE UNLEASHED“ is present in The Callisto Protocol. So if you are deciding whether to play this game...you know, these might motivate you to do so...as it motivated me.

CONCLUSION

So...where lies the problem ? The combat is good, the gameplay is at times great, at times average because of repetetiveness, the world and the atmo. is magnificent, the characters are interesting, the setting is good, the music is unique ...so where is the PROBLEM ? Is it the STORY ? I deliberately left the story for the end…because the story is an absolute…PERFECTION. Yes you heard right, the game has flaws but its not the story…even though you don’t make any own choices the story is so well written…full of ups and downs, moral dilemmas, great protagonist development and interesting characters (Dina, Ferris, Elias)…it keeps you always on the edge, focused on story…”you have to get out of here, you have to survive”, the odds are always against you but you must fight on…

So no my friends…the story is definitely not the problem.

The problem is that the publishers are greedy…you have to pay for the DLC to finish the story…and although you finish the base game…the ending is almost empty…Imagine you are playing for hours, you immerse yourself with the protagonist and the characters and all is for nothing…sure you defeat the boss, some questions are answered but if you want to know the true ending of the story and the fate of Jacob…you have to buy the DLC…I mean… if this is not a dirty cash grab attempt  from the developers…then I don’t know what is… shame on you KRAFTON and STRIKING DISTANCE STRUDIOS... 
...and that’s why I call it a "disappointing" game.  7/10 

Its not a "Dead Space fake" as some people call it because the game is really unique in its own way...but its very similar to it...so you should decide whether its worth it or nah. 

FINAL WORDS
 
Now I know…some of you will say…”Its not a problem for me to buy the DLC”…and you are right…its not a problem for me either…I invested tons of money in games and I don’t regret it. But the game itself was a 7/10  at best, for me…and I don’t feel like buying the DLC because it was not “catchy enough”…even though I finished the game like an hour ago. 

I´m not saying you should not try it…no…I definitely recommend it. Just heed my WARNING…because the cash grab in this case is real…unfortunatelly…and the publishers haven´t delivered the FULL COMPLETE STORY altough you paid them the full price...

review_text:
A lot of my friends and colleagues recommended Bioshock to me since I liked action horror games (like Resident Evil 4) and RPG FPS (like Borderlands). The critics of this game are overwhelmingly good, with a Metascore of 96.

But I don't like Bioshock.

The story seems interesting at first (under the sea, steam punk style, mad inhabitants of a once flourishing city of progress and freedom) and the sound and graphics quality is quite good. More than once I got a racing heart when an enemy lurked around the corner.

The voice quality (English and German synchro) is quite good, if not a little too polished and "clean". The options you have for customizing are pretty good, also the different ammunitions of your weapons add to the rock-paper-scissors gameplay of enemy strengths and weaknesses.

After a while, the game gets boring, though. The story – albeit twisted and unique – gets predictable, the "escape and save the world" tunnel view gives you a feel of limitation. Sure, you can't really expect an open world masterpiece from a game so old, but there were a lot of games with more linear levels which were still more interesting to play.

The enemy types repeat themselves over and over again. After the thirty-third Rosie and the sixhundredth small guy who you have to kill because he respawned and you can't just run past them, you just don't want to kill anything anymore. Which is bad for a first person shooter.

I always play on the hardest difficulty for a challenge, since most of the games nowadays are too easy. Bioshock however isn't _hard_ on the "hard" setting, it's just unfair. I never had the impression I could've killed all the enemies of one floor without dying; sometimes you just run into a horde of enemies or a mean trap and die in less than two seconds. Even Dark Souls made that better, there you always have the feeling you could have beaten this enemy if you were just better at blocking or similar.

I might continue this review when I have played the game through. This could take a while, since I don't enjoy this game a few hours in.

review_text:
I don't normally play point & clicks (or trial/mystery games) so I don't really have the genre savviness for this game, especially the trial in the middle, which seems to lean pretty hard on you coming in with some intuition for the type of game it's riffing on. But the Homestuck writing charm was there, and that carries the experience. Homestuck opens by leaning hard on a bunch of data structure jokes that 90% of the audience is just confused by, it's only fitting that a Homestuck game leans hard on a genre crossover that's going to confuse a large chunk of the audience.

The thing that leaves me really happy with this game and excited for the next chapter is that the sense of tension and suspense is really well handled - the stakes ratchet in a way that doesn't feel forced and has enough valleys to create some salient character moments.

In a lot of ways, Hiveswap Act 2 reminds me of the best parts of Hivebent - if that was one of your favorite parts of Homestuck, you'll probably like this game a lot.

+ Decent combat, pretty environments, and phenomenal character customization.

Everything else, though, is bad.

- Horrible UI, offensive inventory management, "lootboxes" everywhere, a practically non-functioning market board, a completely meaningless early-game, kinda wonky movement, and story/character writing that unironically gave me a headache.

- I suspect that the "real" game begins after the story, after finishing up all the main tasks, but enough core stuff here is so unacceptably broken that I don't see myself enjoying that "real" game anyways.

If you have grown used to the comforts of other AAA MMOs, this will be a painful experience for you. It is as if the developers have not spent an iota of effort into learning from other titles in the genre. It would also seem that public sentiment among even the dedicated playerbase is fairly poor - there is apparently a lack of content and meaningful rewards at endgame.

Pass on this one. There are plenty of other games with just as good combat/graphics/character customization that don't suffer nearly as many of mind-boggling systems issues.

review_text:
I wanted a fun little puzzle game that I could pick up and put down easily, but honestly this one is kind of annoying.  I would give it a 5/10 if there was a side-thumb button, but since there isn't I just can't see myself recommending this to anyone.   

The game is a very simple concept that, like any good game formula, has a lot of depth to it when properly explored (something I think the developers were on the right track with).  After a short time in the game, though, I found myself kind of disappointed with the PC options: resolution doesn't scale (as far as I can see from the UI, and frankly I'm not interested enough in the game to even look for the config files), config options are pretty much non-existant, no windowed mode option, and if you have multiple monitors your mouse can still go off-screen (despite the fact that this is a single-monitor full screen game) and if you accidentally click your game will be minimized (this causes issues when you're trying to edge-scroll from right to left, for example).  If these options exist they were not clearly visible in the main menu as far as I can tell, and with a pick-up-and-put-down game like this I shouldn't have to be spending much time configuring things anyway...Binding of Isaac is a good example of how to do a simplistic PC port.  

Put aside my gripes with the port (the reason I decided to not continue playing the game in the first place) the game just isn't that fun and there are some slightly clunky mechanics that get in the way.  The goo balls are constantly moving along your little wired network so you have to be rather precise with your mouse if you want to pick up a particular one in a crowded area, something that can be a major annoyance with the levels that require you to act quickly.  On top of this it was kind of annoying to discover that when you actually pick up a ball its hitbox is still present in the world, so if you accidentally drag your mouse over a harmful object you destroy the thing.  This turns the game in to one of those stupid games where you drag the mouse pointer through the maze and it detracts from the overall experience I was hoping to get.

TL;DR  it's not a bad game, but when a simple game can't deliver on simple and expected concepts I have no desire to play it.  Hell, if I could play the game in windowed mode I'd probably give it another try because shrinking it down would make it not look like shit.

review_text:
Just Cause 4 might just be one of the most fun games I’ve ever played. The combination of a grappling hook, wingsuit, and parachute creates an unmatched sense of freedom and creativity. Add the DLC upgrades—like a boost jet for the wingsuit and missiles—and you’re practically a one-person army with unlimited possibilities.
The story is another highlight. It’s enjoyable, easy to follow, and keeps you engaged without being overly complex. It strikes the perfect balance of interesting narrative and over-the-top fun, fitting the tone of the game perfectly.
Visually, Just Cause 4 shines. The graphics are stunning, and the lighting makes every environment pop. The map is one of the most diverse I’ve seen in an open-world game, featuring everything from dense jungles and serene forests to snowy mountains, sandy beaches, skyscrapers, grasslands, cordfields and farmhouses. Exploring this world never gets old, and the variety keeps it feeling fresh every time you play.
The challenges are another aspect that keeps me coming back. Wingsuit stunts, vehicle stunts, speed runs, hoverboard courses, races, and other DLC activities add layers of replayability. They’re both fun and rewarding, pushing you to master the mechanics while having a blast.
Honestly, I often boot up Just Cause 4 just to explore the map with the wingsuit. There’s something incredibly satisfying about soaring through the skies, zipping between cliffs, or gliding over the ocean. It’s pure freedom, and the game does an amazing job of making traversal itself a form of entertainment.
If you’re looking for a game where you can unleash chaos, explore a gorgeous and varied open world, and have endless fun with creative tools and mechanics, Just Cause 4 is a must-play. It’s a game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, and that’s exactly what makes it so memorable.

review_text:
Its really tough for me to ultimately have to hit that "Wouldn't recommend" button, as I truly love the Hiveswap universe, and with act two, I really fell in love more with Joey and Xefros.

Unfortunately, here are the reasons that I can't recommend this game.

I ran into multiple achievement breaking bugs where I had to basically backtrack on my save files (I've learned, I was making save files like a madman) Its really frustrating when you can't get one achievement because you talked to someone along the way to the person you actually needed to talk to. Really weird.

The trial. Oh my God. This was at least 50% of the whole game and I'm probably disabled or something (sure felt like it by the end) but I have a really really hard time putting names to faces and with this game not being voice acted, it was hard for me to follow along and understand the story. I ultimately had to piece together a photo of each character with their name under it so I could at least try to get involved and by the end of the whole dang thing I was so flustered that I was just wanting to race through to the end which fueled more of my annoyance cause the only game play aspect at this point is running back and forth on a very long train for dialogue I didn't care for. Now. What I loved, was the ending. I loved the whole dang thing that happened on that final train thing. It took the biggest turn and got me excited for the game again, only for it to end like 10 minutes later.

Which, had me researching of what happened to Hiveswap Act 3, and what made me decide to ultimately have to bid my farewells to this wonderful universe. I'm including my thoughts below though I know it has little to do with the game itself, if I had known this information prior I probably wouldn't have wasted my time on this game, honestly. I made a little mistake in purchasing it back when it released and life happened where I didn't get a chance to really experience it until this year.

This game was released in November of 2020. This was a direct sequel that they released in 2017. Not only did they take three years to releae it, but in that time frame instead of working on act 2, they released another hiveswap universe games that have nothing to do with the main games.

Why am I saying that is a detractor? Wonderful question. Its because the company is essentially dead without funding now and we aren't going to ever see the light of act 3 which really really upsets me as they of course ended act 2 in a cliff hanger.

Now did they know the drama of Hussie would happen after act 2? Honestly, no, I think they were as blindsided as their fan base was and while they did release some art work because they were in the process of doing the deed, that was back in 2021. They haven't made any further announcements, so I think its unfortunate to say it got dropped due to funding.

Maybe if they had focused more on the actual hiveswap games and not the universe, this would have been a different story.I wish it was a different story. 

Honestly, if it weren't for the dang trial sequence i probably would have recommended this game as it was enjoyable up until that point. if you have an easier time with these visual novels and think you could keep up better than I could, and you don't care about act 3 being dead and you want to work hard on some achievements then go right on ahead.

For me though, farewell, friend. X:(

review_text:
The game made by people that don't really understand games.

It offers a high level of challenge, but never any respite, any reward for it. Knowing that certain things can happen without you is great; the lack of control is great since Pathologic is effectively a horror game, but this game doesn't understand contrast. Instead of feeling like you're bravely pushing through against bad odds, you end up trying to outsmart the game itself and its systems.

Some people will defend this, saying that challenge is great. And I agree, I like challenging games. However, if you find yourself quickloading dozens of times to replay a specific day because you keep failing miserably because of things completely outside of your control, there's a problem with the game's design.

Pathologic actively dissuades you from exploring its world or experimenting at all. If you ever ask yourself if you should go help an NPC, explore a new location, try robbing a house, or fight a bandit, the answer is almost always "no." Whatever you do, you almost never get anything useful out of it and only waste precious time (which means more hunger, less health and stamina). There's basically no risk/reward, only dumb luck and a lot of fast running.

Is this suffering worth it? I don't think so.

First, the gameplay isn't better than it was in the original. 90% of the time you'll just be an errand boy. The combat is janky and neither fun, nor engaging, and, like many other things, is rarely even worth getting into: the few weapons you have wear out very quickly, and the repair costs are so ridiculously high that you can basically view them as disposable tools. In the original, with some luck and skill you could battle the bandits at night, even make a bit of money off that, and repairing equipment wasn't such a huge problem, but forget all of that here.

Second, the story. I could stand the gameplay issues if the game was well-written... But it's not!

It seems that tons of people are absolutely enamored with Pathologic 2's writing, but if you've played the original, you'll likely agree it's incomparable. The original Pathologic was subtle, elegant, thought-provoking and philosophical. The game tried to make you feel things and think about things. In contrast, the writing of Pathologic 2 is basically, "You're such a moron! You know nothing about anything, and you're going to fail miserably in everything!" repeated over and over in different voices. The game tries to be mysterious and to make you feel like you're fighting Death itself, but all it does is belittle you and speak in riddles, which gets old pretty fast.

It's funny that Marble Nest, a mini chapter that served as a demo for the game, was a much more complete and well-rounded experience.

And on top of all that... THE GAME IS INCOMPLETE.  And I don't think it'll ever be complete, because Ice-Pick Lodge doesn't understand how game development works. They failed all deadlines, they failed their supporters and they couldn't even fulfill their promises to the backers. Physical prizes? Not received. Digital goodies? Laughable. (Imagine that one of the digital goodies for the backers was one regular item that you can simply make in the game, with no special effects whatsoever. Can you imagine being a Skyrim backer and receiving a single dragon bone for that?)

My verdict: you're better off playing the original.

review_text:
World of Goo is a physics puzzle game where you control a collection of goo particles, and try to get them into a pipe. Building structures by connecting balls of goo together is how you get them to the finish pipe. The unused balls crawl along your structure, and then into the pipe to end each level.

The physics feel great. The unused balls of goo crawling along your structure have mass, not just the components of the structure. Shifting them around is the key to some puzzles. The structures never break from their own weight, only bend, which saves a lot of frustration. Gravity is consistent between levels, except for a short sequence of levels where unique gravity for the level is the main component of the puzzle.

The humor is excellent. Your adventure is narrated by a series of signs written by a character identified only as "the Sign Painter." Their exasperated/humorous narration of the goo traveling through the world lends a lot of charm to the world. The game is very self aware that it is a game, breaking the fourth wall multiple times, each time to great effect.

Puzzle design is good. Challenging at times, but very well designed. Each puzzle takes a few minutes at most to figure out a way to do it, with most having more than one solution. Much more time could be spent on this game than I spent if one wanted to optimize the levels.

There are multiple different types of goo balls introduced through the game, each of which interacts with the environment in a different way. Each one is interesting and unique, and does not overstay its welcome.

Overall, I would recommend this game. I did get it has part of a HumbleBundle, so not sure if I would by it on its own.

review_text:
I bought this game after refunding another game for around $20, and decided I'd play this as a meme to stream to my friends. Then I kept playing it. Then I beat the game, then I started a new game, then another one. Needless to say, this game is really good, addictive certainly, with a gameplay loop that really gripped me.

Lost Ruins is a classic dungeon crawl. The controls are clunky, which perfect encapsulates the idea of being a stupid high school girl swinging a zweihander around. However, the clunky controls are likely the biggest hurdle, and in my opinion they warp what seems like an action game into a strategic one. There are many weapons to choose from, all of which halt your momentum when you use them, forcing you to take it slow. If slow isn't your style, this probably isn't the game for you. You can also lobotimize yourself and make the game a cakewalk by using spells and exploiting weaknesses; there's nothing quite like fighting the first boss, getting annihilated, taking a step back and thinking about the nature of the boss and the arena, and then cheesing the boss to death by abusing the hell out of elemental combinations. This is replicated for most bosses, and even sitatuations, you don't have to bash your skull in and just "get gud", there's different strategies to try, and I managed to make the game a cakewalk before the halfway mark just by minmaxing my stats to godhood. Truly euphoric.

The artstyle... look, let's not beat around the bush. It's anime, monster girls, and the like. I can't even pretend to do the "horny" joke, because I'm not a huge fan of the genre, but I will admit the farther along I got, the more tolerable, and even enjoyable the artwork became. This is a discussion on the artwork, as in still frames, if we're talking about pixel work, dear lord it's amazing. The Japanese anime thing might not be a selling point for some, but it's undeniable that if it could be done justice, they have gone above and beyond. You can tell that Altari Games really care about the game they made here.

So, after having no lifed the game and nearly completed all modes, I can say this game is pretty dang good. I do have some minor gripes with it; for example, I was looking forward to the idea of unlockable characters after the game, and while I did get that, it wasn't really the length I was hoping. Again, what you get it well worth it, I just wish after playing all the modes there was more here, a compliment if anything, and a testament to my enjoyment of the game. Also the story is... not great. It's serviceable, but don't get this game if you want a branching story. The game seems to do best when it does the story of: "small snippets of messages left behind, you fill in the blanks" kind of story telling, the main story itself is nothing to write home about.

Finally, this isn't a particularly long game. Once you figure out what works, the game is going to start breezing, or at least it did for me. Still, with the alternate game types you'll get around 10 hours or so, and even still something you could always boot back up to mindlessly play in the background once you've mastered it. Great game, would recommend, Witch mode is busted.

review_text:
I originally bought this game because I thought it would maybe be an average horror game, but honestly it's bad enough that at some point I was playing it just to have a laugh.  There's a lot of issues with the game. 

- Shimmying through narrow spaces, crawling through vents, or even unlocking doors using the panel are all pointless non-gameplay for what I can only assume is padding. Even more funny is they try to make the vent crawling seem scary with all the scary noises as you crawl, but you literally can't do anything while in the vents so there's nothing scary about it at all. You can't even aim your gun.

-A lot of times there's two paths to go, one progresses the story and the other has treasure. So which is which? I don't know, better hope you chose the treasure path the first time because if not you're locked out of it forever. But it's not like it matters because you can't carry the treasure because you only have 6 inventory slots, it's awful. 

- The pacing is bad. I'm fairly far into the game and have not come across a single boss or even setpiece really. it's all just "run through space corridor, kill some guys" repeat. Every part of the space station looks the same. It might be realistic, but it's not memorable and doesn't create engaging enough visuals. At one point you go into a waste management facility and other than Jacob wading through and getting caked in sh*t there's nothing distinct or interesting about this level. There's not even a great big mutated sh*t monster or something for you to fight. It's just pointless. I'm not even sure if I could explain where in the game I am right now. The chapter is called "Habitat" but it's just a dark metal space station like the rest of the game.

-Most importantly, the core combat sucks. It's all melee focused and it's just hit twice, dodge once or twice, then hit twice again until the creature is dead. Not only that but the fighting feels like a series of QTE animations instead of you feeling in control. There's a gun too but it's clunky, weak, and obviously not what's intended to be used most of the time. Most enemies act the same when meleeing them too which makes it really unfun and tedious. God help you if you have to fight multiple enemies at once. You can block as well as dodge, but the game doesn't explain why you would do one over the other. In fact they don't explain the dodge at all, you will pick up on it eventually (and trivialize every encounter after) but until then it fees like stumbling in the dark, which you already do enough of in this game.

- It's just not scary. Being able to melee enemies means it becomes not a test to conserve ammo, but trying to stay awake during the game's repetitive combat. Melee therefore puts the control back in the player's hands both in terms of not needing to watch your ammo, and also as someone who can easily stand up to the threats, which kind of kills the whole horror aspect. In most horror games if an enemy comes too close to you, you're probably either going to take a huge chunk of damage or just straight up die, but this game insists on you getting up close and personal, which just doesn't work to a horror game's favor. The checkpoint system and linearity help ensure even if you do mess up you can immediately retry anyways. The game tries it best despite this to scare you, often to mixed results at best, but it does so using really overdone horror game tropes and jumpscares. Oh look you just got the power cell you needed to power up the door on the other side of the room, I hope some monsters you've seen a million times don't pop out of vents on your trek back.

- The QTEs are ridiculous. There's way too many monsters that just grab you and force you to mash the button until the enemy is dead or gets off you. You can't even avoid it or get better at them. You just have to watch the animation and mash the button as your health drains, over and over. Every combat encounter in this game feels like a QTE now that I think about it, whether you're doing melee or mashing buttons, it all boils down to the exact same finger dance that you'll tire of in the first hour. Is this 2010 where we need to explain to developers that QTEs aren't fun?

Ok, so what's good? Well, the graphics are honestly amazing and lifelike, and the enemy designs, what few there seem to be, are kinda cool. That's about it. Definitely skip this game.

review_text:
TLDR: The plot is disappointing. If you want long bricks of text about the world of the Trolls of Homestuck, a bunch of fetch quests, and nothing of import to happen, then this is the game for you. The art and music are on the whole good as usual - buy the soundtrack!

Minor over-arching spoilers for the game to follow, nothing specific:

Hiveswap: Act 1 was a very engaging story that happened to take place in the Homestuck universe. As someone who was not a fan of Homestuck, it was still easy to get into, exciting, and well written, while providing enough references to the source material to merit fans of the franchise playing it.

Hiveswap: Act 2 sees you delve deep into various aspects of the world of Homestuck, while exactly nothing happens from a plot perspective. In a grand synopsis of what will ultimately become the entire Hiveswap plot, you could sum up the entirety of Act 2 with "they tried to reach a destination." The game has some enjoyable moments, but leaves so much to be desired from a greater story perspective and leans so heavily into bricks of lore text and fetch quests that it ultimately felt meaningless. The game that took literal years of development hell to release resulted in the player and the protagonists accomplishing almost nothing. I'm left very disappointed in this after my very high hopes coming off of Act 1.

Cutscenes were well animated though their technical implementation left much to be desired (very jittery transitions, weird fades, generally jank). Background art and character art was on the whole superb as the art team is very talented, music is by and large great though due to the majority of the game taking place in one setting with musical remixes in each sub-area it did get a bit samey at times.

Paying $15 for each 5 hour bit of this supposed 8-part opus feels less and less enticing as each part takes years to develop and their plot progress gets smaller with each passing act. Very worrying trend.

Finally, the loss of the certain staff members at What Pumpkin can be felt throughout this game. While the larger elements of the plot might not have been within the purview of this writing team, the character writing is noticeably weaker than in Act 1 (where it shined). A lot of the nuance in Joey and Xefros's characters, both in their chemistry as a duo and in their own stories, was lost in this game. Xefros went from an optimistic but abused character who had a lot to work through, to a nihilist whose long "haha everything sucks lol xd" rants serve to further inject tons and tons of Alternia lore at the player, instead of being in service of his own character. That one example feels generally emblematic of a lot of the writing in this game. It's really, really unfortunate. Hopefully the team can take feedback from this game and make a game that stands on its own merits with its own story, and not one that just revels in being part of Homestuck.

review_text:
Game struggles to find balance between the enemies and the characters you control. No matter WHAT you do, you will make a mistake and be forced to "Quick Load" multiple times to hopefully have an enemy who saw you the first 12 times to finally not register your movements and allows you to proceed. The game is designed for repetition, which it why they shove the "Quick Save" down your throat LITERALLY every minute reminding you that you haven't saved in the last minute! The keybinds are absolutely atrocious! I have never had to rebind almost EVERY key in the game just to make it somewhat functional.

The game also forces cut scenes causing the game to essentially soft lock. For instance, I was to distract 2 "Straw Hat" guards guarding a gate while a normal guard moved back and forth from their path, I proceeded to take out the 2 Straw Hats and then a cut scene forced both my characters past the gate they were guarding, after the cut scene, the regular guard patrolling found their bodies (I was unable to hide them because of the forced cut scene) and then proceeded to call 6 guards who opened the door I was forced through and proceeded to kill my guys and I was softlocked, essentially making it to where if I wanted to get where I was, I would have to start the whole encounter that I spent 20 minutes trying to pass all over again. The game strives to be a "Stealth/Tactical" game but fails in almost every aspect to make things seem flawless and rewarding.

TL;DR The game's terrible keybinds, AI, quick saves/loads, and the constant softlocking makes this game a hard pass.

review_text:
Samorost 2 is an intriguing little point-and-click adventure that stands apart from the genre in a quietly confident way. Unlike most games of its kind, there’s no text, no dialogue, and no character conveniently telling you what they need or where you should go next. Instead, the game relies entirely on your curiosity and intuition. Progress comes from noticing how elements in the environment connect, often in a way that feels obvious in hindsight, yet delightfully puzzling in the moment.

That’s the magic of Samorost 2, its puzzles are simple, almost self-evident, but they require you to observe, poke around, and piece together tiny cause-and-effect chains. It’s a bit like solving a whimsical, minimalist Rube Goldberg machine without being told what the final motion should look like. The game is never truly difficult, if you have a little patience, you’ll naturally work your way from one scene to the next. Some puzzles click instantly and make you feel clever; others might have you scratching your head for a few minutes. But you’ll get there, and watching the little white-onesie protagonist continue his journey is always satisfying.

The art style is one of the game’s biggest strengths. It blends photo-bashed, surreal landscapes with simple, flat-shaded characters in a way that’s strangely harmonious. The contrast gives each scene a dreamy, handcrafted feel. The audio design supports this vibe beautifully, calm, unobtrusive, and atmospheric, it nudges the experience forward without ever drawing attention away from the visuals or puzzles.

Samorost 2 doesn’t overstay its welcome. It’s short, charming, chilled, and consistently delightful. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it, and sometimes, a brief, imaginative escape is exactly what you need.

review_text: Shadow Tactics is Commandos with ninjas. That’s a good thing, by the way. Very few games swim in the same genre pool as Shadow Tactics. There was the Commandos series, and the Desperados games, and that’s basically it. So all Shadow Tactics has to do is take the “shepherd 2-5 killers during their sneak-and-murder spree across a bunch of maps” to Edo period Japan to feel fresh and original. This means that there is only one question to ask if you want to know if Shadow Tactics is worth your time: Would you like to play more Commandos, or Desperados? For me the answer was “It’s complicated”. I played Commandos way back when. I liked the gameplay at first: Sneaking across the map littered with guards until you find the one unfortunate soul not covered by his colleagues and murder the bejeesus out of him, then moving on the guy whose back he was watching, and so on, pulling on the thread of the guard sweater until only a frayed collar remains… It’s like a beautiful puzzle that drips blood for every piece you set down. But the difficulty spikes were brutal, and at times the precision and speed with which a kill was only possible took so many tries for me to get right that I got frustrated and finally gave up on Commandos. These frustrating moments and difficulty spikes are in here, too, but Shadow Tactics does just enough to mitigate the frustrations that I stuck it out. The excellent quicksave system is one factor: not only does it remind you how long it’s been since your last save, it automatically rotates three slots so that when you save in a situation you don’t yet know is beyond saving, you can revert to an earlier save. The adding of banter between the characters is helpful, too. The story might be kind of rote and have a giant plot hole at the center of it, but the characters are well fleshed out, for the genre, and the dialogue script as well as the voice work elevate the game quite a bit. And yes, it helps that I sneak around ancient japanese fortresses and abduct the son **** from a Sento instead of traipsing around european battefields and assassinating **** commanders, again. Success in Shadow Tactics relies on split second timing at times. That can only work if the controls of the game are excellent, and luckily, they are: Switching between characters and ordering them to do stuff is effortless. The art is serviceable to good: Clearly legible, beautiful at times, but lacking any true wow moments. The sound is sparse but well done, the music unobtrusive and pleasing. The voice work is, as mentioned, well above average for this type of game. This game is for veterans of the genre with a taste for more, spiced with a bit of variation. Complete newcomers interested in the genre might as well start here: They might still bounce off Shadow Tactics, but in a genre with very few members, this is as forgiving as it gets. TLDR: Shadow Tactics is a great stealth real time tactics game. If that’s your jam, it has you covered.

I've played every Yakuza game and I would rank this one the lowest, or at least in the lower ranks.

[b] The game is much longer than in previous titles. [/b]
However, it is not filled with entertaining content, but rather with unnecessary sequences, elongated dialogues and lackluster fighting styles.

[b]There are 4 playable characters and each has his unique fighting style. [/b]
This sounds interesting and multilayered, but the design falls through when you realize, that you can only control one character at a time - which means, that you only have access to one combat style at a time. This is much worse than in (some of) the previous games.

[b] The whole Saejima chapter. What a dreadful snail pace.[/b]

From what I could gather online, Y5 marked an anniversary for the developer, which is why they wanted to deliver something big. Instead of only Osaka and Tokyo, they included Fukuoka, Nagoya, and Sapporo. The idea is well meant and the possible greatness of such an undertaking would be remarkable.
However, this is where the fatal flaw shows its head. Because the scale of this game was so big, the quality is stretched thin. Whereas the two cities in Y0 were polished to almost 18 karat, the cities in Y5 are far from it. The same goes for other areas of the game like fighting, side stories and so on.

This game is ~36 hours long, which is double of what almost all other titles are. And it has been a slug to get through it.
I only pushed myself to finish it, because the new titles seem fun and I wanted to finish every main title instead of skipping one.

------------------------------------------------------
[b] Do I recommend it? [/b]
No.

[b] Can I recommend it? [/b]
Only to a hardcore fan, who wants to follow the whole story of Yakuza.

review_text:
This could be an amazing td/rts but why do some developers still insist on using JRE? It's bloated, the garbage collection while revolutionary in 2002 is wonky at best and it handles memory usage in general, terribly because every interaction with the os is third hand.

The dev while I think he or she are/is awesome, pass this off as bloated AI but, after playing the game, I simply disagree. To qualify that statement just play Anno 1404 or even stronghold (a really old game) both of which were well ahead of their times' respectively in terms of graphics and AI, and the quality of the gaming experience are ones that still hold up today, despite their obvious vintage, and exhibit AI qualities I would consider to be far more rewarding and advanced than RtR. 

I have played the game and I do not think the AI justifies the overheads, this is not dwarf fortress, you are asking me for money to fund your hobby in advance.


Furthermore, it seems to be plagued with identical issues in terms of performance Mincraft was a decade ago. Notch knew the JRE was limited, do you?

To cut a long story short, there are many other great platforms to launch this game on, many of which are free and offer significantly better performance so people like me can focus on the gameplay rather than the flaws, please look at them and stop romanticising about JAVA. Use it for JSP or SQL, it's a bad platform for anything other than old school motorola games or server side scripting, please.

Otherwise, good game.

And let me re-iterate. This is no joke, Java is simply a bad platform to make games with. You simply have to examine how sub-optimally it handles memory usage and uses handshakes with the kernel rather than native injection.

Again, it's a great game on a bad platform.

Raybarg, to answer your question fully, I do think this game has potential, but the developers choices force me to give it a negative review. "But why?", you may say. Well. I can appreciate the dev has built the AI from the ground up and to be quite frank, that's ambitious. But nothing alters the fact the capability of JRE will consistently be significantly lower than the developers expectations. It's like an invisible barrier the game will never overcome.

To put that into perspective play Witcher 3 for ten minutes. How amazing does that game look and how interactive and real does the AI feel? Do you think that level of depth is achievable on Java? I can tell you the answer, an the answer is NO.

"But we are talking about AI", you may argue. The developer has suggested the AI is more complex than the likes of Rimworld or Prison Architect but like I summarised, I simply disagree. The difference being Rimworld AI works beautifully, and triple speed doesn't stop a computer dead. I don't own an incapable computer and therefore I do not expect it to be brought to it's knees performing even the most rudimentary operations. But that is not because this is a BAD GAME, that is because the developer is using JAVA.

Why?

You are asking me questions because you feel hurt by the fact I made a negative review. Why aren't you asking the dev why he/she is using Java?

I am a player that plays the game for gameplay and enjoyment with friends, i always skip story because it does absolutely nothing for me. In this context:
[list]
[*] -Allow me to Disable story. -> Don't force it on me, please.  I do not care about it in the slightest, it's just a Press and hold X to progress simulator.
[*] - Game world feels dead
[*] - too many "press and hold X" instances. It breaks flow.
[*] -Why go to the secret market making us wait, walk, press and hold x to 'talk' to people? Just have a dialogue with the character from the quest menu like other less tedious game designs. Too much clutter!
[*] - If we have a 'transfer enhancement' to basically freely (with a fee of 100 currency) put the +10 from 1 item to another, why not have the enhancement on the Gear slot itself? -> less clutter.
[*] -Can't trade with friend i played 10+hours with because he didn't press and hold X enough (to progress in story)
[*] -Enemies just spawn out of nowhere. Why not make them airdrop in instead? more immersive and less dead. "What about caves?" a portal then.
[*] -Weapons lack description. For example 'The Grim Reaper' doesn't say it shoots homing projectiles
[/list]
Nice Sound design. It's alive and playful.

 [h3] Suggestion:  [/h3]
[list]
   [*] -Unless it's already in game somewhere ahead i've not reached yet (because story doesn't allow me, need to press and hold X more!)  a Survival/avalanche of enemy waves could be fun and intense with bosses spawning every X amount of enemies killed in x time to spawn next wave (less staged, more organic this way) Could be fun.
   [*] - Have bosses and enemies respawn in exploration. A 30 second timer could be fun, it skips having to re-match every time if you grinding for an item. Maybe multiply the boss spawn every time?
   [*] -If it needs to have story, incorporate it into the maps the player is going to play anyway. Why break flow and force it onto players as this separate thing outside of 'playing the game'. It seems like a cheap trick locking things behind story progression, you failed to incorporate it into the games flow and now we have to do gymnastics because of it? Making story mandatory does not make the player value it, quite the opposite actually. It prevented me and friends from playing Fortnite STW and the same is happening here now. Friend quit playing because he didn't wanna "press and hold X" to progress story, gain rebel rank to trade with me.

It's surprisingly not satisfying to play. It is very reminding of 'Save the World Fortnite'. Dead islands, different color schemes from 1 area to another. Same enemies different look. Tho they introduced new enemy types every now and then. But they too forced story on player and locked progression behind it.

 [strike] I can't think of the thing this game needs to make it 'pop off' for me.[/strike] [b] Mandatory story is definitely the biggest burden so far. [/b]
[h1] Actually: turn the map into 1 giant one we can freely traverse from 1 mission to another [/h1]
 and explore the world ourselves like in 'Exploration' mode. This would be the best for game flow! Leave and enter area again for bosses to have respawned! Put your story sequences there as non-mandatory dialogue or NPC encounters out in the wild. Never leave your party for solo missions.
