review_text:
There are positives, like the pretty environments and lively art direction, but because of a combination of frustrating elements, the game becomes a frustrating grind that discourages tactical thinking and has you fighting the controls and save scumming constantly.

The maps are large, and the missions typically take an hour or two to beat, but there's no way to see the whole map at once. The zoom is woefully limited, meaning that planning a route through from the start to the goal is impossible. You find yourself taking on every little area one at a time, unable to plan for what's next, and looking back and realizing it would have been faster to go another way. Every guard is watched by at least one other guard. Killing guards becomes a process of tediously killing your way through an entire section of the map just so you can kill one guard that was blocking a gate.

For a stealth tactics game, the maps are also shockingly linear. Sure, it's open, but there's only one path that doesn't lead to certain death. After a time, you get the impression that every map has one main designed path with a few shortcuts, and every area, every section of the map is just a puzzle to solve (and time correctly). I didn't once feel like I could experiment with using different combinations of abilities, or one mission, going vertical, or going sneaking on another. I can't count the number of times I thought "Oh, I'd have loved to have this character right now, I wonder how I could use his explosive with her powder.." etc. except that every mission has a specific loadout of characters. I never felt like I had a creative choice in my use of abilities or characters. And even with the characters you get, working together is pointless. Even the abilities each character has seems unnecessarily limited. Only one character can throw rocks? Only one character can make a luring noise? It's arbitrary decisions like this that make the gameplay uncreative.

The squad mechanics are almost non-existent. I found myself playing most of the maps one character at a time, only changing when I faced a situation that required a different character's abilities. You can only control one character at a time, except to move, and even then it's a disaster because they all have different movement speeds and collide with each other constantly, frequently catching the guards' attention. The only way to use your characters together is using "shadow mode" which allows you to queue actions from different characters so you can execute them at once. HOWEVER, shadow mode only allows you to queue up ONE ACTION per character, making complex planning (i.e. shadow TACTICS) virtually excluded by design. The game wants you to control characters and make decisions in real-time, but making real-time decisions is impossible because the maps are crawling with guards, and this is [i] not a combat game. [/i] If you're spotted by a guard, game over is all but certain. Reinforcements begin to shoot from afar, you cannot fight more than one guard, you cannot run, you cannot become invisible. Even if you do manage to escape, the entire map will be on alert, making the rest of the mission nearly impossible. And your other characters CANNOT HELP AT ALL because again, REAL TIME. If you're spotted, your sniper can't take out the guard, your heavy can't clear the guards, because without that action-planning, by the time you switch to them, it's too late. The game becomes about timing, waiting and save-scumming over and over to get characters across the map, one by one.

That brings me to the save-scumming. It's included in the gameplay by design, even going as far as to include a timer reminding you to constantly save. Some others don't mind this, but I personally found it frustrating and flow-breaking. The game relies on save-scumming because it's the only way the player can time moves perfectly enough to succeed because the stealth, squad teamwork, and combat mechanics are not effective enough alone because they can't be properly planned and executed. It makes the gameplay tedious, and when it collides with the controls, it becomes truly frustrating.

The majority of the game relies on the mouse, and a few clunky hotkeys. Switching between characters takes too long to perform actions across characters in real-time. Executing actions, however, is the true nail in the coffin. I can't count the number of times I've clicked on a guard to kill them, and instead, without my realizing, the kill skill wasn't toggled, and my character walks right up to the guard and sits there, waiting for death. Me too, buddy. Or that I thought I clicked on the ground but instead clicked on a wall, and then my character walks out in front of a guard, reload the save. Or, that I had the wrong character selected, and again, ruined the play. The camera is not suitable for the amount of tight spaces and vertical elements in the game. You can't look top down, and rotating the camera requires stopping whatever else you're doing.

All these elements combine to make the gameplay an absolute grind that discourages tactical gameplay in favor of save-scumming over and over to solve precision timing situations.

review_text:
EDIT: As of 1.1.2, the game has entered a new state of unplayable, the game will now spawn endless boss enemies like Tiger bugs at the start of Arc Slams, amazing work.

Been here a while now, played this game on and off through it's development and enjoyed myself for the most part.

However, this "1.0" release is a disaster. I was worried about it to be honest, the state of the game in 0.8 was nowhere near finished and when they announced 1.0 was the next update I knew it was going to be rough.

As it stands, 1.0 is whack.

Galactic War:
The first day the game would hard CTD at the end of every match, I assume this was because the intel system related to the galactic war wasn't up and running properly yet, then when the galactic war system actually showed up it has to be one of the single worst implementations of a highly awaited feature I have ever seen. It is locked behind a clan system, the new planet is locked behind the galactic war, and when I finally get access to a specific mission I cannot find any players in said mission, in theory this makes this game mode and planet not viable for anyone not running a squad of at least 8 people.

The Performance:
It's bad, 32gb of RAM and a 3070 cannot handle this game on medium in 1080p apparently, I've disabled any form of ray tracing or Lumen (which enabled itself after the update for some reason) but the moment anything drastic happens I'm looking at 24 if I'm lucky.

The gameplay:
It's still ridiculously unbalanced and broken. The fact that a standard warrior can do a charge attack and instakill most of the smaller build classes is one thing, the fact that said warrior twitches, glitches and teleports during said charge however makes it insufferable (it's not even lag, they just wig out constantly regardless of ping). Bugs routinely warp all over or just land attacks through and over objects when terrain gets slightly complex.

Also, the gamemode AAS has some of the most bizarre balancing depending on objective. It's either a complete breeze or you got the high value targets objective and now everyone is stuck in the resupply bunker as a ridiculous horde has literally plugged the windows and doors, leading a game of run to the bunker, hold the trigger with 0 threat and infinite ammo.

The Singleplayer:
This is quite possibly one of the worst tutorials I have ever seen, however if I ever find myself in a linear cave then I am fully trained and prepared. The tutorial campaign is 20+ levels of linear caves that teach nothing, no mechanics, no classes, no bugs, they're the most tacked on content of all time.

Absolute disaster of a release.

Oh, and I still haven't got my early access skin.

review_text:
Really enjoyed this game.  Story is predictable, archetypical, japaneesie, boring.  The characters are stupid and basic.  The character portraits are sexualized as usual and also stupid.   The weapons are almost all boring and possess no individual noteworthy qualities,  Most of the magic sucks, as does casting it until the game is basically over.  Now for the good.  Thank god they didn't try to voice act this.  I do not like the grating voices these types of games assign to their characters.  The fact that it was text based meant I could stand to actually read the cutscenes instead of feverishly searching for a skip button.  There actually is a skip button, and you're not missing much by enjoying its use.  The bosses and enemies are all pretty fun to fight but the bosses can be cheesed really easily.  Like the spider archer lady is completely negated by a shield and summon swords and the ice lady by the fire sword and summonable fire orbs. 
 The visuals are very nice.  Pretty good pixel art.  Cool looking bosses.  To complete the map isn't too arduous and "how do I get over there" to get a treasure chest isn't a huge time sink for the most part.  Load up your favorite magical teleporting christmas throwing ham and... uhh, go ham on some demons!  

Without elaborating much, the only real complaint I didn't already know I was going to have coming into this game was the magic system.  There are equippable accessories that give you constant MP regen you find very late in the game.  Otherwise, your MP NEVER regenerates at all unless you use restorative items which tend to be expensive to buy and somewhat rare to pick up.  The basic (lousy) spells give you up to 4 casts to exhaust your entire magic bar, and the useful ones as few as one or two casts. That's it.  The spells are almost all terrible.  Once you've gotten the two accessories that make magic use practical, magic becomes almost overpowered, one shotting just about any enemy and doing around 1/5th of a boss's health bar per charge if you exploit elemental weaknesses. I don't have a quick and easy solution for this problem.  It just feels like the game developers got lost trying to come up with the magic system, and it's not very good as a result.  You find new spells constantly throughout the game, but it never feels practical to use them at all outside of necessity to open a door or something until you find the items that regenerate your MP.  It would have been nice if there was a scaling up system where spells were either much more useful in the early game when casting them was extremely expensive, there was a very slow regeneration of MP by default, or even a system that regenerates MP for killing enemies so that the player would feel welcome to use it offensively.  Maybe this bothered other people less than it bothered me.  

7 hours to 100% the map and beat all bosses with copious amounts of screwing around in the process.  Definitely worth the 8 bucks I paid for the game on sale. Conveniently, I'd give it a score of 8/10 as well due to the combination of length, cost, and enjoyment factor.  It's a pleasant game that, if you like to get-off looking at cartoon characters with comically inappropriate wardrobes, you'll enjoy even more than I did.  If the story in every anime you've watched or JRPG you've played has blown your mind, then you will love this game because it does not deviate even slightly from the common tropes of that genre.  At 10 bucks, it'd be a solid 7/10.  It is not worth 20 dollars.  Unless you're looking for your waifu or whatever the hell that means, wait for it to go on sale.

"3D cartoon" look to it, which means that it's minimalistic and gives me "free game on an iPhone" vibes. This isn't Commandos, where you'd have like a few interesting areas that are unique per level.

Your team does not listen to your commands, that is if you start an action and someone sees you the game slows down. While you desperately try to click for the idiot to run, he just sits there until the enemy's bar of sight fills up and the enemy starts shooting you with self-loading muskets. Controlling your squad is frustratiing beyond belief.

Not only this, but the player is forced to take care of the enemies, since they cover every single fucking inch of the map, and everyone else is covering them. Only once or twice in the mission is there a way to do things differently and you are not forced into this tactical bottleneck or you don't have to knock out and/or kill literally everyone you see.

Story is shit too. Instead of being a kick-ass band of Ronin, trying to fight the evil KANG of Japan, you are his personal errand boys... with a Samurai who speaks of "Honour" by hiding in bushes and attacking unsuspecting victims from the back.

review_text:
A short metriodvania that delivers on what it sells: a hard side-scrolling dungeon-crawler with cute(ish) monster girls of varying attitudes. It's okay, I am not a fan of the mix of artwork and not a pure focus on sprite-artwork.

[h1] Things to Expect [/h1]

[list]
    [*] A semi-predictable story.
    [*] Punishing combat that gradually becomes easier.
    [*] Very good sprite-work in lighting, effects, and enviroment.
    [*] Extra modes and multiple endings.
    [*] You can sell things to merchants, including the vending machines.
[/list]

[h1] Aesthetics [/h1]
While not the best sprite-work I have seen, it is certainly of high quality! It has the Shantae-issue of hip-shaking and nearly everything dressed in a school-girl's uniform. The music is there and it works to help the mood of each area in the game.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
This game is hard, and this difficulty comes from enemy damage along with a limited kit at the start of the game. As you explore and overcome, you gain various means to make combat easier along with managing damage and magic point scores.

Unfortunately, this is where the Metriodvania qualities end as you gain no extra movement tools, and optional paths to loot either take dynamite(or a fireball spell), or a weapon/spell with long reach (Chain Lightning). Traveling the world is made very simple with a teleport system. The real challenges come from boss fights, but depending on your kit can also be made trivial.

[h1] Story and Characters [/h1]
There is a very simple story here, with creepy implications later on. However, it loses marks from the extra artwork and dialogues you have with various monster girls through-out the game. There is plenty of environmental story-telling just from the sprite-work, but that is lost the farther along you get in the game. The dialogue takes away from the story by explaining the story, which ruins any interest in trying to figure things out yourself. I would have liked it a lot more if the story was told via exploring and looking around, rather than some anime cut-scene girl being glib and just explaining things.

[h1] Opinion and Conclusions [/h1]
I like Metriodvanias, and a good challenge. I disliked the conversation artwork, and the lean on cheesecake character design. Tits have a habit of tarnishing something that was otherwise pretty good. Not to say that this is a bad game, nor a game to be taken super seriously, but it sadly does not marry its over-the-top presentation with its design completely.

review_text:
I played a LOT of Helldivers 2 before I got this game. I was told it was just a much worse version and I shouldn't bother. Then I saw some actual gameplay online, and being a co-op game fan (admittedly due to Helldivers) I decided to buy the game and give it a try. I had a rough start, but soon fell IN LOVE with the game! 

The awesome maps, aesthetic, sounds, weapons, and especially the bugs really sold me. You don't have to be a master of gaming, or know some optimal meta, just hop on and shoot some bugs! The game is also very cinematic, always ending in a massive assault on a base you build with 15 other people. 

Unlocking new perks and weapons is a bit grindy, but that doesn't mean you can't do well with what you have. 

I feel like people compare this game a lot to Helldivers 2, and I don't blame them, it's literally based off Starship Troopers, but if you like that game you'll certainly love this one! 

I look forward to what else the developers will add in the future. 

If I didn't sell you already, this game has a camera man class.

This is a little indie game that is very ambitious. Sadly, it fails miserably in its core feature: the story.
Don't get me wrong, there are many good things about it: how ambitious it is in the premise (you'll love the first 10 minutes or so), the atmosphere it conveys, the soundtrack is very beautiful. It is a cozy little game. But it can not be recommended because due to it being pretty much a walking simulator, the story should be the best element here. It is not. It fails miserably.
How can I explain that to you without spoiling anything?... ok, let me try:
Imagine this game were Back to the Future (this is just a random example, the game has nothing to do with time traveling). Did you? Ok, now imagine it did not bother explaining how is it possible for a man to come back in time, dates his mother, and not ceasing to exist. Do you see what I mean? That was THE CORE ELEMENT in Back to the Future. Because you just can not escape from that! The feeling you will get playing To the Moon, if you have at least a little understanding of logics, is this exact one.
The story starts great, but derails completely and becomes a mess.
You know that strategy in Greek tragedy when the plot was way too confusing and they needed to use Deus ex Machina? Well, To the Moon is much worse than that.
I think I have succeded in telling you why this game is not recommended without spoiling anything.
If you don't want to be deeply disappointed, don't buy it.

Every positive review is correct, the experience of playing and the plot cooperate to take full advantage of 'games' as a medium of storytelling and is a delight. However, the optimisation of the actual game leaves a lot to be desired. 

Playing on recommended hardware, there is often minute long loading screens between entering doors from inside to outside and sometimes within the same building. Combat is not intended to be anything like a natural FPS, but the unique flavour of jank when anybody hits anybody feels unfair in an unintended way and has caused a lot of deaths. 
While Pathologic does make normally boring things like walking and buying food nerve wracking to the most engaging degree, I think there is a difference between that and being put in time out staring at a half loaded door for most of play. Of course if those things don't bother you/hardware isn't an issue and other positive reviews capture you, you'll probably have an interesting time. 

But for those whom this warning applies, I cannot recommend this wonderful game.

review_text:
It's a good engine but bad level design. 

The game is extremely tedious at times but it makes up for it by having some good levels. The beginning intro give you no direction. I spent an hour trying to figure out what I was supposed to do to continue the story. You are forced to play the mini games to proceed. You can leave after joining the extra modes but they don't tell you that. This is also just a bad idea as you have to sit through 6 different loading screens just to continue the story. Why are we forced to play these mini games? If it was some sort of tutorial, that could be a cool idea but there is no direction so it isn't a good tutorial. Also the menu room is also a good idea on paper, but terrible in game. Why do I have to walk across a giant room to get to the sandbox mode? It is a good idea but tedious like the rest of the game. Another gripe I have with the game is that it is more buggy than the first game. I have a 3080, 32gb of ram and a 5800x and am using an Index. There were so many times where I would no clip to the ground or randomly be launched off walls. This is an annoying bug as they have extremely tall ladders to climb. You get all the way to the top just to be launched off. It reminds me of the tedious final level with the giant ladder in the first game. Like I said before, this is an extremely good engine that is held back by it's tedious level design. I would still recommend this game as it is one of the best VR games out there.

review_text:
This game was fun, but not worth $40.

Tunes are sweet and the world is vivid and colorful, but the gameplay stagnates quickly and feels repetitive.
About all there is to do is keep combos going, and this isn't very difficult. Manuals are incredibly easy to do and basically prevent any combo drops. Gonna land? Hold RT and you're safe. Manual timer running out? Press LT and X or B when you have a little meter to reset it. I respect the accessibility, but I wish there was more difficulty.

Story was alright but had some questionable moments towards the last half.

My biggest complaint is trying to switch characters / customize. Why can't I change to the main characters in the hideout? I have to go to one of the other areas and find a breakdance square. But not only that; I also can't have any "heat" or I can't change at all. And if I want to customize my character, I have to go to a restroom, but can only use them once before they close and I have to reenter the area.

I 100% the game in under 16 hours; all collectibles, characters and achievements. Not too difficult, but can be annoying when you need skates when you've got a bike, or vice versa.

 I enjoyed my time all in all, but I can't help being a little disappointed.

review_text:
Sucks, constantly crashes, gameplay is sluggish and the physics are incredibly basic, not letting me even stand on tree trunks and crates without slowly sliding off.

Edit, I decided I fancied a sniping binge after playing sniper elite 4 for a while so I redownloaded the game, and thought I would give it a proper go. Stealth games require two things to be fun, predictability and information. On this game you receive neither. You sneak up behind a big armor clad guy to cut his throat, and no matter how sneaky you are, it's impossible to kill them. Of course the game doesn't tell you this at any point so you have to figure it out through trail and error. Enemy corpses disappear if I respawn so I can simply kill a few guards, go back through a checkpoint, respawn then all the corpses have kindly hidden themselves the only problem then is that you desperately need those corpses for ammo, since in spite of this game being a sniping game, sniper ammo is about as common as unicorn turds, especially annoying if you are playing in a long range section since you usually don't have anywhere nearby to restock, and when you do, you get 10 bullets. You can walk past cameras 3 or 4 times and not get any feedback that they're there, then after you have been laid in front of them for a whole minute trying to get a kill, they suddenly spot you, that is when they're not somehow miraculously spotting you through walls. I've been in gunfights where the enemy have apparently decided to teleport in front of my very eyes to a position behind me. and I spent some of my hard earned money on a drone so I could spot targets without getting near them and it has a tiny 100m range. Although it gives you no indication that you're approaching this range, instead it just shuts off. The AI is just completely random, I've shot a barrel from across the map killing two guards, but then when I go over to the same spot to loot those guards, a stationary patrol who was previously oblivious to his exploding friends manages to spot me. I can shoot out cameras with complete disregard for the enemies realising because in this game the guards are watching the cameras so attentively that if I'm in front of a camera for more than 2 seconds, all hell breaks loose. But if I systematically disable every single camera on an entire level, then nobody bats an eyelid. Why does a throwing knife kill someone instantly if they're facing away from me, but if they spot me for even a moment, it doesn't kill them but bounces off even if I hit them in the face? Are they somehow able to catch knives in their teeth?

The sniping mechanics like windage and bullet drop are great, the world design and futuristic tech is great, but as a stealth game, and in many ways as a sniping game, this game falls flat on it's face.

review_text:
This game combines the feel of classic arcade style sports games (think NFL Blitz, NBA Jam, Backyard Sports, etc.) with a rogue-like campaign format.  Overall the gameplay is solid with simple, intuitive, and responsive controls.  There is just enough realistic physics to make it feel like a hockey game (players can't turn 180 degrees without losing speed/momentum, for example), but otherwise the game is loaded with arcade-y shenanigans that keep things silly and lighthearted.

As the game truly is a melding of two design philosophies (arcade sports and rogue-like), I will judge each separately.

Arcade Hockey Elements:  8.5/10
The controls are easy to pick up and understand, making it accessible to experienced gamers and newcomers alike.  There are no penalties and no offsides rules in the game, so the action keeps moving.  Hockey staples like one-timers and net-front tips are included seamlessly, with the latter happening automatically if the player is in front of the net.  Body checking is generally very effective at knocking a player off the puck, or knocking a player down before the puck gets to them (remember, no penalties).  Players will also stick check automatically if they are close enough to their opponent, so you don't have to rely solely on smashing into your opponents to get possession.

The hockey experience falls just short of 10 due primarily to the AI.  The computer opponent generally has good positioning fundamentals, with certain opponents being more or less aggressive in the campaign mode, forcing you to adjust your strategy.  However, your own AI teammates often make baffling decisions.  Sometimes one or two of them will skate right next to you when you are carrying the puck, getting in your way and also blocking you from making other passes, as they will catch any pass you try to make to teammates beyond them.  They will also frequently overskate the net, taking themselves out of the play and missing out on otherwise golden rebound shot attempts (the opponent AI seems to do this far less frequently).  Finally, the goalie has some sort of bug that makes his passes erratic.  Sometimes he will pass the puck where you indicate, and sometimes he will pass the puck in a random direction (though this appears to affect the computer opponent as well).

Rogue-like elements:  7/10
There are a lot of fun and creative ideas here.  Players have stats that you can increase, and you can gain passive and active talents for players throughout the campaign.  Some of them are far more useful than others, however, with certain talents backfiring on you more often than not.  During the campaign, your opponents scale in difficulty, with each boss and mini-boss having their own talents and abilities that you have to overcome.  Some of these can be quite frustrating to play against, particularly the Act 2 and Act 3 bosses, who both have abilities and rink modifiers that fundamentally change the game, making it feel a little less like an arcade hockey game.  This element of the game loses some points in my evaluation as in these cases the gameplay crosses the line from challenging into frustrating a bit more often than I would like.

Overall this game is at least an 8/10, and well worth the price they are asking.  There is a lot of charm and polish to the game that I haven't listed above (my review would be pages long if I did).  I would recommend the game to anyone who is looking for an arcade-style hockey game, and anyone who enjoys rogue elements and sports games in general.  If you are easily frustrated by rogue-style games where sometimes you just get dealt bad luck, or if you get frustrated by the simplicity and silliness that can accompany arcade-style games, this may not be for you.

Pretty fun and challenging with beatiful pixel graphics and particle/lightning effects. The thing I liked the most is combat. Some people might dislike it and it's understandable, since not everyone likes "clunky and slow" combat, but I personally enjoyed having to think about the way of passing every enemy encounter, including bosses. You can try out many stupid or op builds and since the game isn't that long it has potential for replaybility. I just wish there was NG+, but it might come in the future. 
Another good thing about this game are the graphics. Animations are smooth, particles look amazing, the lightning is beatiful and the enemy designs are of big variety. As for bosses, I will just call their design "interesting". 
The story is pretty simple, but that doesn't mean it's boring, but it has that stereotypical anime plot feeling to it. Some might like it, some might not. I enjoyed it to the point I decided to see all the endings, because I wasn't satisfied with just one (the game has 4 in total).
Do I recommend it?
Yes, but be prepared, that if you expect dynamic hack n slash game, then you can look for something else. But if you want a game that plays the same as Gothic, one of the classic games where at the start of the game you had to carefully choose when to fight and when to run then this game is for you.

With 228 hours playing at the time of writing this (I used to play with the ARC client for a while), a few things I wanna just put out there to anyone thinking about picking up this game. There are a lot of other reviews with very valid criticism about the amount of micro-transactions in this game (looking at you, Mudd). Of course, paying is optional, but pretty much the whole game is free to play. People like to say having (insert item here) is a must-have from the C-store (the real money shop), but really, you don't need it. A lot of good gear comes from missions, reputation, R&D, etc, for free, but some of them do take some time. Waiting/Timer game-play is also a bit of a problem in STO, and I completely understand why anyone would be put off by this. Keep in mind that this game has been around since 2010, and some mechanics/controls aren't explained very well. I know some people will find it annoying, but the STO wiki is your friend. -Player switching is a nightmare.

review_text:
This game is awful.  Absolutely awful.  Completely unbalanced, terrible characters, and .hack// seems to suffer the same problem as Aliens in that every single piece of media tells the same basic plot over and over and over and over.  The only redeeming factor this collection has is that it's at least the full game at one price instead of making you pay full price three times over to get a full game's worth of content (and, no, each individual piece is NOT a full game's worth).

To get into specifics, the game is completely unbalanced.  The amount of experience you get from enemies is mostly flat the entire game, only determined by your level, and the enemy's level.  Unfortunately this is ramped so high that you generally can level every 2-3 fights.  One dungeon can have a few dozen fights.  The maximum level is 50 per game (so 50, then 100, then 150).  I gained 8 levels in one dungeon run.  So you can massively, massively outpace the story without even trying, you can do it simply by doing the side quests.  On top of that, the damage you do has more to do with the level differences as well than your gear.  This is supposed to make it harder to go to a dungeon that's too high for you, as you'll do minimal damage, but ultimately you really can keep enemies locked long enough to kill them anyway even with a sizable difference.  Not that you need to go after high end enemies.

Gear drops don't match the level of the dungeon either, despite what the game tells you.  Your NPC party members can gain quite a bit of levels as well, to 'catch up' while you're not using them.  However, they won't do anything about gear.  You can have someone join your party in the 30's still wearing level 1 gear because you and you alone determine what they use.  In most RPGs this wouldn't be such an issue, but this game is pretending to be an MMO.  But the other characters are dumber here than in most other RPGs anyway.

The story is laughably bad, the same rehashed plot line of "there's a glitch/not-glitch in The World that gives some users super powers and puts other users in comas" and you're the CHOSEN ONE who also has the power so you can counter it.  But the characters in this are absolutely insufferable.  Their personalities are extremely poorly written to the point of parody of religious zealots, pacifists, psychopaths, and the like.

The game is a train wreck on every level.  The original PS2 RPGs (not the G.U. but the set before it) were not masterpieces but they were significantly better than this.  Even the concept of the three keywords just doesn't work well in this, the dungeons it creates are even more lackluster than the original set's.  There's no real incentive to play them either since you'll just end up so far ahead of the plot that nothing matters, you may as well be using the game's built in cheat mode.  For the record, no, I am not using that.  I wanted to actually play the game.  But there's no game here to play.

This game belongs on "worst of" lists.  Just avoid it.

review_text:
After several hours of playing Eastside Hockey Manager: Early Access Edition I can say that it is one of the most enjoyable and addictive simulation games I have ever played.  I always enjoyed various football (soccer for us in N. America) simulations but I love hockey and am so glad that a game developer has introduced (in this case re-introduced) a simulation for hockey fans.   

Pros: The game offers a variety of setting which allow you to establish how many hats you want to wear when managing the team you take over.  You can just manage (draft, develop prospects, sign free-agents, trade players, hire and fire coaches, scouts and other personnel, salary cap) while analyzing endless statistics or micro-manage every aspect of your team by adding coaching responsibilities to your portfolio and establish in-game tactics and select game-day rosters.  The game has an active modding community.  You can download NHL player rosters or other professional league players and team logos for a more realistic experience.

Cons:  
- The game could offer higher resolution settings than the 1024 x 768. 
-  Also while the lower resolution does not detract from game play I have found that when I quit a game the default      resolution setting on my Windows desktop sometimes reverts to the 1024 x 768 resolution setting that the game uses (from my normal desktop resolution of 1920x 1200). Not a big deal to change resolution back to 1920 x 1200 but a nuisance. 
- In rare instances some of the historical statistics do not tally correctly. 
-  Some statistics do not export correctly to a file or printer

Game Improvement:  
- I would like to see some graphical updates made to the game as some of the 2D graphics seem a little dated like when watching individual games.  
- Also would like to see when winning a cup or when a player I manage wins an individual trophy,  it would be nice to have a graphic of a newspaper where headlines highlight the achievement like I have seen in other sports sims.  

Recommendation:  The game for an early access product is well developed and if no further development of the game was offered would still represent extremely good value. review_text:
I've played a number from MMO's from LotRo, ESO, Rift, and SWO and yet none has kept me logging in daily quite like STO has. And the weird thing is that I am not a huge Trekkie either, or should I say I wasn't a huge trekkie before I started. LotR and ES have both had me investing far more time in the past in other games and delving into their lore, but I started playing STO about 3 years ago simply because I started rewatching next generation. 

Star Trek Online is very easy to play in bitesize chunks because of the episodic nature of the chapters and missions, and honestly it is done in a way that no other MMO I have played has ever beaten. In games like LotrO and ESO I found myself logging in after a week away or an extended absence and simply having no idea which quests I was doing or why and so would generally drop them all and start picking up random quests until I found a common story thread to follow. It's not a major issue, but it is a bit jarring when going back to a game after a break. With STO though, the chapters just seem to be more neatly wrapped up and easier to digest and there is a very definite order where you just follow one by one when it comes to the main story. There are other world missions that you pick up on the way too, but are generally repeatable which means they don't tend to affect the main story much. I don't know why but STO just feels neater when it comes to storytelling, and it really helps you not feel overwhelmed. 

The devs also keep constant mini events running where you can earn ships, upgrades and in game items on pretty much a monthly basis which in my view also makes it one of the most generous MMO's I have played. Most games give a daily reward for free, but its usually a one use consumable or something you never would have bought anyway. In this game, the ships alone are worth logging in for the events as each one can be claimed on every character and every ship has a unique trait or sometimes equipment that can help you experiment with builds. I see a lot of "STO is pay to win" but in my experience that just isn't true. They are more than generous with free stuff and they have regular sales on the in game store. Most of what people cry about the cost of seems to be things like rare ships too, which just seems to me like a huge FOMO that they themselves need to either cough up or get over. You can absolutely play this game without investing much at all, as I played f2p for quite a while before starting to spend money on it. 

As well as the in game rewards and freebies, there are regular update giveways on sites like intel, alienware and Steel series and these giveaways tend to have something that ties into the latest game update. For example a recent update was all about the borg and so the giveaways had borg consoles and borg ground weapons that you could claim. What is more every single time they do these giveaways, every one contains a pack that gives you bank and inventory space which means that there is another thing you don't necessarily have to buy in game. These sites always have their own unique updates too giving away different items, and so at each update you get to claim 2-4 different ones and so that is 2-4 different bank and inventory packs. Again, in my opinion just another showing of how overly generous the game actually is. 

There are also in game work arounds to some of the paid content, for example one thing people buy is "cross faction flying" but this can be unlocked for free just by levelling a Klingon KDF character to max level. Once your klingon is max level, every character on the account can fly whatever ship they like so again saves you money after a little time investment. 

As for levelling too, I find this to be one of the easiest games to level characters in personally. I have something like 8 max level characters and most of them I haven't really played that much. They have been levelled mainly through events, random TFO's (group missions) and solo patrols. This wasn't for any other reason than because I wanted different characters of different races to be able to jump in and play when I felt like it and have access to similar skills across them. 

Quite honestly, even as a someone who is fairly new to star trek I can say that this game gives you a lot to log in for and a lot of content to play. It also got me interested in watching other star trek shows such as Deep Space 9 and TOS, neither of which ever interested me before. The fact that the game hires many of the voice actors to reprise their roles got me wanting to know more about them and so it kindled a bit of a star trek deep dive and in turn made me appreciate the whole fandom a lot more. 

My final thought is simply that if you are on the fence about trying this game, just try it. I was and I did, and I haven't looked back.

review_text:
After two playthroughs of the main story, I don’t think The Callisto Protocol is good. "Frustration The Video-Game." The very core of this thing is too flawed. The first half of the game I was convinced this was just not good at all. But…eventually...I admit that despite its many many MANY issues, something about it did come through to me by the end. So while I can’t recommend it at full price, I think on a sale there is something genuine here worth experiencing one day.

Callisto Protocol’s level design is pretty on the surface, but mechanically the more important things are plain, boring, or bad. Graphical fidelity and lighting effects are too good. I’ll say I never get bored looking at this game. Once that trick wares though, there’s not much to grab onto. The entire game is basically one long skinny corridor. If you took any screenshot from the first 5 hours of this game and asked me which chapter it was, I honestly wouldn’t be able to tell you. There’s no backtracking, no unique rooms with memorable sequences, no puzzles, no metroidvania elements, no nothing. Explore if you care about minmaxing. Otherwise you’re not missing anything. It just becomes one linear hallway from beginning to end with a couple branches and hide holes here and there. 

I’m left thinking about what this game’s level design could have been. The devs could have made Black Iron Prison feel more interconnected as a place that had actual structure by making you retread familiar ground and making certain rooms connect to other familiar areas LIKE DEAD SPACE DID BACK IN 2008 FOR CHRIST’S SAKE! Dead Space’s Ishimura was so brilliantly designed. Black Iron prison could have been like that. Instead it has no interest in that sort of mechanical illusion. It feels like a straight line from beginning to end and nothing interesting to see except for pretty graphics and lighting. The exception to this is the game does change it’s scenery with snow and other environments in the later half which made it slightly interesting that I finally wasn’t staring down dark metal hallways anymore. 

Vents...holy crap… I have no idea why the devs thought that making you crawl through 40 plus vents throughout this game was a good idea. Developers, I promise you, vent crawling isn’t fun. It’s a little claustrophobic the first couple times you make me do it in a horror game, but once you’ve made me do it 6 times in the span of an hour and nothing ever happens, then the jig is up. Not to mention, you’re trying to tell me in the far future when we have colonies on other planets, you want me to believe this maximum security prison has huge open vents you crawl through constantly and can reach with your arms everywhere? Seriously?

The story can be summarized the same way I summarized the level design. Cosmetically on the surface it’s good. Its presentation is great with great cutscenes and voice acting. It’s when you look at it closer and expect more depth is when you realize there’s not much there. The characters aren’t that interesting and there’s no plot development until the second half of the game. By the end I did find myself interested enough in the plot, I was intrigued, and I was even invested in the 2 lead characters hoping they would survive. It just took too long to start feeling that way. I’m surprised the game was able to get me to feel that so far in though after a lot of boredom with the story.

Now I could have forgiven a lot of what I’ve talked about so far if the combat was good. But the combat is what done it. Combat is…an absolute abortion. Now, once again just like everything else in this game, its surface level stuff is fun. Animations, finishers, blood and gore, sound effects, that’s all in isolation pretty great. How the combat actually works though and programmed in functionality is a mess. This melee focused combat works fine enough early on when you only fight one enemy at a time but it’s more boring. When the game decides later to throw more than one enemy at you though, it completely breaks, however it's more fun at that point. When you push the attack button to hit an enemy, Jacob locks into an animation with one enemy. So if you’ve got 2 enemies in front of you and you swing between them to try and hit them both, the game will lock you onto one of them, turn you towards them and put you into position so the animation looks better. All other enemies in the arena will simply wait their turn next to you while you’re wailing on one enemy. These are zombies, they wouldn’t wait like that they would just all rush you at once. The devs clearly realized they didn’t create a combat system that can account for more than one enemy at a time very well so they made enemies just stand around while you’re executing melee hits on one enemy until your combo is over. You know what game created a combat system that gave you tools to crowd control and even let you get creative with how you do it AND the space zombies would all rush you at once? Dead. Space. 

Animations won’t even work sometimes. I have so many clips where a zombie starts their attack animation then I decide to attack and see if I can interrupt them. My swing then goes right through them and doesn’t make contact, and then after that instead the game prioritizes the enemy's attack to connect. Why? Because he started his attack before me. So to the game, it doesn’t matter that my attack should have landed first and I should have stunned him, therefore interrupting his attack. Nope. Doesn’t matter. Utterly broken. Also in this game you’re supposed to dodge left, dodge right, dodge left, then hit the enemy a few times, rinse and repeat. The camera during this completely sh**s the bed. The camera jolts everywhere because of the dodge mechanic, and what makes it even worse is that you’re in these narrow corridors most of the time which even further screws with the camera while it’s jolting around during combat. Absolutely atrocious. F minus. Failure. I award you no points developers of this combat. 

I admit though…eventually when I unlocked more moves, some guns, and got the entire combat sandbox revealed to me, I would be lying if I said I never had fun with this broken a** combat. It can be fun in the second half of the game. See the trend here? It’s just a system built too much on making animations connect perfectly for realism’s sake rather than focusing on hit boxes and making the system feel fair.

Look…this game is thin at its core and even broken mechanically. However, even after all of that, I think the reason why I kind of enjoyed it by the end is that this is a game with a lot of effort behind it. I saw it everywhere. The effort and passion is there, and it shows. These guys who made this game are not trying to rip you off or offer you a scam. There’s no insidious plot to get you addicted to spending endless time playing a soulless microtransaction trap. No! It’s just an honest to goodness video game made by people trying to give you an experience worth your money. And so I’m happy some people are coming back and giving this game a little more love than it got at launch. Each of these elements started to glimmer towards the latter half of my playthrough. There’s something to be said about that. The combat at the beginning was boring and repetitive. The level design was disappointing in the first half and waaayyy too many annoying damn vents. The story was basically nonexistent and didn’t move at all for the first half of my playthrough. ALL. Of. Those. Things. Got better, more fun, more entertaining, by the second half. They still had problems, but it started to come together at the end for me. There’s something there. For what it’s worth I started to fall for this game. But I think these devs just made some bad creative decisions early on in this process and it really crippled the core of this thing.

[h1]5/10[/h1]

Though effort and passion alone do not make a good game, I recognize the presence of them.

This game is great and a lot of fun, especially if you like Far Cry 3. However, every time you open up the game or your map/inventory menu, the game tries to connect to the online servers. This game doesn't have online anymore, so it of course can't connect. While I can understand somewhat of the game doing this when it launches, it is absolutely inexcusable to have the game try to connect to the online servers EVERY TIME YOU OPEN UP THE MAP OR INVENTORY. Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun - A Stealthy Symphony in Feudal Japan
Step into the vibrant yet perilous world of 17th-century Japan with Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. This tactical stealth masterpiece, crafted by Mimimi Games, throws you headfirst into the shoes of six unique ronin and kunoichi, each with their own skills and personalities, tasked with eliminating powerful enemies and navigating intricate levels amidst a backdrop of political intrigue and personal vendettas.

A Shadowy Ballet:

Shadow Tactics' brilliance lies in its meticulous blend of strategy and stealth. Every level unfolds like a meticulously choreographed dance, demanding calculated planning and precise execution. You'll spend hours studying enemy patrol patterns, strategically positioning your characters, and chaining their abilities together to overcome seemingly insurmountable odds.

A Gallery of Lethal Artists:

Your six operatives are more than just pixelated pawns; they're living, breathing individuals with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Hayato, the agile ninja, scales walls and eliminates lone guards with ease. Yuki, the cunning kunoichi, distracts enemies and lays deadly traps. Mugen, the hulking samurai, slices through foes in a whirlwind of steel. Each character demands careful consideration, and mastering their synergy is key to success.

A Feast for the Senses:

Shadow Tactics is a visual and auditory treat. The hand-drawn art style is breathtaking, with lush landscapes, detailed environments, and expressive character animations. The soundtrack is equally captivating, blending traditional Japanese instruments with haunting melodies and heart-pounding action cues. Every element immerses you deeper into the world, heightening the tension and the thrill of each successful maneuver.

A Glimmer in the Darkness:

Despite its unforgiving gameplay and punishing difficulty, Shadow Tactics never feels unfair. Each challenge, no matter how daunting, feels meticulously crafted, offering multiple solutions and rewarding experimentation. The satisfaction of pulling off a flawlessly executed plan, perfectly synchronizing your characters' abilities to eliminate an entire patrol without raising an alarm, is unparalleled.

Not Without Scars:

However, Shadow Tactics isn't without its blemishes. The camera controls can be clunky at times, and the occasional technical hiccup can disrupt the flow of gameplay. The story, while engaging, takes a backseat to the stellar mechanics, and the ending might leave some players wanting more.

A Must-Play for Stealth Aficionados:

Despite these minor flaws, Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun remains a masterclass in the stealth genre. Its innovative gameplay, breathtaking visuals, and unforgettable characters make it a must-play for any fan of strategic thinking and nail-biting tension. So, don your ninja garb, sharpen your katana, and prepare to enter the shadows – Shadow Tactics awaits.

Verdict:

Pros:
Innovative and rewarding tactical stealth gameplay
Diverse and well-developed characters with unique abilities
Stunning hand-drawn art style and immersive soundtrack
Satisfyingly challenging without feeling unfair
Cons:
Clunky camera controls and occasional technical issues
Story takes a backseat to the gameplay
Abrupt ending might leave some players wanting more
Score: 4.5 out of 5 shurikens. A near-flawless stealth masterpiece that will captivate and challenge you in equal measure.

Recommended for: Fans of tactical games, stealth enthusiasts, and lovers of beautiful art and captivating soundtracks.

Not recommended for: Players who prefer action-packed gameplay or dislike challenging difficulty levels.

I hope this review gives you a glimpse into the captivating world of Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. Whether you're a seasoned shinobi or a curious newcomer, this game is sure to leave you speechless. So, prepare to unleash your inner shadow warrior and dive into this unforgettable experience.

let me pick up my corpses. there's so many weird decisions in this game: like that picking up things need a long press of E... this is for dialogue games that want to make sure that you don't accidentally click a button and bork your quest-line. NOT FOR ACTION GAMES.

the magic is fantastic, but I never use it. because every time I want to use it, I think to myself: it takes 30 minutes to get off cooldown, so why waste it?
having such insane cooldowns with the most fun aspect in the game is laughably self-defeating. every time I actually decide to use magic, I almost immediately get into a situation where I really needed it and can't use it.

there is so many things that could improve this, like a big mana bar that VISIBLY fills up, albeit slowly, mana potions or the devs potentially deciding that it's ok to just let you use the fun stuff when I can headshot things from a distance. why the ban on letting me freeze things often?

but all of this would not be a reason to rate it down... but losing so much time and so many items I had collected... tons of letters and crosses and such... subjectively speaking, I may as well restart the game. that's how it feels, as ridiculous as it sounds.
it makes not much sense, but that's how I feel and I have no interest in starting over. any time investment into an old looking UE4 title with mechanics that spit on my time investment with BS "now your stuff is gone" mechanics is just a waste

dev: if you pick up an item, even if that item is just converted to gold, NEVER have to be taken away. anything dropped should stay there and be pickupable. no deadline.

but it just does something to my enjoyment when loot that drops despawns (instant down vote for any modern game that does that) or if I can permanently lose items or currency I worked for.

review_text:
Three years after the release of Act 1, the change in writers has made itself quite apparent in Act 2. Gone are the charming flavor texts that sprouted from almost every background element to inspect or trying to get your trusty pidgeon to interact with a piano, and here to stay is a minimal amount of text that says "that won't work" and nothing for human out of water Joey to say about the intriguing designs of the characters around her that weren't introduced in Troll Call. What remains of Hiveswap is a rather lifeless journey through a series of beautifully crafted dioramas of lovingly animated trolls that all have increasingly bizarre yet charming personalities; what's clear with Act 2 is a devotion to character writing, as is common with post-Act 7 Homestuck content, with little effort placed into actual world building. As fun as the characters are, there is little of their characterization from their appearances in Friendsim, so long time fans might be displeased to see this. Many of these characters also end up being not but set pieces of little relevance, which is disappointing given a couple of the trolls' potential connections to future villains. 
Much of the narrative of the game is also quite pointless to Joey and Xefros' endgame goal. A lot of the game could've been cut and nothing would've changed; the entirety of the first third where the two explore Charun and Zebede's hives (both characters cut for time) could've been cut as the only plot-relevant content occurs once they reach the train station. The narrative itself grinds to a halt for an Ace Attorney parody that is also completely irrelevant to the main narrative. [spoiler]The only plot relevant thing occurs when Xefros and Joey and Xefros manage to hi-jack the train, only for the train to be blown up and potentially killing everyone on board, making the entirety of Act 2's plot beats completely irrelevant. The ending also comes across as simple shock value which is the standard Homestuck faire, but even that old trick is becoming rather old.[/spoiler] 
More than anything, the game comes across as wasted potential, and it's all the more frustrating that players will have to wait another three years to see the conclusion to such a disappointing cliffhanger. 
Also again, a game that only added its credits earlier than anticipated due to backlash for even removing them in the first place doesn't deserve your money.

review_text:
I don't actually think [i]The Callisto Protocol[/i] is a bad game. My 'thumbs down' here is not saying the game is bad, I just find the game so painfully mediocre and not worth your time when there are so many better games out there. The game visually looks fantastic (though there is still a stutter issue that never got fixed), but the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired.

My main gripe for the game comes from the general level design. The game, features a lot of slow walking, sliding, and crawling sections. A lot of these sections opt to use fairly cheap jumpscares rather than build any horror through tension or atmosphere. Actually, some of those aren't even jumpscares, but whatever you call those sections where there is some monster/shadow/dead body that just moves off screen around a corner - it's not really a jumpscare and isn't particularly good horror. The game in general lacks any interesting exploration and ends up being pretty linear. By linear, I don't mean that I expect the game to be open world or anything, just simply give me the feeling of actually exploring the world and scrounging for resources. That is what I expect from a survival horror - even if the game has linear story progression, I want to feel like I am exploring the location in some way. I think the fact that Callisto Protocol doesn't have any sort of viewable map really shows just how the game is just linear corridors, you will never need to consult a map because you always just go forwards with only an occasional side path.

A very common complaint around this game is the combat, particularly the melee combat that the game focuses on. I actually don't think that making the combat melee focused is an inherently had idea. In a survival horror game where ammo is going to be limited, I think a strong melee focus can make a lot of sense. I first I actually liked the dodge mechanic, but it ends up being pretty damn repetitive the further in you get in the game. As the game tells you in the initial tutorial popup, there is no timing with the dodge so there is no real skill or challenge in the mechanic. The only mechanic that ever expands on the melee combat is once you get a gun and now you can take a shot at the end of a combo. But the gun doesn't really add much to the melee combo and the game doesn't expand beyond that. Guns in general are pretty boring in the game, the game doesn't really have any mechanic like [i]Dead Space[/i] where you are required to shoot off the limbs, so instead it's just shotgun to the face a couple of times to kill. It's not bad, but doesn't have any of the tension that other games like [i]Dead Space[/i] have.

Inventory management is not something I have an issue with in survivor horrors (not that I play too many of them), but I did find it weird that it really feels like getting more guns is actually [i]worse[/i]. Each gun has a different type of ammo and the game only seems to spawn the ammo when you have the gun. This led to my inventory being filled with ammo, but specifically ammo for four different guns which meant I didn't have all that much ammo for a single gun. The additional guns didn't seem that particularly more useful over the pistol and shotgun, so I think I would've been better off not buying new guns. I never bought the assault rifle because of this - maybe it was good, but it's much more expensive and I didn't want to deal with another ammo type clogging up my already limited inventory.

The story is kinda weird. It's fine and I guess it works for a game, but there are a couple of things that keep me from really caring for it. Without going into any spoilers, it's particularly annoying that there is a bit of a reveal that should already seem obvious to the player. If the player doesn't already assume from the beginning, the game pretty much lays it out before the reveal so so the player should already be able to figure it out before the Jacob (the player character).

If you are interested, maybe the game is worth it on a deep sale, but I think there are plenty of other worthwhile games to play. You would be much better of playing any of the [i]Dead Space[/i] games, or even the [i]Resident Evil[/i] games if you are looking for a survival horror game in general. Maybe if you've already played every other survival horror, then you can go for it, I guess.

The map needs improving and contributes to the frustration when navigating huge levels in search of some missing graffiti, which would be fine if the levels had more fun stuff to discover and play with.

review_text:
I'm in the minority with my views of this game but quite frankly, this game wasn't very much fun. Often billed as a horror game, the narrative kinda blows it's load early. After a scant few jump scares, you pretty much see everything coming. Either that or you hear it coming. Every enemy in this game constantly makes sounds so I can hear the people talking from down the hallway and around the corner. I know well ahead of time whether or not I'm going to encounter more splicers or a big daddy. That kinda takes away the fear and anticipation. Add that to the issue that dying has functionally no consequences and the whole game felt like a boring slog as opposed to a compelling adventure. 

My second issue with it is the atrocious character development. Characters appear and disappear with little more than a, "Hi my name is..." This is a pretty big issue when major plot twists ask you to give a fluff about the secret identities of these bland, boring facades. In fact, *SPOILER* one major plot point involves a character telling you, the nameless, faceless protagonist that no one cares about, are in fact a nameless, faceless protagonist that no one cares about. Shocker. 

Thirdly, we have the gameplay. It's so generic. There's a hefty armory of fairly uninspired guns plus the less than thrilling plasmids, few of which are interesting or useful. Towards the end of the game, after having come to terms with the meaninglessness of death in this game, I abandoned all pretext of strategy and just ran around in circles with a wrench. It was faster.

The game isn't all bad. It certainly looks really nice and probably was even better when it came out (by comparison). But over all, it was just uninteresting and unfun.

I didn't expect to like this one as much as I did. While it unfortunately suffers from an inverted difficulty curve (where a lack of options and power at the beginning of the game makes the first few hours far more difficult than all that follow, even in repeat playthroughs), once it opens up, it feels empowering to find a new weapon or spell or accessory that suddenly makes some other set of tools viable.
It does feel like some of the systems of the game go underutilized. There's a whole system where liquids like oil, poison, or water can spill on the ground and react with fire or electricity, but aside from certain traps, this whole system doesn't come into play too often. It might be possible to work this to your own advantage if you set up your equipment right.
Altogether, a pleasant surprise. Worth pursuing if it looks like your thing, genre-wise.
A word of warning: [spoiler]a quest given fairly early can be easily failed in the very next room, and several other points throughout. Completing it is actually required in order to get the "good ending".[/spoiler]

review_text:
Player-side AI all over is terrible. Your players will not check at all unless you get an upgrade that makes them prioritize checking. Check hitboxes are really narrow/wonky, while enemies have very generous hitboxes.

The really damning part is the game will forcibly change which player you are controlling frequently, and commonly at unintuitive moments. The pass button is also hard-bound to the change player button, so if you want to change players and at the same moment one of your players obtains the puck, you will pass it off immediately.

A minor gripe, but one of the abilities is throwing that player's stick to knock some people down. Because you HAVE to control who has the puck and your teammates never use their abilities on their own, you cannot use this ability while maintaining control of the puck ever.

There's a fun game in here but currently it feels like the game is fighting you in places it shouldn't. I can probably recommend this after significant AI, controls, and player autonomy tweaks/overhauls, but I can't recommend it in its current state. It's just an exercise in frustration currently.

I came to this game attracted by the mods, not the base game itself. As of writing, I have only experienced the vanilla game.

I have never played JSR, so I have no nostalgia for that game in particular. However, this game gave me nostalgia for slightly janky rough around the edges video games your parents bought you based off of the cover. But something in the game was just so much fun and you could ignore everything janky. This game lacks polish is a bunch of places (I don't know what the developpers think is worth 40$ in this game lol, but you know how to buy it for cheaper) and I would argue that is precisely its charm.

The story is almost good, the dialogue is strange in places, some things seem rushed. But you know what isn't rushed ? The movement, and the levels. So good. It just feels good to move around and do stunts in this game. The music is not my cup of tea, but it fits very well. The art direction is commendable.

I haven't played a game like this in a while, so it felt good. And the nostalgia was really nice too...

The meat and potatoes of this game is the movement and the levels. Those are top-notch. You don't need to worry about anything else.

[h1] Edit [/h1]

I now play this to wind down and chill, just messing around with the movement. I have the game modded with a popular modpack that removes speed caps and adds certain moves/tech to better enjoy really high speeds. This is a reaaaally nice way to chill, and the community is super nice and helpful. I really recommend that you give this a try if you already have the game. Don't waste time with customization (it's a rabbit hole), unless you really dig that stuff, and just see what it's like to play modded. I reach for it quite a lot.

review_text:
Might be someones jam, but not mine.  Ground combat I found terrible.  The game does allow you to switch between two combat modes, one more geared for a shooter and one geared for an MMO, but switching between them was tedious and clunky at best.  I found that no matter which mode I was in, I was having difficulty getting anything done.  Shooter mode does not really blend well with interacting with objects, manipulating the environment and using the tools you have.  And MMO mode doe not really blend with a shooter game style.  Plus, ground combat was slow and unsatisfying

Space combat in my opinion was worse.  it felt forced in because it was a Star Trek game, developers should give you a choice if you want to do it, or just "AI" it up and "roll" on chance to hit.  Felt uncontrollable, but I do not play a lot of space sims.

both of these lead to the point that it felt like the game has all these elements forced in because it is Star Trek.  You need to interact with computers, shoot and fly a space ship.  If you dont like one of those components you are stuck, because you need to want to do them all.  If you are down for all of them, and can remember a plethora of keys, you might have some fun...

If it were not for microtransactions.  I get it is free to play, but so much content is locked behind paywalls and by the time you have what you want, you have spent a lot more money than a 60 dollar title.  Not to mention the microtransactions are confusing for a new player, I have no idea what is good, what I want, and the game just kind of throws it all in your face to figure out.

Lastly, the environments were also pretty bad.  Since its an MMO it has to make large, open environments to fit the amount of people that might be coming through, but hallways felt HUGE, like three stories tall on a space ship that should be 1 story tall, rooms that were mostly empty except for a console or two in the middle.  Just not enough life to it.

Bottom line, if you are a Star Trek Super Fan, and love ground combat, remembering lots of keys, space combat, MMO's and figuring it out for yourself, its a good gamble.  Otherwise, wait for them to make focused games for Star Trek (like a shooter OR space flight simulator...will never happy I know).

review_text:
This game's fantastic. The art's phenomenal and the game has several areas with quite distinct atmospheres. There's no dialogue or exposition so you have to piece your own interpretation together.

The puzzles are all challenging but feel fair once you figure them out. There's a bit of back tracking but the game often gives you shortcuts back and you can sprint quite fast.

The combat is the weakest aspect, which does get frustrating once they start piling enemies on you later on. Some enemies twitch too much and are hard to hit, and they take too many hits to die. The boss battle was pretty cool, but a little drawn out. It felt too much like a video game after the other parts were so immersive. The combat helped to build tension at times but other times just distracted you from taking in the environment. 

The music and sound design are very well crafted. The music complements when it should and is tastefully left out at other parts. The sounds are all unsettling and feel like they belong to their sources.

Most of the negative reviews, complaints about the puzzles and so on seem like they're coming from people who don't even like puzzle games and expected an FPS. I recommend this if you like puzzle games and thought provoking imagery.

review_text:
[h1]Wake up. Time to die.[/h1]
Straight up, Scorn is not a game for everyone. It just turns out that this is the perfect game for demented sickos like myself.

The only real critique I have of the game is its price and runtime. The game itself is really only about eight hours give or take (I have a few more hours on the GOG version), which makes it extremely difficult to justify the $60.00 AUD price tag. It is also a shame considering the artbook and soundtrack are also fantastic. Definitely only get this game on a steep discount, especially if you are unsure whether or not you will enjoy this kind of a game.

Scorn also runs perfectly on the Steam Deck. I was playing on the maximum graphics settings with AMD FSR set to performance mode. It both looked fantastic and ran increadibly smooth without any issues or bugs. My only recommendation is to play with some really good headphones, since the audio design should not be missed out on. If you have a Steam Deck, and feel like traumatising the person sitting next to you on the bus, then look no further!

The gameplay itself is very simple. Walking through various scenes and locations broken up between the occasional puzzle and combat encounter. The movements and gunplay are very slow, which might turn a few people off. I did not mind this, but only because I am more adjusted to slower paced shooters anyway.

While on the topic, combat is purposefully cumbersome in this way, and I feel this is where the game loses a lot of people. The majority of players I witnessed seem to have the false impression that they have to kill every single enemy they come across, in the process wasting their scarce resources, and then proceed to complain about ‘forced combat encounters’ when in reality you can theoretically get through most of the game without needing to kill anything. 

Aside from a select few that will encourage combat, the majority of smaller enemies will spawn in on ‘patrol’ and then despawn at the end of their route. If you do not want to waste your valuable health and ammunition, you can simply break line-of-sight and wait for the enemies to move on. If you do decide to engage in combat, get a couple of hits in, run behind cover, let them spit their acid at you, and then repeat. It is dead simple once you get the hang of it.

I do appreciate that there is an animation for almost everything your character does, making the world feel very tactile and real. While I do think part of the intrigue of Giger-esque art is the viewer is only left to speculate what mechanical functions these contraptions have, I think Scorn strikes the perfect balance of intractability with these devices, while still keeping the majority of these machines mysterious. While traditionally gameplay to me is the most important aspect of a video game, I approached this game from the perspective of it being an interactive artbook and was not disappointed in the slightest.

Speaking of which, what can be said about the artstyle that has not been already recited thousands, if not millions of times over? It is gruesomely gorgeous! Wearing the inspirations from both H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński on both its sleeves. Despite the obvious comparisons though, I feel that Scorn does retain its own identity apart from both Giger and Beksiński, and that partially comes from the uniquely strange and esoteric universe the developers have built. In true Giger-esque fashion, you will come across various contraptions, devices, and machines that you can only theorise as to their function. Piles of humanoid and not-so-humanoid bodies clambering up the walls, hinting at some greater struggle, extremely Beksiński-like. In this way, it gives the impression that the developers of Scorn both respect Giger and Beksiński and understand their work, in all its cryptic intrigue.

It is because of this reason, that to me, this is where the real horror of the game is. Naturally, horror is a very subjective concept, what might be scary to me might not phase you in the slightest. This game is a perfect example of this, since to me the true horror comes from the atmosphere, the environment, monolithic structures, and glimpses into atrocity. There is something about the strangely familiar yet completely alien environment that Scorn depicts throughout its runtime that fills me with such a unique feeling of dread and unease, unlike any other horror game has managed to capture before.

While there are a few monster enemies scattered throughout the game, they were not the scary part to me. What was scary was the implications that the world and environmental storytelling convey. The horror that gets to me the most is when there are just enough pieces scattered here and there to get your imagination going and inevitably fill in the blanks between them. An audience’s imagination of what something [i]could[/i] be will always be infinitely more terrifying than any writer, director, or designer could say or show it to be.

This is also true for the story, and the greater lore. There is no dialogue to convey the narrative to the player, no recordings, notes, or documents left behind, which I love. Scorn takes the ‘show, do not tell’ philosophy of storytelling to its most literal, leaving only for speculation into the specifics. This removes the inevitable frustration of bogging down the story with long exposition and endless collectable notes to comb through, and simply just [i]shows[/i] you instead. If you do not understand what you are looking at, good. That is the point! Naturally, this kind of story telling should not be applied to [i]everything[/i], it is perfect for Scorn and the world it depicts.

I only wish we could have seen more of the game, especially the last section of the game that takes place in an entirely new location that is distinctly different from the rest of the architecture prior. One can only pray that an eventual sequel or continuation of Scorn will be greenlit someday. I crave to see more of the horrific lore and witness the rest of this dark world the developers have built.

In summary: Scorn is a short game, so get it on sale. It will not be a game for everyone, but if you are a H.R. Giger or Zdzisław Beksiński fan, you will love it. If you are looking for something completely different, immersive, artsy, and esoteric, you will also love this game. Conversely, you will probably not like this game if you are looking for in-depth combat mechanics, fast-paced gameplay, or an easy-to-understand narrative.

If you are on the fence and buy this game on a discount, simply strap yourself in for the ride and just take your time with it. Look around, drink it all in, absorb the atmosphere and the world around you. I think you will be glad you did!
