review_text:
I'm hardly one for reviews, but I saw a lot of things that justify going this extra mile. The devs have been very upfront and clear about what they want with this game, and this deserves extra love.
Witchfire has a slow start, in my opinion. I know people have feelings about that, but this review is among other things to clear this out: this is a very good FPS/extraction game, but definitely much of it's goodies require some hours of investment. Right now, I don't know how they could make this work in any other way, given the game they want to build. Make first map extremely easy? Honestly, I think that would be deceiving. The first map (as of the writing of this review) is very fair to show what you should set yourself for the rest of the time. It's not a relax experience, that doesn't mean hard, but also doesn't mean you can doze off while playing.
The shooting itself is very satisfying and precise, the different weapons definitely cover a lot of ground in different play styles, and the magic, although still underwhelming for me, presents some options for interesting gameplay. That is to say, the devs are clearly very opinionated on what makes a good shooter, and good mechanics that complement and make this properly challenging.
Devs also have my regards for clearly stating they don't want to lower the game difficulty, admitting this will close doors for some players, but knowing the product they want to launch. This doesn't make the game niche in any way, but clearly a lot of people will prefer a simpler experience.
They also show a lot of concern for eventually doing proper elaboration on the story. Not gonna lie, I'm a bit too tired of the next new worldbuilding/lore dump, so it's definitely not a problem for me. Still, it shows again that they know where they want to go with this game. Buuuut, if this is a concern for you, Witchfire has mostly implicit storytelling for the time, but the studio stated they have the intention of working on this in proper time.
I have mixed feelings for early access games, but I got too many green flags to ignore Witchfire. This is building to be a very fun game, and I trust the 1.0 will be worth every penny when it's launched.

When starting this game, I didn't realize how heavily the pay-to-win lootbox scheme is. You can easily make it through all of the levels without purchasing anything, and technically you can get T6 ships without purchasing them, though it's either during a special event or is a much larger grind than I'm willing to put in.

The issue really becomes with building the T6 ship with components and all. If you're not investing money, you don't naturally get one for free, and it would take months of work. Unfortunately it's really an almost-required thing to progress into the top level content.

I wish this game weren't so lootbox heavy, but just look at the news and see how many announcements have to do with lootbox ships.

Gameplay-wise, it's fine. I enjoy the space combat, albeit it's pretty dull compared to something like Eve online. If you're a star trek fan, most of it feels like star trek, minus the space-science parts.

The ground combat is terrible. Probably one of the worst combat systems I've seen in a very long time. Point to click, some abilities, but it always feels like you never really know what's going on. For example, you'll want to disable the auto fire most likely so it doesn't interfere with your abilities. 

Ultimately, fun for a month, but not really recommended.

[b]IMSCARED[/b], is exactly a combo of both, not only it tries to manipulate you, but also your computer. review_text:
A very cute game that i'm having a ton of fun with.

I do think the comparison to Stardew Valley is weak, as nothing about what it 'borrows' from is unique to that game. I think it's far more fair to compare the game to the sims series. Since it is a living growing village, villagers themselves have no unique stories or cutscenes like in stardew, but instead have traits like they would in the sims. Even farming and seasons, and decorating and growing a family, is something present in the sims, and not something stardew invented.

One gripe i have with the game is that the flow of time is bit rough. If I want to wake up at dawn, pass through the forest and stop in the mine every morning, by the time I finish it is nearly 2pm, and all the shops are almost closed. The mine itself is necessary to stop in for financial gain, but it's such a time sink to stop that I almost wish there was either more down there, it recharged every few days, or some combination of both.

The game is something i truly enjoy, don't get me wrong. I think if you like the sims you'll like this one. Or if you didn't like stardew because every year was the same, and there was no long time change in the village, you'll like this one. I just think that the daily 'loop' could have been improved upon.

I just don't understand how this didn't come up in playtesting.

I don't very often write reviews or take the time to post in forums. I felt the need to for this, though.

On a whim and bored of my library, I decided to buy SGW3 on sale as it was dirt cheap. I poured through the game obsessively in a few days. Sure, it was buggy. Sure, it had all the flaws of the open world Ubisoft genre. But there was was something so satisfying about the gunplay that it kept me hooked despite it's ups and downs. And yet, there was also something else I couldn't quite place my thumb on that elevated the game to great heights during certain points.

After beating it, I decided to buy SGWC1 and hoo boy. I think the devs finally realized what they're good at.

In a couple words: map design.

Ya'll have some of the best map design I've ever seen in games. The gunplay is still satisfying, and I highly enjoy not being forced to play a specific way (with the exception of the challenges).

But the MAP DESIGN.

In other games, areas feel like cheap one dimensional areas with buildings placed from prebaked assets. There's often times only a couple of ways into the location. Enemies don't pop-in until the player is close, and then they stand around and wait for the player to kill them.

In this game, every area is a puzzle, a labyrinth waiting to be mapped out. Most enemies have a wide patrol range, and their paths are very dynamic.

I haven't even beaten SGWC1 yet but am thoroughly enjoying it. I went ahead and bought SGWC2 ahead of time to support the devs.

review_text:
I played the two earlier versions of Eastside Hockey Manager back in the day, and the latest EHM project holds the same charm and appeal with more depth.

Unfortunately, despite the many similarities, EHM hasn't been given the same backing and resources as the great Football Manager series, mainly because ice hockey is a much more niche thing compared to football on a worldwide scale. Therefore EHM has not evolved to its full potential over the years. That is not to say it isn't a worthwhile hockey simulation and management experience, because it really is. It's just obvious it could be so much more developed as far as media and people interaction, training, player personalities, transfer speculations, diversity of many small detail and options, tactical consistency, the graphical game representation, scouting reports, tactical and personnel advise from your coaches etc. go, had it been brought forward through the FM path.

One of EHM's strengths is the wide array of leagues and teams at your disposal. The main focus is NHL, which means that the National Hockey League's trading, contracts, drafting, scouting etc. have been well implemented. If you're looking for a change, then the European leagues offer a freshly different experience; some have league tiers with promotion/relegation structures, and the trading/buying of players differs from that of the NHL franchise. When laying an NHL-based save, I felt the other countries' talented players were nicely included in the Northern America-focused database, and looking for new prospects - whether from overseas or the USA/CAN minors - felt like actually scouting for the National Hockey League.

I have to say the weakest part of EHM is the much dated match engine. In Football Manager I can actually use what I see unfolding in the match as legit info on what small changes to make, who is playing how, which opponent looks dangerous, which side looks like it could be exploited and so on. In EHM the little dots are often skating around much like figure skaters and it could be just my underdeveloped hockey brain, but I cannot make heads or tails of it. I cannot decipher what needs to be changed tactically, and keep getting frustrated by the lacklustre marking and movement of my defenders or the way my forwards - contrary to my advise - lose their man too easily, leave them open for easy goals at the near or far post and slash, hold, crosscheck, hook and trip themselves into the penalty box time and time again.
If only the match engine was remodeled so that it could present more useful and accurate information of the game being played, it would make the coaching so much more sensible.

All in all Eastside Hockey Manager is a very good hockey managing/coaching simulation that yet doesn't fully live up to its vast potential.

This is a gold standard RTS-Base Builder IMO because Rise to Ruins is pretty easy to pick up and start playing, but wow is it hard to master. Come play some tower-defense town making and you'll soon find out how subtle and complicated this game is under the hood.

I'm almost 40 hours in, survived my first year, and I'm still learning whole new ways of organizing and building my towns. It's amazing. It's little stuff like "I should put ammo storage next to my towers rather than the ammo-maker."

Another example: By watching my farmers I realized many were idle. Turns out farms don't take a lot of routine maintenance and I was able to unassign a ton of my farmers (now I have about 0.75 farmers per farm, depending on efficiency bonuses)

Towers are the same way. Position, type, wall design. There's a lot more going on than just "make a maze for baddies." The village's entire economy has to be considered.

Overall 10/10 for being utterly fascinating to play.

review_text: This game is a chore to play. I don't wanna say I didn't enjoy it but it is very very lacking. The stealth is shit, camera's spot you without you even knowing where they are, the handler gets very very annoying if you keep restarting, you have to rely on quick saves that 9 out of 10 times put you in a spot you don't want to be and the fact that you have to watch the briefing every single fucking time when you play a contract is extremely annoying. The story is a cluster fuck that wants me to care about the people I kill while I cant even pronounce their names. The sniping is decent but without a good silencer you cant really snipe up close which is not an issue, but while I was playing this game I found myself not really relying on my sniper instead I went for close quarter kills with my knife and pistol. The assault rifles are lazily added to the game without reason. The only AR that felt somewhat good was the AK but the rest of the guns have to much recoil making them unreliable. All sniper rifles feel the same with small variations there are some rifles who are impossible to use because of their lack of noise suppression. For someone who almost only used a silence pistol in his first playthrough they feel like dog shit. They are good if you want to take one guy out but the second you shoot your second shot it feels wrong like it isn't finished. The DLC feels outrages having to pay for extra guns (that are not viable) and cosmetics you probably don't use because they look awful on your weapon The game doesn't feel finished I can understand that people might like this game but for someone who expected a stealthy sniper shooty shooty assassin game I am disappointed. Just get sniper elite this game isn't worth the price it currently has. Anyone who doesnt think this game is a 4 out of 10 clearly doesn't have any experience with games in this genre, the fact that this game is mostly positive is beyond me. After finishing the game I tried going for a 100% run but quickly found out the challenges are either very very easy or just down right annoying to complete. I tried only killing the target in the first mission to find out after completing that dumb ass challenge that it didn't even register. I have also encountered numerous game breaking bugs like trying to hide in a locker to find myself stuck on the outside unable to move. The AI is abysmal either spotting you from across the map or not seeing you when you are standing right in front of them. Throwing rocks sometimes doesn't work revealing your location. When a single enemy saw you and you don't kill him quick enough the whole area suddenly know's your exact fucking coordinates. I really really tried to like this game but its borderline unplayable. The ending was super predictable if you interrogated all of your targets and was just sequel bait for another broken mess of a game. This game is incredible short only having six levels that blend together. There are only two variants between the levels and the only big difference between them is that you can swim without slowly dying of hypothermia in the green foresty area. This game is not finished and it will never be finished the second game should have been part of this game instead of a completely separate game.

This game makes me sad

I've not played the game a lot and there is a reason for that and i make take some heat from the lovers of this game, but so be it.

The game has a feeling of the late 2000s, the graphic, the story and the sound. This is not a bad thing if you're prepared for it. which i was not. it's certainly not the feeling you get from the pictures and vids here on Steam, now who's at fault for that i do not know or care.
The fact is the game feels bumpy due to the poor control pf thje character, im not sure if it's because it's meant to be played with a controller. I played with keyboard and mouse and it was a daunting task at the best of times. I've not found a way to switch the keymapping, in fact i couldn't find any info on what the mapping where or were.

The game seems to be large, there are many areas to explore, thre is just one prpblem with that, a HUGE problem. You hardly have a reason to explore every inch of the game and that's if you even wanted to. If you want to search every inch of an area you may be paid off with some game credits or an audio of a doctor speaking about a project. There is just far between you finding anything, instead you're rewarded wth having to fight with the poor controls expecially during a fight.

During fight sequences you have no way to avoid a hit, you cannot dodge an attack you can move back to to the side and that's while you're fighting with the camera controls at the same time. There is no joy from fighting, it just becomes another task you just want to move over as quick as possible.

These two things is a huge reason as to why i would never dream of recommending buying this game. If you get no joy from either exploring or fighing when these are two major themes in the game, well then you're truly in trouble. 

The thing that makes me sad is the fact that the game has such huge potential, it could be the next Doom, but only if we go 20 years back in time. The game would have to work on better reasons for exploring the area in wich you're contained and the game would have to work on the controls and the keymapping.

speaking of map, why is there no map? you're disorintated, which may be what the game intends, but with everything else it just becomes annoying. I should perhaps mantion that I've not explored much of the game and therefore moved through the "levels" and that may explain the lack of keymapping, there may be a time in the game where you get an inventory, but i just don't care enough for the game to play through to that level.

I could go on and on with this but there is no point, you the reader have already grasped my point. DO NOT BUY THIS GAME not even at a sale to a good price because there is no good price for a game with a lot of unfufilled potential and poor controls. review_text:
Beat the game after 13 hours on normal difficulty. It started strong with a great setting and introduction that does really pull you in however just over halfway through the game it starts to lose steam. Glenn Schofield was the original creator of Dead Space and after leaving the IP sadly in the hands of EA he set out to create or re-create the survival horror franchise again in The Callisto Protocol. Unfortunately this one too suffered from publisher interference. Schofield would eventually admit that Krafton, the publisher of The Callisto Protocol, forced the game to release early resulting in "two enemy variants and four bosses were cut from the game."

This becomes painfully apparent as you fight the exact same boss encounter 4-5 times throughout the course of the game. It's the same encounter you're forced to redo with zero variation. It's the exact same fight. It's clear they just replaced the missing four bosses with the same encounter. Combat also is interesting at first but becomes a little repetitive as it never really expands beyond the simplistic dodge left/right or block sequence. The final boss was also a let down and anti-climatic. There's a lot of similarities between Dead Space and The Callisto Protocol and whether that's a good thing or not will depend on the individual. I can't really fault Schofield for the similarities as he was the creator of Dead Space and if you liked that game you'll most likely enjoy this one. I did but it's also shame that with so few games in this genre The Callisto Protocol was held back by its publisher rushing it to release. 

If you enjoyed OG Dead Space you'll very likely have fun with The Callisto Protocol but wait until it's on sale for 60-80% off. Not worth full price as the game is too short and and can get a tad repetitive. 
And, there was way to many GD squeezing through pipes/cracks sequences. I don't know they went so overboard that.

It looks a lot like Dead Space, which is great. The story and gameplay were good. I really liked the fighting mechanics, especially with the sword. Although I loved the game, I have a couple of negative comments.

- First, there are no map features which takes away from the exploration. - Although the story was great, our character was the only available pilot to escape the planet, yet people still sent me to do dangerous tasks, as the most valuable person I was sent to do risky things, which felt unrealistic. I understand that in a game we need to do things to keep the player engaged, but the story should still make sense. This was the only thing I didn’t like about the story.

- Overall, the game was fantastic, and I had a lot of fun. However, the last boss was absolutely ridiculous. It felt unfair because I upgraded my sword, which I really liked, but I couldn’t use it in the final boss fight which was a bummer. Instead, I had to use my ranged weapons and it was really easy to defeat it. Ideally, I would have preferred if the last boss didn’t exist at all, it was a boring fight.

review_text:
[h1]Callisto Protocol is a good game, not a great game, but a good game nonetheless.[/h1] 

You play as Jacob Lee, a freighter pilot that finds himself stranded in the moon of Callisto. Having been unlawfully imprisoned in a correctional facility there, our protagonist must flee the titular moon whilst surviving a deadly outbreak that is turning all inmates in deadly, mindless ghouls. As one would expect, this escape is all but a harmless ordeal, and our hero must face many a significant trial and tribulation before reaching his journey's end. 

I dare not say much for fear of spoiling anything about the story, apart from the fact that while it is nowhere groundbreaking, the whole "jailbreak out of an offworld prison infested with zombies" felt as a refreshing take on the horror genre. The story (borrowing from a netizen's comment I saw on Reddit, IIRC), is akin to that of a B-Movie, but that is not something wrong [i]per se[/i] ; the problem, rather, lies with the execution: the game's characters are a somewhat forgettable cast, and their dialogues (and the momentum leading up to many of the game's setpiece monologues) could use some much-needed polishing. Moreover, the game suffers from a ridiculous excess of jump scares, to the point that after 2~3 hours into the game you can predict every single jump scare that is bound to happen in a cutscene.

Needless to say, this detracts significantly from the horror factor, albeit not entirely, for the game (fortunately) does have more tricks up its sleeve: atmosphere is one of them. The sheer sense of unease (and even dread) I experienced when visiting some of the latter portions of the game is right there with some of the most unnerving locations in horror games. The game simply feels disturbingly [i]wrong[/i] in these portions of the game and while nothing truly gaze-averting happens, you do get to experience that feeling of "I shouldn't be here" many horror games try to nail, but ultimately fall short of achieving.

This was a nice departure from The Callisto Protocol's famous, albeit formally unofficial, predecessor: Dead Space. I played the original back in 2008 and was completely unfazed by its predictable nature. This comes from someone who literally suffered playing F.E.A.R. out of the sheer terror that game instilled in me and even later games such as Outlast and Alien: Isolation posed a challenge to my fear-coping mechanics. Not Dead Space; I found it a boring and unenthusiastic tech demo, which often seemed as wanting to showcase what state-of-the-art technology could do, rather than delivering an actual story worth being told. I am currently playing the Dead Space Remake so I can safely comment on the comparison between Callisto and Dead Space and for me Callisto delivers a more ambitious, even if flawed, experience. That is not to say that Dead Space is a bad game, but I find it sorely lacking in inspiration, even if its execution is safer, as you would have it. Callisto seeks to be more and, at least in the horror and fear department, undisputably succeeds.

Not only in these aspects is The Callisto Protocol a solid installment: the game sports some of the most breathtaking visuals ever seen in a game, and while it does experience some FPS dips every now and then, the average FPS count was remarkably stable for such a fine-looking game.

Moreover, the gameplay in this game is, simply put, amazing. It truly makes up for the story's lack of charm. Unlike Dead Space, where you are given a gun and must (boringly) shoot off limbs to render enemies unthreatening before finishing them off with a flurry of stomps, in Callisto it is all about melee combat: you basically have to dodge the enemies' hits left and right, carefully predicting their incoming attack. Should you rather not risk that, you may block them, taking reduced damage. It makes for some fun, but challenging (and surprisingly intuitive!) combos which later on you may compound with firearms and the GRP. The GRP is Callisto's answer to Dead Space's stasis and kinesis. It essentially lets you lift a myriad of things in the air, ranging from enemies to stuff lying about, thereby turning everything in a veritable deadly projectile. Moreover, this opens up a whole avenue of environmental deaths (sorely lacking in Dead Space), such as throwing enemies into grinders, fans and spikes, when not outright flinging them to their deaths at botomless pits. Moreover, this allows you to quickly maneuver enemies out of your reach, so as not to get swarmed by them, for unlike other games, The Callisto Protocol does not have enemies take turns pouncing at you; rather, they attack you all at once if they can. Gameplay, thus, is an exhilarating experience in this game, compensating for some of the weakest bits of the story.

For in the end, The Callisto Protocol achieved to be much more than a horror game: it was a fun experience, as much as it was unsettling, if not outright scary. Ineed, it feels to be the game that Dead Space (or at least their shared creator) wanted to be. It still falls short of its vision and promise, but it has a solid foundation to build upon.

7/10

TL;DR: Awesome graphics and challenging but intuitive combat. Interesting plot marred by a poor execution.

review_text:
Lucius is a third-person adventure/puzzle game, in which you play as Lucifer's son and murder everyone in the manor you live in. The concept is interesting, since it's kinda like reverse horror, but unfortunately the execution is poor. 

The gameplay is pretty much just murdering the people in the house in a certain order and in a pre-determined way and watching a cutscene showing the murder. After the murder cutscene you get a new cutscene, which usually involves a detective, who is put on the case after your first murder. The game could have easily been a point-and-click game, because you just look for items and after using the right items you watch the murder commence.

The game let's you free roam around the fairly big manor between the murders, but there isn't much to do aside from some "fetch quests" called chores and looking for items needed in future murders. After doing enough chores you get some items, of which 2 just give hints for the murder puzzles and the last one is a tricycle. The tricycle let's you move around the manor a bit faster and also let's you use a glitched staircase to get out of the house. 

After each murder you get a new superpower or upgrades to the ones you already have. The game has 4 superpowers: telekinesis, mind control, memory erase and combustion. You will need all those superpowers for the murder puzzles and while you can use some of them for other purposes, they're not really fun. The combustion power is also used in the boss battles the game has and also in some extra mini-game, which seemed to involve priests chasing you (a child) with crosses in a dark forest. I didn't like the boss battles or that mini-game at all, because the combustion power isn't fun and felt a bit clunky to use.

Graphics-wise the game looks pretty good for an indie game, but the devs decided to occasionally use some post-processing effects, which actually made the game look a bit uglier. The lip-syncing seemed to be a bit off, but it didn't really bother me. The voice acting ranged from pretty good to quite awful. The game also has a pretty badly done sex, which looks quite funny as a result and there's some frontal 3D nudity as well. 

The story and dialogue is pretty bad and the ending was probably one of the worst endings ever.

It's a pretty bad game, which could have been so much more. I wouldn't really recommend playing it unless you want to experience some pretty funny glitches. The game is pretty short (took me 5 and a half hours to complete), so it's not like you'd waste a lot of time.

I'm not a fan of classic RPG style game to begin with. But eventhough I believe that beautiful audio and visual are crucial in storytelling, I know the story itself is the most crucial part. Plus the overwehlmingly positive review has encouraged me to give this game a go.

I agree with everyone else that this game has a beutiful story. But there are some factors that bother me:

1. Characters
This game has some notable characters with distinct personality and role, but there are some that are lacking both. This game jumps from one plot to another without giving us enough time to be introduced to the characters. I sometimes forgot the significance of a character. This problem even occurs with main characters. This problem also makes me less 'bonded' with the characters.

2.  The conflict
The conflict, or I should say, the important plot points seem to be stretched. This makes them giving me less impact on each of the plot points. 

3. The details
There are some important details scatered around the story. All of those details supposed to help building the story. But unfortunately, this game isn't so good at 'connecting those dots'. Eventually, those details became some sort of distractions.

4. The mechanics 
The controls seem to be a little floaty. And, within the game, there are mini games that are supposed to be the connectors from one plot point to another. But unfortunately those mini games felt unnecessary and distracting for me.

5. The jokes
To touch the heart through a story, one should make the player laugh and cry. This game has failed me at the laughing part. 

I know there are countless positive aspect of this game. But at the end, those things above can't get out of my head. It's a little bit unfogiving, but I couldn't aprove myself to give this game a thumbs up with those things unimproved.

Very good game. As someone who never played Jet Set Radio and doesn't play a lot of platformers, I did not think i would enjoy it as much as I did. 

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

It follows a story that brings you to different maps that are uniquely themed. In each map, your goal is to reach all the graffiti locations by platforming with your ride of choice. Plenty of collectables and combo challenges. I didn't find the challenges too difficult and this is perhaps due to the movement speed being rather slow. The Steam achievement challenges are more about patience than difficulty in my opinion.

Combat is perhaps the weakest part of the game, but you do this pretty minimally. Boss fights were easier than the challenges. There is a nitpick I have related to gameplay and that has to do with traversal gimmicks. 
 [list]
    [*]There are locations that are clearly indicated that require the player to access using a BMX bike, but somehow the same isn't done for the skateboard and the skates. I don't think these are spoilers, but I shall put them under spoiler text nevertheless.
    [*]Skateboard: [spoiler] If you see a fire hydrant you need to jump on top of it using a skateboard, then perform tricks. [/spoiler]
    [*]Skates: [spoiler] To break glass beneath you, you must slide on manual while on skates [/spoiler]
[/list]

[h3] Story [/h3]
The story is alright, but it is rather short. There are some really nice story-only platforming stages to go with it. I'd say if you are not a collectable or combo challenge type of person, than the game might not be worth full price since you would probably only get ~15 hours of gameplay out this game. 

Overall a funky good time.

I was excited to play this game, but being cautious I waited until the end of the development cycle. Sadly, I didn't read enough reviews to see that most of the positive reviews are only one sentence long (and thus suspect). 

Why do I doubt the reviews?

1. The graphics never stop flickering on any graphics setting.
2. Basic controls are awkward, imprecise and essential short cut commands to delete structures or cancel orders are not explained anywhere and have to be experimented with to find (or looked up via an internet search).
3. Basic resource management is automated, but makes little sense. Most egregious example: raw food is the used both for planting and feeding your people; they will eat their "seed" food with no warning, making farms cease to produce food; once this occurs it is too late to fix since they will be starving and continuously eat everything they grow.
4. Game progress is very slow (and requires you to constantly alt-tab to look up controls), so by the time you figure out reasons 1 through 3, you won't have done anything in appreciable in game, but it will be too late to get a refund through steam.

I love simulation games, but am sad that I spent money on this one. I hope this helps others avoid the same frustration.

review_text:
These twenty-two hours were in one sitting.  Probably not the healthiest, but a super fun game.  Didn't mean to play for so long, but then I got flanked real bad.  The computer was right at the my soft industrial heart so I couldn't stop on an unsure not.  Had to punch threw the flanking line as hard as I could to set everything right.  It took a lot longer than I thought.  I thought I could just keep on going.  It soon got too costly.  I looked up and I was about to starve to death.  I had to fix it. It took 22 hours.  Not to win, just to get back to a comfortable position.  It's a fun game.  

It's a god game.  I've never played one before so I'm happy this was my first experience with the genre.  It's not like a usually rts.  You can't tell your people to go and attack there or take that space over there.  You have to aggressively defend.  

I like how logistical the game is.  You have to think about your supply line.  You'll have food but not where you need it, and people will just start dying. You'll have water somewhere but people will die of heat exhaustion.  Everything will be in the wrong spot and it will take forever to build anything.  

The game is hard but is's generous because it cheats for you.  I would have lost in the winter or at least half the population would have died, but every so often you get a bunch of migrants who seemingly haven't heard how desperate things have been.  You also have your god powers that help you cheat just a little bit in a pinch.  It's never so much as to make the rest of the game feel irrelevant.  It's just enough to keep you playing.  You're always right there though.  You're always right where you're almost about to lose, but there's still a chance.  It's genius.  

The game really taxes your processor at the end.  It tells you that speeding it up is a bad idea at the beginning.  You can still get away with fast-forwarding it until things get real loud.  In both the sense that there's a lot going on and a lot you have to manage, and in the literal sense that my PC was blowing full blast.

It's a good game.  It does everything it can physically do while still being playable.  Not a lot of games push the CPU.  In the twenty-two hour's I played it there wasn't the slightest bug.  The game runs perfectly

review_text:
As a lifelong Trek fan, it pains me to see something from this franchise so full of potential yet so devoid of realization.

While I do agree with other reviewers that this isn't exactly the "perfect" Star Trek game (with a balance of exploration, combat, diplomacy, discovery, etc.), I can appreciate what the devs tried to do with this particular vision; and it could have been something... otherworldly... had it not ended up pretty much stagnating.

STO could be an amazing, beautiful game. For the first few years, I enjoyed the presentation, stories and the flow of combat. Of particular note and commendation is the fact that bringing as many original actors from the Trek universe into the game as they could has given it a particular charm that could not otherwise be achieved - it really does make an infinite difference in how the stories are received, and I would not have enjoyed each initial foray anywhere near as much without those iconic presences.

I had enjoyed it so much, initially, that I decided to buy the lifetime subscription. Despite it being easily the most expensive game content I've ever purchased, I did so with the intention of supporting the devs in this project to hopefully make it better. That is not what the money from the lifetime subscription goes to.

The big problem with this title in my opinion is not the mechanics, the (mostly unaddressed / unrepaired) bugs, or the lack of "perfect" Trek balance. The problem is the lack of new content. The only result of spending real cash on a lifetime sub is the devs putting all their effort into new ships to spend MORE real cash on, and little to no actual content. When one looks at any other MMO and the amount of content produced yearly, this one falls incredibly short. I'd be okay with a lack of original actor voices if it meant some decent, sizeable content produced regularly; it wouldn't be as good, but... at least it'd be something. All players get now is event after event of the same few TFO missions endlessly recycled. Why would _anyone_ want to pay huge amounts of cash for ships just to do the same 3 or 4 events over and over again? The devs need to give us reason to WANT to buy new ships and do stuff, and running TFO  for the 16,000,000th time is not gonna cut it AFAIC.

There is also the issue of the "legendary" ships kinda breaking the game for those who have not spent even more money to get them, as they are (from a balance perspective) broken and severely overpowered. This is a much lesser issue, however, and could be remedied by separating legendary and non-legendary players in all content.

For those who might question my review with the sizeable amount of hours sunk into this title... I loved it at first, but now only keep playing every so often to try for the "free" ships offered by event campaigns to feel like I'm getting something - anything - out of my investment into this game.

Best advice I can offer, given STO's current state: play it free, do all the stories and enjoy the actual content that exists, and then consider walking away. As fun as STO can be - and as much untapped potential as it has - "endgame" STO feels like an empty, windowless room, a couple thousand choices of chairs to hoist one's backside upon, and the same 4 songs on endless repeat. Nobody's spending a Saturday evening in a pub like that, y'know?

review_text:
I had previously purchased Hakuoki: Stories of the Shinsengumi on PS3 and loved it. Even though Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds has the same but slightly expanded storyline (with extra stories from the PS3 version meshed with the existing plot to make it more complete), I decided to get it because of the new guys namely Nagakura Shinpachi, Iba Hachiro, Yamazaki Susumu, Sakamoto Ryouma, Sannan Keisuke, and Souma Kazue.

There are some changes to the dialogue and storyline as well. For example, [spoiler]After Saito's defeat by Kazama in his route, he was utterly humiliated when Kazama pushed his face into the ground with his foot. He was grievously injured and couldn't move. To make matters worse, Kazama even threw the Water of Life serum at him and taunted Saito to drink it. It was extremely unpleasant and I felt really bad about Saito's predicament. That anyone could be so cruel to a fallen opponent is utterly disgusting in my opinion. In this new version, however, it seems that Saito has more of a role to play in his ultimate transformation into a Fury. He had the serum on his person and so, chose to drink it to become stronger. This improved the overall storyline and made Kazama less of a jerk. [/spoiler]

There are extra CGs for the existing guys too, so all in all, it was an extremely addictive playing experience. In fact, ever since I started on this game, my social life has gone downhill. But it's ok because I now have 12 handsome men taking up every bit of my time. Oh and when you buy the game, you might as well get the DLCs too. I mean, since you are likely to become addicted like me, you might as well just get everything to soothe your [strike]menlust[/strike]...I mean bloodlust.

Where Hakuoki: Stories of the Shinsengumi was a complete standalone story on its own, Kyoto Winds is only the first part, so do take note. Edo Blossoms is the second part where the romance really comes into play. You might feel slightly frustrated at the slow pace of romance in the first part, but don't you agree that the initial build-up to romance is what makes love so giddy and exciting in the early days? 

Anyway, I'm really glad that I decided to buy this game and Edo Blossoms. The new characters are utterly adorable and I wish I could spend more time with them. I would also love to see more stories that take place AFTER the good endings. It would be really fulfilling to see how their lives turned out eventually. Maybe a DLC that depicts their cute everyday experiences? 

Pros:
[list]
    [*]Awesome voice acting
    [*]Beautiful graphics and music
    [*]Exciting storyline
    [*]Good endings that are SO sweet I can hardly handle the sugary overflow.
[/list]

Cons: 
Why am I not Chizuru

Buy the game now and I'll see you at the weekly Anonymous Hakuoki Addiction Group.

My advise for Altari Games is to take the momentum and assets built with this one and refine it on a sequel. You guys did a great job.  I can definitely see how this has potential to be even greater if you expand on what you've done with this. 

I give this a pretty solid 7/10.

review_text:
Scorn is a master class of design. Sound and visuals are stimulating enough to keep me interested to the finish. I had a great time discovering the sets of levels and figuring out its story. There is no dialogue, no companions that provide hints and no yellow paint to guide players. Everything is given with environmental storytelling.

Scorn is not a game for players with low attention spans or struggle to pay attention. I have gotten lost once or twice because I was a bit unfocused and it took an decent amount of patience to reorient myself again to make progress. Combat is weird and slow due to long animations and is clearly not its bread winner. Thankfully it is only required in one section of the game but every other time you are better off running away. Checkpoints are sparse between and force you to play your life wisely as you could lose a ton of progress if you die.

Scorn is a short experience with what feels like some bare minimum additions to consider it a game. Art direction was definitely its main showcase. That being said it was a blast to play with a couple backseat-gamers that wanted to solve puzzles and theorize story elements while I traversed its world. I do recommend Scorn if you are a fan of art because this takes the cake. 

P.S. If you have the extra cash, the Deluxe edition is worth it for the Scorn art book.

review_text:
Blade of the Shogun starts out  fantastic. Isometric stealth game play that requires planning and precision. It's incredibly difficult, but the game gives you the ability to save at any point which stops it from being too frustrating. 

Despite all this praise, the game quickly runs thin in terms of game play and quality. As the difficulty increases from hard to harder, the auto save feature becomes a crutch, not to prevent mistakes, but to repeatedly try precise and complicated movements kills. The strategic elements get thinner too as the player relies more and more on cheesier attempts to knock out loners and pull people away from the group. It becomes a pretty stale rhythm. Each level has a unique gimmick to play around, but it only represents a small part of the stage and the rest of the time you are back to the same strategies you use in every stage. 

Outside of the strategic side, the increase in difficulty and precision quickly creates annoyances with the technical elements of the game. Npcs will spaz out on occasion, your characters won't follow your orders quite right, and the camera becomes so cumbersome. The camera controls in this game are AWEFUL. 

The camera lets you switch between four viewpoints, each from one of the four diagonals. But why. Why can't I place the camera wherever I want. Also, your movements can be restricted by the camera because you only have four angles. Certain camera angles will block the space you want to click. Case in point, I had an instance where I couldn't physically click a perfectly legal location because it was blocked by the camera rotations.

Overall, I really do think its a decent enough game, if not enough variety on the strategy overall. But it quickly gets bogged down by an issue most games that require precision and perfection from the player: the game itself doesn't offer the tools to accomplish the needed levels of control. You can't require me to be 100% precise and the controls only offer 90% control. Every time it happens just builds frustration. 

Finally, and most aggresiously overall are the bonus goals. It won't affect most people but holy crap are they poorly thought out and implemented. You have a list of bonus objectives and challenges for 100% completion, and the way they have been implemented is borderline offensive. You have 9 goals and objectives, and it doesn't tell you on your first go around, for no reason I can see. Added to this, many objectives may be exclusive and can't be accomplished in the same try as the others. This means you may very well have to play the same stage five times in addition to the starting clear. Why? Why would you make it like that? And if you did make it like that, why wouldn't you tell us the bonus objectives on the first try to cut down on the repetition. Horrendous. 

Overall, I'm probably making this game sound worse than it is. But on the other hand, I find it hard to believe that anyone who has played this game for a significant amount of time hasn't grown frustrated with it. The core experience is solid, but every little choice and detail surrounding that main experience just wears you down and makes you hate what you initially enjoyed. 

4/10

review_text:
Two hours in and I would recomend this game, but only just. I'd give it maybe a 6/10?

TL:DR
A good example of an otome game; Longer than most and beautifully drawn. However characterisation can be flakey and the protagonist falls prey to all of the usual pitfalls of the genre. 

Pros:
- The art is beautiful
- Music is ok, pretty good
- Seems to be building up to a big story

Cons:
- It can be hard to keep up with whats going on, with lots of unusual terms being bandied about rapid-fire. They're explained in the glossary bit but it's so many all at once that it's hard to keep track. 
- I have real trouble keeping the names straight
- The relationships with the characters don't feel very consistant. 
(NO SPOILER: In one scene one of the guys yells something at me that I, personally, would find unforgivable. Not only is it brushed asside, it's never brought up again. It's also very at odds with the usual interaction between him and the protagonist.)
- Some of the translation is a little lazy. Not too bad, but you occasionally see a line and you're like 'Uuuuh... Ok?'
- Not a lot of options. 
(People in reviews are saying there are a lot of storylines but it seems like a good portion of the story will be the same every playthrough. Also theres one, again spoiler-free, instance where a character is like 'This is the choice I've made' and I'm like 'Ok, you do you dude' but my options are basically 'stop him' or 'make someone else stop him'.)

(Also, the usual otome complaints. Protagonist is a complete passive doormat. (And despite being trained in swordcraft still needs to be saved constantly. The boldest she gets is drawing the sword and freezing up. But she is stated to have been trained (to a passable level as tested by a companion. Like 'Not as good as us, but enough to deal with an average thug' levels.) And the usual wide-eyed 'I'm worried about [insert literally any character] despite the shitty stuff they did, which I won't even mention.')

The game seems to be rather limited in the number of Objects to build. Even the few objects seem to be "permutations" of each other an contain functions of other buildings. I personally did not like that it seems to be rather "fighting" based (zombies etc.) and  i would rather like to see economy of my village grow and spend more time on that... As i said, the idea looks nice but i would have it rather in the dwarf fortress direction (which is rather based in economy than fighting). I did not want to bash your game and will definitely come back to reevaluate it, but currently i would not recommend it, because everyting seems rather limited and not like its worth 10 bucks. No offense but currently i would say that there are free games that give you the same fun and depth and the game rather seems like something you would get for free on a pc-magazine (back in the old days when they gave you CDs with it). An example that would be comparable from the style is clonk which is roughly 10 years old ! Another (also free) example is the latter named dwarf fortress which seems like 10 time the depth of this game.

I know that it is hard to develop a game and please dont get this review wrong ! But if you sell a product for money you have to stand up for it no matter if its early access. And my personal opinion is, that in early access the product should not develop much from the content, but early access is for getting the flaws and small bugs out of the game. Not to actually develop it. I know that most game developers do it like this, which does not make it right. This particular game has a lot of potential, but currently i would not spend money on this.

I personally experience it as a ripoff if the content of the game is developed in the (paid) early access since that is not what it is about. The early access is for fine-tuning the game and get some feedback from the comunity. Its about giving the game its last 5-10% not its last 50%. 

Sorry that all of my all of my bottled-up displeasure about seemingly half-ready games got into this review. I hope that you get point.

Boy is it good to have hockey back on PC. 

Overall, I think this game will satisfy those whose hockey itch has not been scratched in a long time. The game is fun. Really fun. Problems arise, however, in my experience, when playing on expert difficulty. The following are my main complaints.

- Switching is TERRIBLE: Switching between players is haphazard and you never know what you're gonna get; do you want to switch to a specific player? Nah, the game pretty much decides which player you'll switch to.

- Inconsistent difficulty: Yes, this is a rogue-like, and on expert difficulty it's supposed to be hard. I get that. However, I can't help but to feel like the difficulty spikes are totally random - regardless of whether you face a boss or not.

- Lack of deking: No deking. At best, you'll wiggle your left thumbstick to fake the goalie out. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. 

Overall, there's much to be enjoyed (as my playtime might suggest) but if the above mentioned "problems" are either ironed out or at least tweaked, the game would be vastly superior.

review_text:
Really decent game, but there is more complexity to the mechanics than most of the new console players would like to admit, and so the game hasn't been as fun since they launched 1.0 and crossplay. Turning off crossplay doesn't seem to work.
Constant fights over building, players that don't communicate, players that openly sabotage the team, players who feel they are experienced but have no knowledge of the games mechanics, players running out alone and burning tickets up slowly, players who don't want to learn how to play the game, etc, etc, etc.

Every match has become a slog of:

1) Ask/Beg people not to waste initial ore on stupid things, and to place walls around the arc or build command first. (You're lucky if anyone listens)
2) Constantly trying to inform people of the mechanics such as gates aggro'ing bugs, and basically being used solely for crowd control.
3) Encouraging people to climb rather than stand in the middle of a big field where we know like 500 angry, giant bugs are about to spawn.
4) Encouraging people not to do stupid things like building an MG on ground level with previously mentioned angry, giant bugs.
5) Reminding people that they are capable of rezzing others rather than standing on their corpse as a firing platform.
6) Encouraging people to repair before they can openly wonder why we lost the match.
7) Occasionally having to shoot a teammate in the back of the head for trying to randomly dismantle the entire base.
8) Carry matches using classes I don't enjoy anymore (Looking at you, demo.)
9) Wonder why new players don't see the sense in deploying health stims or soft ammo.

The game has been left open running on my pc for like 1300 hours. I have between 350-400 hours in game.
About 6 of those hours were spent playing with Casper Van Dien on his live streams or with 1st MI.

It is an amazing game with mechanics that go beyond your basic shooter. What is currently ruining the game is people playing SST as though it is COD or some other FPS. They don't actually bother to learn to play the game, but are super confident in insisting to you that they know better, and while it was amusing to see the game prove them wrong time after time, it gets rather stale after a while.

I keep finding myself leaving matches due to the same inept nonsense over and over. I do not want to spend my time in this game trying desperately to coach and keep idiots alive, and this isn't a unique opinion from PC players.

Fix turning off crossplay, please. Let the console bros have their own shitshow lol.

Please add a more in depth tutorial to the game.

Maybe some tutorials that show brief build designs you can ask the experienced community to provide?

Right now it is just a gongshow of morons trying to play hero with no idea what they are doing, and the end result is just a frustrating experience as compared to what this game was previously. Fucking sucks, lol. I don't enjoy much in this life, and now this is just another let down.

Will play again, but giving it a break for a while until the chaff moves on.

May 16th 2025 edit - The above still entirely applies, but there are even less experienced players now, so it's even more grating.
The servers seem unstable. Connection issues that hit everyone on the team simultaneously.
Movement feels janky at times, which is a problem when classes like ranger move quickly. It becomes nearly unplayable at times. You can be like an hour into a match and game just closes.
Constant glitches where you have to either pick up an mg ammo box or have someone shoot you and rez you.
Bug spawns not working correctly, so you can't finish side quests.
Bugs spawning in ways and in numbers that make no sense.
Bugs moving as they shouldn't.
Damage counter doesn't seem to count all damage you inflict on bugs at times, which I am wondering if it isn't related to their server and connectivity issues.
Ranger isn't moving fluidly anymore, and so doesn't feel fun to play.
Climbing is currently fucked up.
Stims don't work most of the time.
Timer on Ranger boost doesn't seem accurate, and I wonder if it has something to do with their server/connection issues.

Like, I *love* this game.
Don't get me wrong.

But they can't seem to fix it, and have somehow just made it worse. It's not fun to play anymore, and most of the groups out there where you can find the cohesion and cooperation to play properly/successfully, are full of insufferable people that aren't really enjoyable to play with, lol.
I really just prefer hitting quickplay and doing PUG with strangers, but there is no point in doing it any longer as every mission just seems to be packs of new players that just don't want to learn how to play the game, and if you try to explain on mic, all it takes is one asshole mocking you for being a know it all for all the idiots to turn on you. 
Currently chuffed. Way to fuck up a good game.

I finished this game, so I’ll give it credit for keeping my interest. The story’s juvenile*, but the premise is solid and the steps through the plot are intriguing. And it’s hard to call it a game. It’s more of a pixel hunt for items that usually add little to the plot – just in order to play a set of simplistic games of “Lights Off” to progress linearly. At its best, later in the game, it’s still irritating.

This concept would have been better realized with more sophisticated writing and puzzles that were relevant to the story. Oh and a more thoughtful plot. See below. The art is fine. The music is simplistic and at one point cloying. Path-finding is bad and the cursor implementation is confusing. Also there are limited options for displaying the game.

I’d say avoid this one. A neat idea implemented amateurishly and with some technical problems.

*What do I mean by juvenile? This isn't really a spoiler because it only makes sense if you finish the game, but spoiler warning anyway: what about the wife's memories? What is she, chopped liver? The elated emotions that other reviews say that come from playing the game seem to come to them at the expense of a tragically disposable character. :/ It's the embodiment of an angsty manchild fantasy. Kind of disturbing.

At first I loved this game, as I'm a fan of 2D souls-likes... that said, after a while it feels like a lot of cheap & unfair game play keeps coming up. Very disappointing, this is no Blasphemous or Momodoro. You die too often to situations where skill and reflex mean nothing. For example, you might do some tricky platforming only to be killed by a fireball from off screen while the devs clearly planned for you to be in a position where you can't avoid it, all after you just spent several minutes getting to that point finally! I'm okay dying repeatedly in a game so long as it feels fair, but this game subs clever design for cheap shots...

Update: I've also noticed quite a few bugs related to button remapping. some labels don't update correctly for "back" if you remap the B button, for example. This sucks because the default layout is bad; it uses triggers for map and menu nav and bumpers for combat stuff... what?! So backwards. I tried to give it another chance today but now my L trigger brings up map even though it is clearly remapped for secondary attack in settings and reflects that on screen... So it says press LT equip but when I do the map opens. This sort of thing might be acceptable if the devs were updating the game and fixing issues, but it appears they abandoned supporting this game after a series of patches post-release and zero updates or community communication since.

review_text:
A gem of a F2P mmo, that has done a remarkable job of staying close to, and respecting, its source material. Some parts of the game are showing their age visually, but the scenes in space are still gorgeous.

As for the many complaints you will see in the  reviews here, many of the ships are locked behind a gamble-box pay wall.  It sucks, but that is the way of F2p mmos. There is a small silver lining, in that even as a fully f2p player, you can still obtain several ships through events, including those gameble-box ships. Its time consuming, but still possible. 

With that said, while not the best ships in the game, you can still fly your favorite ships from the show as lower tier ships, and consume tons of content in the trek universe without spending a dime. So, if you're an old trekkie and just want to fly a Defiant class ship while exploring parts of the Trek universe, give Stark trek online a shot. Relax at the Beach on Risa, go through the Bajoran Worm hole, visit Star Fleet academy, watch your character get assimilated by borg, and finish off by smiling at  all the cameos the Trek actors from yesteryear make in the game as voice actors for their characters (Laforge, Dr. Crusher, Janeway, Odo, 7 of 9, Quark, Rom, Martok, and more!).

review_text:
So this game popped up in humble bundle and I thought to myself, "that looks weird enough to try".  Upon starting it up, all I could think of was holy crap this looks amazing and it brought a lot of nostalgia to me considering I loved the Alien franchise.  The artwork on the levels is amazing and anxiety inducing.  The audio!  Wow, the audio is spot on!  They did a very good job of using the right sounds and could easily classify this as a game you should totally play with headphones on in the dark.  I will say the developers did a great job on this title.

My only complaints are the save system...or lack thereof. At least give us the little blip on the bottom to tell us we hit a checkpoint.  I got too tired to continue and have no idea if I hit a checkpoint before I quit.  Also, I am not a huge fan of the combat.  It's like someone gave Amnesia the dark descent a gun.  You may be able to shoot, but you still gotta run away!

I am going to say, this is one of the few titles I have played in the last couple years where A. I didn't turn it off after 20 minutes and refund it and B. Time passed so quickly that I was surprised how long I had been playing and I kept telling myself, "I'll take a break after this next scene".  That does not happen often these days and I will totally keep track of this dev for future titles.  

Great job!

review_text:
I am a big fan of stealth games like Hitman, Sniper Elite, Metal Gear, and Tom Clancy to name a few. I bought this game because a friend told me it was good but oh god. I wasted money on buying the whole franchise on sale. There are so many jarring issues with this game that makes this a grueling experience. I rarely ever write reviews for games but this game just doesn't sit right with me.

- Cameras and guards have ridiculous lines of sight and they see you almost immediately 
- When spotted everybody hive minds to you at once and will try to shoot at you from 200 feet away through multiple buildings
- Main objectives are pickups that are on or near targets making sniping more pointless than it already is 
- So many unnecessary additions that just make the gameplay more complex instead of unique
- You will have to spend copious amounts of hours to unlock skills to make the game "better"
- It's not very well optimized, some areas I will run at a smooth 60 FPS then I just look 2 feet to my left and I'm at 30 FPS
- The save system is possibly the worst feature, with no manual saving and the game barely autosaves every 30 minutes, and not even after completing an objective!
- The skill system is the same with weapon unlocks
- The main character's voice acting is terrible and has no emotion nor does it fit his character
- People can literally spawn right next you
- Despite having futuristic gear you will almost immediately freeze to death in water and you will die in 2 hits
- The climbing system is just abhorrent with you being only able to climb on extremely specific surfaces even if i should clearly and logically be able to climb on something
- The interaction button doesn't always work and will require you to press it multiple times for it to work
- Every feature in this is just stolen from other games that are actually good and the features that aren't from other games are unnecessary and are terrible
- Melee and your pistol will be used way more than your sniper rifle ever will
- Why are grenades bound to F and why are there even grenades in the first place!?!
- There are random traps you can pick up that you'll never use
- The only good and more unique feature is interrogating enemies but that's still nothing new
- The controls are just not great
- You are forced to watch a cutscene that you've already scene if you re-enter and mission and you can't skip it
- If you go to the developer's (CI Games) other games on Steam 90% of them have bad reviews, in fact, there are more games in this specific franchise with bad reviews then there are good ones!
- Only 44% of people have even completed the first mission
- The sniping mechanics are not difficult at all and it basically tells you where to aim and you can line up a shot in 2 seconds flat
- The developers are aware of the bad save system and don't care or plan to change/fix it!
- Despite being one of the best snipers in the world you can hold your breath for ONLY 4 SECONDS!!!! WHY!?

Please if you like other stealth games or having your sanity, for the love of god, please do not buy this game!

review_text:
First I'll say I only got so far as the end of Volume 3 and level 50 of the Forest of Pain. Since the main story is resolved and the Forest is boredom incarnate, I see no point playing this any longer.

GRAPHISMS 6/10
Mostly ok, especially during cut scenes. Quite dull and repetitive though since there are only 4 cities and 4 map layouts (5 with the Forest of Pain).

MUSIC 9/10
Excellent, though the better tracks are usually underused.

CHARACTERS 1/10
Each character is a walking cliche, the voice acting (japanese) is cringe-worthy, especially the first bad guy, who sounds like a bad disney villain.
The main character is espacially annoying during volume 1, I just wanted to reach through the screen and slap him again and again. That's how stupid and infuriating he is.
The character's reactions to the different situations are also quite ridiculous. To give an example, when the second bad guy "dies", the hero is crying... Forgetting this guy manipulated him from the start, was totally amoral, putting lots of players in coma, including the hero's girlfriend... Whatever.

IMMERSION 7/10
You navigate through the game itself, your emails, the forums, the news and a virtual card game. That works well.
However the game itself is lacking. You never see more than 5 other players on screen, even in the starting city. All the environments seem huge but empty. Quite far from the most-played MMO worldwide...

GAMEPLAY 3/10
The avatar battles are cool and refreshing.
The card game is a missed opportunity since the games are automated, so you just rely on cheesy combos to win. No skill involved.
The arena is ok at first but once you're over your opponents levels it gets boring fast. Also the main battles are scripted so you could be trashing your opponent just to lose with one cutscene.
The main battles are fun when they work, that is when you are 5 to 10 levels under your opponents. Once you're at their level, or worse way over it they become a chore... And you level realllly fast (one area gives you 2-4 levels if you're a bit under the general level) so you'll hit max level very quickly.
The weapon change is mostly pointless, adapting your weapon to your ennemy is useless since the differences are not that huge AND you'll be crushing them anyway. You'll also be punished for switching weapons too much since your proficiency won't rise. 
The guns are cool though.

STORY 1/10
The story is full of plot holes (like the main character somehow forgetting all he knew about the game once he goes back to level 1), the ending (as of volume 3) is totally unsatisfying.
The plot itself is boring and predictable: bad guy causes bad AI to threaten the game world, the whole internet and the real world. Good guys trash him, crush the AI. Rinse and repeat.
Too bad, because the main idea (influence of the virtual world over the real world) is brilliant and was quite original at the time.

CONCLUSION
All things considered, I can't recommand this game. I kept playing it to get to the ending but most of my playthrough was quite boring.

PS: if your game runs in slow motion, check which graphic card your laptop is using to run it and change it to the better one. That fixed the problem for me.

Your only other option is to skip the entire scene, which sucks if you haven't played the games before, like me. So I've sat through hours of bad dialog and bad acting and have only made it halfway through the first game. Why do I keep going? Because there is something wrong with me where I have to finish what I start, no matter how terrible it is. [h1] Back in 2007 [/h1]
The first part of the BioShock series of games was born. The game developers squeezed all the juices out of the Unreal Engine, which was popular at that time, and the visual part of the game turned out to be simply amazing! The visualization of water deserves special attention. The game will be a pleasure to play even in our time. I personally completed the game about a month ago and got an unforgettable pleasure from passing it.


Noting the graphic component, I also want to highlight the plot of the game. The main character, who survived the plane crash, finds himself in an underwater town called Rapture and, guided by tips from a certain person named Atlas, plows the underwater expanses. For the first few minutes, the game seemed a little boring to me. The plot was completely incomprehensible, but towards the end of the game a lot became clear, I will not disclose the details - you need to feel it yourself during the passage. In addition, there are several endings of the game. In general, the plot turned out to be full of unexpected twists and exciting moments.

The gameplay cannot be called diverse, but the language cannot be called monotonous either. The combat system is decorated with the presence of plasmids - gene modifications that give the hero Superpowers. As the game progresses, you will find more and more new plasmids. They are bought for ADAM, which you will receive by saving or emptying little sisters. I advise you to save them, it will have a positive effect on the end of the game. I really regretted emptying a couple of sisters at the beginning of the game and ended up watching the worst possible ending.

There are quite a lot of weapons in the game, but they also appear during the game. At the end, you will already have about 8 different types of weapons in your arsenal: from a revolver to a grenade launcher and a crossbow. Killing mutants becomes a pleasure. Combinations of plasmids and weapons make each fight colorful and spectacular. You won't see this in any other game.

review_text:
Animalia Survival is bringing my childhood fantasies to reality. Ever since I was younger, I always played animal games, but my favourite aspect was always doing some sort of realistic sim with it. One of the things I did the most often was creating a biome with Zoo Tycoon 2, populating it with it's proper animals, and then going into zookeeper mode and just living life. Animalia Survival is literally that, but with stunning graphics, and other people. I therefor have to strongly recommend to any other person that used to do the same or similar things to definitely grab this one, but there's a catch.

The [b]Single player[/b] mode is uneventful, last time I tried the landscape was devoid of any NPCs or anything to give that herd/pack feeling or even find food for carnivores (? unsure about this one, if you typically play carnivore, feel free to correct me on this). I'm unsure at the time if NPCs actually spawn or not. Either way, solo mode isn't good for much, except getting a feel for the controls.


[b]Multiplayer[/b] is iffy as well, in a very different way. It depends on if you like to play carnivore or herbivore better, and ALSO depends on if the server you're joining has rules.

Carnivore's are pretty rough at the start, unless you join in with a group, because as a pup/cub, you can't really hunt much. But I find that balances the game a bit more, no complaints. Herbivores, on the other hand, as long as you find a quiet spot, you can probably grow to adulthood/elder on an isolated part of the map, emphasis on the isolated part.

The reason a lot of the smaller species can survive in the wild is the sheer number of them. Survival is rooted in their large groups. Therefor, when over 50% of a server is playing as a carnivore and basically you're being attacked all the time by different groups, makes the few people who actually prefer herbivore have an infuriating time. 

[i]"Why not just go to an other server then?"[/i] you may ask yourself. I wish it was as simple as that, as there's usually only a few servers at a time with over 5 people, and with the size of the maps, you do want interaction. Don't get me wrong! I do love a good chase and squabble, then both go off and lick our wounds, or one of us dies, it's life, it's what I want. But, when two different predator groups gang up on you, it's annoying. When you spawn in and you get killed within a minute or two by a group of predators, it's annoying. 

The strength of the animals, I feel, reflect their real life counterparts. The only problem with that is, with the low amount of people playing herbivores in game, you get none of the support. They see one or two gazelles and it's fresh meat, not a risk at all. A zebra versus a group of predators is no big deal. The larger herbivores don't seem to have this problem, as the risk is higher. 

I've been in a few servers where the rules definitely evened things out, like, if a carnivore is currently hunting something, only them & their group can hunt it. So if you're being chased by a solo leopard, a group of 5 lions can't join in. But there isn't that security in numbers, as most people still would play the larger herbivores or any of the carnivores.

Which sucks, because one of the moments I cherish the most about this game is when me and a stranger ended up going from a group of 2 gazelles, to like 15. When we were in a group that large, most solo predators would think twice before attacking, and when a group of lioness' started chasing us, it flustered them more then if they had 1 target. We even managed to kill a croc by ourselves.

An other large downside with it, is that unlike some other multiplayer games, there's no way to tell how experienced a player is. The first time I played, I didn't realise you could change your spawn, and I kept spawning in as a wildebeest, and kept getting killed every time I tried making a new character. So I switched to a lion cub, as they were a lion, and they killed me yet again.


[h1]TLDR[/h1]
Single player is pretty dull, Multiplayer needs to balance things out a bit, and as usual for any multiplayer games, ganking will happen.

If you like playing carnivore, you'll probably have a ton of fun. If you like playing herbivores, good luck out there.

Take everything I say with a grain of salt, as this is still early access, and can therefor change at  any time.

review_text:
Make no mistake, To the Moon is pure story, more akin to a visual novel than an actual video game - the gameplay offers virtually zero exploration and does nothing but send you on a few fetch quests and have you complete the occasional puzzle.

Now this wouldn't be so bad [i]if[/i] the story was actually good. It has a decent premise and great visuals/soundtrack to go along with it, no doubt. But I feel as though the execution is lacking, because the story doesn't do very much.

Exploration of characters and their motivations is minimal at best (making them feel one-dimensional), and a lot of potentially interesting threads of discussion (most notably the memory-altering technology itself) are never followed. The gameplay, and the occasional pop culture references, often only aggravate the situation by causing mood shifts when they're least warranted, as if the game is trying to excuse itself with "haha remember this is just a game!".

Compounding with the fact that this game has zero replay value, I would recommend avoiding this game entirely. Beautiful? Maybe. But far less so once you stand back and think it through a bit.

I love this game. It's a wonderful game. What the heck am I doing NOT recommending it? Well, honestly, unless you're some kind of purist who likes Left 4 Dead but hates the new features/changes of Left 4 Dead 2, then Left 4 Dead 2 is what you should buy. Why, though? review_text:
Jet Set Radio was a franchise that always intrigued me for its artstyle, soundtrack and cultural status. Despite this, i always kinda hesitated to call myself a true fan of the series because there were plenty of issues i had with the gameplay and mechanics of the actual games: they mostly seemed outdated, gimmicky and clunky. That doesn't mean i hated JSR, i just felt like its limitations sometimes kept it pretty far from its true potential.
This is where Bomb Rush Cyberfunk comes into play. This game takes pretty much everything i liked about JSR, MASSIVELY improves on many of the issues i had, and even provides a compelling narrative that honors the rebellious, counter-culture spirit that birthed the series it is inspired on. 
The gameplay is smooth and addictive, the character design is great and iconic, the soundtrack KICKS ASS, and tagging the world with graffitti actually feels fun and rewarding (instead of a chore with clunky controls) as it is integrated on the gameplay loop in a really nice way. 
I really enjoyed this one. Team Reptile are really good at working with this artstyle and making it achieve its true potential. 
I'd recommend this to anyone interested in games similar to it, or just anyone looking for a fresh experience.
