review_text:
Star Trek Online (STO) is worth a try. [i]If[/i] you're a Trekkie. Otherwise, it's just outdated graphics and stale gameplay. It's entertaining, but quickly becomes repetitive.

There's a lot I could say about the game. Instead, I'd like to focus on the one aspect that led me to leave a negative review: the monetization.

The game is f2p. So, I expected microtransactions, and such. I was totally unprepared. Their in-game store contains [i]thousands[/i] of dollars of merchandise. This is not a game in which you are going to own everything. (Unless you are crazy-rich.)

The pricing is truly truly truly outrageous. Oh ho ho yeah. $30 for ONE ship. $5.50 for a costume. $12.50 to make your ship's bridge look like the Enterprise-D. Everything is just a little more expensive than you would expect.

Fans on the forums will tell you, "Yeah, but you can just grind and buy the stuff for free." This is true. You absolutely [i]can[/i] work to get the items for free. However, the time investment is hardly worth it.

The system is complicated. Try to follow me. 

Tier 6 ships (the highest tier, I believe) cost 3000 zen. 3000 zen costs $30. You can earn dilithium ore in-game by completing daily missions and repeating "Task Force Operations". (Which are equivalent to dungeons in most mmos.) You can refine up to 8000 dilithium ore per day. The refined version can be exchanged for zen. However, the exchange rate is roughly 500 dilithium for 1 zen.

So to obtain a $30 ship for "free", you would need nearly 1.5 million units of refined ore. At a rate of 8k per day, this requires around 180 days. 

Assuming you login and gain the 8k every single day. Which is estimated to take a little under 4 hours. That's 720 hours of your life you are never getting back. For a $30 ship. That's like working for $0.04 per hour. No way [i]I'm[/i] doing that! That's not even remotely reasonable.

(Edit: [b]To be fair,[/b] there's an easier way to obtain a free T6 ship. It's simply a matter of waiting for one of several yearly events. Then completing dailies until you get the required number of points.)

Oh, and loot boxes. With variable rarities. In other words, gambling. Because spending $3 on a box, $1.25 on a key to open it, and then getting a mundane item you could have acquired anywhere isn't at all exploitative.

STO isn't against twisting your arm. They hook me up with 4 bridge officers. Then 2 more, but they won't let me use the new ones. Why? Because I don't have enough "bridge officer slots". The only way to obtain more is to delete one I already have. OR spend money to unlock the slots.

Why even bother? Because my ship has 7 positions for bridge officers. Not being able to fill all the positions puts me at a disadvantage. In particular, my science station is empty. Due to this, I am denied an extra ability in space combat.

So, I need to buy 3 slots. However, the game only sells slots 2 at a time for $3 each. But the game will only sell me zen in amounts of $5 or $10. Which means I need $6 worth of zen for my ship to be fully-functional. So, I'm forced to buy $10, and then have 400 zen left I don't intend to use. Worse, I'm pretty sure you have to spend this with every character you make. (If you want to fill those positions.)

I really wanted to talk about the gameplay. Particularly, the space combat. However, none of it is worth it.

This game wants your money, and everything is centered around getting you to spend. I can't support a game like that. At least, not financially.

I will, however, still play for free. I'd like to see if the game has any more to offer that might change my mind.

Update: Playing more [i]did[/i] change my mind. Started to really enjoy it. Learned about more f2p options. Gonna go ahead and leave this a negative review. Since they arbitrarily decided to make the game cease to function on Windows 7. Despite the game having FULL capability of running on even a Vista. A game with graphics this dated (running on Dx9, no less.) has no reason to do this. No flaws of Win7 are a threat to STO in any way.

Do you dream of long draw out slugfests with repetetive and pointless combat?
Do you want nonsense story where choices does not matter and villains are dime a dozen?
Do you seek a linear game where you are constantly held by the balls by being limited in where you go and what you do and how you do it?

It's fun for a couple of times but after the hundredth time you really get bored. 
In the end the same trash you meet from the start is still just as time consuming and dangerous in the end game.

The first game was many times better. It's hard to put my finger on why but I think it's mostly that this type of very linear game makes a very poor open world style game. Also the story of the first was more focused on a clear goal and villain where this second game has too little focus and the focus shifts too much between different villains.

review_text: Great game and a lot of fun. The themes are pretty obvious from the store page, but it's all just plain horror. No scary content, only unsettling, and it pulls it off nicely. I wasn't expecting the game to be as good as it was. Graphics were great for this kind of game, with the exception of an overuse of dof in cutscenes, and having what felt like a filter to make the game look dark and dreary, instead of just texturing things to look as such. Sounds seem jumbled together and after seeing the amount of sounds that came from freesounds in the credits it seems fitting now. Voice acting felt pretty on par with other games in the genre, and by no means has bad acting, it's just not anything above that. Gameplay only broke a few times. Discovered a glitch where if you drop an item on someone just right they just disappear, which for one of the endings could be problematic but I discovered it prior too so I knew how to avoid it. The game does a good job of slowly unlocking the mansion for you to learn how everything is connected at first, but eventually it's a little overwhelming. You'll be doing plenty of circles looking for items though so it's something you learn quickly. There are some items that I wish had better context clues for finding or were placed a little more obviously, but it wasn't anything I couldn't figure out with a bit more walking around usually. There's also an option for two separate endings, of which I think the puzzle ending is the better of the two. Outside of the one issue with disappearing characters, there were small misplaced textures here and there where you might only realize they were there if you were looking, and if you were to walk through rooms fast enough you could see them loading in, but they load in a split second so it's not a big deal. I saw a lot of reviews about it being a buggy game, but I hardly found any, and the ones I found were fixed by going to the title screen and reloading the level. Great buy otherwise, I'm on to play the next game.

I'll keep this short.  I've tried STO a few times over the years.  Each time, it just didn't hook me for some reason.  I enjoy Star Trek in general.  But the combat in STO felt weird, and a lot of time was spent just figuring out what to do or following the mini map radar around.  I can't point out anything really bad in specific..  I just got bored trying to play it.  I'm actually surprised I even got 22 hours logged, and I think the last time I played was 2017.  Based on this alone, I was largely neutral about the game, and didn't feel strongly enough to want to leave a review.

Fast forward to today however, I saw a friend playing it, so on a whim I thought "Hmm, lets see what the game's like in 2021."  Installed the launcher, ran it to download the game, and the launcher immediately popped up a message saying Win10 would be required to play in February, and made it sound like Win7 users wouldn't even have the option to play "unsupported".  I realize I'm not the majority in this, but that seems pretty silly for a game this old to block all Win7 users.  (Even newer games that don't want to publicly support Win7, are often still compatible unless they specifically need DX12+ or rarely a Win10+ GUI library.)

I decided years ago I wouldn't be going past Win7 and will eventually jump to linux, due to the many controversial things in newer windows versions, and the strides Linux has been making lately in gaming.  But since I'm not using linux "yet", that means I'd only have 2 months to play, and that's a little annoying lol.

So it is what it is.  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯  Maybe I'll try it again on linux some day and update this review.

review_text:
Let me start off by saying that I enjoy this game a lot. It has simple enough hockey echanics that let you do fun and wacky stuff on the ice. The only thing is that if you are going to have simple mechanics, you have to REALLY nail them, and this game does not. 

This may be a bit of a longer review so TLDR: character targetting sucks, events are bad, and expert mode feels like a enemy team stat boost on top of smarter AI

Ok, lets start with mechanics. The two mechanics that I really have a problem with are the targetting on changing character (this includes passing) and the aiming of where the goalie throws the puck after they catch it. Both of these feel awful enough consistently for me to say multiple times a game “that is NOT where I pointed my joystick.” Then I think maybe I actually did, and when I go to run my joystic around its housing, I find that I was actually pointing where I wanted, the game just decided it wasn't that direction. This is terrible when you want to pass to 1 of 2 people that are near each other, and passing to the wrong one means an interception, which gets more punishing in expert mode as I will talk about later. When your goalie has the puck, you can aim directly to either side, and there will just be a chance you throw it backward, into your goal possibly. Why am i throwing the puck like 5° behind my player and into my net. That should not even be possible. If I am aiming there, just have me throw it a bit out so that I can not score on myself. This wouldn't be as much of a problem if it passed correctly out of the goalie though.

These game design mistakes make the game on expert mode just feel suffocating and straight up unfair, instead of an increased challenge to an already fun game.

review_text:
I was a big fan of the old Starship Troopers game, so I was pretty excited about this one. It can be a blast if you pick the right class, have teammates with actual brains and a decent server connection and don't face any of the many below mentioned most common bugs, but that's a lot of "ifs". It's still a long way from being well playable. There are a lot of bugs that ruin the experience (no pun intended, and not talking about the ones actually attacking you).Some of the most common ones include:

- No dropship icon visible on the HUD or on the map. Go for extraction, but where to is your guess.
- Weapon positioning on the HUD being off after switching weapons. Sometimes you just see the grip and the underside of the shaft (usually you can fix this one by aiming down sights)
- Engineer turrets cannot be mounted. You can build them, but when you "use" them, nothing happens.
- Q / Ability / Cooldown not being shown. This happens pretty much every single match. Sometimes you can "fix" it by dying and respawning, but it's really annoying when you're playing something with high cooldowns like engineer and you can't see them.
- Sometimes you get hitmakers for hits but no actual points when the bug in question dies.
- Teammates not being shown in your squad list.In the lower left corner of your HUD, your teammates should be shown. But even with a full squad (4 players), you'll rarely see three other names there.
- Server issues are also common. The ping is usually pretty good, with a delay of about 1 second between "using" something and actually using it. This is already much better than your usual Overwatch experience, but there's still room for improvement. 
The building mode could be easily improved by changing the view a bit (otherwise it's really difficult to place big structures like bunkers, while small structures like wall-mounted turrets need millimeter-fine adjustments in order to be built).
- Currently, the demolisher class seems to be the worst trash ever programmed in video game history. A main weapon & a skill which deal exactly 0 damage and mobility is comparable to a pregnant whale. The only fun thing about this class is the suicide explosion, which deals about 5 damage.This class needs a complete rework or simply deletion.
- Sometimes, you cannot sprint anymore. Usually you can fix this by respawning, but not if you're playing demolisher and got the suicide explosion equipped. In  this case, you can't respawn anymore.
- Sometimes when you join a match not at the start of the mission, you are instantly killed and cannot respawn. You can still switch repsawn locations, but actually respawning is not possible.

I know the game is barely out of early access, but there is still lots and lots to do. Considering all those bugs which really ruin the game at the moment, it's definitely not worth spending 50 euros.

review_text:
The beginning of Ken Levine's console driven spiritual sucessor to one of the greatest games ever created for the PC. Irrational played it safe and decided that since almost nobody in the console crowd at the time would have ever heard of System Shock 2 that they could simply lift nearly every single plot element and gameplay mechanic from that game while simplifying it for consoles and then import it into their new game and nobody would be the wiser. Foor all intents and purposes it seems to have worked. When a game is a "spiritual sucessor" you can just jack everything and repaint it a new color.

In place of Shock2's psionics are the plasmids, in place of hybrids are splicers, in place of SHODAN is Fontane, and in place of cyber modules it's ADAM. 

Bioshock was a highly regarded game inspite of being almost completely unoriginal. Which isn't to say it isn't a playable game, yet it's clear that it was built more with the consoles in mind rather than a PC, mouse controls are never quite right and between each save load or level transition one must wait for whatever personal sensitvity settings you've placed the mouse at to "kick back in" if you've adjusted them from the defaults at all and I most certainly did.

The psionics/plasmids are not too terrible a trade off since half of Shock2's psi abilites end up being skipped over by veterans while most of the plasmids in Bioshock serve some function for the various playstyles a person may choose to adopt in Bioshock. However gunplay and firearms are rather weak and almost entirely propped up by the research, weapon upgrades, and the tonic system. 

One must research the various monsters roaming the city of Rapture to gain advantage of them, often not a big deal as you simply snap photos while being shot at. The real problem comes from needing to keep the very best tonics for your methods of dealing damage and finding all the upgrade machines located in the city while accepting the fact that some weapons are simply more efficent at dealing damage than others. The ability to craft addtional special ammo also helps make up some of the difference at the health and damage of enemies continues to upscale throughout the game and while you can buy newer versions of plasmids it's often better to wait until the third and last version is available before spending any precious adam (an exploit fixed in Bioshock 2).

So at best the gameplay in Bioshock is often just average with the occasional fight against a Big Daddy in order to get a Little Sister for more ADAM breaking up the monotony and even those are trivialized by the Vita Chambers that can bring you back again and again for no penality unless you shut them off (added in a later patch). 

Little Sisters are also where the much touted big moral choice comes into the game, a simple yes or no choice to rescue what's suppose to be a little girl. The problem with Bioshock is that all the human chracters look like cheap melted wax figures and not even close to human. So any attempt to dredge up empathy for me failed abysmally and I happily harvested every Little Sister on my first playthorugh. I later found out that the big moral choice leads to three endings, if you so much as harvest one sister you get the bad ending with a sad voice, if you harvest them all you get the bad ending with an angry voice and if you save them all you get the good ending, those deep moral choices I tell ya.

The plot fares no better since it's just literally System Shock 2's plotline all over again, running around Rapture doing chores for a guy you start to trust who turns out to be the actual big bad of the whole game who then tries to kill you once he has everything he wants. At the same time someone looked at the cover of Atlus Shrugged and decided it would help make the game deep and philisophical and I think the cover is about as far as they got. 

Bioshock is just a pale immitation of System Shock 2, but for a lot of people it's their first exposure to the "Shock" series even though it doesn't belong to it at all.

Boneworks is by far my favourite VR game, so it hurts to see the sequel get downgraded so much.
Levels are super linear with no replayability and tons of loadzones. Boneworks had massive levels with intertwining paths and in comparison Bonelab just feels lackluster.
The focus of this game is on modding and sandbox but they could have atleast given us some decent levels to use mods in, killing NPCs in sandbox gets boring in like 5 minutes.
Climbing is atrocious, it was bad in Boneworks too but they somehow made it worse here.
I'm not sure what they did but aiming has gotten completely scuffed too. I used to be able to hit headshots by aiming on instinct, now I miss even when aiming down sights.
Modding community for this game is pretty weak. I installed a bunch of mods as I was getting back into this game, almost all of them had broken over the course of the last few updates.
Just about the only positive thing I have to say about this game is the music, but it just makes me sad when I listen to it since it reminds me how ass the game it's attached to is.

Honestly, just play Boneworks instead, it's cheaper even.

review_text:
Quite the disappointment compared to the EA showcase.

 You roam maps with random spawns of bullet sponge enemies, your guns are terrible and have low range and low damage, even the rifle has the range of a bb gun, your shots sometimes can stagger enemies when hitting the head but you'll realise that only the dps of a gun matters since everything is a bullet sponge. You'll run out of bullets fighting normal enemies, not to mention the events with lots of spawns or the statues with unlimited spawns. Also if you run out of bullets and try to leave through a portal, enemies can spawn from them, preventing you from leaving. There are ammo chests spawning randomly around maps when you load in and they only give bullets for the gun in your hands, so if you take it and you have 0 ammo on your secondary and 1 ammo missing with the one in your hand you'll get 1 bullet only, you have to remember to switch gun and you will forget.

 The first mini boss you'll face breaks the trinity of enemy balance which is, high speed, high defense, high attack, normally you only give enemies 1 or 2 of these attributes to give them a weakness to exploit, but the first mini boss is faster than you, has a large health pool, shoots very quick explosive projectiles that are impossible to dodge and has a 0.1 second dodge window for attacks. The only way i've found to beat him is by dealing so much damage that you don't need to deal with his mechanics and he just keeps running away to another location until he dies.

The mission to investigate the docks is bugged so i couldn't even make it to the second map and continue to progress.

The enemy variety goes from one extreme to the other, going from useless crawling monster that sprays poison that you can just ignore to swordsmen that can fly away or closer to you and are deadly in cqc. most enemies in the middle a quite generic, skeletons that shoot slow moving guided missiles and zombies that run around randomly and tries to stab you with a knife.

The actual fighting is quite bad, you lose all your stamina when hit with a melee attack, so if you're surrounded when hit you're dead. Your melee attack has an empowered effect with a very long cooldown and sometimes it just goes in cooldown for no reason, so sometimes you'll use your melee attack and realise it did nothing and the enemy will just stab you back.

Trying to use range to your advantage will make you use twice as many bullets, since every gun has a sharp drop in damage after a few meters, including the sniper rifles. The bullet's velocity is also unnaturally low for guns, it's almost like you're using a bow that works like a gun. Since the game forces you to fight close to enemies you wouldn't immediately realise. The proper way to balance guns is by giving them all their own unique advantage in battle. The guns in this game are all boring and terrible, with the enemies being bullet sponges, it makes only the ones with higher dps being viable in any way. 

The event where you defend the crystal will make you waste all your ammo only to reward you with healing the life you lost in the fight and if you don't do anything you get way more crystals if it gets destroyed, so why does it exist in the first place? Just put a chest instead.

I wouldn't recommend anyone to play this game in it's current state, it needs a lot of reworking and the gameplay loop is just not fun. If ammo management is supposed to be important, just make every shot matter, otherwise give unlimited ammo, making enemies bullet sponges while forcing players to manage their ammo is just lazy design choice. Games like Resident Evil and the Metro series were designed in a way that you could avoid fights and conserve ammo while still being able to progress in the game. review_text:
[h1]Casual fun for Trekkies[/h1]
The title I gave is the tldr.
But to gaze deeper into what this MMO is.
[h2]What's fun:[/h2]
+ Abundant variety exploring planets
+ Recurring characters from the numerous Star Trek shows
+ Graphics have a style to them, realism wasn't the aim and that's not a bad thing.
+ Casual questing, but fairly engaging
+ Great race and faction choices, from human to Klingon to Romulans, and more.
+ Satisfactory voiced dialogue.
+ Fair tutorial, making it easy to jump in
+ A lot of effort was put into in-game cutscenes, and that's kinda nice.

[h2]What's not so fun:[/h2]
- Ground and space combat could be refined, but is something you get used to. Though, it appears that it's not the focus
- Downloading the game is manageable, but returning to find the 'idle connection error', and the game didn't finish downloading its resources, sucks. At least, what was downloaded won't need to be downloaded again, but the download percentage won't show you that.
- Railroaded narrative, not branching off with different outcomes.
- Inventory doesn't feel cohesive. If I hover over an item I'd like to see a visual cue of the stat comparison between what I've equipped and the similar item type I'm looking at.  

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Despite the combat, if you love Star Trek and want to have a little taste of something that reminds you of those "strange, new worlds", and its themes of philosophy and morality with sci-fi spunk, you might enjoy this game as I do.
It's 7/10 for me.

[h2]Update[/h2]
The content loop started to wear on me, and stopped playing not long after writing this review, so take that as you will.

review_text:
Dead by Daylight - a name-based breakdown

[b]Dead[/b]
You play in one of two teams (yes, a solo team is still a team), either trying to do the dead to someone or avoiding becoming the dead.
As the killer, it is your job to find people, run in circles of varying radii while dodging pallets thrown at you for at least 10 minutes, attack survivors with often questionable hit registration, and scramble to find a hook in proximity. Rinse and repeat thrice per survivor.
You also get a large cast of characters with increasingly broken and more abundant abilities and perks (scaling with in-game and IRL money cost, of course).
As a survivor, your job is one of: Holding Mouse Button 1 for an eternity and occasionally tapping space, running in circles of varying radii while dodging the killer, dropping pallets and jumping through windows, and enjoying the scenery while [i]hanging around[/i].

[b]by[/b]
By choosing to play this of your own free will, you prove that you are masochistic.
As the killer, the survivors always find some random junk scattered by a tornado to hide behind, and as a survivor, the killer is always slightly* faster than you.
If you are planning to play a killer with projectile or ranged attacks, dont't. Hitboxes in this game have been proven to protrude into the 7th dimension, especially those that don't look that way.
Conversely, survivors have been known to have been hit by attacks through solid objects.
Really shows how our understanding of physics breaks down beyond the third spatial dimension.
Also remember to pray to RNGsus before running through shrubbery, as it might be of the 'solid' genus despite sharing the phenotype of their 'transparent' siblings.
It's also funny how there are never any windows or pallets while you are being chased. Well, back to admiring the level geometry.

The performance is also abysmal. Lowering the graphics settings barely makes a difference, as the game is consistently gobbling up 80-100% of my CPU even while not much or even nothing is happening (e.g. game lobby, transition screens).
Depending on the map, it turns into a PowerPoint presentation as soon as at least one other player is on screen for no discernable reason.
On a positive note, I no longer have to change settings every time I boot up the game, so a big round of applause.

[b]Daylight[/b]
This game is anti-fun regardless of which team you play on, regardless of you win or lose. Good games where neither team is completely steamrolled are few and far between.
It seems like you are placed in the timeout box after dominating too many matches in a row and are free to return after serving your sentence. If that's your thing, good for you, but that ain't it, chief.

Specifically for 2V8 (the only theoretically redeemable mode**) the killer queues are a joke. You usually wait 30+ minutes for a match, and too often just so that the survivors can complete the 'DBD All 8 Generators' 100% glitchless speedrun in 2m 57s.
How is this possible when there is a 5-digit player count at all times? The introduction of 'Survive While You Wait' has done precisely nothing and the priority queue got ditched after one iteration of this game mode for reasons I don't care enough to look up.
At least you may partake in fun activities such as: Holding Mouse Button 1 (but more often because no one else is doing it), getting nothing done while being permanently cornered by 2 killers, and getting ignored by up to 7 players while in a cage collecting hook states (what do you mean that's not the objective???).

I'm being held here against my will by a so called 'friend' who's only into these kinds of games. Please help.

* Top speeds of Mach 3 have been registered.
** Objective fact.

review_text:
In a crowded landscape of modern horror games, it can be rare to find a game that delivers both an intense, visceral experience and a deeply cinematic, narrative driven story. This game does just that while featuring powerful performances from both Josh Duhamel and Sam Witwer. I'm baffled by the amount of negative reviews and the mixed ratings, as I feel this game stands as a unique and exceptional entry into the horror market.
I believe a common point of contention comes from the unfair comparison to the Dead Space series, an understandable but misguided point of view. While it's clear where the dev's roots lie, The Callisto Protocol forges its own identity. It feels like a spiritual successor that further evolves on the formula, creating a unique and impactful experience rather than just being a rehash for old fans.
I've also seen criticism for the melee combat. As for myself, I find it brilliant. Don't come into the game expecting fast paced "kung fu". It feels slow, heavy, and satisfying. There's weight behind each strike from your weapon that emphasizes the feeling of survival that the main character is going through. It makes it feel more personal.
Ultimately, I strongly suggest anyone on the fence pick it up. This is a very cinematic and rewarding horror experience that I can't recommend enough. From the compelling story to the satisfying combat, this is one that stands tall in the market. I'm totally invested in its world and characters and can't wait to play more.

review_text:
I got to this game pretty late since it seemed like Act 3 was never going to happen- so I just kinda didn't feel like checking out the second part a story that won't get finished- and then What Pumpkin went and revealed they're actually working on Act 3 so.  Hey.  Time to play Act 2.

It's fun and cute, a really nice dive into Troll/Alternia stuff for folks who are fans of that, and manages to be a light-hearted adventure while also tackling some less light stuff.  It was really cute seeing Joey start figuring out she's into girls and her friendship with Xefros is really good for both of them.  Didn't feel as short as the first Act, probably because of the trial segment (which I enjoyed but found had a less than satisfying ending since the actual thief doesn't seem to be revealed?), but was paced pretty well.  Hint system's unobtrusive and escalates hints very well if you keep asking for help.  Never felt like I was entirely lost or stuck.

So, it's good.  Worth playing if you enjoyed Act 1, improves on that in a lot of ways.  Feels a bit less ambitious but also a lot more tightly designed in the right spots.  Hopefully Act 3 actually releases someday.

review_text:
NGS: Terrible themepark, good sandbox.

Combat content? Doable, but unrewarding loot. Action is all right, generous iframes, don't expect new classes to come out.

Fashion is very very very good, but F2P money for it is slow, and the market is volatile. You can whale, but there will be scalpers jacking up prices. Otherwise, fashion is the best thing about the game. Many clothes, many animations, many accessories.

The housing (creative spaces) is good too. Extensive options and flexibility in how creative you can get, if you can get into it. Amazing alone to just tour other players' grand works.

NGS story is hot garbage. It takes itself too seriously, and offers nothing compelling to care about.

5.5/10, "recommended" because despite the underwhelming parts, the player creativity carries it. Hence terrible themepark, good sandbox.

Base PSO2 (~60GB free DLC): mostly a free game with years of good content in combat, story, gear, and fashion. Only issue is that the base PSO2 blocks are unpopulated. Good themepark, good sandbox, no players. 7/10

review_text:
Shadow Tactics is an RTS puzzle game that is a mixed bag of some enjoyment but a huge amount of frustration and terrible design.

You get 5 characters throughout the game and they essentially all work the same with the exception of the sniper.  They all have a close range blade attack, a special move only they can do, a different distraction/luring technique, a limited use flintlock, and a 1 time use medkit.  The sniper has limited ammo in his long range rifle as his main attack and a limited number of grenades as his special move.  Early on you only get a couple characters per mission but later on you'll get access to 4 or 5.  Unfortunately the balance isn't very good.  The 2 female characters make the male characters pretty much useless as Yuki's trap/whistle combo can take care of pretty much every regular enemy and once Aiko gets a disguise you'll run around with her killing every lone unit or distracting someone so someone else can kill the person he was watching.  The only time you'll need the male characters is to take out an enemy samurai.

So to get to the frustrations and terrible design.  The entire game is a giant grindy save scum.  You will be quick saving after pretty much every enemy you kill, every time you move to a new position, every time you get ready to set up a new kill, every time you hide a body somewhere, etc.  Then you'll constantly be quick loading as something goes wrong, whether you get screwed over by the god awful camera, whether your character does something completely random you didn't want them to do, you get spotted by some enemy 2 miles away, spotted by some guy who looks like he's looking in a completely different direction, or spotted by some dude who just happened to walk into view range as you started killing.  Anytime you're spotted you're going to press F8 since being spotted alarms enemies.  They swarm the area for a minute+ before they go back to their normal spots.  It's always quicker to quick load.  Fortunately the game quick saves and loads quickly.  I want to be entirely clear here.  I am not exaggerating in any way, shape or form.  On average, you will be quick saving or quick loading at least every 30 seconds.

The cursor and character actions are a gigantic problem.  The cursor will often completely miss what you're trying to do.  Did you tell your character to walk up and stab that guy?  Well instead the game interprets it as you having told your character to walk right in front of that enemy and stand there.  F8.  I don't even want to talk about dragging bodies because this p!ssed me off all game long.  Tell character to drag a body over to a bush and drop it.  Come back to that character later and they're standing in the bush still holding onto the body.  Especially frustrating is when the ninja or samurai do this as they don't duck when holding a body.  So enemies will walk by and spot them standing upright in a bush with a dead body in their hands..... F8.  God forbid you try to get your character to drag a dead body to a door right after killing that enemy.  50% of the time they'll grab the body, then immediately drop it and start walking or running to the door for no reason.  “No you f.cker, that's not what I f.cking told you to do”  F8.  The number of times my characters did completely random things for no reason is too high to count.

The camera might be the absolute worst part of the game though.  Anything blocked by the camera is essentially unreachable for your characters.  On a narrow pathway with walls around it?  Gotta swing the camera so it's centered on the pathway so you can get your character to go down that path.  Want to go around that corner up ahead?  Well you can't just click around the corner, you've got to re-angle the camera so you can see down that pathway.  Want to get into that door around the next corner, gotta re-angle the camera.

The game has a severe problem dealing with ground/building levels.  If the camera is not exactly positioned correctly, character prompts like jumping, dropping down, throwing bodies off something become impossible to do.  For instance, it looks like there's a secret path you can jump to over there.  Well, the camera is off by 10 degrees, so the prompt for jumping doesn't appear for your character.  So you assume that secret passage isn't in play.  Then 10 minutes later at a slightly different camera angle you happen to pass by that area again and now the jump prompt appears.  Gee, would've been great if that would've shown up 10 minutes ago, would've saved me a lot of trouble.  Especially awful is being on rooftops as you must constantly swing the camera to move around.  One mission has you assassinating some enemy and there's a 3 level building nearby him. The game has a massive heart attack trying to interpret your actions up there.  You will constantly walk places you don't want to walk, jump down when you don't want to jump down, hookshot when you don't want to hookshot, etc.  Especially fun is that the prompt for the hookshot spots are always visible so you'll want to walk somewhere and keep getting the hookshot prompt because where you want to walk happens to have a hookshot prompt in the background somewhere.

The game has some inconsistencies with its noise mechanic.  To give a simple example of this, one of your characters has a technique allowing them to whistle.  Guards and villagers in range will be lured by this.  Sometimes enemies who are clearly highlighted blue indicating they'll hear this noise somehow won't hear it and continue along their way.  Other times enemies who are clearly not highlighted and outside of the range will hear the sound and come investigate.

Another problem with the game is that the vast majority of levels play out almost exactly the same due to the lack of enough puzzle elements.  There are only 4 enemies in the game.  Villagers who won't attack but will run away or report your position.  Guards who can be killed by everyone and be lured/distracted.  StrawHats who can be killed by everyone but won't leave their positions by lures and who will only briefly look at a distraction.  Samurai who work like StrawHats but can only be killed by your Samurai or by shooting them and then running up and stabbing them.  Samurai can also see through Aiko's disguise.  You'll have seen pretty much everything by level 6 but there're 13 levels total.  There's just not enough puzzle here to remain interesting and the vast majority of the puzzle is the same exact thing.  Picking off lone enemies or figuring out which enemy you can lure out and kill in a spot where someone else can't see them dying.

Shadow Tactics has some good ideas but the execution is amateurish.  There simply isn't enough new content/puzzle elements to warrant the number of levels in the game.  The camera, cursor, and random actions your characters take will provide no end of frustrations and swearing.  The game simply isn't polished enough to provide a worthwhile experience.

review_text:
Recommended for players who can accept a bizarre slaughterhouse-like fantasy world, built by an advanced but extinct super-race where architecture and science is far beyond from the actual imaginations, 
In here, call it a fleshy walking horror sim with weapon use, you will act some mix of human without skin and much flesh, possessed by some alien crawler what takes over your body piece by piece in ketchup-animated scenes, but closer to the end the extraction from this thing will take place. You start, release yourself, fall down a cliff and without much help, you are on your own to find out of WTF is going on and how this shall end. Mostly you are underground in a well designed environment of futuristic constructions, entangled by a huge alien life-form. The xenomorph maker had a good time in here and once you look closer, the relats to the Alien movies can be seen quite clear. So saddle up and find your way out from this deserted place where only corpses and flesh do remain, master the riddles what are fair and without giving you headaches, upgrade your inventory and interact with anything what pops-up on machinery or buttons of fancy vending-like kiosks. Soon you will encounter the first foes so as learning of how restricted the ammo and health supply will be, avoid any confrontation and chicken-out if you can, no shame for that, but better to conserve your resources to stay alive. The shapeless enemies are simple made but can hurt you quite well, take your choice of how to deal with the individuals. The more you enhance yourself, the tougher it will become, the later fight with 2 robot hosts make fun and the 4 simple weapons shall be used with care as the rough way isn't the best one. Once you will leave the scary underworld and reaches the impressive fortress where some more stands give you a good riddle time. You will be dismantled and rebuild but this play end differently from the expectation as an exit is not always a release, so don't expect more than sadness at the end.
It is worth playing so as it differs from others but has many roots and relations to well known movies and other similar games. I you have no issues with the flesh and blood rich animation along with some cruelty on handicapped lifeforms, this is a good experience and milestone in this very genre.

review_text:
As a huge fan of soulslike games (e.g. platinumed Bloodborne, played a ton of Demon Souls, Dark Souls 1+2+3, Sekiro, LotF, Wukong, Mortal Shell and so on) and also a huge fan of Roguelike and -lite games, I was pretty excited to play this, especially with doom-like looking combat and awesome dark-fantasy visuals.

However the gameplay itself does not make me want to continue playing it, as it doesn't have this addicting feeling of doing another and another run.
Starting a new run does not feel like an exciting opportunity to craft or discover cool builds, more like being tossed into another empty island with some enemies sprinkled on it that you kill with the same weapons over and over and sometimes weird animations (like the musket boys who trace my dash with their shot).

The world and it's vibe are awesome, but the maps feel so empty with only a few objects being interactable like random ammo chests (who would randomly store Preyer ammo in their witch-dominated town?). After the intro sequence, I wanted to feel like I'm this elite mutant fighting on the frontlines of this holy war. kinda like a Black Templar of Warhammer 40k - but instead I was just a dude dashing through levels to farm some souls on samey enemies.

Also the music is great, but isn't nearly as present as I think it should be, as you barely notice it in battle.

Altogether everything except the actual runs is pretty good, but I'm mostly here for fun and fast gameplay - maybe that's my fault for excepting some kind of doom-souls-hades mix. 

Kudos for the optimization though, the game runs perfectly.

review_text:
As often, I wish there were more rating options than just thumbs down or up. I enjoyed playing this game, but there was also the impression that the creators and producers restricted themselves to modest aspirations. In other words, the game lacks content. There are basically only four characters with a name - the protagonist, a tragic loss, one ally and the foe. The nature of their relationships are set after the introductory level and don't change - there is not even a "Ha I only used you to get rid of my opponent and now I betray you"-moment. Furthermore, there a few weapons, no minigames and small variety in the side missions. Plot and story are so flat that they rather imitate 80s Sci-Fi-Action-flicks than poking fun at them. Though there are some funny moments, they are restricted to some dialogue lines. For the final, a cheesy approach was chosen, but I would have preferred an ironical twist - like for example, that a nobody would become a hero and Rex Power Colt would be de-glorified.

Combatwise, there is not so much a lack of content but simply of enemies - it is possible (and quickly happens accidentally) to shoot an enemy from a corner and then watch how the whole garnison of 15-20 foes approaches you in "waves" of 1-2 people, allowing you to take them out easily one after another. Though I played on hard, my Rex died less than five times during the whole game and I would not call myself a pro. So either there should be more enemies or they should have a better AI and target more precisely.

This problem even worsens once you have some of the upgrades. While the enemies are the same from the beginning to the end, Rex can (by finishing the side missions) acquire overpowered weapons. Especially the sniper rifle at full modification allows you to take out most enemies with a body shot (and often killing nearby ones, too, because the bullets become explosive) at a very wide range and even with the swaying of the scope practically eliminated.

Of course, you could also argue that it's only consequent that you are overpowered since the framework is a pseudo-manly and dim lit action title from the 80s. This leads me back to the observation that Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is more a copy than a parody of the underlying matter.

What I liked was the movement, the sound track and the visual style overall. They were worth investing 14 hours at a time where I had absolutely nothing better to do. I really think that this game could have been much better if the humour was more drastic, consequent and widespread and if there was at least some character development and an actual plot. That way, I would have wanted more than just 14 hours.

This game has amazing promise, but right about now I can't recommend this game due to the bugs and cancerous mechanics i've come across.

GAME CONCEPT: It's pretty much Left4Dead in VR you fight multiple zombie types and waves of enemies through the map until you come across a safe point to buy more items and push on to the boss. After finishing a level you are rewarded with possible weapons and weapon mods. 
-You take the fight to the freezing zombies in a 1-4 person crew/fireteam. 

+++++++PROS++++++
You get a nice zombie hunting simulator with your friends or random mates

Fun and engaging allowing for multiple play throughs as zombies spawn in many locations and in greater numbers as the level is increased.

Current guns feel very nice.

---------CONS-----------
Players glitch the map allowing them to cheese the maps while stuck in the walls not taking any damage as they shoot zombies which takes away from players who worked hard and have good coordination. (So now you have someone who potentially hordes needed items and supplies while they create a mission *3 longer than it needed to be)

Players/Host leave quite frequently causing you to lose all your progression on the current level as well as rewards along the way. (Even if you've beaten the boss already)

Servers or peer to peer (how ever the devs are running their connectivity is cancerous) 75% of games end with players unwillingly leaving or being dropped for no reason. 

Long play waits: If you want to try a harder difficulty you can spend 30-160 mins just looking for a team only to get halfway through the level before the host disconnects kicking all players back to the lobby.

Not enough weapons to keep players engaged in the long run. 

The sheer unstability of the game where you can't 100% secure the items you've collected.

The lobby filter is pretty terrible as you get random players or are invited by random players who don't possess the skills for the levels they choose. Getting a team of equally skilled players rarely ever happen.
(Which isn't on the players trying a new difficulty but sometimes the bots are better than the human players)

=====================================================
Right now the BIGGEST threat to this title is its own stability. 

Will I, myself contiune to play yes..... but I enjoy torturing myself for some ungodly reason. 
For new players willing to pick up the game just wait... it's not worth it currently and you can actually progress quickly so you it is not like if you don't join NOW your at a loss (that's simply not true).

I do however looking forward to seeing all of you AFTER the game is fixed and is playable and complete (which it has a ways to go).

review_text:
I honestly don't like it. 

Half Life Alyx has set clear standards to how guns in vr should feel and behave and going from it to this game, it's kind of one big disappointment. 
Before anyone cries out "but it's indie devs", I will have to respond with: pricepoints set expectations. For 40 quid european you get very little game. I'm not expecting the same level of polish, but this game simply lacks polish - and a lot at that. 

At times, it feels very grindy. The controls are unintuitive. I hate the way they've implemented the belt - it never behaves right. Sometimes I grab ammo when I don't want to grab any, and other times I will not, even when I want to do it. 
Putting the ammo belt lower would be a treat,  so it's closer to your waist, but in doing so, you also lower the holster height of your weapons, which means that once I get my ammo belt to a comfortable position, I can no longer reach the weapons.

If you could calibrate both of those things separately from one another, that'd be perfect, but of course, you can't. 

Teleportation is choppy. It seems to me like you have to hold down the trackpad button for a random amount of time before the game decides that you can now teleport. It isn't instant, at least not for me, and thus feels very awkward. You can hardly respond to the waves of enemies when using teleport as a locomotion because of that. 
Using the trackpad works much better, but in games like this, I do feel a little dizzy after doing so for a while, which is why I generally prefer teleportation over linear movement. 

Gun handling feels awkward. There's one defined way of reloading your weapon and that's that. You do what the devs want you to do. I haven't found a menu to change up controls, so I assume it doesn't exist, which is another thing I'm not fond of. I'm using a regular gen 1 vive still, and I would've very much preferred it if they copied the control scheme of HLA. Maybe that'll get better once I have some index controllers, but... we'll see. 

The game doesn't feel as nicely paced out as AZ sunshine. You walk until you hit another wave of enemies where you'll essentially be playing a railshooter and then progress to the next place where you do the same. In a way, it feels like a step backward and in the wrong direction. It's got a much stronger vibe of tech demo (like so many vr games do) that, in ernest, surprises me, considering the otherwise decent track record of the developer. 
AZ sunshine was the first proper non-tech-demo vr game out there, and I feel they've kinda blown it with this game. 

The game is certainly enjoyable in a way, but not enough for me to recommend it. 
At times, I desperately wished the game would let you yeet yourself by pointing a pistol against your forehead and pulling the trigger, but there's no easy way out in this game, I'm afraid.

review_text:
I am sure if anyone reads this they might be confused why I don't recommend this game despite playing it over 100 hours.

I like this game, but I think everyone who would also like this game probably likes it for the same reason I do. I was a big fan of the original series, which are MUCH better games in comparison. G.U. allows for more of the same gameplay, but absolutely does not stand on its own.

Graphics: The game looks pretty great, they did a good job on the remaster. No complaints.

Sound: Some terrific music, sound effects, and the Japanese voice acting at least isn't bad. The Grunty sounds are awful though.

Story: Alright, so here is where it starts to fall apart. The story is entertaining enough, I find myself wanting to see what happens next, but there are so many parts that just doesn't make sense. It is mostly in how the characters act, I understand that role playing is a thing but they act like they aren't in an online game and at the same time, act like they are. There are so many lines that conflict with each other with regards to what is going on in the story. Characters will say something like "This is just a game." and then 3 minutes later they are completely serious. The writing for the main character is atrocious. He's annoying, rude to everyone, and just an overall child. There are times when you think he's gonna stop being mean and then he just says something else. I could do without the awkward online dating storyline too.

Gameplay: Okay so the core combat is just as good as the original game. There's some other stuff added that seems to mostly improve the game...except the bike. The Bike is the absolute worst thing I have ever driven in a game. Luckily, it really isn't required unless you want to complete Ryu Books and it gets slightly better in game 2 since you can mod it, but its still not fun.  The absolute biggest problem with the combat is the game is just too easy. You can ignore ALL the mechanics of the game if you want, in group and solo battles. It is almost impossible to die, I've only had a character come close once and that's just because I wasn't paying attention. There's also a severe lack of actual boss fights unless you play on going out of your way to do side areas, but there's two problems with that. 1.) Doing more than the main story questions will get you overleveled quick, making the game even easier. 2.) Even then, they are barely bosses and more like  regular enemies with more health.

Overall, don't bother with this game if you never played the original 4 games. Its just not good enough without that nostalgia.

review_text:
If you love reading meaningless filler, this game is for you.

I've finished what's considered the "default route", and if I had to describe it in 2 words, it'd be "painfully mediocre". Which is regretful, as the game seemingly has a great setup: a young woman ends up among the samurai forces. There's so much the writers could have done with this... but unfortunately for the heroine, this is a typical Japanese visual novel, so she will spend 4 years cooking and cleaning, only have one day of sword training and call it a day, but nevertheless whine about not being included in armed conflicts and being useless overall.

At first, I thought that maybe this game was intended for Japanese history nerds, but nope. Most of the major historical events only get mentioned in passing, and what you witness instead is lots of petty squabbles with other samurai and boring slice-of-life days. Many characters purposefully keep themselves distant from the heroine (can't blame them, she's annoying), and, in the traditional spirit of Japanese games, she's expected to take their threats and verbal abuse as a wall she's supposed to break through in order to win their affection. Remember that time you were treated like trash and thought "aww, he's only doing it because he doesn't want to show how much he secretly cares about me"? Yeah, me neither. Recommended for people prone to Stockholm syndrome and/or tragically low self-esteem.

P.S. As other reviewers have noted, this is only half of the game disguised as a standalone, so it ends abruptly and on a cliffhanger.

review_text: A pain in the ass. The gameplay is mostly there, but the terrible AI, absolutely disfunctional pathing, and the inability to stack commands or pause time (yes, this is an RTS, but the UI is too shoddy for the devs to get away with that) means that there are constant restarts because the characters won't do what you want them do. The quickload system is the only saving grace for this game, and the only reason its playable, but the fact that it NEEDS something like that is a poor fix to begin with. Not to mention that it gives you the number of quickloads at the end anyway, and throwing this game's mistake in your face, like it was the players fault to begin with, and not a bad design choice. I've long since lost count of the number of times that I've redone one specific point because my characters have a small window to perform, and won't do the commands correctly. The game allows you to check the guards changing viewcones, but only one can be highlighted at a time. If you need to run through several overlapping viewcones, the option given to you is to slap down a marker inside that area...that only tells you if a particular guard happens to be looking at that marker at any particular time. Useless. In short, the UI and AI really kills this game by just making it an excercise in frustration, and whoever was responsible for those departments should have been fired, because the rest of the team actually did a decent job. Shame.

review_text:
"BioShock," developed by Irrational Games and released in 2007, is a first-person shooter that blends innovative gameplay, a compelling narrative, and atmospheric world-building to create a memorable experience. Set in the dystopian underwater city of Rapture, players explore a society that has fallen into ruin, uncovering its secrets and surviving the dangers that lurk within. This review evaluates "BioShock" based on its gameplay mechanics, story and setting, graphical and audio presentation, impact on the gaming industry, and overall entertainment value.

Gameplay Mechanics
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
"BioShock" stands out for its gameplay mechanics, which expertly combine traditional first-person shooter elements with unique plasmid powers, offering players a wide range of combat strategies. The ability to modify weapons and use environmental hazards against enemies adds depth and variety to encounters. The game also incorporates RPG elements, allowing for character customization through gene upgrades, which enhances the strategic component of gameplay. The innovative use of plasmids and the game's approach to combat and exploration set a new standard for the genre.

Story and Setting
Rating: 10/10 - Masterpiece
The narrative and world of "BioShock" are where the game truly shines. Rapture, with its art deco design and retro-futuristic technology, is a character in its own right, rich with history and mystery. The story, exploring themes of free will, human nature, and the dangers of unchecked ambition, is engaging and thought-provoking. The city's descent into madness is revealed through environmental storytelling and audio diaries, providing a deep and immersive narrative experience that few games have matched.

Graphical and Audio Presentation
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
At the time of its release, "BioShock" was praised for its stunning visuals, which meticulously captured the eerie beauty and decay of Rapture. The attention to detail in the environment, character models, and visual effects contributes to the game's immersive atmosphere. The audio design, from the haunting soundtrack to the chilling sound effects and voice acting, plays a crucial role in building tension and enhancing the storytelling, making the exploration of Rapture an unforgettable experience.

Impact on the Gaming Industry
Rating: 10/10 - Masterpiece
"BioShock" had a profound impact on the gaming industry, influencing countless games that followed. It demonstrated that video games could be a powerful medium for storytelling, capable of exploring complex themes and presenting players with moral dilemmas. The game's integration of narrative and gameplay, along with its innovative mechanics and atmospheric world-building, have been cited as inspirations by many developers, cementing its legacy as a landmark title in gaming history.

Overall Entertainment Value
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
"BioShock" offers an exceptional entertainment value, combining a compelling story, engaging gameplay, and a richly detailed world. The game's ability to immerse players in its dystopian underwater setting, challenging them to survive and uncover the truth of Rapture, makes for a captivating experience from start to finish. While some aspects of gameplay may feel dated to players revisiting the game or experiencing it for the first time years after its release, "BioShock" remains a must-play title for its narrative depth and innovative design.

Overall Summary and Score
Overall Rating: 9.4/10 - Masterpiece
"BioShock" is a seminal game that masterfully blends narrative, gameplay, and atmosphere to create an experience that is both thought-provoking and immensely enjoyable. Its impact on the gaming industry and the way stories can be told through interactive media is undeniable, making it not only a landmark title in the first-person shooter genre but also in video gaming as a whole.

Essential for gamers interested in narrative-driven experiences and fans of first-person shooters looking for depth and innovation in gameplay. "BioShock" is a defining game of its generation, offering a rich and immersive journey into the heart of a utopian dream turned nightmare.

review_text:
[h1] History but Sexy [/h1]
First thing is first. This is the first part of a two part game. This is a slow burn romance where you get history and get to know your fellah over the course of a few years. I have played EVERY ending.

Your character is Yukimura Chizuru (or whatever name you give her) and she basically exists for self insert purposes. Honestly, I wish she could do cooler stuff given her heritage. But her behavior generally depends on which route she's in. I do enjoy that she is quite kind. A bit of an airhead at times and you wanna spell things out for her, but she is likable. Not that active, but she does have her goals/mission.

The art is absolutely beautiful. I fell in love with the style. It is a history heavy game, especially part one setting you up for part two. This game is pretty historically accurate, which I found enjoyable. That being said, this is about the rise of a civil war so prepare for some heartbreak. Those of you that liked Nightshade will enjoy this as I think it was actually better.

Characters/Romance style: They're all pretty different. I will block out anything I deem spoiler-y but mostly I'm describing the romance.

Toshizo Hijikata: "Canon." He has the prettiest hair. This romance felt more like you exist as a Greek chorus to watch events unfold since he is a prominent figure of the war. It gets sweeter towards the end.

Souji Okita: I found this to be the most believable route with life just throwing crap his way and Souji dealing with it the best he could. Smart mouth tsundere type. It had its sweet moments. Take a shot for every time Okita says he'll kill you and you'll have alcohol poisoning by the end of this game. That being said, I loved this brat.

Heisuke Toudou: Hilarious start. It's really quite cute as the characters fall for each other. I enjoyed that this character was immediately warm to Chizuru, very much like an excited puppy. This one was a pretty natural progression of feelings that's actually visible in the story.

Sanosuke Harade: MC is SO much stronger in this. There's a mutual sort of respect between the two characters. Sanosuke respects her strength, and even though he's a gentleman trying to protect her, he'll listen to her. Friends to lovers sort of feel.

Shinpachi: F this romance. I'm warning you, this one feels like an older brother.

Hajime Saito: Typical shy guy. Lots of cute moments. There's way more to him and Chizuru helps Saito become more.

Susumu Yamazaki: This guy totally surprised me. Not what I expected at all. Really sweet romance and this character has the potential to become a stronger character because of Chizuru. She has more of a presence in this one because of their [spoiler] similar medical background in healing and she contributes alongside him [/spoiler].

Hachiro Iba: Marry me. Childhood friends trope. Sometimes it is so painfully obvious you want to take Chizuru to the side and say very slowly, "He likes you." He respects Chizuru's desires over what he thinks is best. It's refreshing to have a character who openly expresses their feelings.

Chikage Kazama: I could listen to this man talk for hours. Holy crap the voice actor sends ripples down your spine. My bae. The narrative makes it so Chizuru is out of the loop on a lot of war sh*t, however, the trade off is that Kazama is very dutiful in filling in the blanks about her demon heritage. I enjoyed this alone for learning about that, but he had to have the voice of a sex god so that was a plus. It feels like he's trying to meet you halfway.

Royuma Sakamoto: Eh. He's pretty. This romance is more through correspondence and picks up towards the end.

Kazue Souma: You don't meet this guy for like half of the game. This is more of a very slow growth sort of romance. You get the feeling towards the end that they both [spoiler] like each other but are too shy to do anything [/spoiler]. Nomura is hilarious.

Keisuke Sanan: Okay, he gets a bad rep. Found his route enjoyable but I have a thing for characters that have a dark side growing within them. *shakes fist at Dragon Age Inquisition* You can tell that that the protagonist becomes to Sanan [spoiler] his only source of light and she helps him retain his humanity [/spoiler]. Feels like a romance where the two people like each other but are afraid to cross that line, in Sanan's case it is because of duty.

10 out of 10 would witness a crime and be held hostage by hot samurai again.

I REALLY wish they'd localize the Hakuoki Sweet School Life game where it's this but present day. But I'm still waiting for them to localize the rest of the Amnesia series (World, Later, and Crowd).

review_text:
I should start off with saying that Kyoto Winds is only the first part of this remake of Hakuoki and is essentially only half a game. That being said, there's enough content there to last you a good 40 hours, with a lot of new routes that weren't in the original game.

Hakuoki is an Otome that takes place in the Tokugawa period as certain events lead to the main character staying with the famous Shinsengumi. Nearly all Shinsengumi members as well as most in-game events are based on real-life, which will teach you a lot about Japanese history.

As with most visual novels you start on a common route and choices made will lead you on different paths favouring different characters. Let me say this though: if you're just looking to romance handsome guys, this is the wrong half of the game to play. Kyoto Winds focuses on getting to know each character and building your friendship with them but it doesn't bloom into a romance until the second game called Edo Blossoms. That doesn't mean it's boring though, as each character has their own unique personality, story and background.

The production quality of the game is pretty good, with beautiful graphics, animated lip sync, great voice acting and a very nice OST. My playthroughs were super smooth on the SteamDeck with only a few minor spelling mistakes to note, and it was a great alternative to the Vita never having sales anymore.

Despite only being half a game, this is a solid visual novel and I'm looking forward to the second part. These games are pretty cheap on Steam and on sale a lot, so having to buy two games to get the full story shouldn't be an issue to anyone a fan of Otome games.

-------

The Good:
- Great cast and voice acting
- Dramatic and educational Storyline
- Lots of choices that impact the story, with 13 routes in total

The Bad:
- Only the first half of the game

review_text:
A game that, although good in concept and fun for a while?
Feels bland, empty, and like a demo.

The Early Access period was wonderful, giving a showcase of the bones of a game that needed to be fleshed out and seasoned for it to become more.
Customization felt lacking, the maps were small and limited, and the variety of tricks and ways to explore left plenty to be desired.

It slowly added a new map, a few more customisation options, and then? 

Multiplayer.
A great idea, which made me really keen to see where the game would go.
Although the game hadn't been built on enough for me to recommend it to friends, I did have people in my shared library giving it a go and being keen to see where the team would take it.


Then, full release.
One new map, all customisation locked again, and a progression system that makes you replay the same races, or areas over and over again.
Full release

It feels like this game failed to really develop on the early access release, leaving an extremely barebones final product.
Real shame, as it has no competition and could have easily carved out it's own niche if it had been given more time, and a greater scope. Modding support would be fantastic, but, it isn't really here.

Can't recommend buying it, just not a lot here for the price, coming in at close to $40 in AUS
Will occasionally fire it up on my steam deck as it's perfect for it, but aside from that?
Rooftops and Alleys will be collecting digital dust in my library.

review_text:
I'm not going to preface this with how long I've been a fan. The fact of the matter is SEGA has been sabotaging this game for years. Every launch of this game has been severely botched. Deleted or missing files, unstable servers, limited activities, random ban waves with very little transparency. It's been nonstop.

Now in 2023, when the game should be in a much better place in terms of content and player experience, we seem to be at an all time low. Recycled enemies and quest types, severe gear bottle-necking with no content to justify the effort, no direction for story or future updates. This latest major update that was touted as the evolution of the game ended up being an empty promise.

The new Creative Space feature didn't disappoint, it delivered in ways many players weren't expecting when you consider how poorly they've handled combat and gear progression. However, it seems as though SEGA was expecting this to take the place of all other content. Rather than postpone the update so that it would include combat based content, they pushed through with it and we're left with another empty promise for August. The reality is this new update will not meet the expectations of the player base.

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. Many of the friends that I've made in the few thousand hours I've spent in this virtual space have left because they've gotten tired of waiting for what comes next as every new update just delivers either more of the same or disappointment.

SEGA refuses to learn anything from each update they push. They refuse to course correct. Hundreds of complaints about poorly implemented features will be presented to them with solutions included. If they fix the issue in one update, the following one will include the same mistake. (Impossibly low drop rates. content specific upgrades, quests with drops that don't reflect the effort involved etc.) They run on an outdated business model and are unwilling to adapt with the times.

PSO2 NGS could be the best anime MMO on the market. There's plenty of potential here, but success isn't measured in what ifs. If you want a virtual chatroom with an incredibly robust avatar customization and personal space customization system, you will find plenty to enjoy. If you're looking for an MMO, you might want to look elsewhere.

review_text:
Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is a first part of the story, continuation is held within Edo Blossoms.

Wow, what a wild ride has it been. The story revolves around a girl named Chizuru Yukimura, who's headed to Kyoto in search of her father, but unfortunately (or not) she stumbled upon something she wasn't supposed to witness and it led her to being captured by the Shinsengumi for further questioning, which later allowed her to stay in their headquarters. With time she learns more about the Shinsengumi, their life as samurai and her own life details, which she wasn't previously aware of. I didn't know about the Shinsengumi before this game, so I was pleasantly surprised that this game has historical accuracy, it's always nice to learn about something new through games.

I can hardly consider this part of the game an otome title, as all romance is kept for the second part, Edo Blossoms, but it's a very enjoyable read anyway. You're presented with the ability to build up bonds with one out of 12 available men, so that's still something! 

- The story is awesome, even if it lacks the proper romance in this part.
- Historical setting sprinkled with a bit of fantasy.
- LOTS of different endings since you're presented with 12 men to pick from.
- All characters are very different and it's interesting to see how they open up once they get closer to you.
- Beautiful art.
- Soundtrack is really enjoyable.

Overall, I can say this is a great read, definitely worth a pick together with Edo Blossoms for the full experience.

Much has been said about the art style, which is indeed nice for the most part. Environments are varied and there is a great deal of detail throughout. However the actual modeling, texturing, sound design, and score leaves a lot to be desired, and the atmosphere could have been built to much greater effect with more attention to those detail.
The game play fights against the effort at every turn however, as you are constantly encouraged to sprint through as much of the game as possible: attempting to skip the slog of the combat, trying to conserve the precious health and ammo, and replaying the same parts again and again when you die. God forbid you should try to manually load a checkpoint, which deposits you back at the start of the level, meaning you could lose an hour or more of progress.
The combat adds nothing of value to the game, actively turns the atmosphere from dour to infuriating, and should have been removed altogether.

review_text:
For a $50 game including the Final Transmission dlc which is basically mandatory to complete the story, I have mixed feelings about it. It does some things quite well, but fails miserably in others. Let me break it down, in no particular order.

Story: It's okay - not too bad, but not very good either, especially with the way it ended; (spoiler alert) [spoiler] it effectively killed any chances of a sequel by killing off the main character [/spoiler]. There were a few moments that felt odd, but for the most part it at least felt cohesive and conclusive, and there were a few surprises. It is quite short though, and my biggest grievance is that you need the dlc to finish the main story. There's a lot of wasted potential for a rich world building.

Music/Sound: Actually pretty good, one of the strengths of the game. Though once again, the short length of the game means that there just isn't a lot of it. 

Voice acting and cinematics: Amazing. Easily the strongest part of the game. Character models are extremely high quality, with great voice acting and mo-cap likeness by actual actors, especially Karl Urban. I feel like he carried the game really hard.

Horror: It's okay; there are a couple of really good moments, but for the most part you're just bulldozing your way through hordes of enemies. Player character movement is sluggish on purpose, which is acceptable in these type of games, but I don't think they managed to take full advantage of it. There is some predictability with the horror, mostly because the game tends to shift from gameplay to cutscene so you know something's about to happen. Not a big deal, but I do think if the horror scenes were more dynamic (mid-gameplay) it would've elevated the scare factor of the game. 

Gameplay: The weakest part of the game. I could see where they were going with the heavy focus on the melee combat, but it felt very undercooked. In fact, undercooked is a very accurate term to describe the entire gameplay experience; you're mostly just walking and collecting stuff, with the occasional shooting/hacking at zombies and even rarely so, stealth. Enemy variety is quite low and there aren't a lot of bosses. There's little to no puzzles, and player actions are heavily scripted so you often feel like you're not really doing much. Weapon variety is okay, but upgrades don't feel as substantial as they should because of how shallow the combat mechanics are.

Graphics: Very, very good. The environments are highly detailed and enemies are well designed. There is something left to be desired with the UI and especially tutorials, but I'd be nitpicking at that point.  

Performance: Excellent. Not that the game would run on a potato, but it does run quite well (1080p Medium 50-60 fps) even on 8 year old mid-range hardware like the RX 580 8GB. I mostly played on my RX 6800 machine, and with everything set to the max (RT off) at 1440p I got a very smooth 90-100 fps experience. Beware about enabling RT, it causes a lot of stutters and isn't really that transformative in terms of visuals, so the massive performance drop isn't really justified whether you use Nvidia or AMD.

Finally, there is a severe issue with the game crashing your whole PC. You read that right, the whole PC. I've had it crash on me so many times that I've lost count, and there doesn't seem to be any trigger for it - it just happens whenever, wherever, and quite frequently at that. I thought something was wrong with my machine because I've never encountered a game that crashed my main rig (5800X3D + RX 6800), but after checking on my other two machines (3400G + RX 580 and a 4700U laptop) I got the exact same behavior. Admittedly I only have all-AMD machines at hand, so I cannot verify if this is or isn't an AMD-specific issue, but going through some of the forum posts it does seem the issue exists on Nvidia too. I just don't know, and I gave up trying to troubleshoot. It was a frustrating experience, and I don't think I'll be returning for achievement hunting unless the devs fix it. 

Overall, not really worth the total $50 price tag. I got the Deluxe Edition for just $10 which includes the dlc, so I can somewhat recommend the game on a sale....as long as you can deal with the crashing.
