review_text:
This review is going to make me a hypocrite. But hey, we’re all hypocritical once in a while, right? Oh well, here we go.

This metroidvania is pretty heavy on the “-vania”: there are some really heavy RPG elements that, depending on your level of enjoyment of those mechanics, will make or break this game. Elemental damage and status effects abound here and only the right combination of equipment will make life easier for the player. Depending on the player’s gear, a puddle of oil on the floor can either lead to a quick death to the player or a helpful weapon against any baddies standing in the middle of it. At first, this caused me some really aggravating deaths until I started to get a better grasp of the system. Also, it might be worth noting that the menuing can be a little annoying as the player switches equipment in and out for different obstacles, but all-in-all it’s really fun.

The story is pretty silly, despite some twists here and there. But the characters you meet along the way are pretty great. The psychotic butcher schoolgirl, the zombie fangirls, the katana-wielding goblin slayer: they’re all fantastic. On top of that, the enemies the player faces are memorable as well and each poses a different threat while being vulnerable to different damage types. This game constantly mixes things up and keeps things interesting.

Where this game makes me a hypocrite is that it’s very linear – which is precisely the same reason why I didn’t like [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] and why I didn’t recommend that one. Any real exploration is locked behind sidequests, so if the player isn’t paying attention to those, there is no real reason to roam around the world. On top of that, items needed to complete those quests are marked on the map, eliminating any need to do any real searching. The thing that makes this game more interesting than [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] is that the limited exploration usually leads to a unique piece of equipment or a new spell or something. In [i]Guacamelee 2[/i], exploration lead to either a health pick-up, a stamina pick-up, or (eventually useless) money, and that’s pretty much it. [i]Lost Ruins[/i] does it better, is what I’m trying to say.

In the end, I really had a blast with this game. From the characters, to the maps, to the combat, everything came together to make this one a memorable stand-out. If you’re willing to muscle your way through this often-challenging game, you’re likely to find something you like in here. I know I did!

review_text:
Completely disagree with other opinions regarding this as a masterpiece, or even one of the strongest entries in the Yakuza series.  This is one of the most [i]different[/i] in the Yakuza series, which doesn't necessarily translate to good.  

The problem is, the game is trying to do too much, and be too much at the same time.  This contributes to a lack of focus, poor storytelling, and pacing. 

There are multiple characters to play as this time, and each character has a story, alongside their 'regular activity' simulator.  Kiryu has his story in the first chapter, and along with it, you also drive a taxi.  A lot.  Saejima goes hunting.  But the worst... the worst is Haruka.  There's an entire seemingly interminable chapter dedicated to her.  It's a cliched, trope-filled 'story' as she chases a dream to become an idol because reasons. Instead of fighting, there are dancing minigames in which we have to match button presses as they appear on screen, while she performs passionless robotic movements with dull lifeless eyes gazing out in innocent wonder at the world.   I lost all interest in the game at this point and only continued as I had heard that Yakuza 6 was a direct continuation of this story.

Speaking of which, the stories of each character is supposed to be interwoven, but they decided to go with a cliffhanger at the end of each character's chapter, which results in a rushed, dissonant final chapter.  It doesn't help either that the plot is very convoluted with a lot of references to other people and their machinations, and I am not convinced the writers themselves know what is going on. Several times, they had to rely on expositions and even then it took a long time to get through it.  

The fighting itself, which is the main attraction of these games, is decent in its combos and heat moves.  Each character has their own best moves and combos, but due to the massive gaps in playing between them, I found I was forgetting a lot of what made them strong.  Despite that, I found that the boss fights weren't very action packed or satisfactory, they were just OK and most were quite simple, and over very quickly.

An interesting mechanic that's unlocked this time is the second health bar, filled only by food but not restorable through medicine.  It makes for a nice advantage before you're about to head into a big fight.  

The towns are, as usual, nice to explore; there's a decent amount of detail and places to shop and eat.  But, due to the multiple locations, eventually the exploration became a wearisome task.  


I do hope Yakuza 6 isn't more of this.

equip 20 mods (think this was 50 before, not sure?)

Tier 4 boss raid that rotates aswell.

There is no longer any element restriction in weapons regarding characters, which is good.

These are good changes, and it seems like they have listened to feed back.
1 new character Fuuka.
And 2 new on its way.

I myself am very happy with all these, and i hope it helps someone make a deciscion!

I enjoy the game, for what it is.
I jump in a few hours a day before bedtime and waste some time.

But i get the negative reviews.
This game really needs to add something, if it wants to stay alive.
Becuase yes, at some point doing the same boss raid or co-op quest, will get devestating, especally since the weekly passes demands it, but you only have to do them up to 16, then it doesnt matter.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 is a bizarre entry into the franchise. On one hand there are tons of people who love it and on the other, tons who hate it. Was it the best it could’ve been, no, but it wasn’t the poorest either. It does clearly have big flaws, but I still absolutely enjoyed it. I thought the story was great too, with only a major issue with the ending plot twist and Saejima's part. I heard a good way to describe it is, it has some of the best but also worst parts in the franchise, which sums it up well. I would recommend digging deep into this game with the content you enjoy, and if you really want to, skip the content you don't. Almost every protagonist’s parts I loved, Saejima’s part being the only painful one. And it definitely did have those heartening and awesome moments the series is known for. The exploration was pretty cool, having five cities to explore. There were a few downsides to that though. For example, some of the new layouts were not the best for gameplay (Tsukimino) and their lighting and environment was just very poorly done. The gameplay was done well, maybe one of the most fun in terms of combat. And the side stories were a cool way to introduce an optional side plot to the game. Playing through all besides Saejima’a was amazing. Admittedly I did first dislike the batting minigame but soon grew into it.

[spoiler] At the beginning, that opening scene was a nice way to start. Showing how Kiryu and Haruka’s lives have changed. You can occasionally see how bad not being with his children is affecting him and a few substories add to that. The whole story between Haruka and Kiryu is always still so sentimental to me. I adore getting to see Haruka growing up and their love growing stronger with each game, it always makes me so sappy. Daigo still looks to Kiryu for assistance with leading the Tojo clan, even as Kiryu tries his hardest to leave his Yakuza past behind. I really enjoyed Tadashi and Mayumi, they were great characters. I honestly felt bad for Mayumi, wanting Kiryu as a partner. The whole ending battle was amazing, getting to fight hordes of Tojo members. The entire cutscene of Kiryu going against the Tojo was so badass. And his taxi side story and mini game was honestly really fun, especially the racing. The entire racing storyline was great, Nakajima’s whole past with his wife was so damn heartbreaking.

Saejima’s part was iffy at best, but man, was it really bad at worst. Unlike Y4, I found barely any enjoyment out of his section. The prison here was very slow and not enjoyable at all. Running back and forth, the boring “imagination” section, they were a real slog. The fact that he’s in prison again in the first place is just super exhausting. The snowmobile escape and the bear fight were the only things I enjoyed. Then into the city nothing was enjoyable or fun either. Saejima’s hunting side story was also very slow and boring. Saejima’s whole plot with kidnapping Kitakata was just not engaging. From someone who loves to be immersed and engaged with the stories in games, this has to be one of the most absurd for me. Which is actually really sad too, it no doubt could've been better than it was if they did it differently. He’s a good character, and it really showed in Y4 and in this finale, but his part was atrociously done and didn’t give him anything to go on.

Haruka & Akiyama’s part was also amazing. Having heard this part was very slow mainly from the mini games, but I actually loved doing them. That obviously doesn't mean everybody will, and I completely understand. Before playing, I originally thought it was going to drag on, but really around 90% of the mini games are optional anyway. Haruka’s story was a touching departure from the usual plot, though I know some may find it unappealing since it has nothing to do with the Yakuza plot and focuses on Haruka’s personal life until around the second half, but I always adore these heartening stories. It was adorable, and I feel showing Haruka’s POV was actually really nice to see, and I honestly loved her story more than I’d like to admit. Park being quite cold on the surface, was nice to see her eventually develop a sweet bond with Haruka. Then Park’s death caught me so off guard, especially after all that happened between them, and how brutal she died (no mercy for Ogita). It was great playing Akiyama again, an amazing character to see once more. Only to be reinforced when he meets with Haruka to solve Park’s murder together, that dialogue man. Akiyama is such an amazing wholesome guy, I’m really glad Akiyama and Haruka share a part. I know some would disagree, preferring that Akiyama had his own part, and don’t get me wrong, I’d love that too. But if it had to be anyone besides Kiryu, Akiyama was definitely a fantastic choice. I really wish he got a more balanced screen time though. Akiyama’s ending battle was short but amazing. I didn’t expect to find out that Majima was Park’s ex-husband. I do just wish Majima got more closure for Park in the finale, I felt that’s what was missing by the time I finished.

Shinada was also a fantastic additional character. Once a great baseball player, then permanently banned. 15 years later, starting with only 217 Yen to his name. I loved his part, nice development, nice pacing. His meteor tackle was pretty fun too. Moving through his story is quite calm at first, but soon picks up once Daigo comes to offer him the job of finding out what happened 15 years ago. Over the next few chapters you find yourself trying to put the pieces together one by one to figure out what’s going on. Soon chatting with Daigo which ends in a brawl. Daigo’s boss fight was really fun, maybe the most fun I’ve had fighting Daigo before. Battling along Sawada was unexpected but amazing. Overall, not much to say for Shinada’s part. That’s not a bad thing, it’s just a very straight forward part. A fantastic character with a fantastic well developed story, definitely an awesome addition.

Now the finale. The fighting itself was wildly fun throughout the entire section. [i]Only children believe in dragons.[/i] Oh, and Shinada jumpscare. I loved everyone’s opening sequences, the calm before the storm. We soon returned to Kiryu and Saejima to fight our way up Kamurocho Hills. Kiryu’s dialogue when Kurosawa walks away, ouch man. Then end up back as Haruka, loving her lead up to the Japan Dome. Then the four badasses fight hordes of enemies. Saejima meets with Majima and they fight. Shinada’s crying scene killed me. After a while, one would think that Kurosawa is the entire big bad of the game, rightly so, clearly built up to him from the start of the game. WRONG. It's Aizawa, surprise. The finale was built up to be so good too. The boys come together, Haruka is singing her heart out, and everything is set up perfectly. Then Aizawa, no build up, literally only seeing him a few times in the entire story. His entire character is just him wanting to surpass Kiryu, not even caring that his father wanted to give him everything. Funny enough, Ryuji in Y2 had a similar goal. The major difference, Ryuji actually had a fantastic build up and well developed character arc. However, the actual boss fight at Tojo HQ, although tough, was awesome to do. Moving on to the rest of the ending. I did not expect it to hit me that hard, but it did. Haruka giving her speech was such a fantastic scene. I still ended up loving the finale, ignoring Aizawa. [/spoiler]

By no means was it the best, but it had its charm. No matter the flaws, I loved this game for what it was. Kiryu’s, Haruka & Akiyama’s, and Shinada’s stories were really amazing to go through. This game is one of those that clearly wasn’t done perfectly, but it doesn’t have to be. In the end, I honestly still did fall in love with this game. It still offered an amazing and emotional experience to me and that’s always worth recognition.

review_text:
Title: A Glitchy Grindfest That Deserves Better

Review:
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is four games bundled together—Rebirth, Reminisce, Redemption, and Reconnection. On paper, that makes the $50 price tag seem fair. But honestly, this remaster feels more like a relic that aged poorly than a celebration of the series.

First off, the technical issues are brutal:

No cloud saves (thanks, Bandai, for removing them for some ungodly reason).

Frequent crashes, often during scene transitions or critical story areas.

Huge risk of losing hours of progress, or even your entire save.

Buggy freezes that feel more like bad coding than the “rogue A.I.” storyline.

Gameplay-wise, it’s monotony wrapped in nostalgia. The combat is basically a stripped-down Tales system—okay at first, but quickly stale. Nearly everything funnels you into endless copy-paste dungeons. Need info? Dungeon. Want a boss fight? Dungeon. Trying to progress story dialogue? Yep, dungeon first. Grinding isn’t optional—it’s the backbone of the design.

Story & Characters:
The premise is cool—stopping player killers in an MMO-gone-wrong has superhero vibes. But the pacing kills it. Vol. 1 in particular drags with back-to-back tutorials and a tournament arc where every single match is robbed from you by cutscenes. Characters aren’t bad, but generic; they feel like archetypes you’ve seen in 5+ other JRPGs. The “coma from playing a game” storyline works if you squint and accept “because magic.” Otherwise, it’s pretty juvenile.

There are some good moments—the avatar fights are exciting, Atoli’s crush on Haseo has its cute beats, and the overarching narrative has potential. But the grind, pacing issues, and technical problems bury it.

Personal Take:
I stepped away multiple times out of sheer boredom—ended up playing 7 Days to Die, Pokémon ROM hacks, Hot Wheels & Lego rides with my kid, and Diablo IV with strangers instead. That says it all. As of 8/19/25, I officially retired this game and deleted it from my backlog.

Verdict:

As a movie? Solid 6/10—watch the cutscenes on YouTube or revisit the anime.

As a game? 4/10 at best. Tedious, buggy, and outdated.

If you want to experience .hack//G.U., you’re honestly better off emulating the original PS2 versions on PCSX2 than wasting time on this watered-down remaster. This deserves a true remake, not this lazy port.

Would I recommend it?
❌ No. Not even on sale. I wasted $20, don’t repeat my mistake.

review_text:
[h1] The best Hockey Manager on the market [/h1]

A very fun and addicting manager game that makes you the Headcoach and/or General Manager of your favorite Ice Hockey team. There's multiple leagues to choose from, from different countries. If you fancy playing in Great Britain, go for it! Or maybe you want to guide a NHL team to future Stanley Cups. It's for you to decide. Not a tactical genius? Let your headcoach handle that, so you can focus on being a GM. Trading players, renewing contracts, scouting and drafting prospects. 

A slight concern is the UI, it looks very outdated, similar to Championship Manager 01/02. Changing line players is clunky and irritating. The rosters are not up to date when you start, and there is no EHM Editor like one you would find for Football Manager. However it has a strong community that can provide you with everything you need. 

Perfecting a match engine is difficult. I do however feel like they've done all they can on the match engine, it's very solid. Of course it is not perfect, but it still works well. A slight dissapointment is not being able to see key highlights that doesn't always feature goals, it makes the highlight predictable and boring. Of course you could change it to the one that shows extended highlights, but in my opinon the match goes a bit too slow for my liking. 

Overall Eastside Hockey Manager is the best Hockey Manager game out there, despite competition from Franchise Hockey Manager (That shows a more modern looking UI), EHM wins this battle thanks to the community. 

8/10

review_text:
I have seen many people recomend this game due to its emotional story, it is sort of sad sure but man it is not a good game in any way. Even as a means of storytelling it falls flat in almost every way. Gameplay wise it is not fun in any way, with poor controls on the mouse and the keyboard side the game just feels bad to play. I ran into 2 gamebreaking bugs along the way that prevented me from continuing, being fixed by a restart which lost some progress. The game also trys to pad itself to make it seem longer than a short 3act, 3 hour story.

[h1]Art[/h1]
The game has very sub indie pixel art. And a handful of digitially painted seens which looked rushed and pulled me out of the game world when they did appear. It seems that pixel artists just added a noise filter to everthing they could. It almost hurts to look at some objects. There are also several charecters in the game where they seemed to have applied a noise filter and not toned down the saturation of the noise, resulting in a few charecters being covered in rainbow speckles.
========================
The one redeeming aspect of the games art is the soundtrack which was one of the only things keeping me playing. It is the only thing that pulled emotion out of the dialog, which is very bad as well. But this was ruined several times by having a very hard transition to a different track often for the sake of comedic releif.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It is a game so how does it play? Very poorly. For an rpgmaker game the keyboard controls feel slugish and the mouse controls are infuriating. For the amount of needless walking around the game makes you do the mouse controls feel like they are working against you. You left click to walk, very simple how could it be bad. When walking long distanced you need to click on an icon that takes you to a different scene. The problem lies with the screen always moving the camera is locked to the grid that the charecters walk making the camera jerk as the charecters change direction. There is no smoothness to it making it difficult to click on things while moving. This tied with the charecters slow walking speed and long padded distances makes it feel like you are just waiting and waiting to just get on with the task at hand. The keyboard controls for walking don't feel as bad but the distanced are so long and the speed so slow it is just easier to wait on the mouse.
========================
The puzzles which are placed through the entirety of the first Act are the only type of "gameplay" this game has. You walk around placing the mouse on random objects that act as puzzle pieces, after you collect the necessary amounts you play a really easy puzzle which can be won by randomly clicking around ten times. You do this around twenty times. It is just a time killer a very boring one at that.
========================
Object placement in this game is horrid as well there was one instance where I though my game was soft locked, you normally click on charecters to talk to them or listen to them. This speech icon was just placed on the ground in the middle of to spaced out charecters. Several times throughout the game I had trouble finding the puzzle piece because they didn't even have an icon. The game also pads itself with really long camera pans and slow movement speed on long backtracking paths. With many reused areas that made me hate walking along them again and again. 

[h1]Story and Dialog[/h1]
The game is well know for its sad story. I did not feel a strong enough connection to the charecters throughout the short 3 hours expierence. My connection to them was just barely strong enough for me to drudge through the awful two main charecters dialog to even finish the game. The reason I feel I had no connection the the charecters is due to half the game being a very bad puzzle game. I was hoping Acts 2 and 3 would payoff for waiting through Act 1 but it did not.
========================
I'm going to talk about the dialog now and oh is it bad. Even the non cheesy "comedic" dialog feels like a middle schooler's essay for english class. It is ok but not amazing. But the dialog between the main playable charecters is awful. The game was made in 2009 and it dates itself hard. The writers seemed to have a hard on for name dropping things. They talk about Doctor Who, Animorphs, Google, and many many others. It is just awful and makes the game feel straight out of Tumblr. The game told me to just google something about the Animorphs books after I answered incorrectly. It is so hard to take the sad story seriously when they through garbage references at you.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
The games cult-like following does not hold up, even when overlooking the dated nature of the game. It is not fun and its story simply is not good enough to make up for how awful it is to play. Its so short and filled with padding with its story loosley tossed throughout at 2009 meme and joke ridden trainwreck. This game is not fun, and its story not very good. It wanted to be sad but the only things I was sad about was wasting a few dollars on this. If you do want to expierence its still after reading this whole review just watch a long play on youtube, it wasn't worth my time.

[h1]Final Score:[/h1]
[h1]5/10 Didn't even make me cry[/h1]

Witchfire delivers exactly what I want from a dark fantasy roguelite shooter: combat that’s both great and punishing, with a difficulty curve that feels fair as you push further in.

The art direction is incredible... gloomy, gothic, and full of atmosphere. It’s just a shame it runs on Unreal, but the visuals and mood still carry hard. Guns feel “meaty” and satisfying, progression is fun, and each run pulls me back in.

That said, there are a few rough edges. Some mechanics could use clearer explanations, repetition starts to creep in, and I’m ready for more environments to explore. Still, the core gameplay loop is addictive, and the devs have shown great communication and a clear willingness to expand the game in the right ways.

Overall, Witchfire is a strong early access title and one I can’t wait to see fully fleshed out. Easily an 8.5–9/10 in its current state.

Summary: 5/10, not as bad as the sequel, but very, VERY lacking across the board. I'm glad that I only paid $8 for both this and its sequel, as after beating both of them, I can say with confidence that $10 or less is all that they're worth.

Wow. So, let's try and unpack a bit of this.

The story is not as bad as the second game, but it's definitely more forgettable and vapid. In the end, [spoiler]you get recruited by some vague, nameless group that's on par with the pop culture version of the Illuminati, who have global interests and control in mind.[/spoiler] The characters all hint at something, but in the end, it amounts to nothing, and you are told nothing. The final two "regions" (missions) drag on and are logically disconnected, requiring you to find a battered cardboard box in the middle of the map as "evidence", or wanting you to pick up a stack of papers and books among other debris for "evidence". This is fairly ironic, given how the last two levels in the game tell you to run through them, as both have time-based completion challenges.

The weapons and gadgets are okay-ish, as you never really need to change your weapon past the first or second upgrade, but this also makes the combat and selection feel pointless and shallow. The perks are yet again logically unsound and just gameified stat/abi bonuses rather than semi-logical upgrades. Hey, at least 1/3 of this game's weapons are not paid DLC/P2W, unlike its sequel.

And that kinda leads me to the conundrum: this game attempts to set up a realistic/surrealistic set and setting, but it fails miserably as there's no real justification for anything. Perks that make no sense, innate abilities that make no sense, required weapon purchases because your damage magically dissipates in later levels, characters that give you nothing or speak the obvious when interrogated. It's a shockingly valid example of making a game based on arbitrary mechanics and definitions rather than its own established universe and drive.

Finally, for the Sniper Elite comparisons. Yes, I still stand by what I said for my review of the second game, where if the general concept of these games were done well, it could beat any given Sniper Elite title at its own game. However, this is not done well, let alone to perfection, and the two are quite different anyways. The only similarities are that they're both allegedly based on sniping, and this game shamelessly implements a bullet camera effect that's just as fairly repetitive as Sniper Elite's. Beyond that, eh, more Ghost Warrior.

I am very glad that I spent less than $10 on the pack, as I could not reasonably justify spending any more on it. Given what it is that I did per-mission, I would say that it was worth $1/hour.

review_text:
This game is charming at first. It can be fun and will be fun for the beginning. In all honesty, you will probably have a blast at first. The space combat feels good and is probably one of the best points in the game. The ground combat is a little janky, but it does the job mostly well and I have never had any issues with it. So why do I not recommend this? Well, the game does what a lot of MMO's do and makes the mid-late game near impossible unless you pay money. Now it does take a while to get there, but you will know once you do. It becomes impossible to get new ships (the currency required to get ships beyond a certain point is pay only) it becomes impossible to get new and better weapons (again pay only), and the difficulty of the missions do not decrease to compensate. You can get pretty far, but you will reach the point where you really can't progress any further and you'll know it. 

On top of that, while this is a good MMO game (at least for the early-mid parts) it is NOT a good STAR TREK game. this game involves a lot of combat, gunning, fighting, etc. with most "science" or "engineering" solutions involving hitting the action button in a specific spot. Only on rare occasions does talking actually get you anywhere, you pretty much never have fun random encounters (everything occurs on missions), and, while you can technically explore your ship, it is really empty and not actually there (funnily enough this is where the console version is better because on PC ship interiors are locked behind a pay wall and only the main command spot is open, but on console all the ship interiors are free and you can explore the whole ship without issues as well). There are only a few missions that take place inside your ship, and they don't care what interior you are set to have.

Overall, give the game a try, it is free, but once you hit that pay-wall point, just stop. The game does not improve and it only has a few "that is clever" game design moments. You are probably better off trying out bridge crew or playing EVE/Elite and Dangerous.

review_text:
(Listed playtime does not reflect my actual time in game- I was without internet when I played this)

So To the Moon is one of those games that seemed to have a pretty unanimously positive customer perspective.  The reviews of this game cumulate at a very high rating, noting that it's "simple...full of heart", "absolutely beautiful", and as put by Eurogamer: "How do I explain why it's brilliant without spoiling what makes it so?"  The conclusion that can be drawn from these reviews is that To the Moon is a touching story game with little actual gameplay (since the actual gameplay isn't mentioned anywhere).  OH BOY.  Regardless, I had played some games like that before and I had actually enjoyed them, so I grabbed this at a low price and decided to complete it.  My conclusion after beating it:

To the Moon is an absolutely awful game that I believe would have been much more interesting had it been made in to a graphic novel or animated film.  The few game elements that exist are very poorly executed.  Movement itself can be frustrating and glitchy when using a mouse (I frequently found my character not responding as I expected when clicking where I wanted him to go, and at one point I had managed to walk in to the clouds and I could not get down), the search quests are horrid, and all of the other 'minigames' are trivial and completely out of place.  So, if the bare-bones gameplay elements are minimal and poorly-executed, why bother making this a game at all?  You spend most of your time clicking through conversations anyway; does that make things any more interesting?  I don't think it does at all, and by the end of the 4th hour I was completely overwhelmed at how tiring To the Moon was.  I can't believe that a GAME reviewed by GAME CRITICS recieved such high ratings for nothing other than its PLOT when the GAMEPLAY was this horrid.

Now I don't think anyone beat To the Moon and said to his or herself: "To the Moon was one of the most invigorating gameplay experience of the past year" or anything close to that, so the game was made great by the story (as shown by other reviewers).  Now I must admit that through most of the game I was very touched by the events that transpired; I will reluctantly admit that I teared up at a few moments.  The journey to the end, in terms of plot, was very respectable and  despite the childish "charm" of all the characters and the "click through the words" cutscenes I managed to actually enjoy that particular element.  I would never have given the game a 10/10, but perhaps a 6/7/8.  That was until I beat the damn thing

(SPOILERS BELOW)

To the Moon's story fails in how it wraps up the tale that it tells. You essentially spend the entire game re-living various aspects of a man's life in order to determine why he wants to go to the moon, seeing all of the experiences he'd had over the years that shaped who he was, suffered through major hardships of his life only to erase those from his memory at the end of the game so you can complete your job.  I practically threw my hands up in the air in disbelief when I realized that's how the game was going to end.  The ONLY REDEEMING ASPECT that To the Moon had going for it was smuthered out in the last minutes of this awful title and I would not recommend it to you unless you are the kind of person that likes to marvel at laughably bad titles.  

Bring on the hate, Steam.

review_text:
Very much a step up from the previous two titles in the series. I personally found the game a big too big for its own good, but if you don't mind a bit extra traveling about there is plenty of content to explore and sample. Also, returning is multiple protagonists. Since this is Yakuza 5, there are five.

The core beat 'em up in Yakuza 5 is by far the easiest of the series, It didn't bother me. Since I could up the difficulty. Although, the hardest parts typically were switching a new protagonist's story. Where they are both weak, poor and the player is unfamiliar with their move set. 

Speaking of move sets, Kiryu is pretty much the same with only a slight shuffle. Always a blast to beat down baka that step up to the Dragon of Dojima. Saejima also returns and seems to hit harder but has pityful range and speed. Akiyama is here as well with even flashier juggle based attacks. Finally, new comer Shinada is a combination of weapon and bull rush attacks. He powerful if incredibly spammy.

The fifth protagonist is Haruka as an idol. She doesn't brawl but competes in dance battles. Baically every thing Haruka does is a rhythm game... and none come close to Taiko no Tatsujin, drum arcade game based on the real one from Namco. Hands down the best of the like half dozen rhythm games in Yakuza 5. The only thing I liked about playing Haruka, was bowling people over in the street as a 16 year old idol as well if not better than 200 lb Saejima. I loathed anything involving her and dreaded and scene at the end of the game with her threatening me to have to sit through yet another rhythm game. There were plenty of rhythm based mini-games here.

Speaking of minigames, each protagonist recieved their own. Kiryu drives/races a taxi and makes noodles. The driving ones are tedious with a bit of RNG and the racing is not anywhere close Daytona USA. The noodles is okay, but not my thing. Saejima has hunting up north and can snowball fight. Hunting takes too long to let the player just enjoy it, but when it finally does; it is fun. The controls for the snowball fight are terrible. Shinada has baseball batting and chicken racing. Once I earn the slow-mo and figured out how to hit the ball, it was a lot of fun. Though, too easy with slow-mo and a bit too hard without practice without it for me. Still, best batting cage set in a Yakuza game including the regular batting cage here in Yakuza 5. Shinada also has chicken racing, but in unlocked far too late for me to be interesting is side content.

Which is a huge them with Yakuza 5. There's a ton of side content. But it is both a mixed bat like always, tied to particular characters and made available at differing times in the game. By Chapter 3-4 of each protagonists' story line, I just wanted to move one. And the finale, I just wanted to finish the game. Yakuza 5 felt like 4.5 games glued together. And not all of them I wanted to play. 

Kiryu will always get a pass from me. I enjoy his fighting style, so getting waylaid by bad guys or bit of extra story is fine. Saejima gets robbed with the most uneven story again, with a prison section that takes too long, a hunting section I wanted to ride past to get the story and bit in Sapporo that doesn't add anything. Haruka could have been cut from the game, and I wouldn't feel bad. Akiyama also gets rob in terms of content, but as likeable as he is, I also would have been fine without him. I could see Shinada's brawling being an acquired taste, but he allowed me to finally enjoy RGG batting cages.

I think Yakuza 5 would have been more fun for me if I had more time or didn't have more RGG games, or games in general, to get to. There is a lot to do and explore, but I'd rate only about half of it was stuff I enjoyed. And as a latter day fan, I know the series has better versions of several of the minigames. It doesn't help that so much is spread out over several cities and connected to particular charters. I'd much rather only have one or two hub locations to pick and choose when I want to play some of the side content. And make that side content available as soon as possible. Or at least before the plot ramps up.

Yakuza 5, like Yakuza 4, tries to do too much. Its ambition gets in the way for making a more enjoyable experience. However, unlike Y4,  enjoyed the game sans anything to do with Haruka. I think it was more that I want to get to Yakuza 6 and beyond that pushed me from taking more time with this game. Which was still 70+ hours.  So, I do recommend it. It feels like I am past lows of the series of 3, 4 and 5. I am eagar to start Yakuza 6.

review_text:
[b]Starship Troopers: Extermination[/b] - great potential buried under technical issues. When Starship Troopers: Extermination finally left Early Access, I expected the real “bugs” to be the ones we fight, not the ones in the optimization. Sadly, the game still struggles with performance, connectivity, and questionable system design choices that hold it back from being truly great.
[h3]What’s Good:[/h3]
[list]
[*]Fun co-op gameplay and large-scale battles.
[*]Cross-play sounds good on paper.
[*]Solid atmosphere that captures the Starship Troopers vibe.
[/list]
[h3]What’s Not So Good:[/h3]
[list]
[*]Optimization issues remain largely unchanged even after full release.
[*]Performance drops and stutters in active fights.
[*]Cross-play matchmaking is slow and unreliable.
[*]Random disconnects during loading - including being kicked with “squad is full” errors.
[*]Company (clan) system is overly restrictive: only 30 members, limited permissions.
[*]Regular members can’t start missions, making event participation nearly impossible for solo players.
[*]Players in less active time zones struggle even more due to fixed mission schedules.
[*]Time-limited events feel like a second job when you depend on someone else’s timing.
[*]Paid DLC offering only a few skins/icons.
[/list]
[b]Overall:[/b]
Starship Troopers: Extermination has the foundation of a great co-op shooter, but its technical issues and restrictive systems drag the game down at every step. After leaving Early Access, these problems are no longer excusable - especially when paired with questionable monetization decisions.
[b]My advice:[/b]
If you and your friends enjoy co-op shooters and can tolerate performance issues, you’ll still have fun.
But if you expect a polished experience after 1.0 - be prepared for disappointment.

review_text:
(Played on Quest 2 via AirLink)

[b]This isn't a negative nor a positive review, for Devs visibility. Will update with game's updates[/b] 

TLDR; Very strong foundation but need way more time in the oven.

4 Player shooter with Big hordes of Zs (slow, fast, tough, wide and bosses), ok gunplay, boring runs in recruits and veteran, but challenging runs at Master and Nightmare difficulties, but not really doable until the RNG gods favor you good mods for your weapon.

So many issues I have with the game currently:

• With 2 handed weapon, playing in manual reload and manual hold, when reloading too fast, somehow my off hand grip fail to grab the assault rifle barrel. Which make it very annoying during a fire fight, to be surprised by a huge recoil after a reload, because the off hand, even tho is properly aligned to the barrel and the grip button is hold, isn't gripping the barrel. This is caused by the cocking handle interaction being way too big. 

• There is only 5 maps, and one is quite short (Chinatown)

• To get your loot (weapon mods) you need to finish the map other wise you only get a bit of money. (Which might make Chinatown interesting to farm?)

• You can have duplicate loot at the end of run, which is then converted into money... That can make the 15 / 20 minutes of a run go down the drain. I must have something like 60-75% duplicate in all my runs. 

• Difficulty is strange, there is Recruit, Veteran, Master and Nightmare. I started my runs (with matchmaking) in Veteran with the starter pistol and the runs were a walk in the park. Trying in master, the Zs are faster, encounters have more waves, majority of Zs have ice armor and hit harder. No surprise that a match making team with low qualitys gear can't pass the first encounter. But I can already imagine the thrill of a master / nightmare run with well equiped and coordinate team.

• So to do well in Master or Nightmare difficulty you need a good gear, you can upgrade weapons with mods acquired during runs. Example, you can find a barrel that give 25% more damage which is nice, but then also decrease the firerate dramatically. So you will need (Pray the RNG gods) to find a matching grip that can give you a huge firerate bonus to compensate, otherwise if you equip only the 25% damage bonus barrel, you might end with a DPS lower than the with the stock barrel on.

• There is still game breaking bugs, I was doing a Master run with a good team, it was tense and we had a nice progression. Then one team mate got stuck mid air on zipline, with now way to get unstuck. He ended up disconnecting, leaving behind 1 bot to fill his position (it seems you can't re/connect mid run). No need to say the run didn't fare as good after that.

• Menu options have no descriptiong or tooltips. So I have no idea what some option do.

• The game isn't super smooth on a RTX 3090. Disabling shadows makes it butter smooth.

• You have a wrist missile launcher with 1 charge, work like a super/ultra, it is triggered by holding grip and targeting Zs. Problem, It happens that if you try to distant grab an object while some Zs are in the vicinity it might target them and shoot, wasting your only charge.

• You can fall thru the map when jumping down on some map, with the only option to kill the game.

I'll definitely play a bit more and hope Vertigo bounce on this, because then it might be a must have VR game if they can polish the experience.

A big, yet empty, map with a bunch of markers that, at the end of the day, creates tedium rather than engaging content. The shooting is the typical hitscan garbage we have gotten used to (which is rather problematic when the enviorments are this large and empty...) and the stealth is just as undercooked as usual (meaning that there is just a quarter circle that fills up and a giant neon sign is magically attached to the player once you get detected). There is nothing old school about the actual gameplay no matter how cute the introductory parody on modern tutorials may be. At least you are not tortured by the presence of Jason Brody this time around.

review_text:
Great game. Fantastic gunplay. I thought I wouldn’t be able to play it because of the insanely high difficulty. And yeah, at first, it really was tough. But then I started getting into it. And after that, I just couldn’t tear myself away. I love literally everything: the environment design, the enemies, the weapons, the music, and that thick, grim atmosphere. This is the Painkiller 2 we wanted.

At the start, I thought I was really missing those sweaty brawls with dozens of enemies on screen, but that didn’t last long — once I got into the more serious locations, I ended up in fights where for a couple of minutes you literally forget to breathe, locked in a bloody dance of destruction, tearing through everything alive.

If you understand how the game works, you’ll have a blast. But if you try to play it like a regular shooter, without using literally everything the game gives you, you’re in for a rough time. I often caught myself thinking that most shooters I’ve played let you ignore most of their mechanics — just shoot and you’re fine. But here, using your entire arsenal is absolutely essential. Without it, you’re in for a quick and stupid death.

And once you find your favorite weapon, upgrade it, and put together a build that feels just right for you — that’s when the real flow starts, especially on the highest levels of Gnosis.

Highly recommended for anyone looking for a deep and dynamic shooter.

review_text:
The team behind Witchfire understands game design better that most. I usually avoid two things: Early Access titles and Roguelikes (although this is technically a Roguelite). The approach to difficulty and difficulty scaling is immaculate. The game is challenging but continues to give you new tools and ways to interact with that challenge. Build-crafting absolutely works and the game offers a Cornucopia of toys to choose from. 
The game has several different "leveling" systems that all interact with each other in a well balanced way. I have never once felt like the game was wasting my time, which is one of the main detractors for Roguelikes for me.
Conquering a Witch's Familiar is as rewarding as any Souls-boss out there. Each of the levels on offer are unique and thrilling to explore. Secrets never felt obtuse and each expedition gives the player plenty of choices to sink their teeth into. 
Throughout my play I have continuously been surprised. If being "okay" is a death knell in the current gaming market place, Witchfire goes well WELL above that.

review_text:
It pains me to mark this as not recommended, but I am just not feeling it.

The game is visually stunning and I can't name many other games that surpass it in terms of art style. Sadly that's where most of the praises end. Sure it has a fittingly oppressive atmosphere and it provides a niche horror experience, but they really aren't well experienced with gameplay design.

Where the game excels artistically, it falls short with giving the player a fun time alongside it. The combat is geniunely some of the worst I've seen. It's incredibly clunky, sluggish and not rewarding in the slightest. Enemies are more of a chore and annoyance, meant to frustrate the player, than they are a fun and integral part of the game. Honestly, you could've taken them out completely and probably be left with a better, more engaging experience overall. It also doesn't help that you can't tell the recharge on your basic weapon due to the color choice and that same recharge is incredibly slow as is everything else in this game. Not to mention the abhorrent range on that thing. I missed more stuff at near point blank and ended up getting hit back as a result because it's so absurdly short. It also doesn't help that there's little clutter everywhere on the ground that you can easily get stuck on resulting in getting hit more. It only leads to a more frustrating experience. 
And that's not where the shortcomings of the combat end. Switching weapons is also very slow and you can't dodge anything while doing it, so good luck switching to another weapon after running out of ammo mid fight. Also the reloads are slow as hell as is everything else and it's even worse since you can't reload cancel. Once you start reloading, you better believe you're putting every bullet you have into the mag even though you only needed one to finish off the enemy. It also doesn't help that enemies are inconsistent with their health. Sometimes they take 2 shots, sometimes 4. I know it's probably due to the crit spots, but I swear, sometimes I shoot them in the exact same places and they either survive or they just die. This only leads to more unpredictability which can be a detriment to the player and cause more health loss. It really doesn't help that the game is pretty stingy with giving the player healing and that the checkpoints are spaced apart quite a bit.

Apart from that it's also easy to get lost in some of these places. They tend to be quite large, although linear, but most of the areas look the same. Since the game requires quite a bit of backtracking at certain points, you'll be finding yourself blindly searching for where you're supposed to be going. The game doesn't tell the player anything at all. It won't hold your hand and that is completely fine. Sometimes it will leave a better impression if it allows player agency even if it is a linear game, however, it would help if some of the areas weren't so similar looking and maze-like.

The game is also kind of buggy. Sometimes the bullets phase through the enemies, leaving them unaffected. I'm pretty sure the enemies don't have some kind of i-frames, but I could be wrong. Either way it's really annoying missing a shot that clearly hit and then losing precious health because of it. Apart from that, I got stuck in place twice after certain cutscenes for seemingly no reason, resulting in me needing to restart to the latest checkpoint and one time the game didn't allow me to interact with anything even though it was giving me the prompts, leading to another soft lock and reset. It really took away from the overall experience, especially since these bugs were really only a waste of time.

(minor spoilers for the ending) The game is very ambiguous with its story. It doesn't tell you much and only poses more questions than it answers, but it definitely ends with a very negative ending that could be unsatisfying for some, especially because of what you have to go through only to end the game with it. I could bet everyone (myself included) were expecting something very grandiose, but were left disappointed with such a cruel outcome.

Overall, the game has tons of potential, but is too clunky and unsatisfying to play as is. I really do care about it, hence why I'm writing this much. I hope that the developers improve upon the annoyances of this game in their possible future titles and combine such an astounding visual style with good gameplay to form an extremely palatable horror experience.

Being a fan of PSU as a child, I was hyped to play the Base game [PSO2] years ago. I spent ages on this game when It hit global, finally glad they actually did it, and rubbed it in those who had no hope for a western release. Fast forward to a few years, I was surprised to hear that New Genesis was coming.

Never thought PSO2 would get a PSO'3' in a sense, so when I played the demo, I was really hyped.
When the full game released I was... questionable to say the least. the lack of content really threw people off.

I was also happy that the original game retained the data. But I will say this hot take: New Genesis has superior combat, while PSO2 has the better story. Not bashing the story of NGS, it HAS grown on me, but it took a while. NGS gives you so much better movement and the combo game is satisfying and the open world brims with enemies and wandering bosses. There are points of interest with lore and crates. Multi Weapons also spices up the combo game even more, even allowing you to use weapons as classes that can't use them, (you just can't use Photon Arts) The sad part about NGS is that you don't have as many photon arts in PSO2, removing the customization of skills. But the skills we have in NGS is pretty good. 

I do suggest if you're just getting this game. Play PSO2 FIRST, not New Genesis. The basic mechanics doesn't change between the two.

review_text:
So. Bomb Rush Cyberfunk. As someone who absolutely adored the original Jet Set Radio growing up, I was super pumped that this came out. And, I gotta say, it is absolutely a spiritual successor to that game.

For good and ill.

Going back to JSR after years away from it, it has jank. Hella jank. 1 analog stick on the dream cast controller, so only a trigger for camera recentering. Janky movement and acceleration, mildly irritating hitboxes and physics. In the modern age, it is not a good game. But it had something that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk doesn't, and that's failure states.

In JSR, each mission is a timed score attack mode. You have only a certain amount of time to get points, and combos and graffiti tagging are how you do it. More lines, better combos, more complex graffiti, more points. You're racing against the clock, and you can fail, drop your combo, or fuck up a graffiti spray and lose the points for that spot.It also had the problem that it was EXTREMELY linear. If you don't get the Jet rank in a mission, you have to wait till you hit that mission again in new game plus.

BRC got rid of that, at least... mostly by not having any real missions at all. The time attack portions, if you could even call them that, are few and far between, and you'll spend most of your time exploring the open world and mindlessly tagging spots. Even the spray painting, which is probably one of the more important parts, was dumbed down to "just mash at the wall". You get more multipliers if you graffiti new murals during a combo, but you're not actually doing anything skilful, and even if you don't do a new mural, you're not locked out, you can just try again at the next. You can't even fall while doing tricks. Sure, you'll lose your combo, but you can't die unless you fall into water, or get hurt by the cops.

Right, the cops. Eventually the cops will come out in greater force, and (so far what I've found) the only way to deescalate them/escape them is to wipe the stars entirely. Because the way that JSR did it, you have stakes as you try to eek out the last points before the cops kill you on a timer, escaping them. In BSR, you just reset them, because they got rid of the timed element. And then they immediately come back in, each successive mural giving you another star (with the small cutscene taking you out of the action to let you know that SHIELD GUYS ARE BACK for the fiftieth time).

It really feels like BRC is "open world JSR" but without the necessary gameplay changes and improvements needed to facilitate that change to a new style. So much taken out, nothing added back in. Time pressure removed. Graffiti skill checks removed. Level rankings removed. No differences in characters. Revamped spray can resourcing (nah, just kidding, removing it). 

So what does it add? 
- A boost system, which would be good if it let you keep your speed (it doesn't). after you finish a boost, you immediately brake back down to a standstill and have to reaccelerate in your normal movement style.
- A new combo multiplier system. This is potentially the one place that I want to 100% commend. Unlike Tony Hawk style games, where each new trick gives you combo multiplier, meaning you are incentivized to do the "infinite manual", BRC only gives you combo multiplier for new corners, wallrides and half pipes, meaning you're incentivized to make your combo go all around the play area. this is a great change.
-A terrrrrriiiiibbbblllllle cell phone camera.

BRC is great if you wanted JSR to open up and just be a place where you can skate around and listen to cool tunes and see cool art, but little else has changed in the last twenty years.

If I had any changes I'd want to make:
- More character differentiation. Even the movement styles (rollerblades, skate board and bmx) don't feel that different.
- Score/Time Attack
- Reasons to care about the murals you're painting
- Less "cutscenes" that stop the action. Don't need one for every heat level, don't need them for the tiny "crew member name" tag spots, potentially don't need them for the "hey kid, do this line" missions.
- Make the police something that you can't just deal with with a bathroom break.

review_text:
This game is my definitive parkour game, taking the spot from the Mirror's Edge series, both fantastic games in their own regard. For me, this truly captures what it feels like to be a parkour/free-running practitioner. Seemingly borrowing design philosophy from the Skate games in regards to how detailed the mechanics are for parkour specifically, the game definitely has a learning curve, but once it clicks it becomes an astoundingly in-depth parkour experience. 

The gameplay is phenomenal and easily the highlight of the game. Every button movement of the stick is tied to movement in some way, creating a parkour system that is far more in-depth than any other of its peers, even ones dedicated to it like Mirror's Edge. The tricking system feels cool and the game encourages you to blend both disciplines of parkour, which focuses on efficient movement and freerunning, focusing on creativity and expression, to perform optimally in the many challenges on the map. That being said, this is all optional buy in, so players more dedicated to performing flips and tricks over efficiency can play their way at no penalty and vice versa for efficiency focused players like myself. The maps are all well crafted for the purposes of verticality and flow and I am excited to see what is added in the future. 

A big part of why I enjoy the game is how it makes me feel. This is coming not just from a gamer but from someone who practices parkour myself. I was out with an injury that stopped me from training and found this game. As I went through the settings I found realistic camera mode for first person and never looked back. Using this setting, it felt exactly as I would feel in a training session and is a feeling I cherish even to this day. Not only did this get me through the injury period but it also gave me a drive to return to training, all this because of the care that went into how accurately this realistic first person camera mode worked. Needless to say, the game truly captures how it feels to be a traceur. 

The graphics are simple but do the job, being a cell shaded style that gives the game it's own personality. Combined with the soundtrack, it creates a very cool atmosphere that lends itself well to just unwinding as you run around the map in your own way. That being said, I do personally love throwing on the Mirror's Edge soundtrack and reliving the days of when Mirror's Edge Catalyst had servers and still worked. 

Perhaps my only gripe being the progression system, unlocks are locked behind feathers that you now collect from using challenges, a stark contrast to the freeform system in the early access period. While I understand the need to have a progression system to keep people playing, I do wonder if there was a more elegant way to do this. Beyond that, multiplayer is also a treat, the maps feel great to run around with friends with and the tag game mode in particular is a lot of fun. 

Overall this game truly captures the parkour training experience with a robust, in-depth system that keeps me coming back whenever I want to get into the flow and relax at the end of the day.

FINAL SCORE: 9/10

review_text:
[i]The Callisto Protocol is a third person horror brawler, from the creators of Dead Space, which very much wants to be Dead Space while its creators are desperately trying to avoid accusations that they are coping Dead Space, and players going into it are mostly looking for more Dead Space. [/i]

[h1]Flows[/h1][list]
[*]The game looks bloody great. The environmental effects are just eyecandy.
[*]The developers are very clearly building on the foundations of Dead Space, evolving many of its original ideas. Transitional vents now may contain death traps, the protagonist is suffering psychotic episodes which are very trippy, there are attempts at stealth sequences, etc.
[*]The actors just look great. There is absolutely no uncanny valley effect.
[*]The female lead is Japanese while the protagonist is a westerner. More of this kind of diversity please.
[*]Telekenisis is pure sex. It was good in Dead Space as well, but here it's just perfect (WHEN the developers take care to make it an option).
[*]Truly high tension environments in many areas. The game does not hold back on punishing stupid plauer decisions, like being greedy. The prison cells segment in the DLC was just fantastic, as were the stealth segments in the main game, in the old abandoned colony.[/list]

[h1]Flaws[/h1] [list]
[*]The story is paper-thin. Long gone is the lovecraftian touch of Dead Space, the nihilism and the alien aspect of the horror. Here it's just a virus, and your enemies are more or less zombies, which you have seen a million times already.
[*]The player is imprisoned, then immediately the outbreak happens. So the game neither throws us in an already derelict, haunted environment like Dead Space, nor does it allow us to see a "normal" day in the prison so that we can then compare it to the chaos of the outbreak. As a result, you are thrust into action pieces with zero context. The chaos around is as new to the monsters and the people as it is to you, the player.
[*][spoiler]At some point it is (falsely) revealed to the female lead ~who had made our ship crash~ that we were in fact innocent. At that point, from her perspective, she had just f@cked over a completely innocent man in the worst ways possible, getting our partner killed, ruining our business and our ship, and getting us imprisoned. The b!tch just offers us no apology. Instead, she and the protagonist just become friends awkwardly fast from that point on.[/spoiler]
[*]The weak point of your enemies are tentacles sprouting from their chests after they take damage, which you must shoot fast or they transform into much tankier enemies. A good idea to add tension to the fight, except it's much less remarkable than Dead Space strategic dismemberment. 2)It very rarely matters, because the transformed tank enemies can be thrown with telekenisis to multiple instant-kill spikes, fans or death drops.
[*]Survival horror, like Dead Space, needs you to be on close proximity to your enemies, not RIGHT in their face. Enemies are meant to be close enough that you are afraid they will reach you with melee attacks, and you are therefore stressed to deal with them before that happens. Callisto Protocol actually plays as a brawler. You will be fighting enemies one on one with melee, while enemies off-camera basically stand around (even if they are right next to you). Instead of trying to stay away from enemies, you will be intentionally running towards them. The horror aspect is immediately ruined.
[*]Survival horror's dark, claustrophobic environments are a very ill fit for arcade action.
[*]Imagine having to deal with nonsense like invincibility frames or animation mismatches in a survival horror game. Every time I swing or shoot at an enemy climbing up the rails and my attack just passes through them, my excitement vanishes.
[*]The game's difficulty is pretty much determined by how much the environment allows you to abuse telekenisis. Some are filled with spiked walls that give you free insta-kills, others don't have as much as a bucket for you to pick up and throw at your enemies.
[*]Enemy corpses will often be in spots designated as non-interactive. So because the zombie you just killed is hugging the wall, you can no longer loot it, despite it being in front of you.
[*]Severely lacking enemy variety. There's just zombies, the launching head-traps and the spider enemies. Dead Space 1 by comparison, had about 4 times the enemy types.
[*]The game could have used a lot more prison-bot segments. They are a nice change of pace from the regular brawler gameplay.
[*]The DLC's ending is just a middle finger to the players.
[*]The combat basically boils down to blocking till your enemy finishes his combo and then scoring a few hits. It sounds boring, it plays even more boring.
[*]Very limited weapon customization, and no armor customization.
[*]At least in max difficulty (which was my first and only playthrough) there are certain segments, especially in the DLC, which will will drive your patience to its limits. A certain room right before the end, where you are made to fight the new hybrid boss enemies in pairs of two (half-robot, half-zombies that are VERY tanky and are immune to telekenisis) in very close quarters, almost made me uninstall (we are talking 30-40 retries to get through that f@cking thing).[/list]

[b]Thumbs down for a purchase. Callisto Protocol is not Dead Space, despite it trying very hard to be. The environments nail the horror aspect, while the gameplay ruins it with the bizarre brawler approach it has. The difficulty swings from piss-easy to controller-throwing hard, seldom finding the right balance.[b]

review_text:
Honestly, 7 hours in I had lost all the will to continue, I was constantly hoping that it would end soon. 



Gameplay :

The stealth sections are way too easy, enemy being really dumb with extremely exploitable vantage point/grate takedown, alongside the extremely overpowered Detective vision just made it a matter of patience with barely any thinking required, since you can just hide easily because of their AI, there is usually no risk in getting caught cause you can just go inside a grate or repeteadly jump between vantage points, and rinse and repeat. 

The combat is really good and I played the entire game in hard difficulty, however the severe lack of enemy types just means that 3 hours into the game you've experienced the entire gameplay. There's the one armed thug, which I have no idea if they're supposed to make it harder, I mean, the only thing missing is for them to tell you when to dodge because you can't block it. Then the swinging "titan" which requires another different input to fight. Then the ones with the blade, which requires another different input to fight. Now these sounds good, but they were never really utilized in a way where they all perfectly work together to challenge the peak of the player's skill. I don't think they were willing to fully commit, which for me, really hurt the potential of the combat and almost made the game unbearably boring to finish. It was fun for sure, but after a while I stopped caring because I couldn't get engaged when the game barely throws anything my way that will require more than three brain cells to do.

The bossfights were decent if not bad, the entire point of the combat is a 360 degree combat, with emphasis on awareness. The bossfights being some sort of cuphead projectile dodging game was way too outside what the gameplay is about that it felt jarring, this isn't Dark Souls where'd you spam roll to dodge, doing that in the Clayface and R'as al ghul fight was just too awkward. However, the bit in the bossfights where you'd have to dodge Clayface while fighting off multiple small clayface was good. Because you know, it challenges the skill you've been honing during the game. Uniqueness and variety is good, but doing it for the sake of just doing something differently even thought the entire core of your game does not support it is not. This is the equivalent of platforming with suddenly breaking floor and dying instantly as Bed Of Chaos in a game about learning your enemies' moveset, dodging and counterattacking which is Dark Souls.  The Mister Freeze fight was tedious, you only need to take him down twice, to know all that you need to do. Doing it 8 more times was boring. He's extremely smart and dumb at the same time, adapting so that a trick will not work twice, but not learning to change his approach. 


And there's the hacking part, if you can call that gameplay. They exist to slow down the game, they're not engaging in any way. A few of them is fine, but they are way too prevalent in the entire game. 


STORY 

Story is decent, held down at being good because of Hugo,  I just couldn't get myself invested with the whole Hugo Thing, how he speak is just so annoying, he has zero charisma, and he speak so "smart" but doesn't sound threatening, he's so one dimensional in his dialogues and delivery that it was painful. The Joker part was better, his lines were good, delivery was good and when he talks you want to listen. It's because of his attitude, how he acts and carries himself, which if you put Hugo Strange in there, is a statute when it comes to being alive so I have no idea why he was even there. The twist was eh. There's another one, great. Totally didn't see that one coming because of the Joker looking deathly sick and healthy as a horse in another scene. Let's be honest, There being two doesn't matter. In detective stories, twists are good, because throughout the story, you're not just given clues, but you are also given misdirection. So when the reveal happens, you think yourself an idiot, not because there's a twin brother that you didn't catch up on, but because you suspected his sister. In Arkham City, the twist is just that there's a twin brother. Even if you pick upped on the clues, the only question you ask is "Wait, is there a different Joker or something?" You don't ask yourself the why. because there is no why, he just did it. That could be the real Joker holding down Talia, but instead of all that stuff, he just shoot her down instantly. Which would result in the same thing, no twin twist needed. 

Overall, I'd give it a 6/10. With the Joker and the combat being the sole good parts of the game
